Ancient skeleton shows woman in imperial China had her nose amputated

New Scientist September 17, 2026

A woman who lived in China about 700 years ago had her nose cleanly sliced off, perhaps as punishment for stealing horses or cattle. She lived for at least a few years after the incident and may have worn a prosthetic nose over the hole. The archaeologists who found her remains, buried face down in a cemetery, think this may be the only known physical evidence of punitive nasal amputation from ancient China.

“I suspect she lived a difficult life, facing stigma and social challenges,” says David Shaye at Harvard University, who wasn’t involved in the study. “Facial deformities can profoundly affect identity, social interaction and a person’s place within a community. In this sense, this archaeological finding connects very directly with challenges that people continue to face today.”

Ancient Chinese legal texts describe cutting off a person’s nose as one of the “Five Punishments”, along with decapitation, limb amputation, castration and facial tattooing. By the end of the Yuan dynasty, which ran from AD 1279 to 1368, the law prescribed it mainly for theft of high-value livestock, or for repeated offences involving the theft of less valuable animals.

Advertisement

High-tech archaeology shows we aren’t the first to endure hard times

Yet despite ancient texts documenting thousands of cases, there’s never been physical evidence of it actually happening, says Qian Wang at Texas A&M University.

In 2018, surveys ahead of construction of a trade school in central China’s Henan province uncovered a cemetery containing 299 tombs. Fei Yan at the nearby Sanmenxia Institute of Cultural Relics and Archaeology and colleagues rapidly excavated the site and stored the skeletons at Zhengzhou University. An archaeologist there, Yawei Zhou, noticed one skull had a strangely wide nasal opening with missing bone and healed edges, suggesting the woman’s nose had been cut off during life.

By 2024, Wang had joined the investigation. The researchers identified the remains as belonging to a woman by features of the pelvis and skull, while tooth wear and skeletal indicators put her age at 40 to 45. Radiocarbon dating of her right femur placed her death between 1298 and 1404, spanning the late Yuan and early Ming dynasties. The design of the tomb itself is consistent with the Yuan – the Mongol dynasty founded by Kublai Khan.

Subscriber-only newsletter

Isotope analysis of the skeletal remains suggested the woman ate mostly millet and little animal protein, consistent with relatively low socioeconomic status.

CT scans revealed that large amounts of bone and other tissue around and inside her nose had been cut away, apparently from bottom to top, says Wang. The healed and remodeled edges showed she survived for years afterwards, although probably with difficulty breathing and moving her upper lip.

The woman must have had good medical care: the fact that she survived suggests caregivers controlled bleeding, prevented infection and probably managed her pain, says Wang.

“If initially bleeding was controlled, the wound would slowly heal on its own over several months,” says Shaye.

A bizarre skeleton from a Roman grave has bones from eight people

Small lumps of extra bone – known as bone spurs – formed around the nasal opening. These could reflect chronic inflammation, but it’s also possible they chronicle pressure from an artificial nose. “This woman had a normal diet for a commoner and might have worn a nasal prosthesis to cover the scar – indicating that she tried to get back to normal life,” says Wang.

Only later, examining the lone photograph from the hasty excavation, did the team realise the woman had been buried face down, says Wang. None of the other bodies in the cemetery was buried this way. The practice is sometimes associated with punishment during the Yuan dynasty. Wang suspects she was buried isolated from her family or community, possibly face down to hide her disfigurement.

DNA from plague bacteria has been identified in graves from 1338 in Kyrgyzstan, and these pathogens appear to be the ancestors of those that caused the Black Death

“We believed there was a discriminatory attitude,” he says. “It could be a decision of disapproval.”

Wang adds that there may be other explanations for the woman’s injury, including disease, accident or even self-mutilation. However, the researchers found no telltale signs of such alternatives. If their interpretation is correct, the skeleton provides the first physical evidence of punitive nasal amputation in ancient China.

Beyond showing that a gruesome punishment described in historical texts was actually carried out, the discovery offers a rare glimpse into how the ancient Chinese punished, treated and ultimately regarded convicted criminals, says Wang.

Plug-in solar panels still have safety risks in the UK despite legalisation

New Scientist September 17, 2026

It is now legal to buy and use plug-in solar panels in Great Britain, but safety concerns surrounding them haven’t yet been addressed by the UK government. This is according to one of the leading engineering institutions, which says the legalisation has been rushed through without creating proper legal standards and has created an increased risk to life.

With plug-in solar panels, you simply buy a kit, place it in a sunny spot and plug it into a wall socket. There’s no installation cost, no certification and no planning permission. The devices are popular in many European countries and the UK government legalised them on 27 August to boost renewable energy generation and cut down on household bills.

Prior to this legalisation, Mark Coles, the head of technical regulations at the UK Institution of Engineering and Technology (IET), told New Scientist about several potential issues. One surrounded residual current devices (RCDs), the safety devices found in fuse boxes that sense when current is leaking to ground – a sign of electrocution or a short circuit – and almost instantaneously cut power. Most RCDs used in the UK aren’t suitable for current flowing in both directions and so could malfunction if used with plug-in solar panels.

Advertisement

Another of the IET’s concerns is what happens if there are multiple kits in use in an area and a power cut occurs. In theory, the plug-in kits should also shut down in order to prevent “islanding”, when one home’s power stays live. But if they are still generating power, then they could deceive each other into thinking the grid is live and keep running. The problem then is that power can jump past the fuse box and electrocute maintenance workers in the area fixing the outage.

The IET made these concerns clear to the UK government both before and during the consultation by the Department for Energy Security and Net Zero (DESNZ) that ended on 30 June. But Coles says the issues weren’t addressed and now present a risk.

“It was a done deal before it went out, I’m sure,” says Coles. “It’s been rushed. There needed to be time to develop a proper standard for these things, because we feel under certain circumstances that there’s an increased risk to life.”

Plug-in solar is coming – how dangerous is it and is it worth it?

Coles says the risks emerge only when there’s a perfect storm of problems, but that this will inevitably lead to an injury or a death over time if plug-in solar panels are widely adopted.

Extensive scientific studies have been carried out to determine how quickly damage is done within the human body from electric shock. Based on that research, UK RCDs are required to trip and cut off current within 40 milliseconds. But there are no similar standards for plug-in solar panels, which Coles suggests could – if things go wrong, and in very limited circumstances – take longer to shut down.

“You could be exposed to the electric current for longer than you should have been,” says Coles. “You’re in the danger zone.”

The IET’s advice is to get an electrical inspection prior to committing to plug-in solar in order to minimise risk.

Free newsletter

A DESNZ spokesperson told New Scientist that “we have funded an independent contractor to fully test the electrical safety of plug-in solar devices on UK electrical house wiring practice, which found these products to be safe”.

The department added that it had looked at testing with older household electrical safety devices and found no evidence that their ability to provide protection was affected when used with the type of plug-in solar systems sold in Europe.

Coles agrees that tests were carried out, but says that they focused on plug-in solar kits sourced outside the UK, because none was legal here at the time, and with brand new RCDs. That has two problems: legal RCDs in the real world can be much older, and of older design, and there was no clear definition or regulation for plug-in panels that were tested, meaning that ones now for sale may act differently.

“They spent this money on getting these units tested, but these units were non-standard units,” says Coles. “So it’s not like I’m testing something that’s been made to a product standard and I’m seeing how it conforms to this product standard. So I don’t see the point of spending the money. From our point of view, it’s being rushed.”

SpaceX’s Starship will orbit Earth for first time during next flight

New Scientist September 18, 2026

SpaceX’s reusable rocket, Starship – the tallest and most powerful ever launched – will orbit Earth for the first time within days. And because it will also release working Starlink V3 satellites, it will be the first commercially useful Starship mission.

The company has announced that a launch window will open at 7.15am CDT (1.15pm BST) on 22nd September, during which Starship will launch from the company’s Starbase site in Texas.

The flight – Starship’s 14th – will reach an altitude of 275 kilometres and complete six orbits of Earth over 10 hours, with re-entry and splashdown targeted in the Pacific Ocean, to the west of Chile.

Advertisement

SpaceX’s 1 million satellites could avoid environmental checks

This will make it by far the longest and most ambitious test flight of Starship to date. All 13 previous Starship test flights have been, at best, sub-orbital.

Starship is made up of two parts: an upper stage, confusingly also called Starship, and a lower stage, called Super Heavy. Currently, SpaceX is testing the latest third generation of each section using a fail-fast, learn-fast strategy more common to Silicon Valley than the conservative world of space exploration.

SpaceX is several years into its development programme for Starship, intended to be a rapidly reusable and extremely powerful launch vehicle that will take over the rollout of the company’s Starlink satellites and be a central part of NASA’s Artemis moon missions.

Free newsletter

The 14th flight will also see 26 Starlink V3 satellites launched for the first time. Thousands of these new devices will join the existing constellation of satellites that provides internet connections around the world. Until now, Starship test flights have launched only dummy test satellites.

Davide Amato at Imperial College London says that an orbital test is indicative of confidence within the company that the rocket will at least survive the journey to orbit and the release of satellites. But he says that re-entry, where the company has faced problems during recent tests, may be another matter.

“In short, they’re making good progress towards introducing Starship as a successful commercial launcher,” says Amato. “Whether Starship will be ‘revolutionary’, as promised by their CEO, will depend on whether they will be able to achieve a high launch cadence and on whether their design is cost-effective.”

SpaceX is about to launch tallest and most powerful rocket in history

Leah-Nani Alconcel at the University of Birmingham, UK, says that the 14th test flight will be a key step for SpaceX. Not only will the release of V3 satellites help the company update its Starlink constellation – the new satellites fly in a lower orbit than existing Starlink satellites and have higher data capacity – but their larger size than previous models will go some way to showing whether Starship is up to the task of launching its proposed Starmind data centre spacecraft, which are substantially larger.

“I don’t think it’s a huge jump in operational complexity for the launch vehicle, but demonstrating the Starlink V3 delivery to orbit is a significant step,” says Alconcel. “It may not be as flashy as the ‘chopstick catch‘ for the vehicle stages, but it would be a big boost to their commercial capabilities to have both the already-established high-cadence Falcon 9 and a proven Starship in their repertoire.”

A rocket launched last year is thought to have smashed into the lunar surface this morning, creating the moon’s newest crater

Three of the satellites due to be released on this flight have been modified to include cameras that can scan Starship’s heat shield whilst in orbit and transmit images to engineers on Earth.

During the 13th test flight, the booster stage made its ascent as planned, but during descent only eight of the 13 engines intended to slow its fall reignited, causing it to make a hard splashdown into the ocean rather than the planned gentle simulated landing on water. Neither the booster nor upper stage will attempt to make a controlled landing on the 14th flight.

Only two Starship flights have taken place so far in 2026, with flight 14 due to be the third. The upcoming flight will also be the second since SpaceX’s flotation on the stock market, which made controversial founder Elon Musk the world’s first trillionaire. The number of flights has fallen far beyond bold estimates made in previous years; SpaceX officials hoped to launch as many as 25 Starship test flights last year. In reality, only five test flights occurred that year.

SpaceX didn’t respond to a request for an interview, but the company says on its website that “there have been several modifications to hardware and software to address issues seen on the previous flight”.

Physicists are scrambling to make sense of possible dark matter signal

New Scientist September 18, 2026

We may have finally spotted a dark matter particle – but figuring out exactly what kind of particle it was is a daunting task. Even as researchers race to confirm they really did detect an unknown particle, physicists around the world have already started working out what sort of dark matter particle it might have been.

The potential particle in question was found at the LUX-ZEPLIN (LZ) detector in South Dakota and announced on 1 September. The detector uses a huge tank of liquid xenon to look for signatures of dark matter particles smashing into the nuclei of xenon atoms, which are expected to produce a burst of light in response to any collision that would then be picked up by the arrays of cameras surrounding the tank.

The LZ group recorded only a single burst of light, and there is about a 1-in-200 chance that the signal was a fluke event rather than evidence that dark matter was there – but nevertheless it is tantalising.

Advertisement

Unexpected hints of dark matter should breathe life into particle physics

What makes the signal even more intriguing is that it was at a higher energy than would be expected if the particle were a standard weakly interacting massive particle, or WIMP, the simplest proposed type of dark matter. “It’s an anomalous event,” says Henning Flaecher at the University of Bristol in the UK, part of the LZ group. “It’s not what you would expect from the most general dark matter models.” The fact that this high-energy event was spotted, with no accompanying lower-energy collisions, makes it exceedingly unlikely that this particle, if it exists, is a “vanilla” WIMP, he says.

In the weeks since the announcement, theorists have released scores of papers digging into the data, searching for answers. “The large number of papers is less a statement that theorists believe the event is a [true] dark matter discovery and more a reflection of the fact that, if it persists, its energy already tells us quite a lot about types of physical processes that could produce it,” says Juri Smirnov at the University of Liverpool in the UK.

Many of those papers debate the possibility that the particle could be what is called a higgsino, a type of non-“vanilla” WIMP. It arises from a theoretical framework called supersymmetry, in which every known particle is proposed to have a “superpartner”, with some similar properties but different spin. In supersymmetry, the higgsino would be the superpartner of the Higgs boson.

Subscriber-only newsletter

A higgsino is the simplest WIMP explanation still available to explain the LZ signal, according to JiJi Fan at Brown University in Rhode Island. “It gives rise to a wealth of signals that could be searched for at different experimental frontiers.” Plus, a higgsino detection event is predicted to be unaccompanied by a host of lower-energy collisions, matching the signal detected by the LZ group.

However, the higgsino has its problems. The most basic model of that sort of particle that could explain the LZ detection seems to be ruled out by constraints from other experiments. This doesn’t mean the particle couldn’t have been a higgsino, but it does suggest the higgsino in question would need to have had a much higher mass than expected.

Many other models have been proposed to explain the detection, though. Among them are several models of dark matter particles originating in extra dimensions. While this may seem an unnecessarily complicated line of enquiry, these models were already being studied to solve other problems in particle physics, says Lisa Randall at Harvard University, a co-author of one such paper. “In some sense, the data looks like it’s calling out for something like this: it avoids the pre-existing constraints and fits quite naturally.”

Particle collisions are inherently quantum, but much of that character is lost when we turn them into classical data. Sarah Alam Malik explores whether preserving more of it could help us spot signs of dark matter and other new physics

An extra-dimensional dark matter candidate could both fit the LZ detection and explain why the fundamental particles have the masses they do, a long-standing puzzle, she says. Other models propose a whole dark matter sector, with multiple types of dark particles.

Right now, there is no way to tell which, if any, of these models might be correct. “I don’t think the data currently justify saying one of these is ‘the’ explanation,” says Smirnov. Some of them do come with additional predictions, though, which will be particularly useful when trying to pick through so many ideas, he says.

As the LZ team and other teams at detectors around the world continue to analyse their data, looking for additional events to confirm that the dark matter particle was real, all of these ideas could help them know exactly what it is they are looking for. “Anomalies could come and go, as we all know,” says Fan. “My take is that they provide us with some concrete targets to think: is this expected? Are there new territories/questions in theory or experiments we should cover? No matter whether the LZ event is confirmed, some of these topics would lead to long-term research.”

Fishapod fossil shows early elbows came in a variety of forms

New Scientist September 18, 2026

An ancient fish that lived just before the first four-legged animals walked on land had a pointed forearm bone and a hinge-like elbow joint, adding to the growing evidence of trial and error in early arm formation.

The 350-million-year-old animal was one of several “fishapods” – creatures with fins that had evolved some limb-like features. It might have used its fins for actions other than swimming, such as moving along the bottom of rivers.

“We keep uncovering more and more variation in the shapes and geometries of these bones,” says Thomas Stewart at Pennsylvania State University. “The more we study the diversity, the more we realise there’s just a range of unusual forms of animals living in and exploring their ecologies.”

Advertisement

Extraordinary ichthyosaur fossil shows its last meal was a pterosaur

In the past two decades, scientists have found fossils from dozens of distinct species of finned tetrapodomorphs, or fishapods. These animals lived in water and had fins that contained bones similar to those found in the limbs of today’s four-legged animals. The most iconic fishapod – Tiktaalik roseae – has been nicknamed the “crawling fish” because it could probably use its fin-limbs to crawl out of water, capturing an important step in the evolution of vertebrates.

But the story of how fish evolved into land animals is anything but a straight line, Stewart says. For instance, Qikiqtania wakei, which he and his colleagues described in 2022, was a fishapod that appears to have initially evolved weight-supporting fins but then evolved to be a full-time swimmer.

Now, the team has analysed another unusual fishapod. So far, the animal is known only from fossils of a single isolated fin that was discovered on Canada’s Ellesmere Island. The researchers CT-scanned the fossil and compared its arm-like bones with those of 16 other known fishapods. The isolated fin didn’t quite match any of them, suggesting it came from a distinct species.

Subscriber-only newsletter

The radius – which, in humans, runs from the elbow to the thumb side of the wrist – was long and triangular, coming to a sharp point at its far end – where the wrist would be in a tetrapod. Other bones and tissue would have led from here to the fin’s tip, but the shape of the radius itself would have provided little support for pushing against the ground, says Stewart.

At the elbow end, the radius lacked the rounded knob seen in other fishapods, but instead was narrow and “shaped like a bean”. The upper arm bone was missing, but the radius’s shape suggests the joint between them would have worked like a simple hinge that largely bent back and forth in a single plane. This is more restrictive than the elbows of other fishapods: they could twist and rotate their elbows, like we can, to provide greater flexibility of movement.

The fossil also contained the intermedium, a small bone seen in fishapods that scientists suspect eventually evolved into part of the wrist. In the fossil from the unknown fishapod, the intermedium was relatively longer than in Tiktaalik and its close relatives.

Hidden fossils reveal secrets of oceans before major mass extinction

Exactly what the animal was doing with its unusual fins isn’t clear, says Stewart. The restricted movement of the elbow might have been a kind of experiment in evolving appendages that could have served this particular animal’s needs, in its environment. But this doesn’t necessarily mean the elbow joint was perfectly suited for its role.

“When animals begin to explore new kinds of movements, they might be kind of awkward,” he says. “They might not be the best at it, but they’re still good enough. It’s a matter of sufficiency, not optimality.”

Julia Molnar at New York Institute of Technology, Long Island, says she was excited to see the new specimen. “The question of when and why the fin-limb and water-land transitions occurred is still very much up for debate,” she says. “I would not be surprised if this wide variation in radius shape represents different approaches to the problems and opportunities of this changing world.”

Palaeontologists have found new evidence that the early ancestors of amphibians, reptiles and mammals did not have a larval stage with external gills like modern frogs or salamanders

Importantly, the variations shouldn’t be interpreted as different attempts to evolve limbs for a future life on land, but rather to suit their own current environment, says Brian Swartz at the University of California, Berkeley.

“A fish like this one might use its fins to ‘walk’ in shallow water or push through vegetation,” says Molnar, “allowing it to escape large aquatic predators and prey on smaller fish and arthropods at the water’s edge.”

Journal of Vertebrate Paleontology DOI: 10.1080/02724634.2026.2708076

Our brain evolved from two primitive nervous systems that merged

New Scientist September 18, 2026

Our brain may be a hybrid of two ancient nervous systems that were packaged together hundreds of millions of years ago. This is based on the finding that the front and back brain regions in people and several other species develop from two distinct cell types in embryos, instead of sharing the same developmental origin, as previously thought.

“Our research suggests that evolution took two existing neural systems and pushed them together spatially,” says Kyle Loh at Stanford University. “Having the brain as one organ would probably be more efficient, but we rely on this primordial way to make the brain as two separate pieces.”

Human brains may have got bigger for no particular reason

Loh and his colleagues studied early stages of mouse embryo development and found its brain develops from two types of early progenitor cells, proliferative cells with a limited capacity of self-renewal. One type expresses a gene called OTX2 and turns into the neurons found in the front part of the brain, comprising the forebrain and midbrain. The other expresses a gene called GBX2 and becomes the neurons in the back part of the brain, the hindbrain.

Advertisement

The researchers then conducted experiments using human cells in a dish and found that the neurons of the hindbrain and those of the forebrain and midbrain also develop from different progenitor cells. “We’ve shown for the first time that the front of the brain arises from a totally different progenitor cell than the back of the brain,” says Loh.

This explains why it has been so hard to grow human hindbrain tissue in a lab. “It was actually a summer student’s failed experiment that got us into this,” says Loh. Researchers have typically tried making hindbrain neurons from the progenitor cells that are destined to become forebrain and midbrain neurons, which doesn’t work, he says.

Subscriber-only newsletter

Armed with this knowledge, the team was able to grow functional human hindbrain motor neurons in a dish for the first time by starting with the correct type of progenitor cell.

The hindbrain coordinates fundamental life-sustaining processes, such as breathing, sleeping, eating and the beating of the heart, whereas the forebrain is the centre of higher-level thought. Conditions like amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS), the most common type of motor neuron disease, and spinal muscular atrophy cause speech and swallowing difficulties because they affect the hindbrain. Recently, scientists also discovered that GLP-1 drugs like Ozempic and Wegovy suppress appetite in mice by acting on the hindbrain.

Now that it is easier to grow human hindbrain neurons in a dish, it should assist ALS and spinal muscular atrophy research, and allow us to investigate the precise mechanisms of how GLP-1 drugs work in people, says Loh.

When does your brain reach adulthood? We’re now understanding the many ways the organ continues to mature decades after society first deems you an adult

The researchers also studied early-stage embryos of chickens, zebrafish and acorn worms, and found their nervous systems are similarly derived from two different types of progenitor cells. This suggests our shared two-origin brain system arose at least 550 million years ago.

But jellyfish, which we diverged from around 600 to 700 million years ago, have two separate nervous systems. These may have joined up in our distant ancestors because it improved their overall processing power, says Loh. “You get more efficient communication when things are closer together,” he says.

Having our brains develop along two separate pathways might also have facilitated the evolution of complex thought, says Loh. While the hindbrain was taking care of all the basic functions for keeping us alive, “evolution could play around with the forebrain, and make mistakes and give rise to all the fancy things like memory and creativity”, he says.

Nature Neuroscience DOI: 10.1038/s41593-026-02433-7

National’s policy includes:

Netball player in battle over protection order against ex-boyfriend while at the court

New Zealand Herald September 19, 2026

A young netballer has struggled in her sport after she was granted a protection order against her ex, an umpire, but got no support from the local netball centre.

Sarah has dreamed of being a Silver Fern since she was 5 years old.

But whereas netball used to be her “happy place”, now she says it’s overshadowed by what feels like a lack of support from her netball centre.

Sarah* successfully applied for a permanent protection order from the Family Court this year, after a bad breakup with a young man whom the court found had difficulty taking no for an answer.

A Family Court judge, deciding whether to impose the order, found that the young man had engaged in acts of family violence against her, including through coercive control.

But the young man works as an umpire for the same netball centre where she plays.

The judge allowed conditions for him to be present at the netball courts while Sarah was playing, given his work as an umpire, provided there was no contact between them.

He is required to use his “best endeavours” to ensure he doesn’t referee Sarah’s games; if there’s no other option, the communication is only to be within the context of refereeing.

Sarah agreed to the condition and contacted the netball centre to let it know what had happened.

She’d earlier sent through the temporary order, and with it having been made permanent, she requested a meeting with management.

She says she asked if they could “work together” to put a “safety plan in place”, so she could continue to play netball and have reassurance about how to keep some distance between her and the young man.

She says she told them that while it might appear nothing bothered her, she was “scared of him and the judge agreed this was valid”.

However, an email sent on behalf of the centre’s board said that while the centre would comply with the conditions of the permanent protection order, it could not “interfere with or extend the Family Court’s decision”.

It concludes: “If you want a more extensive safety plan, then you need to go back to the Family Court”.

An email sent a month or so later did inform Sarah of his role umpiring an upcoming event.

Sarah and her parents remain confused as to why the centre would not even meet with them.

They had hoped for some practical steps – for example, that the young man would be put on a court on the other side of the facility from where she was playing.

They expected more support for Sarah, given she’s a young netballer who has “done nothing wrong”.

Sarah said she never wanted the young man to stop umpiring – in an early email when the protection order was yet to be made permanent, she told the club she “does not want to stop or get in the way of [him] doing what he loves, which is being an umpire. I am happy for [him] to live his best life, just without me”.

She said she never wanted anyone to have to take sides; she just wanted things in place to limit the contact.

Instead, she and her family have been left feeling like they’re the ones in the wrong – that the centre thinks they’re troublemakers.

Sarah pulled back from some aspects of netball to protect her mental health, and feels her confidence has taken a hit.

“I can’t think, and I can’t play,” she said.

“And he just walks around like nothing’s happened ... like, cool, so you get to live your life and do what you want and not have to worry, but with me, I have to worry where he is, what he’s doing ... I’m always on alert.”

Sarah said she’d had supportive responses from Netball New Zealand, but the local centre remains in control of the practicalities – including the umpire rosters.

“We just don’t understand why they’re not trying to work with us or even talk to us,” Sarah’s mum said, later explaining they previously had a really good relationship with the centre’s management.

Sarah’s parents say they’ve observed the young man watching Sarah while she’s playing and feel like he’s not making any effort to distance himself.

But because the protection order allows him to be at the netball courts, they feel there’s little they can do.

They’d hoped the netball centre would assist in holding him accountable.

Sarah’s parents have to accompany her to netball, even though she’s a young adult.

“She’s having to be careful of where she goes and what she does, but she’s done nothing wrong,” Sarah’s mum said.

She feels the “netball centre has completely protected him and made him feel like he can do whatever he wants ...”

She said there was one instance where the young man had turned up to umpire one of Sarah’s training games – this was not allowed by the special conditions, which were in place for competitive matches only.

Sarah’s own team management and coaching staff had been really supportive, and they stepped in and asked the young man to leave.

They claim they observed him sitting in his car, and that his younger brother came in and watched the whole game.

Sarah is considering next steps for what police have advised likely constitutes a breach of the protection order – but that would require a statement and Sarah giving evidence in court.

Contact the Open Justice team

That in itself is a big hurdle for Sarah.

She and her family remain bewildered by where things have landed – they thought with a permanent protection order, Sarah would have space to heal and move on.

Instead, it seems to them to have created a grey area where her expectations do not correlate with reality, and she feels left in limbo.

Despite this, Sarah hopes to continue playing next year.

“Since I was a little kid, I’ve always wanted to be a Silver Fern. So I’m not just going to give it up just because of him, but at the same time, I was like, this is really bad for my mental health.”

Protection orders are granted by the Family Court to prevent family violence and abuse by those in close relationships.

They can be applied for to protect someone from a partner or spouse, a family member, a flatmate, a carer or caregiver, or anyone the person shares a close personal relationship with.

The main conditions usually are no family violence – which includes threats of harm, as well as physical, sexual, psychological, or financial abuse – no contact, and no weapons.

Before making a protection order final, there is usually a hearing, where the judge will hear from both parties and their lawyers.

In Sarah’s case, both she and the young man gave their versions of events.

The judge concluded it was “clearly a relationship in which two young people, inexperienced in intimate relationships, struggled for different reasons at the time of their separation”.

However, he was concerned about the young man’s attitude that if he “badgers enough”, he can get his own way.

He found that both the young people were “impressive young adults” and would succeed.

He’d noted that early intervention, noting family violence included coercive and controlling behaviour, helped stop and prevent family violence, and this was appropriate for the young man, who was required to do an assessment for the Living Without Violence programme.

The judge’s written decision concluded that it was “important for [Sarah] to know that she has some breathing space as she still works through the ending of this relationship”.

However, Sarah’s family feel things haven’t played out in the way the judge may have anticipated, given the conditions allowing the young man to be at netball.

The centre was asked by NZME what its policies or procedures for managing situations involving protection orders were, and what measures were taken to minimise contact between the parties – in particular, ensuring that, where possible, the young man did not umpire games Sarah played in.

It was also asked if any support was offered to the player, as the protected person, and how the centre balanced the rights and safety of all participants in such circumstances.

However, the centre said it would not provide any comment.

Netball New Zealand was also contacted, but did not respond.

The chief victims adviser with the Ministry of Justice, Ruth Money, said protection orders could be “notoriously difficult” to enforce when the parties remained in the same community.

“We get it often with cultural clubs, churches, that kind of thing, where again you have clubs who are reluctant to, as they see, interfere with a court order,” she said.

And in fairness to those organisations, she noted they often didn’t understand the law.

“Some orders can unnecessarily put the onus on the environment to manage the risk and any alleged breaches or, you know, interactions, which is not safe and is not wise because what does the church [for example] know about managing ... risk?”

She said organisations and employers could use resources and guidance from Shine, a charity that supports domestic violence victims, to understand things like protection orders.

“I always recommend that any club has safeguarding and ... training ... these things are so prevalent that they will be happening in your workplace,” she said.

“If you don’t have the education to be able to have these safe conversations and kind of navigate these things safely, then [what will] happen is what you’re dealing with here, where you have someone feeling really quite unsupported and not sure where they can turn.”

*Not her real name.

Hannah Bartlett is an Open Justice reporter at NZME. She previously covered court and local government for the Nelson Mail, and before that was a radio reporter at Newstalk ZB.

Number of meth pipes, bongs seized by Customs soars

New Zealand Herald September 19, 2026

The number of meth pipes and cannabis bongs confiscated at the border is soaring.

By Peter de Graaf of RNZ

New Customs figures show importers are trying to bring a soaring number of meth pipes and cannabis bongs into the country, despite a law banning the sale or importation of drug utensils.

Over the first seven months of this year, Customs seized just under 40,000 pipes and bongs at the border – more than the 37,000 seized during all of last year and a massive 25 times more than 2024.

Earlier this year, RNZ visited vape stores, $2 shops and dairies in two Far North towns, and found roughly two-thirds openly sold glass pipes for smoking the class A drug methamphetamine, also known as meth or P.

Most shops had no age restrictions in place and some displayed the pipes on store counters, next to children’s novelty items.

Anecdotal evidence suggests similar availability around the country, despite a law in force since 2014, making it illegal to import or sell meth pipes, hash pipes or cannabis bongs.

Customs northern inspections manager Jared Nicholson said prohibited drug utensils could arrive through any border pathway, including air cargo, mail, sea cargo and passenger luggage.

He said Customs used intelligence and risk assessment to identify goods and people of concern. Frontline officers then carried out targeted inspections and searches based on those assessments.

Critics of the ban on importing drug paraphernalia said it wouldn’t solve New Zealand’s drug problems, but Nicholson said minimising drug harm required action on several fronts.

“By seizing prohibited drug utensils at the border, Customs helps prevent them from being used to administer drugs or sold for criminal profit,” he said. “Customs takes the illegal importation of drug utensils seriously.”

If the offending was serious or commercial in scale, the people responsible could be investigated and prosecuted.

In May, Customs intercepted a shipping container at the Port of Auckland containing roughly 1600 three-litre canisters of nitrous oxide, 21,400 meth pipes and 219kg of illicit tobacco sent from China.

As a result, three men, aged 35, 39 and 44, were charged with importing and possessing prohibited goods and defrauding Customs revenue.

In another case, an Auckland couple were sentenced that same month for the large-scale importation of thousands of illegal weapons, bongs and meth pipes.

The 50-year-old man was sentenced to eight months’ home detention and their company was fined $45,000.

Nicholson said the number of items seized each year could fluctuate, depending on how many commercial-scale consignments were intercepted.

While Customs has enforced the import ban for several years, an RNZ investigation this year found widespread confusion among police, politicians, councils and retailers about whether it was legal to sell meth pipes.

RNZ inquiries bounced around government departments and ministers, before a briefing paper prepared for Health Minister Simeon Brown finally confirmed selling drug utensils was against the law.

First issued in 2014 and updated in 2020, the Misuse of Drugs (Prohibited Utensils) Notice makes it illegal to import or sell cannabis bongs, hash pipes or meth pipes.

The notice spells out the physical characteristics of each type of pipe, so retailers cannot escape prosecution by claiming the pipes are intended for another purpose – such as decorative ornaments, ingesting herbs or tiny flower vases.

The maximum penalty is three months’ jail or a fine of $1000 for an individual, or $5000 for a business.

Possession of a meth pipe is a different matter. That is illegal under the Misuse of Drugs Act 1975, but police must prove the person caught with the pipe intended to use it for smoking meth.

Customs could not break down how many of the almost 40,000 utensils seized this year were meth pipes and how many were for smoking cannabis. Some utensils could be adapted for use with either drug, making it difficult to arrive at separate figures.

Customs data shows the number of seizure operations is falling, which suggests consignment size is increasing sharply.

Mauao landslide: Why holiday parks are reviewing their natural hazard plans

New Zealand Herald September 19, 2026

Six holidaymakers died in January in a landslide at Mount Maunganui Beachside Holiday Park at the foot of Mauao. Photo / Jason Dorday

Holiday parks nationwide are reviewing their natural hazard plans after the deadly landslide into a Mount Maunganui campground.

Six holidaymakers died when a section of Mauao collapsed into Mount Maunganui Beachside Holiday Park, owned by Tauranga City Council, about 9.30am on January 22 after record rain.

The council’s external review of the fatal landslide, led by former High Court judge Paul Davison KC, found the tragedy was “preventable”.

Davison identified reports of landslide risk and rockfall hazards to the campground going back to 1999.

The 1999 report by rock engineering consultant Dr Laurie Richards said heavy rain could cause debris flows into the campground.

“The risks of injury or fatality from slope failures to sleeping persons in fragile accommodation (tents/caravans) is quite high, and the owners/operators of such facilities would have a duty of care to ensure their safety.”

A 2006 rockfall and landslide risk report from Avalon Industrial Services said an 8000-cubic-metre slip above the campground, in the area where the January slip occurred, had a risk of killing 21 people.

The January landslide involved about 12,000cu m of earth.

Tauranga City Council formally accepted the findings and 10 recommendations of Davison’s review on September 1.

Chief executive Marty Grenfell told a council meeting that it accepted them “without qualification” and was committed to implementing every recommendation.

New Zealand Motor Caravan Association national manager James Imlach said the landslide was a reminder that risk management was an ongoing responsibility.

The association operates 66 private parks and three public campgrounds nationwide.

“Operators have a duty to adopt appropriate safety measures and respond when new information indicates those measures should be reviewed.”

Imlach said member safety was a key priority.

“We have processes in place to assess risks, implement site-specific safety and emergency procedures where appropriate, provide safety information to members, and proactively respond to developing issues such as severe weather events.”

Those processes had resulted in precautionary park evacuations. The association had also notified members travelling nearby to avoid affected sites for safety.

“We also review and update our procedures as circumstances change and new information and tools become available.

“Most people understand that natural hazards exist throughout New Zealand, but they also expect campgrounds to take reasonable steps to provide safe places to stay.”

Imlach said the landslide reinforced the importance of vigilance and ongoing risk management.

He said, at this stage, demand for motorhoming or camping had not been affected.

The Department of Conservation manages more than 300 campsites nationwide. Eamonn Whitham, its acting director for visitors and heritage, said many campsites were in natural or remote environments.

“Natural hazards are an inherent feature of some of these places, and managing risk to visitors is an important part of how we operate our sites.”

DoC assessed and managed risks using local knowledge, previous events, inspections and specialist advice.

“Where a hazard is identified, the response will depend on the nature and level of risk and can include monitoring, warning signs, and visitor information, restricting access, carrying out physical works, or temporarily or permanently closing a site.”

Whitham said sites could be reassessed after weather or natural hazard events, or when new information about a potential hazard became available.

DoC was considering lessons from Tauranga City Council’s review alongside its existing approach to managing visitor safety and natural hazards.

“It is too early to determine whether the Mauao landslide or subsequent review will have any effect on visitor numbers at DoC campsites.”

Whitman said DoC would not speculate on potential economic impacts for the wider camping and holiday park sector.

“DoC campsites will continue to operate in line with our existing visitor safety and risk-management processes.

“Visitors should check current alerts and conditions before travelling and follow any safety information or restrictions in place at individual sites.”

Holiday Parks New Zealand said its member parks were independently owned and operated, with health and safety responsibilities.

“Across our industry, we regularly share best practice through resources, guidance and events.

“We take the responsibility of hazard management across the sector seriously and will continue to support operators in this space.”

Tasman Holiday Parks and Top 10 Holiday Parks were both approached for comment.

Bijou Johnson is a multimedia journalist based in Bay of Plenty. A passionate writer and reader, she grew up in Tauranga and developed a love for journalism while exploring various disciplines at university. She holds a Bachelor of Arts in Classical Studies from Massey University.

Rotorua’s Capers Cafe farewells Carolyn Grammer after health diagnosis

New Zealand Herald September 19, 2026

Carolyn Grammer has retired from Capers Cafe + Store after 25 years of service, since the day the cafe opened. Photo / Kelly Makiha

The red lip, the wild curly hair and the husky laugh after classic one-liners.

Anyone who has been to Capers Cafe + Store in Rotorua in the past 25 years will know Carolyn Grammer well.

She’s been the one at the front counter under her signature crochet black hat, eagerly encouraging you to get the cake if you’re having a bad day.

As her workmates put it, “Caro is Capers”. She’s been there since the doors opened in October 2001.

But at 65, she’s retiring – not because she wants to stop working but because she has been diagnosed with chronic heart disease and chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (emphysema).

She blames kissing a bloke with strep throat 10 years ago – that was her first one-liner for the interview.

Or maybe, she said, it was all the “ciggies” she smoked in her earlier years. Either way, she admitted her health wasn’t great.

“I’m on borrowed time ... I’m on tonnes of pills every day to keep me alive.”

The solo mother of two said she wouldn’t change the past 25 years for anything and was grateful for the ride.

Born and raised in Palmerston North, Grammer did a horticulture and gardening apprenticeship upon leaving school before working for the council’s parks and reserves team.

She was a proud member of the Mothers MC Gang – “an actual gang,” she said.

She spent a couple of years working in Gisborne before embarking on a trip to Europe.

Returning to New Zealand in the 1980s, she got married “because some princess in England got married so everyone wanted to get married”.

The marriage lasted 12 years before she flew to greener pastures, arriving in Rotorua with her children.

She landed a house in Hamurana and had locals chin wagging at school drop-offs when she’d “rock up” in her leather miniskirt, low-cut top, dyed blonde hair, red lipstick and waving her signature cigarette holder.

For six years she worked weekends at the Quality Hotel, and recounts the great days of partying after work at nightclubs such as the Ace of Clubs, Windjammers and Monkey Joes.

But she needed a full-time job to support her children, so she started working at a cafe at Trelawney Garden Centre on Fairy Springs Rd.

She said they did a catering job one night attended by Pig and Whistle owners Gregg and Susan Brown. The Browns loved the food so much, they bought the cafe, on the condition that chef Cherry Te Kiri and Grammer came as part of the deal.

Grammer was then brought on staff at their new venture – opening Capers Cafe + Store on Eruera St.

She said she was grateful to have crossed paths with the Browns all those years ago.

“They are what I call good people. World peace people really.”

She said great bosses were so hard to come by, and she never once thought of leaving.

She said they employed many travellers over the years, whom she got to know well, and felt like she had travelled the world without leaving Rotorua.

“Every day was a good day.”

Capers Cafe + Store general manager and shareholder Rosie Harding said the business employed many staff who had been there a long time, but Grammer was particularly special given she was there since the doors opened.

“Caro is Capers for all of the customers. Everyone knows her and she’s been the face of this place for 25 years.”

For now, Grammer is adjusting to her new life of not working around the clock.

“I cry but I try not to think about it. Most of the time I smile and laugh and I think that I have had it good. Great people and great food.”

Kelly Makiha is a senior journalist who has reported for the Rotorua Daily Post for more than 25 years, covering mainly police, court, human interest and social issues.

Taskforce Kiwi: Former Napier City Council CEO Steph Rotarangi volunteering in flood-hit Nepal

New Zealand Herald September 19, 2026

Steph Rotarangi is part of a specialist Taskforce Kiwi team of three helping in the Nuwakot region. Photo / Taskforce Kiwi

Former Napier City Council chief executive Steph Rotarangi is in Nepal helping to restore water to communities destroyed when an avalanche of ice and rock triggered a deadly flash flood.

Rotarangi, the council’s first female chief executive, has been in Nepal since leaving New Zealand on September 8.

She is part of a specialist Taskforce Kiwi team of three based in one of the “worst-hit areas that we have information on”, in the Nuwakot district.

She said it had been raining and was humid as they faced monsoon season in the area.

“There are two towns, Bidur and Trishuli ... and they have been absolutely torn apart, so from where we are it’s sort of where the road ends and that road used to go another 65km up a valley that was home to 13,000 people plus up to the border.

“When you stop to think about it, and lift your head up out of what you are doing, it’s an enormous scale.

“There are entire communities that have been killed or are missing.”

The team are working alongside Taskforce Kiwi’s local NGO (non-governmental organisation) partner, Noble Compassionate Volunteers (NCV), to support the relief operation.

They are primarily supporting those displaced by flooding, helping to establish, improve and maintain displaced persons camps.

More than 5000 people remain missing, with the death toll topping 1350 last week.

Conditions are austere, with major concerns about sanitation and drinking water for those displaced, including a large number of unaccompanied children.

“We are working to co-ordinate services like water, sanitation and hygiene,” Rotarangi said.

“There are relief centres here for survivors who have no running water, so we are water quality, water quantity.”

The team is working to improve conditions as the risk of water-borne diseases such as cholera increases.

“It’s very hard to articulate without using a lot of cliches, but it is absolutely unprecedented; the scale is really hard to comprehend.

“The locals that have survived described it like they thought the mountains were coming to engulf them.”

She said they “didn’t imagine anything like this could ever happen”.

Amid the devastation, she had experienced community strength.

“It’s so humbling, even in the face of a disaster such as this, the manaakitanga that we have been shown is next level.

“One of the first things that happened when we arrived is people coming out of their houses to give us cups of tea.

“They are a very strong and calm culture.”

Rotarangi has been a volunteer with Taskforce Kiwi since its founding in 2022.

She led a team to Hawaii after the 2024 Lahaina wildfires.

She brings vast experience from her career with Fire and Emergency New Zealand, and her time in Australia as chief fire officer and deputy emergency management commissioner for Victoria. She was also deputy chief fire officer for the state’s Country Fire Authority.

“Honestly, like every New Zealander that was watching the footage [from Nepal] that we saw, we just felt that we needed to be able to offer assistance.

“At any time in New Zealand we could have our own disasters, so the international connections that we make by doing this sort of work teach us new things and they help us potentially have a wider network of people to work with when, if we need it in Aotearoa.”

Conditions remain difficult in the affected areas, with damaged infrastructure limiting material aid reaching thousands of displaced people.

Michaela Gower joined Hawke’s Bay Today in 2023 and is based in the Hastings newsroom. She covers Dannevirke and Hawke’s Bay news and loves sharing stories about farming and rural communities.

Inside Opureora Orchard, Matakana Island’s 8ha avocado block

New Zealand Herald September 19, 2026

Shareholder Pania Wilson with Popsy the dog. Photo / Kelly O’Hara

While avocado blocks in Bay of Plenty are commonplace, the location of one is particularly unique.

Opureora Orchard is on the southwestern tip of Matakana Island and occupies 8ha within a 10ha land block known as Opureora 1B7B3.

It is Māori freehold land owned and operated by Opureora 1B7B3 Land Trust, with orchard operations separated into its own business structure and the trustees’ focus on governance.

Trustee Pania Wilson said there were about 800 avocado trees planted in the 8ha site, alongside 10 homes in the papakāinga (intentional communal living on ancestral Māori land – “a nurturing place to return to”).

It also includes an orchard shed which was recently renovated into an accommodation space for use by shareholders and their whānau, as well as orchard workers during picking season, and three bays for storage of orchard vehicles, resources, tools and equipment.

“The space is aptly named ‘Te Whare Manaaki’, a place of welcome, hospitality and community,” Wilson said.

The trust’s immediate history goes back to May 1998, when a hui was called on the island by the Tauranga Moana Māori Trust Board for all registered owners/shareholders in five blocks, including Opureora.

Board members were trustees of the blocks transferred to them by the Māori Trustees’ Office, and they wanted to hand responsibilities back to the rightful owners/shareholders.

A new land trust was formed to govern Opureora 1B7B3 in January 2000, and in 2004, trustees, with the agreement of the shareholders, entered into a joint venture lease agreement for 18 years to establish an avocado orchard with a well-known orchardist family business from Katikati.

“We were introduced to avocados by the joint venture partner who approached the chair of our land trust at the time,” Wilson said.

“The orchardist had kiwifruit and avocado crops in Katikati but said the climate on Matakana Island is up to 3C warmer, making it an ideal location to grow avocados.”

Across the Island, the main fruits and vegetables grown commercially are avocado, blueberry, corn and kiwifruit.

“Operations/orchard manager Raatu Samuels keeps good relations with our distributor, who provides great, trusted advice and guidance as we’ve been with him since the joint venture 18-year lease agreement ended in 2023, and our land returned lock, stock and barrel – but also $40,000 in deficit,” Wilson said.

“However, the trustees, our orchard team and whānau rolled our sleeves up and, working with a distributor who gets our vision and why we do what we do, we are happy to advise the business is doing okay, despite the challenges, including some of the severest weather events we have ever experienced.”

The fruit is taken to market using the Matakana Ferry II, a ferry/barge service which operates between Matakana Island and Ōmokoroa.

“This travel accounts for up to 20% of our business costs, but we have no choice if that’s the only way to get product off the Island and into the marketplace,” Wilson said.

“There have been discussions about a collective investment in our own ferry service, and perhaps that will become a reality one day.

“But for now, the focus is on the business and our shareholders/owners.”

The off-season presents a time to clear and refresh the orchard through pruning and weeding.

Raatu Samuels lives on the island and contracts one to two locals for orchard care, but for the current harvest the owners have commissioned professional contractors from the mainland.

Wilson said the land trust did not have shares in any other business on the island.

“However, there is a connection of our shareholders to the other land blocks”, she said, and “that is through whakapapa (genealogy)”.

Matakana is a long, flat island, 20km in length and about 3km wide, forming a sand barrier between Tauranga Harbour and the South Pacific.

It protects the entrance to Tauranga Harbour and stretches from Bowentown to Mount Maunganui.

Matakana Island has two distinct parts – 2023ha of farm and orchard land – including Opureora 1B7B3 land block – on the inner harbour (where most of the population lives) and 4047ha of forest-covered coastal land exposed to the Pacific Ocean.

Combined with nearby Rangiwaea Island, it has a population of more than 300 people.

Wilson said everything from people to product came over on the barge, while the island hosted its store, post office and health clinic.

There are five marae on Matakana and Rangiwaea islands: Opureora, Kutaroa, Oruarahi/Te Rangihouhiri, Rangiwaea, Oponui, and five hapū (sub-tribes): Ngāi Tuwhiwhia, Ngāti Tauaiti, Ngāi Tamawhariua, Te Whānau a Tauwhao, and Te Ngare. All five belong to Ngāi Te Rangi Iwi.

“Despite our relative isolation and challenges to access necessary health and social services, our whānau are resilient and resourceful,” Wilson said.

“We have te reo Māori experts, environmental warriors, experts in regenerative planting, fishermen, entrepreneurs, carpenters, nurses, lawyers, teachers, accountants, plumbers, drainlayers, farmers and orchardists.”

Opo, red socks and the Wahs: Why NZ needs another feel-good obsession - Glenn Dwight

New Zealand Herald September 19, 2026

Could the Warriors become the next unlikely force to unite the country? Photo / Photosport

This article is based on no scientific evidence whatsoever, but I have this feeling that something changed for the world after Covid.

There was BC, Before Covid, and then came AD, After Distancing, and somewhere along the way we took the distancing too far and ended up divided.

Even down here, in our little corner of the South Pacific, the Land of the Long White Cloud doesn’t seem quite so much like one big long white cloud anymore.

We’ve become more of a collection of cirrus, cumulus and the occasional dark and angry-looking cumulonimbus.

Politics divides us, sport divides us, we still can’t agree whether that dress was blue and black or white and gold, and our love of putting pineapple on pizza is probably enough to end a potluck dinner and possibly diplomatic relations with Italy.

So, it’s time we un-divided ourselves.

Now, my basic understanding of mathematics is that multiplication is the inverse operation of division, so if division is the problem, surely multiplication is the answer.

I should point out here that most of my Form 5 maths education was spent typing 58008 into a Casio fx-82 calculator and turning it upside down.

Still, I think the theory is sound.

We need to multiply the things that bring us together. The good news is, we’ve done it before.

Every now and then something has come along that, for reasons nobody can entirely explain, captured the imagination of the whole country and somehow brought us all together.

Take Opo.

In the summer of 1955-56, a young bottlenose dolphin started hanging around Ōpononi, playing with swimmers, following boats and generally having a bloody great time.

I like to think Opo was simply on a classic Kiwi summer holiday at a mate’s undersea bach in the Hokianga.

Nothing flash, just a little two-bedroom place, seaweed curtains, a couple of bunks for the kids and one of those signs saying “Life’s A Beach”.

After three days of rain, punishing games of Monopoly, the kids fighting over the top bunk and everyone getting on each other’s fins, Opo did what any sensible holidaymaker would do and headed into town to see what the locals were up to.

Whatever the reason, word got out that our mate Opo was in town and New Zealand went mad for her.

People piled into cars and buses and travelled for hours along dusty, unsealed 1950s New Zealand roads, presumably with several children fighting in the back seat, no air conditioning and Dad threatening to turn the car around, all because somebody had told them there was a friendly dolphin at the other end.

And they came in such numbers that the local campground filled up, the hotel was booked out, and hundreds gathered on the beach hoping Opo might make an appearance.

Opo played with beach balls, swam with children and became such a celebrity that songs were written about her.

When she died in 1956, there was genuine national sadness; a girls’ hockey team in Whangārei even wore black armbands.

A dolphin had brought New Zealand together.

Sadly, I’m not sure Opo could happen today.

For starters, the moment she arrived there would probably be orange cones around half of Ōpononi.

DoC would quite rightly tell us to keep our distance, somebody would launch a Givealittle page, there would be a Facebook group called “Opo: The TRUTH”, and within 48 hours we’d somehow be arguing about whether the dolphin was woke.

So perhaps another dolphin isn’t the answer.

But 40 years after Opo, New Zealand found something else to unite behind.

This time it was a pair of socks.

Sir Peter Blake’s lucky red socks became the symbol of Team New Zealand’s 1995 America’s Cup campaign, and before long they were everywhere.

New Zealanders bought them by the thousands, helping put money into the campaign, and wore them to show their support.

Prime ministers wore them, bus drivers sported them, kids wore them to school.

For a while we had accidentally created a national uniform.

Black Magic then thrashed Dennis Conner and New Zealand was once again a nation of seamen and women, even if the closest many of us had come to a nautical endeavour was wiping out on a Warehouse boogie board at Ōhope. Always swim between the flags.

We knew the names of the sailors. We understood what a tack was, or at least pretended to. And when that boat crossed the finish line, it genuinely felt as though the country had won something together.

That was Peter Blake’s great trick. He somehow made everyone feel part of it.

When you bought those red socks, you weren’t just watching Team New Zealand; you were helping New Zealand.

Team New Zealand is still extraordinarily successful, but I’m not sure that same connection exists anymore.

The modern America’s Cup is incredible, even if the boats do look a bit like a frog stretching its legs first thing in the morning.

They’re carbon fibre, cutting-edge technology, helmets and enormous corporate budgets. But somewhere in that metamorphosis from yacht to carbon-fibre frog, I think we lost a little of the connection.

In the red-socks days, ordinary Kiwis felt like part of Team New Zealand.

These days it can sometimes feel like we’re watching Team New Zealand (by name only) instead.

Unless, of course, you happen to have a billion-dollar business and room for your logo on the side.

Maybe that’s unfair, but I miss the socks.

Then there was Shrek the Sheep.

Only New Zealand could turn a sheep that had successfully avoided a haircut into a national celebrity.

Shrek the Sheep hid away on a South Island station for six years, and when he was finally discovered in 2004, he was carrying around 27kg of fleece and looked less like a sheep and more like one of those pom-poms we all made by wrapping wool around two bits of cardboard in Sunday School.

And naturally, we loved him.

He was shorn on live television, raised money for charity, became internationally famous and even met Prime Minister Helen Clark.

And that’s the New Zealand I want back.

Not because everything was better then. It wasn’t. But every now and again we seemed capable of collectively deciding, “You know what, this is fun. Let’s all get behind it”.

Maybe that’s the secret.

We don’t necessarily need something important to bring us together.

In fact, history suggests we’re much better at uniting around things that aren’t particularly important at all.

A dolphin.

Some red socks.

A very woolly sheep.

Simple things that gave us something to talk about with the person next door rather than something to argue about with them.

I’ll throw one possibility out there. Maybe it’s the Wahs.

They’ve already managed to turn “Up the Wahs” into something close to a national greeting, and if they ever go all the way and win the NRL, just imagine it.

Five million New Zealanders suddenly discovering they’ve always been league fans, strangers hugging in the streets, more mana waves than a Raglan left-hand break and a choir of 5 million belting out: “We are the Warriors 100%.”

Whatever “it” is, it doesn’t need to fix the economy, solve our problems or have a position on pineapple.

It just needs to make us smile, get us talking and remind us that, despite all those different clouds floating around up there, we’re still living under the same sky.

And perhaps, as the Opo song put it all those years ago, it’s time we were once again “friendly as can be” and a whole lot less divided.

‘Growth is good’: The towns avoiding the rural death spiral

Sydney Morning Herald September 20, 2026

You have reached your maximum number of saved items.

Remove items from your saved list to add more.

Towns are born, and towns die. Behind the Great Dividing Range, towns are on life support. In once-prosperous farming towns, six hours between Melbourne and Sydney, the pubs are shut, and weatherboard homes are boarded up.

The rain has come, turning pastures into fields of green. But resentment runs deep: over illegal clearing prosecutions, net zero, fuel prices, stagnating local economies, and a city-country divide that is fuelling distrust about decisions being made in the capitals.

Fewer jobs mean fewer people. Now there aren’t enough of them to staff critical services in regional areas across NSW and Victoria.

“If you bring the people out, then services come as well, but they can’t come out because there are no bloody services,” says Keith Rowe, a farmer in West Wyalong, a six-hour drive from Sydney and Melbourne.

“We really need more new people coming into our town. And we don’t care how that mix is made up.”

No political party has been able to break the economic cycle of decline in parts of regional Australia. Fewer people means schools and shops close. Children leave. In 1960, the median age in West Wyalong was 26. Now it’s 43. In nearby Grenfell, it’s 52. The impact compounds as the years roll on, then steams home when those left behind realise all they once knew might one day be gone.

“I think about it a lot,” says Rowe. “It’s a real serious dilemma we’ve got.”

Rowe’s friend, farmer Rod Hardie, issues this warning: “The current system, the current economy, the current way things are running – we won’t be here.”

Once upon a time the Nationals were the natural representatives of the vast tracts of land spanning Nicholls and Mallee in Victoria and the Riverina and Parkes in NSW. One Nation’s victory in the Farrer by-election in May and its surging support in national polls mean that all four are now in play.

In One Nation’s regional policy mix, immigration falls behind water buybacks and anti-net zero. Nevertheless, on a national scale, the party has harnessed the emotional impact of the perceived threat of immigration to its image of Australia, regardless of whether the large cuts it is proposing might do more harm than good to the economies it wants to represent.

Betty Wu has owned the last Chinese restaurant in West Wyalong for three decades. Now she is voting for One Nation.

“I’m voting for the lady,” she says, referring to One Nation leader Pauline Hanson, who once claimed Australia was being “swamped by Asians” like Wu. “Something needs to change.”

Wu, who migrated to Australia from Guangdong in South China, once had multiple competitors along West Wyalong’s main drag. Nearby restaurant Lam and May has gone takeaway only. At lunchtime on a Thursday, Wu sits alone in a banquet room, hoping someone will walk in.

“It’s hard,” she says. “There are no people. It’s so quiet.”

Nearby, in the regional hub of Cowra, once a postwar centre for Eastern European migrants, the shift from farmhands to an increasingly mechanised workforce has reduced the working-age population, while its retirement-age population has surged.

“I suppose we are the old WASPS, the white Anglo-Saxon Protestants and Catholics; that’s virtually what the town is these days, and that’s probably why we’re so conservative,” says mayor Paul Smith.

More than 75 per cent of Cowra’s 12,000 residents have parents who were both born in Australia; those who weren’t were mostly born in England, Scotland or New Zealand. A quarter of the town is aged 65 or over.

Meeting the needs of that population has become more challenging.

“I go to mayors’ conferences, and they’ve all got the same problem,” says Smith. “We have a brand-new hospital, which is more attractive to young graduates. The thing is, to get a doctor here, you have to have work for their partner. Now, if they’re another doctor, there’s no trouble. But if they are an engineer … that can make it difficult.”

This is the paradox facing One Nation. Newly elected One Nation Farrer MP David Farley is grappling with an electorate bordering the Riverina that already lacks enough workers to pick fruit, let alone staff hospitals. Now his party wants to cut immigration by 750,000 temporary migrants, and put Australia into three years of population decline before stabilising at 130,000 a year, 100,000 fewer than the government’s target.

It remains unclear if that 130,000 figure will exclude backpackers, nurses, Pacific Australia Labour Mobility workers and other skilled workers needed in the regions, as Farley suggested last month. His leader, Pauline Hanson, did not respond to requests for an interview.

The story across the country is not uniform. Shepparton is two hours’ drive north of Melbourne. It sits within the federal electorate of Nicholls, bordering Farley’s seat of Farrer.

Hanson has a foothold here too. Shepparton’s placid CBD is home to the office of Victoria’s only state One Nation MP, upper house member Rikkie-Lee Tyrrell.

Polling suggests Tyrrell could be joined by up to 11 more One Nation MPs after November’s state election. Some union-commissioned research has suggested the party could win up to 30 seats.

One Nation’s vote has jumped on the back of its anti-immigration message, Resolve Political Monitor polling shows, but a lot of that support is driven by anger that has nowhere else to go. It’s a lot easier to blame migrants than it is to blame the faceless forces of inflation and globalisation.

“It’s a story as old as time, where people feel insecure and when purse strings are tight,” says Professor Alan Gamlen, the director of the migration hub at the Australian National University.

“The world is changing too fast for people to comprehend, and they need a simple explanation. And it’s always been the case that blaming the outsiders, the witches, the infidels or the plague of locusts has been a really successful political strategy.”

Shepparton’s One Nation voting may be surging, but it has avoided the economic fate of West Wyalong and Cowra through waves of immigration that continue to this day.

Sunny Uppal’s family moved to Shepparton from India, via New Zealand, in 2003. “We always wanted to do farming because it’s in the blood,” the 41-year-old says.

For generations, Uppal’s family grew potatoes and wheat in Punjab. In Shepparton, they started with 30 acres of apple orchard and today have almost 200.

“I love seeing something grow out of the dirt,” he says. “The trees start to flower, the seasons change. A year goes by pretty fast here.”

Uppal estimates around 30 Indian families own farms around the Shepparton area.

They follow in the footsteps of Greeks, Italians and Albanians who came in the 1920s, then Turks in the 1960s.

Punjabis started arriving in the 1980s. In the 2021 Census, 1549 people living in Shepparton reported speaking Punjabi at home, the most common language after English, and representing 2.3 per cent of the population.

Uppal manages his orchards with his two brothers. In their large sorting shed, 30 workers are packing pears and apples into wooden crates for distribution around the country.

All are from overseas; some have migrated to Australia permanently. Others are on working holiday visas, fulfilling their 88 days of mandatory regional work – a critical supply of labour for one of the country’s largest fruit-growing regions.

Between 2000 and 3000 workers from the Pacific Islands also travel to the Shepparton area every year to work through the PALM scheme too.

“We don’t have enough working people here, that’s why we’re getting people from overseas,” says Uppal.

“Imagine if we don’t have them, we won’t have fruit for anybody. We need truck drivers, we need forklift drivers, fruit pickers, fruit packers. There’s so much that goes on there, and without them, we won’t be here.”

Shepparton has a constant demand for migrants to support its manufacturing industry, which includes fruit canneries and dairy processors, and essential services for the town of just over 65,076 people.
