4:22

Immigration nation: How Australia's immigration success story became its biggest political fight

Labor, the Coalition and One Nation are heading towards an immigration election. This is how we got here.

Over the past five years, the Committee for Shepparton has run a program helping 850 professionals move to Shepparton – the vast majority of them migrants – and links them with local sporting or social clubs.

The goal is not just a warm welcome; it’s to encourage workers to put down roots and stay put.

“It’s an essential contributor to the success of our economy,” says its CEO Linda Nieuwenhuizen.

Goulburn Valley Health, the only public hospital and main health service in the area, was struggling with a 20 per cent staff vacancy rate in 2023 but has brought that down to 8 per cent, mostly through international recruitment.

The anaesthetics team consists entirely of migrants. Ma Lenie Estrella, a nurse originally from the Philippines, worked in the United Arab Emirates for a decade before moving to Melbourne in 2023 and Shepparton in 2024, and has a working visa sponsored by GV Health.

“At first it was a culture shock. The main thing is communication. Sometimes Australians try to shorten things – like telly, bikkies, cuppa – so I’m not used to that,” she says. “But over time it gets better.”

A walk down Acacia Street punctures another tenet of Hansonism: the myth of Australia’s monocultural past.

Albanian Muslims started moving to Shepparton in the mid-1920s to work on the orchards and have been part of the town’s DNA ever since.

In 1956, the Albanian community started constructing Victoria’s first purpose-built mosque here. When it opened four years later, it was surrounded by fields furrowed for tomato plants; today, the cream-brick building sits in a pocket of tidy suburbia.

Enver Sabri and Riddy Ahmet were born in Shepparton to Albanian parents. They could barely speak English when they started school – but that wasn’t unusual in the 1950s and 1960s, when classrooms were a melting pot of Anglo, Greek, Turk, Italian and First Nations kids.

“If you talked English inside the house, you’d get your ears chopped off,” recalls Ahmet. His father would say: “When you come inside, you’ve got to speak Albanian because we might go back.”

The first wave of Albanians thought their time in Australia would be temporary, part of a long-standing cultural practice called kurbet, where a man would travel abroad for a few years before returning home. World War II and the communist takeover of Albania made returning too dangerous.

So they stayed, holding on to their Albanian culture and adapting to their new environment. Ahmet and Sabri worked the orchards, attended mosque, and on weekends performed in their country and western band.

Shane Sali is the second Albanian-Australian to serve as Greater Shepparton City Council’s mayor. He stood down in September, ahead of running as a National Party candidate in November’s state election.

“Shepparton is an excellent example of what strong multiculturalism looks like,” Sali says. “Our region’s history demonstrates the enormous value that migration can bring to the economy, workforce and community life.”

One hour south of Cowra, Young is another town that is anathema to the picture of Australia pushed by One Nation.

Between its rolling hills and cherry farms, a minaret is being lifted onto the newly renovated mosque on the town’s outskirts.

“It’s going to be the biggest building in town,” says a beaming Abdul Ghoneim, a member of the mosque’s committee and one of the organising forces behind the renovation.

The mosque, initially opened in the early 1990s by Lebanese immigrants, had become too small to accommodate the surging Muslim population in town, and has been renovated to expand the praying space and improve its facilities.

Ghoneim says the mosque has acted as an anchor for the steady stream of Lebanese and Muslim families leaving Sydney for Young.

Slowly but surely, their internal migration has reshaped the town into a unique regional migrant hub, complete with Lebanese bakeries and ethnic grocers.

Since 2006, the number of residents who were born overseas and with parents born overseas has doubled in Young, supercharging the demographic shift.

And it isn’t just Lebanese or Muslim communities, with increasing rates of residents speaking languages such as Chinese, Hazaragi, and Dari.

That steady stream has also meant Young has avoided the stagnation that has plagued surrounding towns, with population growing by over 8 per cent since 2001.

This demographic shift has had an obvious impact on the town’s economy, with steady growth in agricultural output, household salaries and rates of employment.

The town hums in the way a western Sydney suburb might, only with a regional tint. Muslim women in hijabs wander about with their children, greeting other townsfolk, while young people mill about outside the local manoush shop (the only such bakery for hundreds of kilometres).

Next door, at Maz Mart, an ethnic grocer that specialises in Arab goods including tinned chickpeas, Lebanese bread and tobacco for shisha, both Anglo and Arab locals shop.

“The non-Muslims shop here almost as much as the Muslims,” Abdullah AlShammari says as he helps a customer. “They buy everything, tomatoes, rice, even the sweets. They are our siblings, and we love it.”

“We are a Muslim community, but we are a part of Young, and we are proud of that,” Abdullah Sultan, one of the members of the Young Mosque committee, said at the opening ceremony.

Brian Ingram, the mayor of the local council, Hilltops Council, was also at the opening ceremony. He smiled broadly throughout the event. He said the steady flow of immigrant and Muslims families into Young has been nothing but a positive, fuelling economic growth and a vibrant cultural shift.

“They buy homes here, they pay rates here, they buy stores and supplies here, and that’s what it’s all about. And on top of that, they have some developers amongst them that are creating the opportunity for more housing, which is essential,” he said.

“Growth is good,” he added.

Young and Shepparton have positive stories. The challenge for Labor is selling them.

As immigration minister for more than a decade, Philip Ruddock travelled around the country holding town halls in cities and regional communities.

Political and international editor

“Too often the debate is also shaped by prejudice, fear and, at times, blatant racism,” he says.

Ruddock says it’s time for Home Affairs Minister Tony Burke to do the same and visit cities and regional areas.

“One of the frustrations of national immigration policy is that national averages can conceal local realities. Sydney and Melbourne may experience congestion and pressure on services, while smaller states and regional communities are desperate for people,” he says.

“Every government faces the same temptation: to simplify the issue, to speak only to one side of the argument, to pretend that generosity requires no limits or that control requires no humanity. Neither position can sustain a nation-building immigration program.”

Ruddock, the longest-serving MP since Billy Hughes, says Australia faces a demographic truth that cannot be ignored.

“Advanced economies are ageing, with falling rates of fertility, and working-age populations shrinking or growing more slowly,” he said.

“That is why I found so much of the public debate frustrating. Critics often speak as though multiculturalism were a policy for migrants. I see it as a policy for Australia.”

‘I had been completely ripped apart’: Julia Busuttil Nishimura’s shock postnatal diagnosis

Sydney Morning Herald September 20, 2026

The mother of three has enjoyed huge success over the past decade, but it’s been tinged with struggle and sacrifice.

You have reached your maximum number of saved items.

Remove items from your saved list to add more.

Julia Busuttil Nishimura is a hugger. As soon as I enter the bustling cafe where we’re meeting, she’s up from the table and trapping me in a warm embrace, her mass of dark curls brushing against my cheek.

Here are some other things the 38-year-old Italian teacher and food blogger turned cookbook author is fond of: tennis (both playing and watching), lamps, and headscarves. And peaches. She really loves peaches.

“I do like a peach; I think I mention one in all of my books,” she says over lunch at Florian in Melbourne’s Carlton North, not far from the home she shares with her Japanese-born husband of 12 years, Nori, and their three boys, aged 11, six and nine months.

1:03

Julia Busuttil Nishimura's Sunday ritual

Sunday Life catches up with Julia Busuttil Nishimura at home to chat through her favourite Sunday rituals and recipes.

In fact, it was here they recently road-tested eating out as a family of five. “It was kind of chaotic, but it was cute,” she says, laughing.

Enjoying food, both making and eating it, is something she’s keen to instil in her children while they are young. Her strongest food memory is from when she was 22 and working in Italy as an au pair. “The family would make this cherry tomato pasta with garlic and basil with paccheri [a short, tubular pasta], and good olive oil – simple things,” she says.

For Busuttil Nishimura, whose career and personal life have been on a warp-speed trajectory for the past decade, simplicity is more than a buzzword – it’s her whole raison d’être. “Cooking for your friends and family doesn’t need to be fancy or stressful,” she says. Nor does simple have to mean – dare she say it – basic. “The kind of cooking that I do is so understated that you have to have the confidence that you can use just four ingredients, and it’s going to be delicious.”

But if not for a chance meeting at a local farmer’s market with her now-publisher, Mary Small, who had been a fan of Busuttil Nishimura’s mid-2000s food blog, Ostro, she may have remained content in her former career as an Italian teacher.

“It is quite uncommon now to have been discovered, and not go through MasterChef,” she says. After her 2017 debut cookbook, Ostro, came out to rave reviews for its celebration of unhurried, simple cooking (Jamie Oliver and Nigella Lawson were fans), she still didn’t know if she could make food her full-time job.

“I was a nobody, really, I had my blog, it was the very early days of Instagram,” she says. “I never really set a timeline or had a plan, which for a Virgo, and someone with anxiety, [is rare].”

This month Busuttil Nishimura will release her fifth cookbook (she also wrote an award-winning children’s book, Sundays Under the Lemon Tree), Simple Pleasures. She hopes fans will see it as a balm for these “crazy” times. “We’re so inundated with the news and the busyness of life – it is so overwhelming,” she says. The recipes in the book, which range from hearty soups to chocolate mousse, are about “coming back to what actually is meaningful and brings us pleasure”.

For Busuttil Nishimura, that means leaning into her softness, both physically and emotionally: “This idea of slowing down, but not in an arduous way,” she says. “The small moments that punctuate our day are what makes cooking – and life – so pleasurable.”

Aside from the sleep deprivation of having a young baby, life is in a good place for Busuttil Nishimura. But, as we tuck into our plates of cured salmon, soft egg, and pickled fennel and cucumber, she tells me the past decade has been punctuated by periods of postpartum anxiety following the births of Haruki, now 11, and Yukito, 6.

“When you have a baby, you’re very raw and emotional – it makes you reflect a lot on how you grew up. My anxiety’s all around health stuff, because my mum was really unwell when I was little.”

Born in Adelaide as the youngest of three children, Busuttil Nishimura was two when her mother developed breast cancer at age 40 (her parents separated when she was six). Even as a child, food offered her a place of “peace and calm and escape”.

“There’s something about the beauty of food, nature and the reliability of mostly knowing how it’s going to turn out – there’s something special about that,” she says.

Becoming a mother at 26, before any of her friends and with Nori working long hours as a chef, was an incredibly lonely time. “It’s really isolating,” she recalls.

Since then, she has worked with a therapist, and says her third pregnancy was her best yet. “It took me three goes to really figure out what I needed to ask for … to have a great pregnancy and a great postpartum time.” She remembers thinking at the time: “I’m the most settled in my career that I’ve been, and everything feels like the jigsaw puzzle has fit together.”

But a shock came about a week after Mikoto was born, when Busuttil Nishimura developed jaw and neck pain. Initially, she dismissed it as a delayed reaction to labour, but then she started dribbling while trying to drink water. Then one eye wouldn’t close. “I just remember thinking the worst case was a clot in my brain,” she says.

After tests ruled out a stroke, Busuttil Nishimura was diagnosed with the autoimmune response Bell’s palsy, which affects up to one in 2500 people each year, and is more prevalent in women in late-stage pregnancy and after giving birth.

“It does all flash before you,” she says of the health scare. After spending a week in hospital for treatment, Busuttil Nishimura remembers “standing at home, wearing disposable underwear, leaking through my bra, I’ve got an eye patch on, and I’m holding my baby, and thinking, ‘What is this?’ I just felt like I had been completely ripped apart and put back together.”

It took about three months for her to make a full recovery, and despite not being able to smile at Mikoto in his first weeks, weirdly, she says, the experience “sparked something inside me to stay positive”. Even so, she worried about the impact the illness would have on the book, which was already in production, and future work.

“You already feel so self-conscious postpartum,” she says. “Ideally, I wouldn’t be 13 weeks postpartum on a cookbook shoot.”

She concedes that not having an official period of maternity leave is the price of running her own business. “But conversely, I feel so lucky that I can do what I do, and it’s so flexible.”

Part of why it works is that Busuttil Nishimura and Nori, 39, who now works as a tennis coach, have taken turns being the primary earner (she dislikes the term “breadwinner”) and caregiver. But her cookbooks, media commitments and the children have limited her husband’s opportunities to travel overseas where there are better coaching opportunities.

She says their success as a team lies in seeing her work as a family business, rather than as a solo pursuit. “We’re trying to build something for the both of us, and for our kids. It’s a big juggle … We both can’t be at the top of our game while the kids are so little. And it just works.

“We’re just the most perfect fit – I can feel it in my bones, just how matched we are and how supportive of each other we are,” she says of her husband, whom she met in Melbourne while working in the same Collingwood restaurant. “We go through these seasons, and mostly I have benefited from it. He’s really sacrificed a lot for me to have the career I do have.”

The success of her first four cookbooks has opened doors for Busuttil Nishimura to also work with fashion and beauty brands, including Lee Mathews and Mecca, and to dabble in television presenting. “I actually can’t watch [myself on TV] … I am unpolished, but it’s just real,” she says, laughing. “If you try and be something that you’re not you can come across as being a bit contrived.”

While she’s keen to do more TV, writing remains her core passion. “I’d like to write books forever,” she says. “I just want longevity, really. I don’t want to do things too fast. I’m really big on thinking things through.”

Between answering DMs about readers’ recipe dilemmas, walking the occasional red carpet, writing regular magazine columns, and developing recipes in her kitchen while her eldest two are at school, Busuttil Nishimura always comes back to the one word that brings her the most happiness: simplicity.

One of her most treasured family moments happened during a recent blackout, when they played Uno by candlelight and ate all the ice cream in the freezer before it melted. “My work is so consuming, and I’m always doing a million things at a time,” she says, “so when I can put that away to just be with the kids at home – to me, that’s the best.”

Simple Pleasures (Plum) by Julia Busuttil Nishimura is out September 29.

The strange story of Norfolk Island’s super-sized sharks

Sydney Morning Herald September 20, 2026

You have reached your maximum number of saved items.

Remove items from your saved list to add more.

At Norfolk Island Airport the signs say “welcome to paradise”. The super-sized tiger sharks that live here must surely agree.

In the pristine waters around this South Pacific outcrop, 1400 kilometres from the Australian mainland, the tiger sharks grow fat on juicy mutton birds and beef offal. They roam freely across thousands of kilometres from New Zealand to New Caledonia, with the occasional jaunt to the Great Barrier Reef. And left unmolested by humans, they grow to a ripe old age.

And that’s even before a proposal by the federal government to expand the area of marine sanctuary around Norfolk and Lord Howe islands.

The result is that Norfolk’s tiger sharks are among the biggest in the world. The median length of a Norfolk tiger was 4 metres, in a Flinders University study of 35 tagged sharks. The largest female was 4.5 metres while the largest male was 4.1 metres.

By contrast, the largest female shark in a 2022 East Coast study of 66 sharks was about 3.8 metres, and the largest male was 3.3 metres.

Professor Charlie Huveneers at Flinders University, an ecologist specialising in shark research, says the Norfolk Island tiger sharks are extremely large. Since his paper in Marine Environmental Research last year, scientists have also studied large tiger sharks in the Maldives, but Huveneers says the Norfolk population is remarkable for having so many in a small area, without the influence of wildlife tour operators using food-based attractants.

“The primary reasons for these tiger sharks being so large is likely because they are old individuals which had the opportunity to grow to these large sizes,” Huveneers says. “These sharks would have also needed the right nutrition to grow and their time around Norfolk Island likely facilitated the consumption of nutritious prey.”

What was that prey? The reason many Norfolk Island locals point to is the offal chute at Headstone Bay. There are free-range cattle all over the island, but nowhere to dispose of the carcasses without poisoning the groundwater, given the island is just eight square kilometres. The skin and offcuts often get dumped down a chute into the ocean and the tiger sharks devour the beef from underneath.

Tien Dat Do, 28, a nurse who moved from Vietnam to Norfolk Island about nine months ago, goes rock fishing four or five times a week. Headstone is his favourite fishing spot on the island, and he sees the chute used at least weekly.

Do has seen the remains of up to four cows dumped into the water, and the tiger sharks demolish it all within half an hour to an hour.

“They smash from the bottom and when they finish the bottom, they keep going until there’s nothing left,” Do says.

Huveneers and the team used biochemical tracers from the muscle of tiger sharks to find out what they ate. Only about 5 per cent of their diet was identified as organic waste from livestock. Seabirds, including wedge-tailed shearwaters known colloquially as mutton birds, made up 70 per cent of their diet. Twenty per cent consisted of turtles, sea snakes and fish.

The tiger sharks like to hang out in Headstone Bay regardless of the organic waste disposal, acoustic underwater monitoring found. Huveneers says this could be because it is where the largest shearwater colonies are found on Norfolk Island, with the offal being incidental.

The researchers also found that dusky and Galapagos whaler sharks visited Norfolk Island’s fishing piers at various times of day, especially in the afternoons when fishers clean their catch along the piers and throw the scraps into the water. There are also white sharks around Norfolk Island, but not studied by the Flinders team.

The tiger sharks are around Norfolk mostly between October and April, satellite tracking found, while dusky and Galapagos whalers remain there year round. Tracking found that nearly nine out of 10 tiger sharks across multiple seasons returned to Norfolk Island at least once.

One intrepid individual tiger shark swam between New Caledonia, the Great Barrier Reef, Norfolk Island, the Chesterfield Islands, and New Zealand, at least 17,000 km in 468 days.

Luke Fitzpatrick, 30, takes tourists out fishing in his charter boat, but uses a more resilient aluminium boat to do the shark tagging with Huveneers and the scientists.

“We catch them and they get them up to the side of the boat and then they put a couple of ropes and hoses around them so it doesn’t hurt them and then they put the tags in their fins,” Fitzpatrick says.

“They’ve got a tape measure that goes from its head to its fins, one person each end. They’re pretty cool creatures, the big ones.”

It does not surprise Fitzpatrick or anyone else on Norfolk Island that their sharks are bigger than anywhere else in the world. It seems everyone who grew up there has their “you’re gonna need a bigger boat”, or Jaws, moment.

For fisher Scotty Greenwood, 37, of Greenwoods Fishing Adventures, it was about a decade ago when he was out with a friend on a 14-foot plastic boat.

“We were just drifting, and a great white hit the boat like a seal,” Greenwood says. “It hit the back of the boat, nearly tipped us out. It still had enough momentum after glancing off the boat that it was airborne beside the boat. We thought it’s going to be hurt and take off.

“No, it landed, turned around on a dime, came back and hit the boat again. At this point, we were terrified and just got out of there.”

He later found out that male great white sharks hit the females in that manner to turn them upside down and mate with them.

By contrast, Greenwood says Norfolk’s tiger sharks are “quite placid and predictable”. Despite the size and number of sharks, there has never been a shark fatality recorded on Norfolk Island.

Spearfishing guide Jamie Ryves, 44, agrees. Unlike in places where they do cage diving for tourists, such as Hawaii, the Norfolk Island tiger sharks are “actually very timid”, he says. Diving with them is all about getting your body language right.

“You’ve really got to keep your body streamlined and be very slow and dive away from them and let them come into you to even get close to them,” Ryves says. “I don’t really feel threatened being in the water with them.”

Caitlin Fitzsimmons and Audrey Richardson travelled to Norfolk Island as guests of the Australian Museum for a separate story.

Ed Davey takes aim at Reform and Elon Musk as Lib Dem conference begins

The Guardian Sat, 19 Sep 2026 21:37:52 GMT

Leader says party ‘won’t give up the fight’ to defeat ‘nasty populism’ in first-day speech to delegates

The Liberal Democrats’ leader, Sir Ed Davey, took aim at Nigel Farage’s Reform UK and Elon Musk on the first day of his party’s annual conference, saying that they “won’t give up the fight” to defeat “nasty populism” and the far-right party’s “£72m arsenal of hate and lies”.

Speaking from the main stage at Brighton Centre, Davey called on the assembled delegates not to be deterred in the face of Reform’s hope “that the anger and the hatred and the lies will grind us down until eventually we just give up”, and praised earlier speakers for showing “why we care and why we fight”.

He contrasted this with Reform, which “care about their own bank balance and they fight because two crypto billionaires gave them 72m quid”.

Davey, who entered conference season having to address frustrations over his leadership expressed by some Lib Dem MPs, also used the speech to recall his early political life as a student campaigning successfully for his university college to boycott Barclays, due to its investments in apartheid-era South Africa.

He spoke of his “visceral shock [and] overwhelming anger at seeing human beings treating other human beings with total contempt” and drew parallels between that experience and the need to not look away “when we see human dignity under attack”.

Davey said: “Today – we are back. Fighting again the fight that fired me up at university. The fight to end injustices. In our country and around the world. The fight to defeat the nasty populism of Trump, Le Pen, the AfD and the rest.

“The fight to stop the world’s richest man who learned racism in apartheid South Africa from funding racism around the world.”

Referring to recent abuse from far-right agitators aimed at the RNLI, Davey also pointed to the “fight to defend the Royal National Lifeboat Institution after volunteers for the coastal rescue charity were recently targeted online amid anti-migrant protests”.

He said that “Reform know they don’t speak for the real United Kingdom” and what Farage was “counting on to get him to No 10” was that people would get “tired, depressed, fed up of seeing Zia Yusuf on BBC Question Time week after week”.

But Davey said he hoped Reform were watching and would see “a party that won’t be ground down. That won’t be deterred. That won’t give up the fight”.

Also during the first day of the conference, Lib Dem health spokesperson Helen Morgan set out a £600m plan to improve maternity care, including proposals to bring in one-to-one midwifery for every woman in labour backed by a round-the-clock senior consultant.

The party said the measures will pay for themselves by reducing how much the NHS has to spend on compensation for maternity negligence claims every year – totalling £1.3bn in 2024-25.

Munira Wilson, the Lib Dem education spokesperson, said the party would introduce a guarantee to provide 100 hours of work experience for students from GCSE age to 18 to tackle the crisis of young people not in education, employment or training.

Israeli president pardons combat medic who shot dead wounded Palestinian attacker

The Guardian Sat, 19 Sep 2026 20:32:17 GMT

Elor Azaria’s conviction in 2017 for manslaughter of man who stabbed soldier continues to divide country

Israel’s president has pardoned a combat medic who shot dead a badly wounded Palestinian attacker who had stabbed a soldier in the occupied West Bank, in a case that divided the country a decade ago.

Elor Azaria’s conviction in 2017 for manslaughter and his release after serving two-thirds of his 18-month sentence drew enormous attention in Israel, where military service is compulsory for most Jewish men.

In his first interview after his release, Azaria said he would “act exactly the same, because that’s how I needed to act”.

Azaria had approached Abdel Fattah al-Sharif as he lay on the ground, unarmed and badly hurt, after stabbing a soldier in the city of Hebron. A mobile phone video captured Azaria shooting al-Sharif in the head.

The office of president Isaac Herzog said in a statement on Saturday that he acted on the recommendation of defence minister Israel Katz. The statement cited the time that had passed, and the spirit of the approaching Yom Kippur, or Day of Atonement, holiday as among the factors in the decision.

Herzog’s office also said that Azaria, who was 20 when he was sentenced, had “expressed his sorrow” in his request. The statement noted that in an earlier request, he called his gunshot an “operational error”.

In a separate statement, Katz called it a “right, humane and fitting decision” and said Azaria had been in a “complex operational mission”.

But the military’s chief of staff, Lt Gen Eyal Zamir, had said in a letter to the defence minister that the pardon should not be granted, Israeli media reported.

The conviction was a rare case of a military court ruling against a soldier for deadly action taken in the field. Top generals had pressed for his prosecution, while many in the Israeli public supported Azaria at a time when there had been a series of stabbings and car-ramming attacks by Palestinians or Israeli Arabs. Some supporters protested outside his trial.

On Saturday, Israel’s hard-line national security minister Itamar Ben-Gvir said in a statement that “cancelling the criminal record of someone who killed a terrorist makes me emotional and very happy”.

Some Palestinians and human rights groups had described Azaria’s sentence as far too lenient. Prosecutors had sought a sentence of three to five years.

The statement by Herzog’s office on Saturday said that his decision “does not constitute a reassessment of the case”.

The divisions over Azaria’s case led to public polling and political pressure that led the defence minister at the time, Moshe Ya’alon, to resign.

After the verdict, Israeli prime minister Benjamin Netanyahu called for Azaria to be pardoned.

After the sentencing, the Palestinian government minister in charge of prisoner affairs, Issa Karaka, called it a “joke”.

The moment I knew: On a bike ride, she did a bunny hop over a speed hump – her pure joy for life delighted me

The Guardian Sat, 19 Sep 2026 20:00:57 GMT

Anna Malos and Georgie bonded over their shared love of travel and horses. By their third date, an awkward encounter cemented their relationship

Find more stories from the moment I knew series

Georgie and I met at a kick-boxing club in London in 2004. We sparred together in a few beginner classes, just hitting soft pads. Although I didn’t pay her too much attention initially, I immediately recognised she was tall, elegant and very good looking.

It wasn’t until the club’s Christmas drinks that things kicked off between us. We started talking and couldn’t stop. We’d both travelled and worked in Latin America, and also loved horses – Georgie had volunteered with a horse-riding business for tourists in Ecuador. The sparks were flying all over the place.

A friend of mine was deejaying at a gay club nearby so we headed there and continued chatting, dancing and flirting. About 2am we found an all-night cafe and talkeduntil daybreak, then went our separate ways. But we planned to meet again.

On my way to our third date, my housemate called saying we’d been burgled. I had to return home and call the police. When I explained this to Georgie she suggested coming to mine instead. When the police finally arrived, many hours later, I introduced myself as one of the occupants. One of the constables asked Georgie who she was. There was this awkward silence – on date three was she my girlfriend? I think we went with “friend”. But she didn’t go home that night.

Things moved quickly from there. One morning in early spring we took a bike ride through a nearby park that had little speed bumps. Like us, our bikes were very different – mine was a lightweight touring bike and hers a hard-tail mountain bike.

I was riding just ahead of her but when I looked back I saw her doing this funky bunny hop over the speed hump. I can picture the jacket she was wearing – dark grey, heavy canvas – and her focus as she flicked her bike over the hump. It was that joie de vivre that delighted me. Her embarrassment when she realised I’d seen was also so very her – wanting to be cool, but so much more than that. This was someone who couldn’t contain her enthusiasm. It crystallised what I loved about her.

After a couple of years of living together in London we moved to Melbourne. She loved the city and fitted right into some sports and footy clubs here. But she found it hard to get work for her niche in sports community development. So she went back to the UK for work and our relationship became long-distance.

Nearly a year later, in 2009, she found out she had breast cancer. She was only 32. Within a fortnight, I gave up my job and moved to the UK to be with her. She absolutely knew I would upend my life to support her at a time it really mattered.

She did recover well initially. A couple of years later we made it back to Australia and this time we both found work that suited us. We also took many great trips – camping in the Northern Territory and Western Australia, cycling trips all over including from Cairns to Cape York.

But a couple of years later she was diagnosed again, and a bit later the cancer metastasised. At the tail-end of 2019 her doctor advised her that she may only have six months to live. It was time for her to head home to the UK and I went with her. It coincided with Covid lockdowns, so we got to spend a tremendous amount of time together in a small town near her family.

Georgie seemed to be improving but then she started to get breathless and her specialists couldn’t work out why. She was in hospital for scans when she had a brain haemorrhage and lapsed into unconsciousness. Two days later, in July 2020, after some intensely moving times in ICU with her family, she died.

I feel so much gratitude for the time we spent together. Just three days before the brain haemorrhage she had cycled to see her GP – so fitting, being active was so important to her. It was her irrepressible energy I loved, and I am a better person for having known her.

‘I feel like I’m cancelling out her life’: the wrenching work of clearing out a parent’s home

The Guardian Sat, 19 Sep 2026 20:00:56 GMT

From old love letters to pieces of string, our homes are stuffed with stuff. When it comes time to empty a parent’s home, sorting the junk from the memory can be overwhelming

Soon after her marriage in 1952, Ellen Rogers’ mother, Fay, bought a coordinated bedroom ensemble – a floral dressing gown and matching bedspread. The day I talk on the phone with Rogers, she has made a tough decision – she is putting the gown and bedspread in a garbage bag to be sent off to a charity shop. “I feel so bad,” she says.

Fay died in May aged 97, and had lived in the same terrace house in Camperdown in inner Sydney her whole life. Rogers grew up in the house and returned three years ago to be a live-in carer for her mother. Now she’s cleaning out the house so it can be sold. The decisions she must make are endless; which pile for what item – family, rubbish or charity? “It’s overwhelming – there’s so much,” Rogers says, “including every bloody card she ever received.”

Through winter, Rogers moved through the house alone, trying to focus on the task but not always succeeding. Her three brothers are elsewhere. “It’s quite lonely and I hate this house because it’s so cold. I just wish I could speed up the process but I can’t. Some days I’m right on to it, and then other days I just can’t, because it’s very emotional – and I’m not really an emotional person.”

I’ve been in a similar situation. I know the emotion and loneliness of emptying a family home. After my father died in 2010, my mother moved to a smaller place on the Queensland coast. The large family home in Toowoomba where I grew up remained – overflowing with my parents’ household items, their collections (beer steins, fabric, books, Royal Doulton figurines), as well as every last item from my grandparents’ home which arrived in a large removal truck when they came to live with us.

It took me 12 years to empty what came to feel like an emotional halfway house; I flew up from Sydney for a fortnight or more a couple of times a year. My mother was with me, but absent too, lost in memories and completely incapable of making decisions about anything. We argued over everything. We argued over a piece of string. “That’s a perfectly good piece of string,” she said one day of a fragment maybe 10cm long.

I moved through the silent house feeling the ghosts of the family’s past, the grief-filled shadows, the immense weight of possessions, of stuff.

But Rogers and I are not alone in the challenges we’ve faced. The global population is ageing and members of the so-called “Silent Generation” – those born before 1945 – are now in their 80s and 90s and either moving into care or dying. (Deaths in Australia have risen by 20% over the past decade.) This is the generation that came of age during the increasingly affluent decades after the second world war. They bought stuff – lots of stuff. And now, emptying out their homes is becoming a rite of passage alongside weddings, anniversaries and funerals. (Are Australia’s charity shops ready?)

The four women I spoke to for this story (research suggests women are more likely than men to manage estate admin alone) use similar words to describe the grief-edged process: “wrenching”, “gruelling”, “overwhelming”. For others, especially in families riven with tensions and fractures, it can be explosive.

“Get a skip [bin], clean it out while your mother’s not there,” a close family member who made no contribution to the clean-up told me. (I was enraged.) “Throw it in a skip,” people told Anne (she asked that only her first name be used) as she and her siblings started to clean out her mother’s home in Sydney’s southern suburbs in July.

Anne’s feelings about the presence of a skip on a footpath are similar to mine. “The earth’s too fragile” to just toss things into landfill, she says. Among my many recycling triumphs, I found a charity to take a pile of old spectacles that emerged during my cleaning; Anne has organised for more than a hundred of her mother’s X-rays to be recycled for their silver and PET plastic content. “I would do that for every single item in the house if I could.” But she has had to compromise with her sisters and allow some things to be discarded. “The stress for me is looking over my shoulder all the time and monitoring what’s happening; my sisters are wonderful but they have a different approach.”

Kathy, a former Sydney public servant who asked that I not use her real name, inherited her late mother’s house after she died in 2024 and has been living in it while trying to clear it out. She has also found herself unable to simply toss things away. “The problem with getting rid of Mum’s stuff is I look at it and think, ‘I can’t just throw it into a skip’ … It’s like, someone will want this.”

She thought she’d found a home for her mother’s extensive collection of vases when a friend said her Japanese floral arranging group was looking for big vases for a demonstration. “Have I got big vases for you!” Kathy told her. She pulled them out of a cupboard. Her friend looked at them. “Oh no, none of them are suitable,” she said.

The women I interviewed have all had another concern: paying respect to possessions that carried layers of meaning for their parents. A house full of things is not a house but a memory machine; things are not things but layers of recollection of self.

Melbourne woman Adrienne lost her mother in 2022 (she asked that I only use her first name). But even before her death, she had already started to tackle her mother’s house. “I completed a ‘Swedish death clean’ at my mum’s house over three stifling January days,” Adrienne wrote in an email to me. Her motives were pure – to make things easier for her mother, who was expecting visitors to stay – but she regrets now her vigour.

“She watched me, sat forlorn at her kitchen table, while I ruthlessly moved things on. I did not empathise with how much meaning might be attached to stuff I was basically calling worthless. I see now that objects can store all sorts of nostalgia including several versions of self – old interests and enthusiasms, even unrealised aspirations. I store the picture of her sitting at the kitchen table and can see her grief during the process. I wonder if she was also reflecting on her eventual end as well?”

My mother also bore witness to the moving on of things invested with meaning. Like Adrienne, I was ruthlessly efficient through the process, driven by a wild rage at the staggering physical and emotional scale of the job left to me, the absence of my sibling, and my mother’s shifts between pigheadedness and shilly-shallying. But an image of Mum sitting at her kitchen table, looking lost, remains with me too. As is something she said as we went through a pile of Dad’s old clothes: she remembered, she said, the feeling of his dinner-suit jacket brushing her arm as they walked down the aisle on their wedding day.

But a parent present in spirit only can still exert a powerful psychic influence. Anne, as the oldest child, felt responsible for ensuring that her mother’s possessions received “due acknowledgment” as stitches in the fabric of her life. As Rogers builds piles in her late mother’s Camperdown home, she is flushed with guilt. “Well, I said to my brothers when I was getting cranky the other day in a group [chat] … I feel like I’m cancelling out her life.”

The women’s stories reveal something else: the exercise of emptying out a family home has come to reveal a deep generational gap in attitudes towards stuff. What’s frequently described as “brown furniture”, for example, holds no appeal for members of the Ikea generation. But frugal memories and habits, and a sometimes almost reverential respect for material possessions, were embedded in the Silent Generation’s psyche. Frequently, a shiny new item signified status, a step forwards and upwards.

My mother, born in 1936, reminds me frequently how little she had growing up. I heard the old lessons as we waged a battle over kitchen cupboards and linen closets. “When sheets wore out, we’d cut the sheet down the middle and sew the outer edges together to give it new life,” Mum told me more than once. Soap, she said, was removed from its wrapping paper so it hardened and lasted longer.

Kathy has also found that her mother’s lessons are sticky. “There are still things in the kitchen that she used before she was married in 1967, and the good wedding china does not have a broken or chipped plate amongst it; everything she had is in good condition because we didn’t grow up with much money.”

She thought clearing out her mother’s things so she and her partner could make the house their own would be straightforward. “It just isn’t.”

Kathy found that dealing with her late father’s hoardings – old speciality books related to his profession and “a garage full of things to fix stuff or build stuff” – was simple. But in the kitchen, she came to a screeching halt over casserole dishes.

“I unpacked them on to the bench, and I just thought, ‘right, which of these will I keep?’ And then I just looked at them and thought, ‘I can’t,’ … it was just like a whole shutter came down in my head,” she says.

“They’re so tied up with memory; I thought, ‘I know what she used to put in each one, I know the difference between the one she made lemon delicious in and the one she made chocolate pudding in, the one that was always out at Christmas with the tomato casserole.”

For Rogers, the emotional trigger was discovering cards her father had written to her mother. “He passed away when I was six. I’d never seen his handwriting. That gave me a little cry.”

The clean-up has made Anne realise that she places little store by possessions. “I’m not really interested in the jewellery or anything expensive, I just want the mementoes,” she says.

“In Mum’s knitting bag, for example, I found a bunch of letters that Dad sent to Mum and vice versa, when they were courting. I don’t particularly [want to] read them but I fished those out – they’re important and special.” She has kept one of her mother’s childhood books in which she found an inscription: “my favourite book – do not throw out”.

I still have nightmares about the process of clearing out my family’s Toowoomba home, fever dreams in which endless stuff – books, bags, china, chairs, figurines, forks, photographs, paintings – hurtles towards me. But what madness is this – at the end of it, I took ownership of hundreds of items from the house – my great-grandmother’s sideboard, hundreds of my father’s books, my great-aunt’s dinner service, my grandmother’s old mixing bowl, my mother’s 1950s cocktail shaker … and on, and on …

My apartment has become a museum of family stuff and stories. Once, I couldn’t bear to let the stuff go; now I feel suffocated by it. I look around and feel panicky. My nieces and nephew are unlikely to be interested in anything I’ve kept or the stories attached to them.

I think of Rogers: one of her nephews wanted her mother’s Charles and Diana tea caddy and a couple of her grandkids took some figurines, but her brothers seem not to want anything. I think of Kathy, who says her brother and niece only took away a box or two.

And I think of an elderly relative who never married, did not have children. After he died, family members went to clean out his home. There was almost nothing left. The man had released them from the burden.

Suzi Quatro: ‘It is absolutely crazy I’m not in the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame. But I’m in good company!’

The Guardian Sat, 19 Sep 2026 20:00:56 GMT

The 76-year-old rocker on her pre-gig routine, the one reality show she’d go on and who she’d cast as herself in a film about her life

Your new album is called Freedom and the title track interpolates The Girl Can’t Help It. You’re going to be rocking until they take you out in a box, aren’t you?

When I was 35, a journalist stupidly asked me, “When are you going to retire?” I said, “I will retire when I go on stage, turn my back on the audience, shake my ass, and there’s silence.” This followed me my whole career, so when I got to 65, I said, “I will retire when I go on stage, turn my back on the audience and my ass shakes by itself.”

I’m 76 now but at 75 I gave my final quote on this subject, and it was serious – I will retire when I go on stage and do not deliver to my standard. When I feel that, I’m done.

There’s also a cover of MC5’s Kick Out the Jams, with Alice Cooper. Tell me a bit about Detroit in the 60s, where you had Motown on one hand and yourself, Alice, Iggy and MC5 on the other? What a time to be alive!

What a city! We had Motown, which we all bowed down to, we were weaned on it. But all the white rock’n’roll groups, they all had that danger, that edge, that foot-on-the-gas desperation. I’ve talked about it with Brother Wayne Kramer, who passed not long ago, and Alice, and we don’t know why that is, but we can never get rid of that. It was a special time.

What’s the most chaotic thing that’s happened to you on stage?

We were doing a show once, going down a storm, and I have a section with the drummer where we’re both playing, because I’m a trained percussionist, so it’s like Gene Krupa and Buddy Rich. Then the PA blew, and all the audience could hear were drums. We looked at each other, and went, right, let’s go!

So, we did a 15-minute drum solo together, because whatever happens on stage, the golden rule is you use it – you have to make it work. Finally, somebody from the side of stage put his thumbs up, and we went back into the song. Everybody thought it was part of the show.

You’re a veteran road hog. What’s the first thing you do when you get to your hotel?

I set up my room. The computers go on the table. My diary gets opened. My stage clothes get hung up on the hooks. My boots get put out. My pyjamas go on the bed. I turn the bed down, then before I leave the room for the gig, I close the curtains and check all the lights to get the correct ambience. That way, when I come in after the show, it feels like home.

How about your most chaotic encounter with a fan?

Most of them are great but this wasn’t nice. A couple of years ago I was coming out to do my final song, and everybody had their hands up for a high-five. So did a little bit of that, and one girl grabbed my hand, held on to it with a death-grip and tried to pull me off the stage. I tried to pull back and my entire jumpsuit ripped, right across my ass.

I finally got free and I walked backwards to my monitor – very professional! – and I sat down and did the rest of the song, not moving. As soon as the song was over, the monitor guy came and put a towel around my waist, and I walked off. I wish I could find that girl because I would love to give her a piece of my mind. I was really upset.

There has already been a documentary about you. If there was a biopic of your life, who would play you?

We’re working on that right now, we’re doing the screenplay as we speak. Scarlett Johansson springs to mind. But whoever plays me, I would have to meet them, because I would need to feel something that you can’t act, and that’s the Suzi Quatro vibe. Don’t ask me to explain it but I would have to feel they have that vibe about them.

If you had to appear on a reality TV show tomorrow, which one would it be?

There’s only one — Strictly Come Dancing.

Before you went solo, you were in a group with your sisters, the Pleasure Seekers, whose best-known song is What a Way to Die. Was that inspired by the Who’s My Generation?

I don’t know who inspired that; it was just about getting drunk and crazy. But what I love about that song is that I was only 15, and my style was set right from the beginning. It wasn’t something I developed through the years. Nobody ever told me how to stand, how to sing, how to play, what to do. I always just did what I felt, and I like that about me.

What’s an album you always return to?

I’ve got a few. Bob Dylan’s Blonde on Blonde. Jackson Browne’s Running on Empty. And Tom Petty’s first album. Those are the three that just popped to mind that I will play nonstop and never get tired of.

Tell me why you’re not in the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame.

It is absolutely crazy. It used to bother me but now I’ve read up on lots of people who aren’t in it, and I’m in good company! I always thought it was a no-brainer, because there was never a woman playing an instrument in a rock’n’roll band with world success before me. I just hope they’re not waiting for me to die so they can do it posthumously.

Suzi Quatro is touring Australia between 14 November and 6 December. Freedom is out now

When friends become good neighbours: the Melbourne families who transformed one home into three townhouses

The Guardian Sat, 19 Sep 2026 20:00:56 GMT

In a novel approach to urban housing, some residents have pooled their time and finances into redeveloping single dwellings. It’s a herculean task – with feel-good results

Melbourne architect Chris Gilbert had run out of eggs. He texted a neighbour and within minutes, he says, their child arrived with some. “Then I made brownies and my kids took some over to the neighbours’ house.”

It sounds like a flashback to a bygone era, but this neighbourly exchange took place this month, at the Davison Collaborative, a novel housing project in the Melbourne suburb of Brunswick. In 2020 the townhouse development replaced one past-its-prime brick veneer house with three architecturally designed three-bedroom family dwellings, trebling the lot’s density and future proofing it “for at least the next 50 years,” says Liam Wallis, from the sustainability focused property development and consultancy company Hip V. Hype.

In 2018, times weren’t so idyllic. Gilbert was bring outbid at auctions week after week. Each Monday he’d arrive despondent at his shared working space with Wallis, and Wallis’ business partner Peter Steele.

Wallis had already been mulling whether pooling resources to redevelop single home lots into multiple dwellings could increase density, while saving families money.

“I said ‘hang on a minute, let’s just do a project. Let’s see if this works. Let’s figure out how hard it is,’” Wallis says.

The collaborative eventually bought a postwar home, owned by the same family for 50 years, at auction. The parents had died and their children were selling. Two years later, the three couples moved in. “And each of those homes were the same size as the original dwelling,” Wallis says.

As Wallis, Gilbert and Steele were moving in, a similar plan was unfolding in another inner-north Melbourne suburb. During lockdowns, a close-knit group of friends and colleagues (with experience in architecture, interior design, project management and a tradie among them) who lived within walking distance of one another in Carlton North, were spitballing ways to parlay their collective professional wisdom (and their finances) into a similar proposition.

Four years later, Sarah Birthisel and her husband, along with couples Sarah Cosentino and Stephen McGarry, and Tanya Smith and Neil Clarke, moved into their tri-townhouse venture, Northcote Townhouses.

Sitting down with Birthisel and Cosentino, the pair are obviously pleased with how things turned out. Knowing such an endeavour wouldn’t be feasible in Carlton North, the group looked to the adjacent municipality of Darebin. Fewer heritage overlays, larger lots and cheaper prices, they explain, made the area far more suitable.

After agreeing on their vision and drafting contracts, the consortium bought a 638 sq metre property that backs on to the Mernda train line in Northcote. Their first order of business was to make their intentions known to other residents on the street. “It was really important to us to connect with our neighbours, to make them aware that this wasn’t going to be something that we would be flipping … That this would be our home, and that resonated really well with the community,” Cosentino says.

Then they went to the council with a strategy that Birthisel says was “very sympathetic to the streetscape and continued the rhythm of the streets”. Development approvals went smoothly and they broke ground in 2022. When it came time to move in, they staggered that process so each couple had some time to settle in.

Cosentino and Birthisel say that while the communal aspects of the arrangement were alluring, each family also wanted a sense of privacy. Two years into their experiment, they feel as if they’ve achieved that.

“I love the security of knowing I’ve got friends at my doorstep. I also equally love that sense of retreat and sanctuary; we could be in the house the whole weekend and feel like we’re not around everyone else at all,” Cosentino says. On the flip side, last summer, they say, was full of plenty of balmy evenings where private gatherings with family and friends spilled into common areas, and impromptu alfresco meals were shared, with their children playing in the communal garden. “Those incidental interactions are so beautiful and bring such a buzz.”

These two projects have been nominated for a slew of awards – the Davison Collaborative was a finalist for the Victorian premier’s design awards, while Northcote Townhouses received a commendation in the Houses awards. While they underline how collectives with the right professional and financial capital can leverage their resources into remarkable housing solutions, they were no small undertaking.

“It’s very difficult for just anyone to do it, unfortunately,” Wallis says. Their project was stalled at planning, and then at the Victorian civil and administrative tribunal (Vcat), for a year. And, like the Northcote venture, the professional experience of the members made all the difference.

In an effort to keep friendships intact, the Davison Collaborative deferred broad spectrum project management to Hip V. Hype because “it’s impossible to run a complex project if you have to go back to someone with every decision, but there are select, important decisions that need collective agreement and so we carved those out [early on],” Wallis says.

For less prepared consortiums, Tim Riley is in the business of filling knowledge gaps. His company Property Collectives has worked on 11 collaborative housing projects around Melbourne and charges a fixed management fee to guide groups of families, friends and occasionally strangers through the process of property development, right through to final fixtures.

He says the kind of people who use his service “aren’t seeing the sort of homes on the market that they would want to live in, at a price point that makes sense to them”.

“There’s an acknowledgment that if we want to create this little co-housing community of 10 or 20 households, we need to do it ourselves.”

While participants often save upwards of $100,000 compared with buying a similar home in a similar area, Riley says these homes are not “capital-A affordable”. But beyond design and financial imperatives, he believes there is something deeper at play.

“I think it is all rooted in a belief that having more meaningful social connections with your neighbours is a really valuable thing to have in life,” Riley says.

“For the young families that are involved, the desire to have a place where their kids are growing up in a supportive community with a range of people in different life stages is really attractive. And similarly for the older generation, they’re not wanting to go to a retirement village, they’re wanting an intergenerational community.”

Riley says his company keeps contracts as standard as possible “so that lenders, builders and the whole ecosystem doesn’t see it as being terribly strange”.

On an interpersonal level, Riley thinks consortiums are most successful when participants share a clear vision. Typically they employ “sociocracy”, which establishes from the outset which decisions need to be unanimous and which require majority approval. Each household has one vote. “And that can reduce a lot of friction through the process.”

The company then walks all participants through a plan of work that has seven decision gates, starting with strategic vision and ending up in operations. He says that “chunking” the herculean task makes the process less daunting. The process from forming the group to moving in takes on average four years.

While no longer a resident of the Brunswick project, Wallis believes every block on Davison Street could easily accommodate similar ventures, turning nine homes into 27.

“We did a bit of an exercise and looked at, within a kilometre radius, how many blocks of land were on laneways in Brunswick with the same attributes as our site. There was something like 500. We could turn 500 family homes into 1,500.

“We don’t need to build 20-level buildings to increase density. We just need to use what we have more effectively.”

Belmont Park is back: inside New York’s $555m bet on horse racing

The Guardian Sat, 19 Sep 2026 19:50:19 GMT

The storied Long Island racetrack, rebuilt with a $455m state loan, is smaller, sleeker and designed for a changing audience. Can it create the public needed to sustain it?

Henry Miller stood on the trackside apron of the new Belmont Park on Friday trying to decide what he thought of the place.

“It has to grow on me,” said Miller, a 59-year-old retired sanitation worker from Brooklyn’s Bedford-Stuyvesant neighborhood who has been coming to New York racetracks for 47 years. “For me, it’s too much concrete. I don’t think it’s as friendly as the old Belmont.”

He missed the familiar trees and the ivy-covered brick facades. He missed the old bar and grandstand. Most of all, he was still mourning Aqueduct, the ramshackle Queens racetrack that shuttered in June as part of the $555m experiment that has made the reimagined Belmont possible.

“That broke my heart,” Miller said.

For the first time in more than three years, horses were racing at Belmont Park on Friday. But almost everything else about the 121-year-old race course just outside New York city limits had changed.

The cavernous grandstand that once loomed over the home straight is gone, replaced by a smaller, glass-fronted building designed for a sport that no longer expects tens of thousands of people to turn up on an ordinary afternoon. The old Belmont had a footprint of roughly 1.25m sq ft; its five-storey replacement is less than a quarter of the size, at about 300,000 sq ft. Even Big Sandy, the famously deep mile-and-a-half dirt track that became synonymous with the grueling final leg of US horse racing’s Triple Crown, has been relegated to the past, recreated with the same soil composition used at Saratoga with the finish line repositioned for a longer stretch run. There are four rebuilt racing surfaces in all, a paddock 50% larger than its predecessor and roughly 20 acres of newly accessible green space.

Inside, the aesthetic is almost aggressively modern: bright white walls, gleaming floors and long, clean expanses that feel more THX 1138 than old-school racetrack. As one Fox Sports production assistant could be overheard describing it: “It looks kind of like an airport, but it’s beautiful.”

It is a dramatic break with the Belmont that has stood on this corner of suburban Long Island in some form since 1905, a piece of New York cultural furniture along the Queens-Nassau County line whose hulking structure and sweeping turns were recognizable even to people who never studied a racing form. Secretariat surged into history by 31 lengths here, generations before American Pharoah ended a 37-year Triple Crown hoodoo. The track appeared on screen everywhere from multiple Woody Allen films to a Frederick Wiseman documentary to Godfrey Reggio’s Koyaanisqatsi.

What opened on Friday was not simply a renovated sports venue, but New York’s half-billion dollar wager that horse racing can shrink its physical footprint, upgrade the experience and find enough new customers to survive a gambling landscape that has largely moved beyond it.

The $455m state loan that financed the reconstruction was accompanied by another $100m from the New York Racing Association, the nonprofit that operates Belmont, Saratoga and, until recently, Aqueduct. The state money is to be repaid from NYRA’s cut of slot-machine revenue from the Resorts World casino, which sits alongside the now-closed Aqueduct property, only nine miles from Belmont.

At a ribbon-cutting on Friday morning, New York governor Kathy Hochul called the loan a calculated investment in the future of the industry.

“Three and a half years ago, we made a big bet on Belmont,” Hochul said. “We made the bet because we saw the enormous economic potential.”

She described the goal as an “international racing hub” that could double as a concert and entertainment space – “a versatile venue” intended not only for racing fans but “the entire community”.

The bargain came with significant consequences. NYRA consolidated its downstate operation at Belmont, bringing an end to 132 years of racing at Aqueduct and leaving New York City without a thoroughbred racetrack for the first time since the 1821 opening of Union Course in what is now Woodhaven, Queens. The roughly 100-acre Aqueduct site is being returned to the state for redevelopment, with Hochul’s administration planning for a mixed-use redevelopment of housing, retail, community facilities and open space.

Belmont itself has been reconceived around a blunt reality. The old structure, which re-opened in 1968 after a five-year rebuild, was engineered for crowds of a scale that rarely materialized outside the biggest racing days – like the 120,139 who turned out for Smarty Jones’ doomed Triple Crown bid in 2004. Its replacement will hold roughly 10,000 people inside, while access to the infield and temporary seating will allow the property to accommodate around 50,000 for the Belmont Stakes.

The new facility will stage a 46-day fall meet featuring 72 stakes worth $17.7m, before the Belmont Stakes returns next year and the Breeders’ Cup comes back to New York for the first time since 2005.

Fittingly for a venue being pitched as an international racing destination, the first winner at the new Belmont on Friday afternoon was a UK product. Lisa Joy, a British homebred owned by Andrew Rosen, won the opening mile-and-a-quarter maiden on the inner turf for Hall of Fame trainer Shug McGaughey and jockey Antonio Fresu.

McGaughey, a stalwart of New York racing who denied Sunday Silence the Triple Crown when Easy Goer won the Belmont in 1989, was enthusiastic about the rebuilt track even as he acknowledged the place was still finding its feet.

“I think it’s a beautiful place,” he said. “It’s different than what I expected. We just need to get the kinks out and get the people in it and it’ll be really special. I think it’s going to be great when everything gets settled in.”

For longtime patrons, getting used to the new Belmont may take a little longer.

Kathie Riccobono, a 74-year-old from nearby Garden City who has been coming to Belmont for half a century, was impressed by what she saw but immediately identified what she missed about the old place.

“The crowds,” she said.

“It’s a big change,” Riccobono said. “Change is good, but you’re not going to have the old Belmont like we used to. The old people, there’s not many of us left. And the new group don’t know nothing about horses.”

Attendance was capped at 6,000 during opening weekend and will drop to 4,000 beginning next week while construction continues. Right now only the first two floors are open, while the remaining three are expected to be finished early next year.

The transformation is perhaps most obvious in the way spectators are distributed. General-admission customers occupy the first floor, apron and backyard, with bars and food concessions including Big Red’s, Silks, Homestretch Market and the Trackside Lounge accessible without reservations or cover charges. One floor up, the Turf Club, Overlook and Stretch View require reservations. Above them, still under construction, will be the suites and boxes.

The prices rise accordingly. A box seat runs between $55 and $75, while the Overlook and Stretch View can cost $100 to $150 more per person and the Turf Club charges $75 per person, climbing to $150 for its premium menu.

General admission, at least, remains cheap. After opening weekend, tickets will cost $7 in advance or $10 at the gate, the same price NYRA charges at Saratoga. Yet some regulars say the cost of admission tells only part of the story.

Miller was among them. Parking, he noted, costs $20. Factor in other costs like admission and a program and the economics begin to look different.

“You’re spending $35 or $45 before you even make a wager. It’s not going to get people in the doors when you have the other option to stay home and gamble or bet on the app,” Miller said. “That $45 is going on a parlay.”

The same tension can be found in the new backyard. NYRA has promoted a space roughly five times larger than its predecessor as a communal gathering place, but coolers and outside beverages are prohibited, eliminating a longstanding way for families and groups to keep the cost of a day at the races down.

For anyone who spent time at Aqueduct, the distinction is significant. Miller called it “the poor man’s track”.

“I don’t know if there’s another racetrack that you could take public transportation to, directly to the track,” he said. “Everybody knows everyone. The jockeys are even closer with the guys. It’s more interaction.”

Belmont, he said, had always been “more prestige or boutique”. And he had noticed the same trends surfacing elsewhere.

“I was down at Gulfstream, I was at Churchill [Downs]. They’re all gearing towards this boutique kind of thing,” Miller said. “The average horseplayer, the nickel-and-dime guy who keeps the industry going is going to get squeezed out.”

Aqueduct was nobody’s idea of luxury. By its final years it was dim, dilapidated and increasingly swallowed by the casino next door. But entrance was free, the A train stopped outside and patrons could bring their own food. Regulars carved out territories around particular tables, simulcast monitors and betting windows.

That accessibility helped make Aqueduct an increasingly rare thing in American sport: a third place where anyone could walk in off the street and stay the whole day without spending very much. Its democratic crowd reflected the borough that surrounded it: a racially and economically mixed collection of horseplayers, families, retirees and obsessive handicappers. Belmont remains accessible by public transport, with the Long Island Rail Road stopping at the neighboring Elmont-UBS Arena station. But Aqueduct’s location directly on a major subway line gave it a different relationship with the city.

On Aqueduct’s final day in June, 6,866 people came for what felt alternately like a celebration and a wake. Many posed for photographs in front of the Secretariat mural or pocketed small keepsakes. Others wondered aloud whether they would make the trip east to Belmont at all.

“Probably not,” one retired horseman turned Aqueduct regular, Robert Bourget, said that afternoon when asked whether he would go. “They’ll charge too much to get in.”

Not everyone on Friday regarded the transformation with suspicion. Joseph Gillespie, a 60-year-old retiree from Levittown who was at the track with his wife, Eileen, has been coming to Belmont for 35 years and said he expects to visit even more often now that he is retired. He called the new building “very nice” and was unbothered by what he had seen of the prices: even a $12 beer, he reckoned, “is not so bad these days”.

Gillespie also understood immediately what NYRA appeared to be aiming for.

“I think they’re trying to make this like a Keeneland destination type of thing,” he said. “People get fancied up. Hopefully you don’t get the riff-raff. Not that there’s anything wrong with that. Hopefully it thrives.”

The question extends well beyond New York. More than 40 American racetracks have closed since 2000 as the sport has contended with an aging fanbase, declining attendance and a gambling marketplace that bears little resemblance to the one that made horse racing a mass spectator sport.

Another signpost of the contraction arrived this year when FanDuel TV, the former TVG and for more than two decades a central hub of American racing coverage, announced plans to wind down its television operation. The network, which reaches about 30m households, is cutting its workforce by roughly 60% and plans to eliminate studio production by the end of the year before ceasing linear racing broadcasts altogether in 2027. FanDuel’s wagering platforms, meanwhile, will continue operating.

For much of the 20th century, the racetrack possessed an enormous house edge: in many places it was one of the only legal ways to gamble. That monopoly began disappearing with the spread of lotteries, casinos and off-track betting and has been obliterated in the mobile sports-betting era. Americans wagered nearly $167bn on sports in 2025, compared with roughly $11bn on US horse racing.

The irony is that Belmont’s rebirth comes as horse racing itself loses ground, but that may be precisely the point. Across American sports, venues have increasingly become anchors for year-round economies of restaurants, shops, hotels and entertainment rather than self-contained destinations. Belmont now has its own version: a $455m racetrack only footsteps from an expanding luxury shopping village and UBS Arena, the 17,255-seat home of the NHL’s New York Islanders.

Miller didn’t need the statistics to understand racing’s demographic problem.

“I’m 59 now, so like my cousins say, ‘I’m in the departure lounge now. I’m not in arrivals,’” he said. “So you got to get the younger people to get more involved.”

He could remember when Aqueduct on an otherwise unremarkable Wednesday or Thursday might attract 15,000 or 20,000 people. The Meadowlands on a Friday or Saturday night could be the place to be even for people who had little interest in gambling. That, he believed, was the challenge facing the new Belmont in an age when the casino is already sitting in everyone’s pocket.

“You got to give a person a reason to come,” he said.

Some of the arrivals Miller was talking about were plainly visible on Friday for a re-opening that was intended as a showcase. On a sun-splashed 83F (28C) afternoon beneath a cloudless sky, a sold-out crowd of about 6,000 filled the partially completed grounds, country singer Dierks Bentley performed an abbreviated set and the nine-race card was built around the $1m Jockey Club Gold Cup and one of world’s most famous equine athletes today.

Forever Young arrived at Belmont as a bonafide globetrotting star. Friday marked the five-year-old Japanese horse’s 16th career start at his 10th different track. The strapping bay stallion had won 11 of his first 15 races, including the 2025 Breeders’ Cup Classic, never finishing outside the top three.

This article includes content provided by Instagram. We ask for your permission before anything is loaded, as they may be using cookies and other technologies. To view this content, click 'Allow and continue'.

His following had traveled too. Hordes of younger fans crowded the paddock and apron for a glimpse of him, including many groups dressed in elaborate anime-inspired cosplay – a strikingly different image of the racing enthusiast from the aging horseplayers the sport has spent years of hand-wringing about losing. They were not the traditional railbirds Miller remembered from Aqueduct, but neither were they indifferent newcomers being coaxed into caring about the sport with trackside concerts and food vouchers.

Forever Young duly supplied the reborn Belmont with its first marquee moment, sitting comfortably behind the early pace before sweeping to the lead around the far turn, winning by three and a quarter lengths and pushing his career earnings beyond $32m. Even that was apparently not enough to satisfy his famously demanding trainer. Yoshito Yahagi pronounced himself only “50% satisfied”, estimating Forever Young at about 80% fitness before his attempt next month to become only the second horse after Tiznow to win back-to-back Breeders’ Cup Classics.

“I think I will never see again a horse like this in my life and my career,” Yahagi said through a translator.

The mania around Forever Young offered one glimpse of the audience NYRA hopes to cultivate, but attracting a new generation of fans is only one part of its attempt to remake Belmont for a changing sport. The physical plant itself has been designed around year-round use. Alongside the traditional mile-and-a-half dirt track and two rebuilt turf courses is a new one-mile Tapeta oval that will become the exclusive racing surface during the winter, allowing NYRA to consolidate a calendar once divided between Belmont and Aqueduct onto a single property.

Even the Belmont Stakes itself may not return unchanged. NYRA is considering shortening its signature race from its traditional mile-and-a-half distance to a mile and a quarter, with NYRA CEO Dave O’Rourke arguing that the historic distance no longer reflects what modern breeders are producing.

Taken together, the changes make Belmont an unusually literal experiment in the future of American horse racing. The old model was a gigantic betting hall that happened to surround a racetrack. The new one is smaller, brighter and more flexible: part racetrack, part entertainment complex, with the biggest crowds concentrated into a handful of destination events and premium spaces available for customers willing to pay for them.

There were signs Friday that the experiment might work. Riccobono, for all her nostalgia for the old Belmont, was struck by the mood around her.

“Everybody is cheerful,” she said. “And that’s how it always is at Belmont.”

After 50 years of coming here, she was less interested in delivering a verdict than appreciating the fact that she had made it to another incarnation of the place.

“I feel lucky to be alive,” she said. “I feel lucky I’m here.”

For one afternoon, at least, the formula clicked. Six thousand people filled the grounds. Families spread across the new backyard, old horseplayers filled the tables and benches at trackside and toiled over their forms (or tablets), while younger fans celebrated the Japanese stallion who had made his name around the world. Whether the same energy can be reproduced on an ordinary Thursday in November – without a $32m global superstar, a concert or the novelty of seeing the place for the first time – will be the more consequential test.

Dutch riot police dispersed several hundred far-right protesters in The Hague on Saturday after violence erupted and local authorities banned a planned march in the city against immigration and asylum policies.

Justice minister David van Weel called on X for an “extremely firm” response to what he described as “disgusting scenes” at the protest, organised by the far-right We Are the People organisation.

He said demonstrators made Nazi salutes, chanted antisemitic slogans, and attacked and threw fireworks at police.

“Thanks to all the police officers who are once again standing up for our democratic rule of law,” he wrote.

The Hague municipality banned the march after violence broke out among demonstrators gathered at the Malieveld, a park in the city centre, and later ordered the crowd to disperse.

Those arrested were detained for various offences, including failing to comply with the order and illegally possessing weapons.

Police reportedly used pepper spray and a water cannon on the rioters.

Saturday’s unrest came a year after rioting erupted during a rightwing demonstration in The Hague.

A police car was set on fire during the clashes between black-clad protesters and police. The headquarters of the centrist D66 party – whose leader, Rob Jetten, is now prime minister – was also attacked.

Jetten said on X that the demonstrators deliberately sought confrontation with the police and chanted “abhorrent” far-right and antisemitic slogans.
