The Guardian Sat, 19 Sep 2026 19:01:51 GMT

Queen speaks of love of reading at festival for charity she founded after success of her Instagram book club

Queen Camilla has spoken of her love for books with a “life-enhancing power” after a series of allegations were made about King Charles in extracts from Earl Spencer’s memoir about the life of Diana, Princess of Wales.

Camilla was welcomed to Chatsworth House in Derbyshire for the first day of the festival for the Queen’s Reading Room, a charity she founded after the success of her Instagram book club during the pandemic.

She told the guests: “I created my Reading Room simply because, like all of us here, I love books and their life-enhancing power and I want to share that love with others.

“In those early days, I had no idea if anybody would be interested but six years on, we are a global community of millions from over 180 countries, swapping recommendations, undertaking research and donating thousands of books to women’s refuges and homeless shelters.”

Camilla’s speech about her love for reading comes after Spencer made a series of damning claims about the king in a new memoir chronicling the life of his sister, Diana, that prompted an “unprecedented” response from Buckingham Palace, which said: “The pain of fraternal grief can cloud reason”.

Camilla will also feature in the BBC Arts programme The Book That Changed My Life, which is due to air next month as part of the National Year of Reading 2026.

The BBC has said the documentary film will follow Camilla as she meets four remarkable people whose lives have been changed by books at moments when they most needed them. The latest details of the show were revealed on Saturday at the Reading Room festival.

During the event, she spoke to Ian Kirby, one of the contributors to the documentary, asking him about his experience of finding community and hope through reading.

Kirby, from Gateshead, fell into depression after a traumatic incident at home, but discovered a new perspective on his own experiences after joining a local book club and reading the autobiography of local boxing champion Glenn McCrory.

Speaking in the documentary, he says: “That is the beauty of a book. It can give you experiences you’ve never experienced, but they can also be an inspiration.”

The BBC has previously said the documentary would “feature individuals from a wide range of backgrounds who all share one thing – moving stories of resilience and renewal, fostered by reading”.

“From finding solace in a book while in prison, to overcoming deep depression through the connection of a local book club, or finding the inspiration to completely change their life, these stories reveal how books offer salvation, hope, joy, deep connection and fresh perspectives when people need them most,” it added.

It said the film would also explore the growing scientific evidence of how reading can improve health and wellbeing.

The documentary was first announced by Camilla during a Clarence House reception celebrating the fifth anniversary of her Queen’s Reading Room book club in March.

In a speech, Camilla described how her literary project was launched to share her “lifelong conviction that books make life better”.

At the festival, alongside the journalist Reeta Chakrabarti and broadcaster Gyles Brandreth, Camilla revealed her four book recommendations for autumn – Finding Belle by Chakrabarti, The Picture of Dorian Gray by Oscar Wilde, Whistler by Ann Patchett and Sashenka by Simon Sebag Montefiore.

In the Sculpture Gallery, Camilla also attended a reception with literary figures taking part in the festival, including Lee Child, who wrote the Jack Reacher novel series, and Turkish-British novelist Elif Shafak.

The Book That Changed My Life is expected to air on BBC Two on 14 October.

Arsenal were mightily relieved as a 95th-minute Smilla Holmberg volley rescued a point at home to a much-improved Manchester United side, but the draw will not be enough to eradicate concerns about how far behind the leaders Manchester City Renée Slegers’ team are slipping already and how frequently they seem to struggle to break down a low block.

A defiant Manchester United stunned the north Londoners as Eva Olid’s side claimed the first point of her tenure with a performance that defied all of the pre-match scripts, but it was very nearly a victory, had it not been for Holmberg’s last-gasp back-post finish from Leah Williamson’s deep, diagonal ball into the box, which finally broke the visitors’ stubborn resistance.

Widely criticised for their dismal displays in their opening two defeats against London City Lionesses and Chelsea, Manchester United were heavily tipped to struggle again at the Emirates but an encouraging defensive effort and an against-the-run-of-play Julia Zigiotti Olme strike gave them a precious lead in a display that will buy the former Hearts manager Olid plenty of time to continue working on her style on the training ground and quieten those doubting her.

Instead it will be Arsenal now facing scrutiny as they failed to win at home for a second straight game and slipped four points behind the defending champions, Manchester City, after just three rounds of fixtures. Last term, Manchester City dropped points in only four games and the early-season leaders have a 100% record so far. Arsenal’s next two WSL games are away to Chelsea and Manchester City.

“It’s not ideal, it’s not what we wanted at all, four lost points,” Slegers admitted, reflected on consecutive home draws, but she added: “It’s round three in the WSL, there are a lot of games left to play. Let’s see in May, how it ends. Not converting dominance into wins, that’s something we have to look at. We believe in the quality of the squad. When that starts clicking, it’s going to be really good.”

In truth, this was a result that Arsenal could ill-afford, especially after last weekend’s goalless draw at home to the newly promoted side Crystal Palace, where the north Londoners were surprisingly wasteful in the final third. Slegers’ team had scored just one goal from 43 shots across their opening two league fixtures. Surely, therefore, a home match against a side who conceded five goals last time out was the perfect opportunity to banish any concerns of a lack of clinical quality in the final third? Think again.

The hosts did create good openings and looked to have control of the midfield. Their winger Lisa Baum shot straight at Phallon Tullis-Joyce early on and was providing dangerous crosses from the left. Mariona Caldentey also went close, curling just wide and Tullis-Joyce made a fine save to keep out Stina Blackstenius’ header. Nevertheless, it had been United’s Elisabeth Terland who went closest in the first half, being thwarted by two excellent Misa Rodríguez saves in quick succession.

Arsenal stepped up the pressure after half-time but Georgia Stanway – one of Arsenal’s better performers for the rest of the game – made a costly error as she tried to play a simple pass back towards the centre-back Steph Catley that carelessly rolled the ball into the path of Zigiotti Olme instead. The grateful Manchester United midfielder confidently stepped the ball around Catley and slotted through the legs of Rodríguez. The Emirates was astonished. The United bench, jubilant.

No, but seriously. Maybe Frank Lampard and Coventry can achieve Premier League survival. The club’s first top-division win since April 2001 was celebrated rapturously, victory an object lesson in unsettling opponents for whom confidence can waver. Jay Dasilva’s excellent goal was built on the foundations laid by a battling defensive performance that must be replicated on a weekly basis. Coventry, dogged throughout, blunted Nottingham Forest’s creativity, though could thank a late video assistant referee call that enraged the City Ground crowd.

Lampard declared, with his broadest grin: “I feel great, I feel amazing.” Next, as is his way, back to serious business. “The reality in football is you have to fight for it, you have to work for it, you have to have organisation.”

Coventry’s troubled start to the season had revived doubts in his capabilities as a Premier League manager and far too many echoes of a quarter century in the wilderness. Whatever happens, their fans, under the weakening, early-evening sun, were determined to enjoy themselves. Even if it’s for a single season, why not make the most of things? “Something we have to build on and not get too carried away,” said Bobby Thomas, having personified that rearguard effort.

“We are a team with a lot of players having their first stint in Premier League football,” said Lampard. “Not everyone is a Wayne Rooney or a superstar that can just own it.”

Forest’s home league record in 2026 continues to be wretched: only Burnley, in April, have left in defeat. He remains ignored by Thomas Tuchel despite verifiable claims of being the most in-form English No 10 around, only Pascal Gross creating more chances in the Premier League this season, though like his team as a whole, Gibbs-White is doing his best work away from West Bridgford. Forest hit 26 shots on Coventry’s goal, just three on target.

“We struggled with scoring,” was Oliver Glasner’s simple diagnosis. “Today was the first time I could feel the heaviness of the past, it was very quiet in the dressing room. When we conceded the goal, everyone was nervous, the entire ground was nervous and I think the reason is last year.”

An early deft header to Liam Delap and a cogent flick to James McAtee had suggested Gibbs-White was in the mood but Forest never found the momentum to crack Coventry’s defensive shield. McAtee’s talents have never quite found their position but playing deeper as Gibbs-White’s creative partner has suited him. However, the duo were far less in tune than the previous week. Delap has shown signs of being the player glimpsed at Ipswich but was another lost in heavy traffic, Forest reduced to potshots such as his snapshot wide.

• Coventry earned their first Premier League victory of the season – it’s their 100th win in the competition overall, and first since April 2001 (1-0 v Sunderland).

• Jay Dasilva scored Coventry’s first Premier League goal of the season. Assisted by Carl Rushworth, it’s just the second time a team’s first goal in a campaign has been assisted by a goalkeeper, after Peter Schmeichel for Manchester United in 1992-93.

• Nottingham Forest have failed to score in their first three home games in a league campaign for the first time in their history. Opta

Coventry’s kick-off for the second half saw their players line up in a formation resembling that for a rugby union dropout. It achieved little but previewed the long-ball tactics that brought about the breaking of their 25-year duck.

Loum Tchaouna, a half-time arrival, cutting inside to shoot, if too weakly to beat Matz Sels, might have served as a further warning to Forest, as within moments, Dasilva, showing admirable strength for someone of such diminutive dimensions and a beautiful first touch to beat Daniel Muñoz, blazed to a diagonal ball from his goalkeeper, Carl Rushworth. The finish was just as adept, the celebrations deafening. Coventry’s previous Premier League scorer had been Mustapha Hadji in a losing effort at Aston Villa that confirmed relegation.

Caribbean nations draft action plan to push UK to redress reparations over slavery

The Guardian Sat, 19 Sep 2026 17:00:14 GMT

Caribbean nations are drawing up a multi-pronged “action plan” with legal options to push the UK into negotiating a decades-long slavery reparations deal, officials at a reparations conference have said.

Leaders in the region are hoping the UK would agree to targeted and constructive negotiation talks at upcoming Commonwealth and UN summits, but they are ready to take the matter to international courts if Britain continues to resist diplomatic options.

Earlier this month, a spokesperson for Andy Burnham reiterated the British government’s long‑held position that “the UK does not and will not pay reparations”.

Ralph Gonsalves, the former prime minister of St Vincent and the Grenadines, said the Caricom Regional Conference on Reparations, which took place this week, hosted by Barbados with the Caricom Reparations Commission (CRC), was key for agreeing a unified strategy to bring Britain to the negotiating table. Gonsalves is now an elder and adviser for the Repair Campaign, a social movement for reparatory justice.

He said that slavery happened over centuries and reparations had to be realistic and set over decades. “We need a concrete, multigenerational plan,” he said.

On the legal options available to the Caribbean, Gonsalves challenged arguments that Britain did not violate historical laws during transatlantic slavery, adding that the UK’s signature on contemporary UN conventions had established a binding legal obligation for reparative justice.

“The fact is that the consequences of slavery fall squarely under the Committee on the Elimination of Racial Discrimination, which obliges states to help address the consequences of native genocide and slavery,” Gonsalves said.

In March this year, 123 nations voted for a landmark UN resolution that described chattel slavery as the gravest crime against humanity. The UK was one of several European countries that abstained from voting in the resolution. But, last month, a UN committee on the elimination of racial discrimination said countries were legally obliged to consider reparations for the transatlantic slave trade and take other ⁠measures to address the enduring ⁠legacy of racial ​discrimination.

David Comissiong, the deputy chair of the Barbados National Task Force on Reparations, said the Caribbean nations were considering “several legal strategies”.

“You’ve had Jamaica trying to engage with the national legal judicial system of the UK, the privy council – that is one strategy,” he said, adding that going to the international court of justice for an advisory opinion was another option.

Prof Sir Hilary Beckles, the chair of the CRC, said reparations was a matter of justice, adding that countries in the region were forced to create viable democracies “out of the mess” of colonialism, which was still having an impact today.

“When Jamaica took its petition to the UK, we had to surround that petition with the fact that when Jamaica became independent in 1962, 80% of the black people in Jamaica could not read or write. After 300 years of British colonisation, they moved into independence with 80% illiteracy. How do you build a modern nation, not even a competitive economy, with 80% illiteracy?”

Speaking at the conference, Mia Mottley, the prime minister of Barbados, said the Caribbean had “no desire to bankrupt anybody”.

“But we have a desire for justice,” she said.

Earlier this year, Barbados commissioned a report which showed that Britain stole 25 million years of life and labour through slavery in the country.

She added: “The British government took almost 200 years to repay the debt that it incurred when it paid the slave owners £20m.” Mottley pointed to the fact that Germany paid $95bn (£71bn) to the Jewish community because of the horrors of the Holocaust.

Mottley said that she did not want “anybody to diminish the fact that in this country here, which I have the honour to lead, that from settlement in 1627, 400 years ago next year, for 211 years, not six, people were treated as chattel”.

“If they dared to speak or to do things that were displeasing, their lives and limbs were put at risk. The evidence is clear. What is absent is the will,” she said.

Still unbeaten, yes, but for England this was anything but business as usual. The Red Roses remain undefeated in 40 Tests, but, for once, there were no victory speeches afterwards. For the first time since 2022 they have failed to win an international fixture, bringing to an end one of the purest winning sequences in world sport.

A wonderfully committed Canada fully deserved a share of the spoils and, in some ways, were unfortunate not to depart with more. The outcome was still up for grabs deep into the final quarter and England were indebted to two first-half tries from their Exeter wing Claudia Moloney-MacDonald.

With the clock ticking down and the scores locked at 26-26, however, it appeared as though England might have located the necessary key, only for their forwards be held up over the line and then denied by a loudly celebrated Canadian ruck turnover.

In the final analysis, though, they lacked some of their customary forward dynamism and their frequent match-winner Ellie Kildunne was consistently denied the luxury of space and time out wide under grey, drizzle-threatening skies.

The can-do Canadians, by contrast, all enhanced their reputations and will now be looking forward with even more eagerness to hosting England in two further WXV series Tests this autumn. Here was another reminder of the ability and spirit that took them all the way to last year’s World Cup final, with the openside flanker Julia Omokhuale, the centre Florence Symonds and the perennially excellent Sophie de Goede all outstanding.

The draw also ended England’s 100% home record against Canada and left John Mitchell with the unfamiliar task of reflecting on a disappointing result. “We were certainly in a ding-dong, weren’t we?” said the head coach. “I thought we owned a lot of the second half. We were applying huge pressure, but we just didn’t convert. Greater things will come as a result of this. One Test match isn’t going to take us away from our purpose.”

Both were the product of close quarter pick-and-go pressure, precisely the kind of thing England love using to their advantage, while a couple of costly dropped balls also did little for home momentum.

They were not at their slickest in other areas, either, but did strike back via a ninth-minute try for MacDonald wide on the left and a no-nonsense barging score from Hannah Botterman. The Mitchell plan is clearly to speed up the team’s tempo and add more variation to their game, but sometimes nothing beats the tried-and-tested basics.

Both sides then had a potential try apiece ruled out, the first when MacDonald was unable to ground properly a bouncing chip ahead and, more contentiously, when a beautiful weaving 45-metre solo score by the athletic Asia Hogan-Rochester was nullified by a marginal forward pass. A one-handed six from Jos Buttler sealed the deal and a delighted Harry Brook said yes, it absolutely did feel like he was in charge of the new No 1 T20 side in the world.

“Everything is running so smoothy, especially in the field,” the captain said after England’s eight-wicket win over Sri Lanka. “Lads are taking it upon themselves to make sure they’re in the right spots, buying into everything we’re talking about in the outfield especially, putting 100% in and that is all you can ever ask for.”

He acknowledged that holding on to the crown after leapfrogging India may be a little more difficult: “We got to stay motivated, try and keep that spot as long as possible. We probably don’t play as much T20 as other nations, especially India who play a hell of a lot, so keeping that might not be as easy as it sounds, but every opportunity we get we try and dominate whether the conditions are in our favour or not. And we’re getting really good at, when the conditions are not in our favour, still managing to scrape a win.”

The conditions were in England’s favour at Old Trafford, where an unchanged side did what they had done twice before, and seven times this year: beat Sri Lanka with a flourish. Brook’s 23rd win in 26 completed matches since he became captain was an exhibition match: a win with more than 10 overs to spare, leaving the good-natured crowd in the autumn sun looking around for more entertainment as the ground packed up around them.

Such was England’s dominance that the huge expanse seemed to shrink when they were fielding. In their mismatched navy blue trousers and royal blue (and red) tops, they were everywhere, long-legged praying mantises patrolling the damp ground. Here Liam Dawson avoiding Jofra Archer’s footwork for a neat run-out of Eshan Malinga; there a double-handed diving effort by Brook at short midwicket to get rid of the dangerous Pathum Nissanka. And there the giant form of Jamie Overton blocking Kamil Mishara’s attempt to clear the rope.

England’s bowlers ran smoothly through their paces. Sonny Baker continued the fantastic impression he had given this series with two for 17 from his 3.5 overs – Brook calling him “awesome” – while Overton’s miserly four overs, one for 15 may cheer up his brother, Craig, whose County Championship ambitions were near-ended by Yorkshire on Friday.

With the bat, it was business as usual. There were three stinging fours by Aneurin Donald, but he missed the chance to ink his name on a winter tour after advancing with ambition at Tharindu Ratnayake, and turning round to find he had been stumped. That brought Brook and a throaty cheer, and he wasn’t hanging around. Twenty-one runs came off Nuwan Thushara’s over, a wristy flick for six followed immediately by a wide spray through the keeper’s gloves for five wides and then another four clipped off the boots and an extra cover carve.

Take your pick of the rest: Buttler flaying Malinga without moving his boots for four down the ground; or swatting him for six, like a September wasp in the kitchen, to bring up his fifty off 30 balls. Sri Lanka’s effort was a comedy of errors, wides and misfields, though they did manage to run out Brook before the close as he gambled on a quick single and was beaten by Wanindu Hasaranga with a nimble turn-and-throw, for 33.

Eighteen holes sit between Rory McIlroy and an impressive piece of symmetry. In September 2025, McIlroy claimed a second Irish Open title in euphoric scenes at the K Club. Five months earlier, he had won the Masters.

At Wentworth on Sunday, McIlroy will take off in hot pursuit of a second PGA Championship crown. As was the case last year, he is the reigning Masters champion. Another season that will inevitably be defined by Augusta National could find itself with a cherry on top.

“I’d certainly like to win again,” said McIlroy. “The Masters feels like quite a long time ago. I have had half-chances here and there since then, but tomorrow is a great opportunity.

“It is a tournament and a place that means a lot to me. I first came here as a 10-year-old to watch the World Match Play with my mum and dad. I have played this tournament so many times, I have been able to win this event and now I have a house on the estate. I have a lot of history here, a 27-year history.” Indeed, the 2014 point at which McIlroy won at Wentworth feels like a lifetime ago.

On a wonderfully compacted leaderboard, McIlroy will begin round four two shots adrift of a pair of unlikely lads. Filippo Celli and Manuel Elvira are 358th and 294th in the world rankings, which makes their 54-hole prominence here rather extraordinary. Both made birdies at the last to reach 13 under par.

Alejandro del Rey, Johannes Veerman and JJ Spaun are one shy of the lead. Spaun arrived in Surrey with a point to prove after being overlooked for the United States Presidents Cup team. Del Rey and Veerman shot 64 on day three. So, too, did Kristoffer Reitan, who has Joaquin Niemann, Adam Scott and Davis Bryant for scoring company alongside McIlroy at minus 11. For the second time in three days, Scott missed an apparently straightforward eagle opportunity on the 18th green.

In testing conditions, McIlroy’s day was the slowest of burners. He was one over through 11 holes and irritated by subsequent missed opportunity before closing with a bang. McIlroy birdied the 17th in straightforward fashion. At the last, he fired a 230-yard four iron to tap-in range. With that eagle secured, McIlroy signed for a 69.

“It was a frustrating day,” he said. “It was hard to get the ball close to the hole, but if you look at the last few groups, I think everyone has struggled. We had the most of the wind and those first 11 holes were very, very difficult.

“It was a day when you really needed patience. That patience I tried to show all day was rewarded with the birdie and eagle.”

How the galleries roared. This is a fine tournament to attend if you fancy a close-up view of some of the best in the world who are not McIlroy. It feels as if 95% of the gallery follow him. “The crowds and the atmosphere have been absolutely incredible,” McIlroy said. “Great tournaments need great crowds and, honestly, this is one of the best atmospheres we play in all year.”

Toby Samuel beats Andrés Andrade 4-6, 6-4, 6-1

Wimbledon semi-finalist wins for 2-0 day one lead

Arthur Fery’s return to competition on home soil for the first time since his glorious summer at Wimbledon took place on a different surface, in a different format and on the opposite side of London. The emotions it generated were all the same as the British No 1 led his team to a 2-0 lead over Ecuador by defeating Álvaro Guillén Meza 7-5, 6-0 in Great Britain’s Davis Cup qualifier tie in the Copper Box Arena.

The victory for Fery, a Wimbledon semi-finalist, was preceded by a solid debut for the British No 5, Toby Samuel, a late injury replacement for Cameron Norrie. Samuel opened the tie by overcoming a nervous start to set the tone with a 4-6, 6-4, 6-1 win over Ecuador’s No 1, Andrés Andrade.

A successful opening day means Britain stands one win away from the Davis Cup Final 8, the decisive knockout stage of the competition, which takes place in Bologna between 18 and 23 November.

“You get goosebumps walking out,” said Fery. “I don’t know how many people that was, but it made a lot of noise. It was great playing here in London. A lot of support from everyone.

“It’s always different playing Davis Cup. You’re playing for a whole nation. There’s more responsibility on your shoulders. You know that it’s going to impact the team result as well, how you play. It’s a weight I can carry on my shoulders and I felt confident. It was never too much of a burden.”

Great Britain will now call on its impressive doubles team, the world No 1, Henry Patten, and last week’s US Open champion, Neal Skupski, to seal the tie in the first of three potential matches on Sunday.

As a result of Norrie’s late withdrawal, a packed and forceful British crowd witnessed a new Great Britain singles lineup, with Fery’s singles victory in Poland last September the only Davis Cup match he or Samuel had played. Despite their inexperience, the home team, in favourable conditions, was heavily favoured to defeat an Ecuador team without a player inside the top 200.

Still, no tennis competition springs surprises like the Davis Cup and Ecuador had already showed it should not be taken lightly. They earned their place at this stage with a 3-1 win against Australia in Quito on clay in February. An away tie in east London on indoor hard courts, however, is a different challenge.

Last February, Samuel was ranked outside the top 1,600 and was competing on the lowest rung of the World Tennis (formerly ITF) Tour as recently as November. He has been one of the fastest-rising players since then, winning nine titles in the past year at all levels, including five ATP Challenger titles.

Arsenal were attempting to record an eighth successive victory in all competitions to start the new campaign for the first time since 1903 when they were still known as Woolwich Arsenal.

Instead, it is Brighton – inspired by first-half goals from the veteran stand-in captain, Pascal Gross, and the exciting teenager Charalampos Kostoulas – who find themselves in third place, two points behind Arsenal. New signing Chema Andrés made the points safe from a corner 12 minutes into the second half. The home supporters waved blue and white flags before kick-off as the players swapped their usual kits for a deep blue limited edition shirt that was inspired by their first season in Southern League Division Two in 1901. That has caused controversy among fans after originally being listed on sale for £150 in a package that included a letter of authenticity from the club owner, Tony Bloom, and a keyring. Given this is the only time they will wear it, those who shelled out will be pleased they did now.

Georginio Rutter returned as a late substitute, but the damage had already been inflicted by then thanks to Gross and Kostoulas.

Jurriën Timber looked leggy on his first start since March and Bruno Guimarães was disappointing on his first Premier League start for Arsenal. Myles Lewis-Skelly’s energy and drive in midfield was sorely missed in the week he was recalled to the England squad.

UK politics increasingly funded by billionaires as mega-donations surge

The Guardian Sat, 19 Sep 2026 16:00:50 GMT

Exclusive: A total £179m has been donated by wealthy individuals since 2019, research reveals

British politics is increasingly being funded by individual billionaires with a wave of mega-donations having flooded into UK political parties over the past two parliaments.

A total of £179m has been donated by wealthy individuals since 2019, research reveals.

The figures from the IPPR thinktank show how big money is playing an ever more influential role in Westminster, with a particular rise in mega-donations of more than £1m.

The research found that contributions from individual donors have accelerated since the Brexit party received £10m from the Thailand-based billionaire Christopher Harborne and the Liberal Democrats were given £8m by David Sainsbury, the supermarket tycoon, who has now returned to Labour.

Between 2001, when donation records began, and 2018, the total donated by individuals giving more than £1m averaged £3.9m a year.

But between 2019 and 2025, that figure rose to £13.1m a year, almost three-and-a-half times as much, and far outstripping what would be expected with inflation.

The research found 72% of all £1m-plus donations from individuals since records began had come since 2019.

Guardian analysis found that in some years, such as 2023, almost £7 out of every £10 in reported private donations to political parties came from wealthy companies or individuals who gave more than £1m in a calendar year.

The figures are likely to raise fresh concerns about the influence of a small groups of wealthy individuals, which have already been heightened since two crypto billionaires, Harborne and Ben Delo, said they had each given £36m to Reform UK this month.

Reform UK has said it is trying to redress the balance as the other parties have taken millions in mega-donations in past years. The Conservatives’ biggest donors include Frank Hester, who gave more than £20m before the 2024 election, and Labour’s Gary Lubner, who has given more than £9m in total.

The IPPR figures draw on Electoral Commission data since 2001 and Transparency International analysis, plus the two record donations of £36m each to Reform UK from Harborne and Delo.

There is increasing concern among Reform UK’s rivals about the issue of donations of more than £1m, with some Labour MPs pushing for a cap of £100,000 or £500,000 a year.

Some Labour members are intending to push the issue at the party’s autumn conference, and proposals for a cap are likely to be tabled when the government’s current elections bill goes to the House of Lords this autumn.

No 10 has been reluctant to include a cap amid opposition from some trade unions who fear it could lead to restrictions on them being able to donate so much in future.

However, the government has recently pledged to deal with the issue of mega-donors having an outsize influence on politics. It has already introduced a cap of £100,000 a year for donations from overseas voters.

Harry Quilter-Pinner, the executive director of IPPR, said: “Something fundamental has changed in how British politics is funded. Million-pound donations were once exceptional. However, since 2019, mega-donor money has become a much bigger part of our political system.

“Reform’s extraordinary fundraising has accelerated that trend, but this is much bigger than one party or two enormous cheques. This is the Americanisation of British politics, where political parties can become dependent on a handful of people with exceptionally deep pockets.

“Britain should draw a clear line. The government should introduce a £100,000 annual cap now and bring it down over time, so that no individual can bankroll a political party simply because they are incredibly wealthy.”

Civil society groups have urged the government to fix the issue for good, after the government said earlier this month a new taskforce would examine the issue of mega-donations.

Dr Susan Hawley, executive director of Spotlight on Corruption, said: “Without urgent action to limit the amount that wealthy individuals can give to political parties, we’re going to continue to see a staggering inflation of money – and the influence it buys – flowing into the coffers of political parties … The taskforce needs to take decisive action to get big money out of our politics in a fair and even-handed way, so that power and influence is returned to ordinary voters, where it belongs.”

At the time of the £72m in donations to Reform UK, Duncan Hames, senior director of policy at Transparency International UK, said the situation with big donations was “completely out of control, and makes an irrefutable case for government to bring forward an annual cap on political donations, and fast”.

The Guardian Sat, 19 Sep 2026 15:41:39 GMT

British Museum chair tells Big Brue festival he thought no one would find out about the private viewing

George Osborne has said he thought no one would find out about a private viewing of the Bayeux tapestry he organised for the tech billionaire Peter Thiel at the British Museum.

The former chancellor, who is chair of the museum, told the Big Brue festival in Somerset that he had been on holiday when Thiel was shown the medieval artwork.

Thiel, who supports Donald Trump, is the founder of PayPal and Palantir, a software company that builds data integration, analytics and artificial intelligence platforms for government agencies and large corporations.

Palantir has a swathe of British public contracts, including, most controversially, a £330m deal with the NHS, which it has held since 2023.

The company also works for the US, Israeli and UK militaries. Its use of AI-powered software to support military strikes in Gaza and Iran, US Ice immigration raids and its access to NHS data has stoked concern.

Of the viewing, Osborne said: “It wasn’t like we expected anyone to know about it.” The museum’s director of development, Charlotte Appleyard, hosted Thiel at a VIP viewing of the tapestry before it opened to the public on 18 August.

The visit was revealed in the Guardian shortly after it happened.

When asked what the museum might have got in return, Osborne said: “The short answer is he hasn’t offered any money, and were he to offer money, the board would consider it and have to take into account the pros, you know, receiving more income, and the reputational risks.”

Osborne, who lives in Bruton, near where the festival is taking place, complained that people treat the British Museum like the Foreign Office when they protest about donors who are thought to support the Israeli government.

He said: “The critique was that [Thiel] was a supporter of the Israeli government … I mean, this is the most difficult, and almost all the protests that happen at the museum … When I started five years ago, they were climate protests, Just Stop Oil and that kind of thing. Now they’re almost universally Gaza.

“You know that is the moment I would say the most sensitive, difficult political issue for the museum, and you know we try and navigate it, and I keep trying to point out we’re not actually the Foreign Office.”

He said the museum has to take money from companies such as BP to be able to operate.

“You cannot say we want museums to be free, and then one of the biggest British companies offers us £50m, BP, and we go, oh, don’t, because we object to oil exploration. Where is the money going to come from?

“You’d shut down the British Museum. People do say this. They say you shouldn’t take tech money, you shouldn’t take oil money. You can’t take any money from the banks. We want the museum to be free. The museum would shut down.”

Denmark and Greenland say US military agreement will not compromise Arctic territory’s sovereignty

The Guardian Sat, 19 Sep 2026 14:43:07 GMT

Statement sought to clarify Trump’s announcement that US will have ‘permanent control’ over Greenland’s security

Denmark and Greenland have said any agreement with the US to develop a significant military presence in the strategic Arctic territory will not compromise Greenland’s sovereignty.

In a statement on Saturday clarifying an announcement by Donald Trump that an agreement had been reached to give Washington “permanent control” ⁠over Greenland’s security, Denmark and the semiautonomous territory ⁠expressed hope that a deal would end friction with the US over the issue.

Greenland’s prime minister, Jens-Frederik Nielsen, said that he was pleased with the proposed deal. “The agreement recognizes the sovereignty and territorial integrity of our kingdom and ​the right of the Greenlandic people to self-determination,” he said ​in a post on Facebook.

“Next week could be a good week – for Greenland, ‌Denmark and the United States,” Denmark’s foreign minister, ‌Lars Lokke Rasmussen, said in a statement, also on Facebook.

“A time of uncertainty will hopefully give way to a binding agreement that strengthens security ‌in the Arctic and the north Atlantic, and thereby our shared security within Nato Europe – while respecting the Danish kingdom’s red lines,” Rasmussen said.

The US, Denmark and Greenland said late on Friday they had reached a deal to allow the US to develop a significant military presence on Greenland, while prohibiting US adversaries from building their ⁠own bases on the island.

The deal is expected to be signed during the UN general assembly next week.

Key details of the agreement have not been made public, including the degree of the US military presence in the self-governing Danish territory and whether any formal power over foreign policy and resources would be ceded to Washington.

Trump said on social media that under the deal, “the United States will FOREVER have the complete ability to do what is necessary in Greenland in order to secure and defend the security of Greenland, and the United States of America”.

He added that the agreement would give the US “permanent control over security, and all ‌other needs, in Greenland”.

The security and mineral resources of the vast northern island have been subject to Washington’s foreign policy and attention since the start of the second Trump administration, with officials citing national security, access to valuable natural resources, including rare earth minerals, and control over emerging Arctic shipping lanes.

The island had a significant US military presence in the 1950s, when fears of annihilation in a US-Soviet nuclear exchange required that long-range nuclear bombers and early-warning systems be based on Greenland.

The US still maintains a reduced military presence at the Pituffik space base, formerly known as Thule, on the island to monitor for missiles.

Mikkel Vedby Rasmussen, a political science professor at the University of Copenhagen, told Reuters that the Denmark-US deal “is probably not the end of President Trump’s ambitions for Greenland and certainly not the end of US strategic interest in the territory and its resources”.

Rasmussen added that if Copenhagen cedes any formal power to Washington over Greenland, which it has held for 1,000 years, it would raise questions for Greenlanders of whether “this is the beginning of replacing the colonial relationship with Denmark with a colonial relationship to the United States”.

US ambitions for greater sway over the Arctic island have strained relations with Nato. In January, European member nations sent military personnel to Greenland to demonstrate military readiness. Eight European allies issued a joint statement confirming their commitment to Arctic security. Negotiations followed.

A Nato spokesperson ‌on Saturday said the alliance ​welcomed the agreement, which would “help advance security, ​stability and cooperation in this vital region”.

Small boat arrivals are ‘wealthy men’ who do not deserve help, says Reform’s Danny Kruger

The Guardian Sat, 19 Sep 2026 14:30:58 GMT

The fact that some migrants pay people smugglers thousands of pounds makes them well off, MP claims

Asylum seekers who arrive on small boats across the Channel are “wealthy men” who do not deserve the help of the British state, according to the Reform UK MP Danny Kruger.

The former Conservative, who defected last year, said the fact that some migrants were paying people smugglers thousands of pounds – often using their life savings or borrowed money – made them well off. The claim was immediately dismissed by charities who support refugees.

Speaking at the Big Brue festival in Bruton, Somerset, Kruger said: “By the way, most of them [are] comparatively wealthy and fit young men who’ve crossed safe countries to begin the journey to the UK.”

Asked by the event’s moderator, the editor of the Independent, Geordie Greig, how he knew these men were wealthy, Kruger said: “Because they’re paying thousands of pounds. They’re paying thousands of pounds to people smugglers to get here. Comparatively wealthy, compared to the people who I think most of us can regard as really deserving of the compassion of the British taxpayer.”

Seema Syeda, a Joint Council for the Welfare of Immigrants spokesperson, said it was untrue that most asylum seekers who arrive on boats are wealthy.

She said: “The reality is that most asylum seekers who arrive here are denied the right to work, live off as little as £8 a week, and can end up in destitution. But in the end, whether rich or poor, people fleeing war and persecution deserve to be welcomed. The right to safety is a human right.

“Many people arriving here have been forcibly displaced due to war, genocide or imperialism that the British state has, past and present, funded or supported.”

Earlier this month, Reform politician Matt Goodwin, the party’s unsuccessful candidate at the Gorton and Denton byelection, caused outrage when he said at the party’s annual conference that the “best and the brightest” of the British population had been replaced by “drug-dealing goat-herders” through immigration.

Kruger said Goodwin was correct to make these incendiary remarks. He said: “There are some drug-dealing goat-herders who we’ve admitted to this country, so I mean, it’s factual.”

Asked by Greig if he accepted that language, he said: “Yes I do.” He added: “And they don’t like our country.”

Kruger said he was concerned “about kind of massive cultural transformation. And yes, the admission to our country of many people who do not share the values that we all love, and I’m afraid to say it’s not just recent migrants.”

The Reform MP also complained about second- and third-generation migrants.

He said: “In fact, I think recent migrants are probably more pro-British because they’ve come here for a reason. They want to be here. We’ve got a problem with second- and third-generation immigrants because they are, and it’s a fault of politics that … this has happened.

“We have an alienated generation, many many people, millions of people, for whom they don’t love their country, they don’t think that Britain is great, and they don’t feel that they are part of the mainstream society that we have here, and that is our challenge.”

He further claimed that current policies would cause a civil war. “We continue down the path of segregation and of you know elite virtue signalling, pretending we’re all a lovely multicultural diversity is our strength, and it’s rude to even point out any problems,” Kruger added.

Rachel Millward, the co-deputy leader of the Green party, said: “Reform is a party funded by billionaires that chooses to attack the most vulnerable in our society – people fleeing environmental breakdown, famine and war.

“Instead of stoking division and hatred, just days after anti-immigrant protests brought violence and disorder to our streets, politicians need to step up and offer solutions. We’re calling for more safe routes so that those who need asylum can apply for it before they leave their own country, and never have to face a dangerous crossing in a small boat.”

Trump’s battle to rename the Kennedy Center has put its future at risk

The Guardian Sat, 19 Sep 2026 13:30:48 GMT

The president has threatened to block renovations and suggested the landmark could be demolished after courts ruled against his bid to rename it

It was born with the world premiere of Leonard Bernstein’s Mass. “Young people will come here and they will see this cultural centre,” Rose Kennedy, the mother of slain US president John F Kennedy, said at that opening night gala. “They will carry some of these ideas back to their different communities.”

More than half a century later, the potential death knell came just after 4.30pm on Tuesday with a perfunctory announcement on the public address system: “The centre is now closed to the public. Please exit the centre by way of the Hall of States.” Soon barricades had been erected and security guards were blocking access.

The John F Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts in Washington DC, once filled with the buzz of audiences and children, had fallen as silent as a mausoleum. Now a high stakes legal battle is under way to prevent Donald Trump from taking a wrecking ball to the building that is both national arts complex and living memorial to the 35th president.

The current White House occupant, incensed that courts have prevented his name being added to the Kennedy Center, told reporters this week: “I think that the Trump administration should certainly have recognition. Because frankly, if we don’t do that, it’s going to close. It’ll end up being ripped down.” On social media, Trump declared the venue “destined to doom” without his intervention.

The once unthinkable threat became more thinkable when an Agence France-Presse photographer took a picture of Trump aboard Air Force One, holding a placard with ominous red text: “Kennedy Center DEMOLIS...” The rest of the word was obscured by the plane’s window frame. Below was a big picture showing a yellow heavy construction vehicle scooping rubble from a torn-down building.

Trump has no legal right to demolish the facility, which was established by Congress. Critics say he is acting out of spite because he cannot get his way. Kerry Kennedy, the former president’s niece , said: “Like a child who can’t play with a toy, he wants to stomp on the toy. But this is not a toy. This is the living memorial to a slain president.

“It would be like adding the Trump name to the Trump-Lincoln Memorial or the Trump-Jefferson Memorial or Trump-Tomb of the Unknown Soldier. The courts have spoken, he cannot demolish it, he cannot put his name on it and he should be focused instead on his job.”

The Kennedy Center did not respond to requests for comment.

The 100ft structure opened in 1971 on the banks of the Potomac River. Since then it has presented ballet, children’s theatre, comedy, contemporary dance, hip-hop, jazz, international festivals and educational programmes. The annual Kennedy Center Honors have hosted past presidents and a who’s who of US arts and culture.

Trump seized control of the facility in February 2025, claimed its finances were in dire straits and fired board members who did not align with his “vision for a Golden Age in Arts and Culture”. Deborah Rutter, the centre’s president, was ousted and replaced by Ric Grenell, a Trump loyalist and former ambassador with no experience in arts management.

An initiative created in 2020 to promote anti-racism and community outreach was shut down and its 10-person staff dismissed. Citing “drag shows specifically targeting our youth”, any programming perceived as “woke” was purged. It was a commercial disaster as audiences, performers and philanthropists deserted the centre in droves.

Lawyer Norm Eisen, who has litigated against the administration’s attempts to impinge on institutional independence, said: “He slapped his name on there and destroyed the lifeblood of the Kennedy Center: audience and artists.”

In January, the Kennedy Center hosted the world premiere of Melania, a documentary about the first lady, with the Trumps in attendance. Three days later, the president announced that he would be closing the facility for two years for $257m repairs and renovations.

The Trump-appointed board backed the move and also voted to rename the venue the “Trump-Kennedy Center”. Trump’s name was duly added to the exterior marble facade, before the US district judge Christopher Cooper intervened and ruled that only Congress has the authority to rename the memorial. The name was removed but the result remains hidden by giant scaffolding and tarpaulins.

Asked about Trump’s motivations, Eisen of Democracy Defenders Action added: “You would need an authority in abnormal psychology to get the answer to that question but he appears to have developed an obsession because he’s not used to hearing the word no.”

On Tuesday this week, Judge Cooper again ruled that the Trump administration could not put a new Trump sign on the Kennedy Center’s facade or rename its plaza for the president “without Congress’s blessing”.

Hours later, the centre’s board voted to close the facility for two years, citing the need for $257m of repairs and renovations. The centre’s executive director, Matt Floca, ordered an immediate seven-day emergency closure, citing “acute risks to public safety resulting from continued structural deterioration”.

But Democratic congresswoman Joyce Beatty and Senator Sheldon Whitehouse allege that the closure is a “pretext” to hide a financial “death spiral” caused by artist boycotts and dwindling ticket sales.

In an interview on Friday, Whitehouse, the top Democrat on the environment and public works committee and an ex-officio member of the Kennedy Center board of trustees, said the events represented three phases of Trump’s assault on the complex.

“One is what I call the mob bust out gone wrong, in which they tried to take over and run the Kennedy Center, give themselves and their friends big contracts, charge expensive goodies to Kennedy Center accounts, do political favours using Kennedy Center facilities for Trump allies, and that was extremely damaging to the business of the centre,” he said.

“Then they moved into the renaming fiasco and that seems to have struck a lethal blow to the centre’s business model – a predictably damaging blow that they failed to consider at all. Now they’ve moved into a third stage in which they are threatening the actual destruction of the Kennedy Center if they don’t get their renaming.”

Whitehouse added: “It has gone from bad to worse but the through line in all of this is that these trustees are under a legal duty to put the welfare of the centre itself first and, if they fail in that duty, they create a legal environment in which courts can and ultimately likely will step in to make sure that the centre is run lawfully.”

The legal battle intensified on Thursday, when Judge Cooper issued an order requiring the Kennedy Center to give at least 30 days’ notice before making any major physical changes to the building, including demolition.

Whitehouse said: “There’s a contrast between the thuggery and bullying world in which you could countenance a threat to tear down the Kennedy Center if your name doesn’t go on it and the actual legal world in which actions have to be approved by a board that has a fiduciary duty to put the welfare of the institution first. Those two are irreconcilable at this point.”

Still, Trump ordered the demolition of the White House East Wing to make way for a ballroom, despite opposition from preservationists and questions over the administration’s authority to proceed without Congress. He is now threatening to cancel the renovation of the Kennedy Center, and warning of its possible demise, if his name is not restored to the building.

Chris Raleigh, an organiser the Hands Off the Arts movement, which is mobilising grassroots resistance, said: “That’s what you do when the hostage takers can’t get what they want. There comes a point where the hostage is inconvenient. Look at it: the people who have fought back have pushed Trump to the brink here.

“In no way at all is he winning. His name is not going up on the building. There is somebody in the White House every day who says, before they walk in that building, ‘Oh god, please don’t let there be another Kennedy Center story today.’”

Raleigh added: “Everyone in Trump’s life should be telling him: ‘You gotta to get out now. This is not going to help you.’”

And even if the current peril passes, it will be difficult to restore the centre to its former glories. On Friday it laid off about a dozen staff, the Washington Post newspaper reported.

Michael Kaiser, who led the centre from 2001 to 2014, warns that even a two-year closure will be damaging. He said: “When you don’t have audiences and you don’t have donors participating for two years, those individuals go elsewhere. When you have no staff, even if there’s a time in the future where we can return to a more sense of being normal, it’s not going to be so simple to reopen a building of this size and complexity.”

Some critics see the attack on the Kennedy Center as part of a broader assault on institutions and freedom of expression. On Friday, Trump announced that the media outlets CNN, MS Now and Politico would be banned from the White House and, with health secretary Robert Kennedy Jr standing behind him in the Oval Office, railed against the Kennedy Center again.

To Kerry Kennedy, who has worked in the human rights arena for 45 years, the president is a “petty tyrant”. Asked to consider the possibility of the Kennedy Center being lost, she reflected: “It would be devastating for my family because we love Uncle Jack but in the end Trump is not going to hurt my family. He is hurting our country and he’s hurting our world and he’s giving permission to tyrants everywhere to shut down arts centres and silence critical voices.”

On Friday evening thousands of protesters gathered outside the Kennedy Center in view of the marble facade that remained concealed by scaffolding and tarpaulins. The speakers included a drag queen.

Against the setting sun, protesters beat drums and waved signs that read: “Keep your tiny hands off our Kennedy Center”; “You’re no Jack Kennedy”; “Our center not DJT’s”; and “Wicked starring DJT”.

Maga wants more babies. But they don’t seem too worried about miscarriages in ICE detention

The Guardian Sat, 19 Sep 2026 12:00:47 GMT

Officials lack data on miscarriages after October 2025. Detained women aren’t getting the prenatal healthcare they need

Maga men have babies on the brain. They may not all be interested in changing diapers or hands-on parenting, but they’re very keen on population growth. “[W]e want more babies, to put it very nicely,” Donald Trump said last year.

Trump, who has called himself the “father of IVF” and joked that he will be known as the “fertilization president”, surrounds himself with people who profess a similar fondness for children. Only a few days after being sworn in as vice-president, JD Vance declared he wanted “more babies in the United States of America” and went on to make pronatalist policies a theme of his time in office.

Meanwhile, the administration’s favourite moneyman, Elon Musk, is doing his own part to increase the population. Ashley St Clair, the mother of one of his many offspring, has claimed he once told her he wanted to have “a legion of children before the civil war”. At least one of Musk’s kids has denounced him, so I’m not sure he’s considered that they might not all be fighting on the same side.

While the Trump administration may want a baby boom, it won’t shock you to hear that, when you take a closer look at their particular brand of pronatalism, they don’t actually seem to want “more babies”. What they really want, judging by the way in which pregnant immigrants are being treated, is more of the “right” type of baby.

A Guardian investigation published this week revealed that ICE is arresting a record number of pregnant women and teenagers. These detained women are reportedly not receiving the prenatal healthcare they need and, alarmingly, ICE does not seem to have records of how many of these women have suffered miscarriages.

“ICE recorded 18 miscarriages during the first nine months of the Trump administration,” the Guardian writes. “[B]ut the agency has no data on miscarriages after 3 October 2025.” Let me just reiterate that: we have no idea how many women in ICE detention have lost their babies over the past 11 months.

It’s very strange that ICE seems to have just stopped tracking miscarriage numbers; the agency, and the Trump administration, is normally very big on surveillance. Last year, the Guardian reported that pregnant immigrant women were turning up to hospitals to deliver their babies wearing location-tracking smartwatches as part of an ICE monitoring program. One of these women was diagnosed with pre-eclampsia, which can cause major swelling, and hospital staff were worried that the smartwatch would cut off her circulation. “She was in tears about [the idea of taking the surveillance device off],” a hospital staffer told the Guardian. “She had this deep fear that ICE was going to come to the hospital and take her baby.”

Surveillance also extends to the broader pregnant population. When Dr Erica Schwartz was confirmed by the US Senate as director of the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) earlier this year, she emphasized: “Abortion surveillance is absolutely a critical component of what the CDC is currently doing.” While the CDC doesn’t require states to collect data on abortions, 44 states plus Washington DC have some sort of mandated abortion reporting, according to the Guttmacher Institute. This isn’t necessarily sinister but, following the overturning of Roe v Wade, there has been growing concern that this data might be weaponized to punish abortion patients and providers, who are increasingly being treated like criminals.

And that concern is hardly unfounded. In the first two years after Roe was overturned, prosecutors in 16 states charged more than 400 people with pregnancy-related crimes, a 2025 report by the group Pregnancy Justice found. The report also noted that there are likely far more cases of miscarriage criminalization than have made headlines.

Funny, isn’t it? If you suffer a miscarriage in ICE detention, possibly because of systemic medical neglect, the US government will apparently shrug and look the other way. But if you have a miscarriage in a state that has fetal personhood language in its abortion laws, you may find yourself facing a police investigation and criminal charges. Once again, there is nothing pro-life about this administration. They are solely pro-control.

“These profiles were incorporating imagery of a ‘traditional wife’ aesthetic and listing specific interests in an attempt to appeal to … individuals in law enforcement,” an internal FBI memo warns. “The objective was to lure affiliated law enforcement personnel into an online or in-person interaction under the guise of a date, after which the individuals would be publicly exposed and doxed online.” Oh dear, my heart bleeds for these poor ICE agents.

Starting last Sunday, Turkish police raided the offices of LGBTQ+ rights organizations and HIV-advocacy groups. Then they arrested people protesting against the raids and journalists covering the protests. “This is the widest crackdown on LGBTQ+ people in recent years,” said Emma Sinclair-Webb, of Human Rights Watch. Homosexuality isn’t illegal in Turkey, but the government seems to be weaponizing “obscenity” laws to target the community.

The “ceasefire” continues.

New research from the University of St Andrews found that women have significantly unequal medical care. Men are far more likely to be offered treatments such as strong painkillers or surgery, according to the analysis.

Does the podcaster not realize that his support helped get Trump elected? Lack of self-awareness aside, it’s amusing to watch some of Trump’s former supporters turn on the president.

Female students who miss swimming because of their periods need to have a parent submit a note “stating the length of the menstrual duration” so they can make up the day. If you don’t comply, your grade is at risk.

One hundred and forty-six women, aged between 20 and 58, make up the Power of Mama, which protects the biodiverse region of Indonesian Borneo. “Because we are housewives, we are the ones that feel its effects most,” one member said of what motivated her to fight fires. “I thought I had to do something about it.”

Patel told a Senate judiciary committee oversight hearing that the FBI “did not want to punish victims of bestiality” by automatically disqualifying them. At one point of this absurd hearing, a senator from Louisiana asked Patel whether the change “disqualified the animal” from FBI service. Just when you thought US politics couldn’t get any more stupid, it goes and surprises you.

Hunk – or ‘unc’? What magazine covers of Michael B Jordan and Tom Cruise tell us about manhood

The Guardian Sat, 19 Sep 2026 12:00:45 GMT

Images of two actors on front of Vogue and GQ land at a time when masculinity is increasingly dominating headlines

Tom Cruise and Michael B Jordan share many similarities as box-office powerhouses known for their death-defying action hero stunts. But this week the two stars went head-to-head, or more accurately chest-to-chest, on magazine stands.

In one corner there’s 64-year-old Cruise on the cover of GQ, his first for the magazine in 20 years. Posing in an unbuttoned shirt, one hand running through his tousled hair, the other gripping his belt buckle, this is Cruise playing the role of sexy Cruise.

Despite his efforts, and Cruise previous having been crowned the sexiest man alive, the internet, usually a place of deep division, has unanimously agreed that the resulting image is deeply unsexy.

“Never sharing Tom Cruise GQ cover because I have compassion for others,” reads one comment on GQ’s Instagram. “What horrors did I do to get this in my algorithm,” adds another. Others have nicknamed him “unc” – internet slang for someone out of touch.

Meanwhile, 39-year-old Jordan makes his Vogue debut (the sixth man to be given a solo cover) lying down and laughing on a bed of flowers, the blazer of his suit unbuttoned to showcase his many, many abs and a flash of his right nipple.

Most of the comments are NSFW (not suitable for work). An example from the tamer offerings: “I aspire to be a flower.”

The covers land at a time when masculinity is increasingly dominating headlines. From toxic masculinity to looksmaxxing and performative males, the conversation is being driven by increasing concerns over the manosphere and what exactly being a man means and looks like today. Cruise is a boomer. Jordan is a millennial. Both have added further fuel to the masculinity fire.

Dr Ashley Morgan, a masculinities scholar at Cardiff Metropolitan University, says despite there being “a massive range of masculinities”, people tend to focus on one type: the white male patriarch.

“That is what Cruise is selling on this cover,” she says. In contrast, “Jordan presents a range of masculinities including ideas around Black masculinity. He’s wearing a suit but it’s very suggestive. His cover is more universally attractive to men, women and others.”

For Andrew Groves, director of the menswear archive at the University of Westminster, there is a clear fashion distinction. “Everything in the Cruise image is constructed to make it appear sexy, yet somehow it isn’t,” he says. “Cruise is given clothes rather than fashion. The worn shirt and old Levi’s belong to a masculine language of work and labour. Jordan is allowed fashion, decoration, jewellery, and softness. His masculinity is constructed through a much wider set of codes.”

When Adam Baidawi was named the new editor of GQ last year, he said he wanted to restore the magazine to “its rightful place as the North Star of masculinity”, and that GQ would be “a magazine for and about men”.

His debut cover in September featured the actor Jeremy Strong wearing a hoodie and holding a steel archery bow. It chimed heavily with what Baidawi’s predecessor, Will Welch, set out to do. One of his most popular issues was “The New Masculinity” edition in 2019, which starred Pharrell Williams on the cover in a gown-like coat.

A year later, Harry Styles appeared on the cover of Vogue wearing a dress. Six years on, Styles has ditched his signature sequined jumpsuits for suits and ties on his world tour while Trump’s Maga movement is being driven by tech bros and a model of manhood that champions traditional patriarchy.

Alona Pardo, who previously curated an exhibition exploring masculinities in photography at the Barbican in London, says the two latest covers highlight “how the media continues to codify and reinforce normative ideals of manhood”. Pardo says the image of Cruise defying ageing is particularly reductive as it reinforces “the standard that a man’s worth is linked to physical vigour and perpetual dominance”.

Jessa Crispin, author of What’s Wrong with Men, says Cruise’s cover reflects his role as “the dad of Hollywood”. In the accompanying interview he talks about teaching young actors how to navigate the business, including giving actor Glen Powell a six-hour instructional film. “It’s a very kind of traditional man-as-steward masculine role,” Crispin says. She compares the “tame” Jordan cover to Cary Grant, “masculine with a sense of humour, and not really anything revolutionary”.

Pardo says both are disappointing. By using the visual language of virility they reassert “traditional patriarchal authority”. Framed against social movements including #MeToo, Pardo says the images “function as a reactionary bid for male solidarity” and ultimately reassert “traditional patriarchal authority in direct opposition to movements challenging systemic power dynamics”.

US fashion CEO resigns after physically restraining animal rights activists

The Guardian Sat, 19 Sep 2026 11:58:01 GMT

Steven Kolb of the Council of Fashion Designers of America was filmed during an altercation at New York fashion week

The chief executive of the Council of Fashion Designers of America, Steven Kolb, has resigned after he was filmed physically restraining two animal rights activists during an altercation at New York fashion week.

“After 20 years leading the CFDA, I have made the difficult decision to step down as CEO and president,” Kolb said in a statement. “I am enormously proud of what we have built together and believe this is the right moment for both me and the organisation to begin a new chapter.”

Kolb had been placed on leave on Tuesday pending a review of an incident during a COS show at New York fashion week on Sunday.

In a video, Kolb could be seen trying to restrain two People for the Ethical Treatment of Animals (Peta) protesters who attempted to disrupt the show in a demonstration against the use of wool by the H&M group, which owns COS.

Kolb pushed a protester, identified as Mason Melito, and covered his mouth. Kolb also wrestled a second protester to the ground, using his arms and a leg to restrain her and putting his hand over her mouth.

Speaking to the Guardian after the incident, Melito described the situation as scary and said Kolb’s behaviour had been “completely uncalled for”.

The CFDA is a non-profit organisation that supports and promotes US designers and brands. It also organises the official New York fashion week schedule.

A statement issued by the CFDA board, which includes designers such as Ralph Lauren, Thom Browne, Tory Burch and Michael Kors, said: “Steven Kolb has been a dedicated leader and tireless champion of American fashion throughout his more than two decades at the CFDA, including 15 years as CEO.

“We respect Steven’s decision to step down and are grateful for his many years of leadership and service to the CFDA and our industry. He leaves the organisation well positioned, with a clear mission and dedicated team, to carry out the important work ahead as we look to the future of American fashion.”

The group is yet to name a successor.

“We will still be meeting with Mr Kolb, and hopefully others in the industry will meet and take meaningful steps to stop this epidemic of cruelty to animals for nothing more than a look.”
