Don’t be afraid to be masculine, laugh more, and phone your mum: letters to our sons, by Stephen Graham, Riz Ahmed, Danny Dyer and other wise men

The Guardian Sat, 19 Sep 2026 11:00:46 GMT

The Adolescence actor and the psychologist Orly Klein asked fathers to write to their sons. The results – from famous dads to the wisdom of strangers – were moving and motivating. Here’s a selection

What can I say? From the moment you and your sister were born my heart has been full of a love I never thought was humanly possible. As a baby you were filled with wonder and so much energy. You had a beautiful, mischievous and inquisitive nature, which has always made me smile. You were climbing, running and jumping everywhere. You’d walk into a room wearing shoes that were four times, five times, 10 times too big for you … Sometimes they were ye mother’s.

The sound of your laughter is one of the most beautiful compositions made by nature. I am so blessed to be a part of your life, and our friendship is something I hold dear to my heart. That beautiful bouncing boy has grown into a man who brightens up a room whenever he walks into it.

I have had the pleasure of watching you grow, of watching you learn the lessons of life, like how you conducted yourself when your heart was broken for the first time. To watch you navigate that pain with compassion and come out the other side appreciating your worth without holding on to any resentments, showing your vulnerability to me and your mother and allowing us to guide you through – that was truly admirable.

You’re the glue that holds friendships together – you give 110% to all of your relationships. You are a fantastic listener, never judgmental. You have the humility to sit with a prince or a pauper and treat them both equally with dignity and respect. I think one thing I’ve passed on to you is the quality of a proper hug, and anyone who knows you would completely agree.

You’ve got funny bones. The little voices you do, your silly impressions, and I love watching the double act you and your mum have created, especially when yous take the piss out of me (I am 5ft 6in). One of my fondest memories is when you and me went out to play football. We climbed over the school gate, wheeled out the goals and had the best game of shootie the world has ever seen (I think I won 10-9). When we got home and knocked on the front door we were covered from head to toe in mud. I’ll never forget your mum’s reaction: “What the hell have you two been up to?!” You and me looked at each other and burst out laughing.

My hopes, dreams and aspirations for you are already being fulfilled. Keep being you because you are brilliant. You constantly embody what your nana used to say: “No one is ever above you and no one is ever beneath you.” Always be true to yourself and to who you are. The only advice I could ever give you is to keep doing what you’re doing, always be willing to learn, always be open-minded and always be honest.

I love you so much – you’re one of my best mates. I love you to the moon and back for ever.

All my love DadStephen Graham, actor

Drew, actor, Merseyside

a few words to you, my son. My only son. My son and heir. Unfortunately for your sisters, you get the lot. All my readies. My hard-earned dough. What a result.

Just wanna thank you, really. For being a brainy little fucker. The smartest in your class. Never something I could claim to be. The way you can think logically is amazing to me. The way you can retain information brings a tear to my eye. Yes, you’re on the spectrum but ain’t we all. It’s what makes us unique.

There’s a lot of wrong ’uns in this world. I know that you won’t be one of ’em. I’d call you my prince. But as we’ve learned, princes can be noncy fuckers.

So proud that you’ve come from my nuts. It’s the greatest thing my testicles have ever done.

Don’t ever be afraid to be masculine. Always be considerate and kind and thoughtful to anyone you meet coz you never know what they’re going through.

Love you, my boy. More than you’ll ever understand. Dad

Danny Dyer, actor and presenter

Martin, retired, Hampshire

Marc, project manager, Bristol

Now that you are 21, I feel as if I can speak to you as one adult to another. I have dozens of reasons to write this letter, but one outweighs them all: the constant sirens and explosions that can be heard in the city every week. Even back when I was working as a journalist at the front, recording interviews right in the trenches, I had already accepted the possibility that I might die. But what frightened me most was something else – that I might not have time to talk to you again, to tell you what truly matters.

I no longer live on the frontline, but hundreds of kilometres away from it. Yet rockets and Shahed drones reach this far every week. I’m afraid I won’t be able to do everything I’ve planned in life. And I’m afraid I won’t be able to tell you what truly matters to me. That’s why I’m writing.

First and foremost, you might be wondering why I remain in Ukraine, knowing that my life is at risk. Indeed, I had the chance to leave. But I would have lost all respect for myself if I had. It’s as simple as that. An enemy has attacked our country. And it wants either to destroy us or to turn us into slaves. It’s just like in The Lord of the Rings – the orcs have come for the people. I have taken up the fight. My weapon is not a gun, but words. I want to tell people the truth about this war. I truly believe that it is the truth that will help bring it to an end.

That is why I stayed. That is why, for two and a half years, I risked my life, travelling along the frontline, helping foreign journalists cover the war, and writing reports and even a book on what I saw. That is why I joined the army, to serve my country. Once again: I could have left. Men of conscription age are not allowed to leave the country, but I have an exemption because I am a father of three children. One thought always stopped me: what kind of life would await me in Europe? The life of a refugee, odd jobs in a restaurant, canteen or care home – just to keep a roof over my head and food on the table? I wouldn’t even be able to support our army. Right now in Ukraine, everything comes down to one simple truth: you are either in the army, for the army, or against the army. That’s the reality of war. It’s as simple as that – there are no grey areas; there isn’t room for doubt or debate.

So, there you have it – that’s what I believe. This doesn’t mean I think our country is perfect or wonderful. There is much I dislike – the way things are run, the behaviour of some politicians and commanders. But I remember John F Kennedy’s words: ask not what your country can do for you – ask what you can do for your country. I stayed to fight for my country’s freedom. So that one day, when the war is over, you can come back home and live in a peaceful and free country. In the country for whose freedom your father fought. It may sound a little grand. But you cannot speak about values and faith without a certain grandeur.

Sometimes I look at our old photographs and recall the past. Sometimes I remember the first days after you were born. Your mum and I invited many friends over. We were the first in our circle to have a child, and it felt like everyone wanted to congratulate us. One of my friends asked me, “Do you feel like a father yet?” I didn’t know what to say. I was overwhelmed. There was suddenly a new person in my life, a person born out of your mum’s love and mine. My first feelings as a father were wonder, awe and anxiety. I was afraid to hold you in my arms, afraid to bathe you. You were a tiny baby, completely dependent on us. You cried – and your mum nursed you. You fell asleep – and she could finally rest. For a time, her entire world revolved around caring for you. I will never cease to admire this almost sacred power in women – the ability to create life, nurture it and sustain it.

It makes me sad that I have to write this letter at all. It is yet another visible and obvious confirmation that I am not with you. After all, if you were living with me, I wouldn’t have to write any letters. I would simply talk to you every day; you would see how I live, how I interact with people, what I do and why – and that would be enough. Children don’t remember our words, but our actions, and they adopt our way of life. Or they leave it behind, if we behave unworthily. The hardest thing about these years of separation isn’t the shelling, rockets or power cuts. The hardest thing is opening the front door after work and not hearing, “Daddy’s home!”

I wanted to write to you about raising children – but you know more about that than I do now. You’re training to be a nursery teacher; you’re with children every day. All I ask is that you don’t repeat my mistakes with your own children. Spend time playing with them while they’re still small. Be there.

We parents like to think we know which moments shaped our children. We’re usually wrong. It turns out the things that stay with you are the ones where you were watching and we didn’t even know it. Let’s talk about this soon. I have a fortnight’s leave coming, and I’ll be there to see you. I don’t know what you think you’ve learned from me, but I know what I’ve managed to give you: how to read, think and explore the world. And smaller things, like how to ride a bike. We went swimming together, and I decided to find you a coach. Now your breaststroke is faster than mine. You’ve learned languages and left me behind. That’s the greatest joy for me as a father: when my children become better and stronger than me.

Your ever-loving father VladVladyslav, Kyiv region journalist Translated from Ukrainian by Marta Gosovska

Gareth, chef, Bedfordshire

I don’t even know where to start this letter, son. I’ve never written to you in prison. It never felt right. Maybe because deep down I didn’t know how to. Maybe I never really learned how to be a father. My mum and dad were never there for me, and I guess I carried that on without meaning to.

But I need to say this straight. I’ve always been proud of you. Always. From the day you were born.

When we first had you, life was mad, but there were beautiful moments too. You walking round the estate in that little denim outfit, beanie on, that bit of baby jewellery I brought back from Miami – you looked the part, proper cool. Maybe that was my ego a bit, but you really did light up the place.

When me and your mum fell out, everything changed. It was chaos and I didn’t handle it well. I thought by leaving, going to America, searching for peace, chasing art, I was doing something right. But really I was just running. I thought you’d be safe with your mum on the estate, but I didn’t see how fast things were changing.

I still remember painting that walkway by your school, the same path you used to walk down every day. When they shut that school, it broke me. That place was the heart of the estate, and when they closed it, it felt like watching the soul of the place die.

And, you know what, Jamie, that’s where so much of this started, I think. The pressure. The madness. Kids from different estates suddenly turning on each other. It used to be a few scuffles, a black eye, a busted lip, and you’d move on. But it changed. Somewhere along the line it went from fights to life and death. From 0 to 100. Either him or me. I never really saw it for what it was until you said it yourself: it was either him or me, Dad. That hit me hard. Because I realised it wasn’t just about violence or choices. It was about there being no alternative. No space. No outlet.

When I was your age, we had youth clubs, breakdancing, graffiti, music. We had places to put all that energy and pain. That’s what saved me, Jamie. Art saved me. It gave me somewhere to throw all that chaos inside me. That’s why I’m still here. But when they closed the schools, shut the youth clubs and cut the funding, what did they expect was gonna happen? They ripped the heart out of those communities and then blamed the heartbeat for bleeding.

So yeah, there’s blood on our hands. But it’s not just yours, son. It’s a whole generation failed. A country that turned its back on you kids and then acted shocked when the streets turned to fire. I don’t say that to make excuses. I just want you to know I see the bigger picture now. And I see you in it, not as a monster, not as a mistake, but as part of something much bigger that went wrong.

Then came the call. The one that said my son had taken someone’s life. Jamie, that broke me in half. My heart just sank. All I could think about were two doors: one with your mum answering, hearing you were wanted for murder, and another mother opening hers, being told her son was dead. Two mothers gone that day. That weight has never left me.

I didn’t visit for a long time because I was angry, not just at you, but at myself. Because when I looked at you, I saw that bright kid who used to paint beside me, the spark in your eyes, the laughter. There’s a photo of us, me leaning over you while you’re painting in your little pyjamas. That one still gets me.

When you came to stay with me in Hertfordshire, I tried to show you my world: the records, the dogs, the art. I thought maybe I could keep you out of trouble, get you into something new. But the streets were always calling, same as they called me when I was young. And when the police came, asking if I’d seen you, saying you were on the run, I can’t even describe the feeling. All that success, the house, the money … none of it mattered. I’d failed where it mattered most.

You know that old saying, you can drag a horse to water, but you can’t make it drink. That’s how it felt. I tried, but maybe I didn’t try in the right ways. Maybe I just didn’t know how.

But I’ve seen you changing in there, Jamie. I’ve felt it when we talked. There’s more calm in you now, more understanding. The groups you’re doing, the reading, I can tell it’s helping. That’s why I wanna send you more books. Things that might speak to you like art spoke to me.

You said something the other day that stuck with me, about feeling anxious about getting out. I understand that now. Freedom’s a strange thing after you’ve been trapped for so long. It’s gonna feel weird, but you’ll find your feet. One step at a time, son. You’ll get there.

You’ve always been the stamp of me. Everyone says it. The look, the laugh, the way you move. You’re my son through and through.

And I love you. I’ve always loved you. Even when I was silent. Even when I didn’t show it.

Maybe next time I’ll start my letter with that, instead of ending with it.

I love you, Jamie, from the bottom of my heart.

Goldie, musician and artist

Stewart, East Sussex, trainer

Sign up to Inside Saturday

The only way to get a look behind the scenes of the Saturday magazine. Sign up to get the inside story from our top writers as well as all the must-read articles and columns, delivered to your inbox every weekend.

after newsletter promotion

When I was your age, I remember being really let down by my dad, because of the way he had let down my mum, and it shook me to my core. Up until that point, I didn’t think that dads could make mistakes. We didn’t speak properly for a while after all that, but then my relationship with him got a lot better, because I then saw him for what he was – a flawed human being who loved us very much. It is partly because of this that I have tried to be as open and as honest with you as I can about my mistakes, flaws and doubts, and many of my flaws I have demonstrated without meaning to – but it all helps!

You mean so much to me. I have seen all three of you grow into different strong, funny, charming, kind and loving personalities, and every single day I look at you and can’t quite believe that you are my sons. While I worry about how you are going to get on, and what pain you might feel in the future, and what heartbreak you might suffer, I never worry about what you are going to put into the world. You are three people who I couldn’t be prouder of.

I have been lucky enough to spend most of my working life doing something I love, and I would implore you to do the same. Work is hard even if you love it, but doing something you love or care about is one of the best ways to spend your life in contentment. I have never dreaded a day’s work, and I really wish that for you. Choose something you care about and chase that thing until you make it happen, at whatever level that may be. We all get caught up in successes and triumphs, but the greatest triumph is doing it at all. The greatest gift I can hope to give to you is to get you to stop caring about outcomes, and throw yourself completely into what you’re doing. That is much more enriching than any awards, fame, money or recognition.

More than that, though, the best advice I can give you is to show love and respect to everyone you come across. If you only think about bettering and helping yourself, I promise you, you will find life unrewarding. If you instead spend your time looking to make connections, supporting people around you, showing people love whether they’re your friends or not, celebrating their successes as if they were your own, you will find happiness follows. What you give to other people will come back to you many times over. That has been my experience, anyway. But please remember, most of the time I’m not sure I’m right.

I am sorry for every day that I spent not being with you. I am sorry for every moment that anything took me away. You are my best friends and I would trade every single achievement I have ever made at work for a breakfast together. Maybe not a breakfast. A holiday. An all-inclusive holiday.

My sons, you have become what you are not because of me, but hopefully not in spite of me. A happy accident maybe. Plus, let’s be honest, Mum is the better one, isn’t she? I know it’s easy to forget, but please make sure you find some way to show gratitude to her. She has spent every waking moment since you were born thinking about the best and most supportive ways to love you. And I think we can agree, she’s smashed it, despite being slightly obsessive about tidiness. I often agree with you on that, but don’t tell her I said that as she and I have to present a united front.

Thank you for being who you are – kind, loving and almost-as-funny-as-your‑dad boys who I’m so beyond proud I played a small part in bringing into the world.

With all of my love A flawed human being who loves you very muchRomesh Ranganathan, comedian

Anonymous

One of my biggest dreams growing up was to become a parent. I imagined reliving what I had with my dad and hoped that one day I could be even half the parent he was to me: someone who was always there for me at all of my competitions, waving a massive union flag.

As I learned more about myself, I thought that dream might never become a reality. But the two of you have brought so much love and joy into your papa’s and daddy’s lives. With so much love, and with the help of your amazing “tummy buddy”, what once felt impossible became real.

We have always tried to be as honest and open with you as possible, answering your questions whenever they come. And if we have one piece of advice to give you, it’s to continue to stay close to your incredible tummy buddy, the wonderful woman who helped make our dream of having a family come true.

I cannot wait to see the people you grow to be, although not too quickly, because time already feels like it’s moving far too fast. You make me so proud to be your papa every single day.

I love you both so much. Your papaTom Daley, Olympian

Alex, creative, London

John, scientist

The place I would always rather be is with you.

I know it can be hard to feel that when I have to be away so much to work. I can’t promise to always be there physically, but I promise you’re always on my mind and in my heart. You are what drives me forwards, and brings me back to anchor me.

No matter what, I am always with you. Always.

The love that I feel for you is unlike anything else. Putting you on my back is my deepest joy. Long after you’re too big for me to carry you, I hope I can still give you that feeling. That you are able to stand taller, see further and climb higher, because of the love that supports you.

Being a man means many different things. You will work out what it means to you. You don’t need to follow anyone else’s template. Just remember the non-negotiables. Self-respect, respect for others, respect for our environment.

It also means facing challenges. That’s part of life. And when you do, remember it’s OK to share your feelings and reach out. Draw strength from your family, friends and community. Vulnerability is brave, beautiful and powerful. We aren’t supposed to pretend it’s all OK. Taking off the armour helps us connect.

Each obstacle is an invitation to deeper connections with others, but also to grow, and to unearth the deepest parts of yourself.

More than anything, our challenges are a reminder that life’s river is one we don’t control, and that there is a greater current guiding our lives. Surrendering to its flow, swimming with the current, can sometimes bring us more peace, power and purpose than fighting it.

I’m always here for you, proud of you, and grateful to be on this adventure with you.

Please make time for joy. Seek it, share it, create it for yourself and others.

You are beloved and worthy of love. BabaRiz Ahmed, actor and rapper

Chris, Berkshire

It’s all right being a bloke. Let’s face it, we don’t have the odds stacked against us like women do. But it can still be confusing. So here’s a few wise lessons I’ve learned through 50‑plus years of being stupid.

The first thing is, you can be who and what you want. It’s all good. Life is much more fun if you try things out from different angles and ignore the voices of the cool, telling you, “Nah, no way!” I’ve passed on to you a few things that you’ve accepted already. You know to respect others and to care about the world around you. This is good. I wonder how this will manifest itself as you grow and change, and the world grows and changes around you?

You stand up to prejudice. You’re basically decent and kinda leftwing. You don’t like the Tories. Which is good, because that really is a red line. But back to the first point. I do like football. I also like motorbikes and beer and mountain climbing and other bloke stuff. And I know you quite like some of that, too.

But I also like cheerleading and pole-dancing, long walks, drag, books, foreign films, fake eyelashes, art galleries, socialism, fur coats … I know you hate some of that and can be mortally embarrassed by me, but, believe me, my life is much more fun and interesting for all of it. Try anything you might be intrigued by and sod anyone who tells you it’s weird. Weird is good.

My dad once told me that he realised too late that he was actually a good guy – someone he could like and be proud of. And actually quite good-looking. He told me that I was, too. He told me too late and I believed him even later. I hope I haven’t told you too late and I hope you believe me now.

Believe in yourselves. Love and respect yourselves and others. Stand up to injustice and ignore ignorance. Be who and whatever you want to be.

I love you.

Mick, trade union organiser and cabaret performer, Sussex

James

This is an edited extract from Letters to Our Sons by Stephen Graham and Orly Klein, published by Bloomsbury (£22) on 24 September. To support the Guardian buy a copy at guardianbookshop. com. Delivery charges may apply.

‘Just cut the wires’: why UK conspiracy theorists are destroying traffic scanners

The Guardian Sat, 19 Sep 2026 11:00:45 GMT

Sensors that monitor vehicle volume are said to be ‘electronic assault weapons’ by the ‘Blade Runners’ group

At the top of an extendable ladder on a quiet street of Ilfracombe, in Devon, an older woman dressed smartly in cropped trousers, a red rain jacket and matching red socks is chopping at some wires at the top of a set of traffic lights with a small pair of pliers.

A grey-haired man holding a takeaway coffee supports the ladder, while others, filming their activities, give encouragement from behind the camera. “Yeah, that’s how you do it,” says one man. “Just cut the wires.”

Posted to social media after the incident on 28 August, the footage rapidly attracted attention. To some, it was an act of straightforward vandalism; a woman in her 60s and man in his 70s were later arrested and bailed on suspicion of criminal damage and causing danger to road users.

Others, however, believed the woman should be lauded. “Not all heroes wear capes,” reads one Facebook comment on a supporter’s page. “Bideford and Barnstaple next, please,” reads another.

Most people view traffic lights as helpful landmarks that keep road and pavement users safe. To a group who call themselves “Blade Runners”, however, the traffic scanners installed above them increasingly conceal a sinister purpose: to install “phased array electronic assault weapons” on city streets that they claim can carry out mass surveillance and even cause cancer, dementia and sudden death.

Previous activists claiming affiliation to the movement have targeted Ulez cameras in London, resentful at their surveillance and the resulting emission zone charges; there have also been sporadic attacks on 5G mobile network towers, inspired by conspiracy theories that include the suggestion they spread Covid.

Ilfracombe is not the only town where traffic scanners have been attacked. In May, police in Cambridge appealed for information about a suspect after nearly 200 traffic detector units were damaged. In the same month in Sleaford, Lincolnshire, 10 units were vandalised in a week, with the council describing the conspiracy claims as “ridiculous”. In County Durham, a pensioner is facing trial after allegedly damaging units on eight sets of traffic lights.

To Susan Grant-Muller, a professor of technologies and informatics at the University of Leeds’s Institute for Transport Studies, hostility to traffic scanners is puzzling because “this technology, in its most basic form, has been around since the late 70s”. Activists targeting traffic lights do not generally damage the familiar green, amber and red stop-go systems, but instead target additional sensors installed on top that monitor vehicle volume and, in some cases, pedestrian numbers, to allow lights to be phased to help traffic flow smoothly.

“The cameras aren’t recording any personal information at all,” says Grant-Muller. “They aren’t recording faces or any details about the car. They just detect that there is something there, a car or person, and the length of the queue that people are waiting in.”

They are generally only installed at junctions with a history of traffic flow problems, she says – often at the request of concerned local residents – and are welcomed by Living Streets, which promotes pedestrian safety. “Better monitoring technology improves pedestrian safety at traffic lights and crossings, [particularly] when enforcement technology is used as part of a wider approach to road safety,” says Tanya Braun, the charity’s director of external affairs.

Sign up to First Edition

Our morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it matters

after newsletter promotion

None of this convinces those who see a more nefarious purpose behind them. Conspiracies about these scanners fits into a broader fear of surveillance and limits to individual freedom. This is part of a “super-conspiracy” that believers call “the great reset”, says Clare Birchall, a professor of contemporary culture at King’s College London, who has written extensively on technology and conspiracist thinking.

“These super-conspiracies draw all sorts of different things together to give some kind of shape to a whole bunch of different anxieties and fears,” says Birchall. “We’re all worried about technological overreach. Lots of people are worried about datacentres. And I often read conspiracy theories as a vernacular form of critique. It’s an everyday version of what we’re all trying to grasp.

“I’m not surprised at all that [some] people need to find a narrative to find their way through it, because we’re so disenfranchised when it comes to the collection of our data or what happens to that.”

Conspiracies often form in response to frightening events, agrees Stephan Lewandowsky, a professor and chair in cognitive psychology at the University of Bristol, “and if you can assign that to a bunch of evil-doers who are responsible, that can provide psychological comfort for certain people, because they’d rather have bad people do bad things, then realise that the world contains effectively random events that you can’t control”.

‘Everyone assumed it represented a poo emoji!’ 27 writers on the greatest cake of their life

The Guardian Sat, 19 Sep 2026 10:00:44 GMT

From the blissful threat of ‘death by chocolate’, to a book made of sponge and the lemon drizzle to end them all, these are the bakes that left the biggest impressions

The Sorting Hat sponge I made for my son’s Harry Potter party is not the best cake I’ve ever tasted. That would be anything baked by my granny, or the coffee religieuse (a choux pastry puff) I ate in Boulogne-sur-Mer with my mum. But it’s the most surprisingly edible cake I’ve ever made – a vaguely Jamie-Oliver recipe with buttercream filling and tinned mandarin slices. It didn’t only work; it tasted great, and wasn’t quite as teeth-screechingly sweet as expected. My one regret is that I over-pimped the decoration: it looked so sinister in the fridge with its cold, Sorting Hat stare that the next day I stuck on googly eyes and further sparkles. This perhaps explains why everyone assumed it was a poo emoji cake, despite it being a Harry Potter party with heavy-touch theming. That people thought I actually wanted children to eat shit is a shame, but it still remains my greatest culinary success. Catherine Shoard

My dreams of a cake fit for Marie Antoinette came true on my 35th birthday: with a single baby-blue tier, whimsical white piping and glace cherries for a welcome dash of gaudy. After taking it home in a taxi from Lily Vanilli bakery in London, I proudly displayed her for all to marvel at. Inside, the vanilla sponge had a raspberry and buttercream filling. It felt like my wedding day when I cut the first slice. By the end of the night, after everyone had tucked in and I was about 10 tumblers of prosecco deep, I fulfilled another lifelong dream: face-planting a cake. (Well, half of one.) I picked at those sugary remains for days afterwards. Hollie Richardson

My most treasured Christmas present of 1992 was the Hamlyn All Colour Cook Book. While I don’t remember cooking any of the savoury recipes – sherried kidneys and turkey in aspic weren’t quite to my 10-year-old tastes – the “family favourite cakes” chapter was a different story. I started with Mary Berry’s classic Victoria sandwich and graduated to her triple-decker chocolate button cake. But I found the ultimate in sophistication, decadence and all-round deliciousness in Audrey Ellis’s “fancy cakes” section: a glorious orange cream gateau. I lovingly baked two orange-zest sponges, sandwiched and smothered them with orange-juice buttercream, and decorated the top with jellied orange and lemon slices. It looked, and tasted, like pure sunshine. Rachel Dixon

The monumental creation is Nigella’s pear, pistachio and rose cake, expertly reinterpreted by my friend Sian. This entity represents the three all-important ingredients of the perfect bake. First, it was made by someone whose cakes always taste as good as they look (a difficult achievement), the kind of person who is tired of everyone saying to them: “You should go on Bake-Off. No, but really, you should.” Sian very much ticks this box. (She really should.) Second, it is part of the grand tradition of “birthday swim” cakes to be eaten with friends at 7am after a freezing cold dip. And third, it features the inventive use of a single candle to represent the numeral “one”. (It is a 51st birthday cake.) No cake could compete on taste, suitability-for-occasion or creativity. Viv Groskop

Before my father died, I had never had to organise a funeral. The strangest element was choosing items for a funeral buffet when I was so choked with tears that I could barely swallow. But my mother was keen that we offered a good spread for my foodie father’s send-off. I chose iced gingerbread mainly because my dad loved ginger. But a mass-catered cake sounded unpromising. Imagine our surprise when it turned out to be one of the most heavenly bakes I’ve ever eaten. Tasting as if it was homemade, it was perfectly moist, with a good kick of ginger and cinnamon. The showstopper was the melt-in-the mouth lemon icing. There was loads left over and it offered us some solace in the gloomy days afterwards. Anita Chaudhuri

The best cake I ever had was a replica of the notorious “Forg cake” meme, surprise delivered to my door by a friend who had never baked before. I was in the middle of a full nervous breakdown, and had been hooked up for a 24-hour blood pressure test the day before that had brought me to the edge of sanity – so this gentle, generous act of friendship restored my faith in better things to come. It was delicious, too: a superlative victoria sponge hidden underneath droopy pastel icing. Madévi Dailly

It’s not my fault I’m not a cake person. When I was growing up, after the birthday kid had blown out the candles, my saturated-fat-fearing aunties (it was the 90s) would scrape off the cream before serving the naked cake slices to my unimpressed cousins. One upside of adulthood is cake (and cream) whenever I want. On a recent child-free day with my husband, we went to Cafe Lewi, a tiny venue in Lewisham, Sydney, where they serve homemade bakes and pastries, as well as enticing meals and drinks. Their “vintage” cake is a thing of beauty – layers of chocolate sponge with a sultry crumb, sandwiched together with a chocolate ganache and raspberry curd, and thickly slathered on all four sides with a snow-white Swiss meringue buttercream, all embellished by someone who knows their way around a piping bag. We ate it for breakfast. Yvonne Lam

Every year since my son’s third birthday, I’ve put together a fancy fondant based on one of his fleeting interests: on my first attempt, when the theme was Pokémon, my Pikachu was so lumpenly misshapen that my son burst into tears. It turns out, though, that if you practise something once a year (with a few clay modelling sessions) and watch a lot of videos, you do improve. This cake, made by my wife, was a victoria sponge with buttercream and jam filling, but the wrapping – modelled, of course, on video game hero Kirby when he turns into a car – was all me. It tasted like triumph. Joel Snape

As a child, I had one currency: chocolate. The more the better. Nowhere offered a better exchange rate than my mum’s cakes, not least her chocolate hedgehog birthday cake: chocolate sponge, chocolate buttons for spikes and a chocolate-icing face. It became the best bit of birthdays, until I got too old for candles, left home and somehow went 30 years without a birthday cake from Mum, hedgehog or otherwise. Luckily, I’ve corrected this terrible injustice by telling her that all Guardian journalists are now required to have their mum bake them a cake … and she believed me. Thanks, Mum. Happy birthday to me. Rich Pelley

In April 2000, I turned four while on a family holiday to Nepal to visit my grandparents, who were living there. My parents had explained that it might not be possible to get me a birthday cake while we were away. For an almost-four-year-old, this was a huge tragedy, a fact that I shared with almost everyone we met. When the big day arrived, the hotel staff surprised me with a huge cake decorated with green, pink and yellow icing. I was overjoyed. I can’t remember what it tasted like, but I know I’ve never been so excited about eating a cake. My tiny mind was blown again soon after, when it turned out that my grandparents had also arranged a cake for me. Then my mum baked another when we got home. I couldn’t believe my luck – three birthday cakes! I was on a high for weeks. Lucy Knight

It was my friend Anastasia’s birthday party. We were watching Eurovision and had just finished stuffing ourselves with pizza when she brought it out. A vegan chocolate cake, covered in edible purple flowers, plump strawberries and juicy blackberries, it was more a work of art than a simple gateau. She had baked it using a recipe by Nigella (who else?) and the glossy chocolate icing oozed on to the plate. From the first spoonful, I knew I had finally found it – a vegan cake that didn’t taste like a vegan cake. As someone with an extremely sweet tooth who is lactose intolerant, I have tried many over the years. Usually, they’re too dense, too dry, or taste too virtuous to feel like a treat. But this was rich, creamy, and ridiculously indulgent, even without all the sinful dairy. I savoured each chocolatey bite. Ann Lee

I was 16 and on a school trip to Westminster. During our lunch break, I visited Caffè Nero, which, in the early 2000s, still had an exotic Italian appeal and a hint of sophistication. In a hurry, I made an impulse purchase – an individually packaged slice of lemon drizzle cake. It was so delicious that I still think about it all these years later. The cake was moist, with candied lemon peel, topped with fondant icing, and contained what I can only describe as bursts of lemony icing sugar balls within the sponge. I can’t remember much about the trip except for that slice of lemon heaven. I have yet to find a lemon cake that matches it. Georgie Wyatt

For decades, this no-bake wonder has been the birthday cake in every Spanish household. It’s perfectly sweet, moist and beautifully balanced, with alternating layers of milk-soaked biscuits, velvety vanilla custard and the smoothest chocolate ganache. Easy to assemble and incredibly forgiving with measurements, it is the perfect introduction to cake-making for little kitchen helpers. I’ve enjoyed it hundreds of times (I have a very large family), and it remains my favourite – not just for its wonderful taste and lovely texture, but for the fond memories attached to every bite. Esther Gomez

I’d worked for four years to write my second book and, like every author, was looking for attention. What I received from my mum was more than I could have hoped for: a facsimile of my book Who Wants Normal? made entirely in cake. The real cover was recreated in orange and yellow icing wrapped around sponge pages, and even the endorsement was piped on. It was akin to that episode of the Bake Off where contestants make roast dinner gravy out of chocolate, except that this was baked by a professional my mum had hired. Was it a book? Was it cake? I could never write anything so delicious. Frances Ryan

My very first memory, at the age of two and a half, is of a black forest gateau. No chocolate cake could have prepared me for it. It stopped me in my tracks; a vast slab of dense, dark chocolate-and-purple-stained cream dotted with posh, burgundy cherries – all far more sophisticated than the sticky glaces I knew from fairy cakes. And it was on wheels (a dessert trolley). I told the waiter I wanted a “big slice”. He tapped me on the head and said I had to wait. Strangely, my memory doesn’t stretch to eating it. Perhaps it remained a feast for the eyes alone. Either way, it set the cake bar for life. Emily Retter

after newsletter promotion

While I’m not a big fan of cakes, there was one that bucked the trend: a baklava cheesecake. I tasted this melt-in-the-mouth delight when I was working at Nuba, a Lebanese restaurant in Vancouver. Its flaky filo pastry pistachio base was perfectly complemented by a soft cheesecake centre. Three years on, I’m still waiting for the pastry chef to send me the recipe. Gabriel Stewart

In terms of looks, this cake is pretty underwhelming. It’s brown on top, and brown inside. There’s no icing, decoration or fireworks. But it tastes fantastic. It was the cake my mum always made growing up: a simple loaf with sultanas and raisins inside and, crucially, tea. The fruit gets steeped in it. Not surprisingly, it pairs well with a cup of tea and sends me back to the Sunday afternoons of my childhood. I think this cake’s feelgood vibes have seeped in deep, because whenever I want cheering up – not being much of a cake maker – I put the kettle on. Paula Cocozza

One of my best friends baked me a coconut cream cake for my 26th birthday. I’m dairy intolerant, so this type of whippy treat usually sends a shiver down my intestinal tract. But she made it vegan by replacing all the milk ingredients with coconut, even using coconut milk powder in the icing. It was buttery, subtly sweet, featherlight but satiating, with toasty, nutty notes. Five years later, my family still talks about it. My friend had been so nervous it would be horrible that she also baked me a backup cake. A fine testament to friendships in your 20s. Lana Crowe

Can there be anything more thrilling to a child than a cake trolley? The anticipation as it works its way towards you, pushed by a smart and austere waiter, laden with cakes lavishly decorated like something out of a children’s picture book. My sister and I, both about 12, were with my dad, who was working in Salzburg for the summer. One day he took us to this grand cafe, all retro Mitteleuropean magnificence and good manners. I chose a black forest gateau, probably because it was the biggest. I actually don’t remember eating it, so perhaps I was underwhelmed. It’s the delight of the trolley I remember, and – rare for a child – being able to choose what I wanted. I remember its name: schwarzwälder kirschtorte. The words still pop into my head, on repeat, like a spell. Emine Saner

When I was growing up, I was allowed to choose the cake I wanted for my birthday each year. At five or six, that meant a mermaid cake. Chocolate-coated popcorn “rocks” covered the sponge, on top of which perched a (non-edible) Ariel doll, her legs obscured within the cake itself and a mermaid’s tail fashioned from “scales” painstakingly cut out of icing. I seem to remember she also wore a shell-shaped icing bikini top. It possibly wasn’t the most sophisticated cake in the world, but I had chosen it from a recipe book and my mum had somehow made it real. I was thrilled. Leah Harper

I was in San Sebastián for the night – though it felt more like a week as we hopped from one pintxos bar to another. Ending the evening at La Viña, we joined a 20-strong line for Basque cheesecake from the restaurant that invented it. Sitting on a shop stoop with violently coloured Patxaran cocktails in hand, we carved our way through the slab. It was a dreamy custard mousse with a caramelised cut-through from the burnt outer layer, descending into a centre more liquid than solid. A rare dessert that felt both light and decadent at once. Emma Elsworthy

For my birthday earlier this year, my bestie Alix baked me a cake that I’m still dreaming about (and drooling over). Nigella Lawson’s chocolate Guinness cake brings together the three defining features of any of her recipes: it’s indulgent, unpretentious and sumptuous. The sticky cocoa sponge balances the subtly bitter taste of Guinness with enough sweetness to give an elephant a sugar high. And the sponge’s delicate hint of chocolate is offset by the sourness of the unfussy cream cheese topping dolloped on the top – making the cake look like a creamy pint of Guinness. Louis Staples

In 1970s York, children’s birthday cakes came in one shape (round) and in one of two colours (yellow or brown). Then, one day, there was Dougal. Bettys tearooms’ version of the character from The Magic Roundabout blew my mind – I had no idea a cake could be dog-shaped. Dougal was also a taste sensation: his shaggy coat skilfully fashioned from feather-light butter cream; his innards from sophisticated dark chocolate sponge; his face from a meringue disc with a cheeky, pink piped-icing tongue. Although now tragically discontinued, this exquisite cylindrical trailblazer will long remain in the hearts of many York children. Dougal walked so Colin the Caterpillar could run (crawl?). Emma Beddington

The grilled banana cake at Milk in Balham, south London, was the ray of warmth I was looking for last winter. Paired with silky whipped halva and pumpkin seed tahini, it worked divinely with a slightly smoky, yet delicate, sweetness that melts in the mouth almost instantly. Who knew a banana milkshake came in cake form? Kieran Yeow

Cake was never on the menu when I was a kid. My mum was, and remains, an anti-sugarist, who ran a tyrannical campaign of snack and confectionery suppression. But a memorable exception was made when I was around nine years old. I was invited to a friend’s birthday party at the local swimming baths, but my folks muddled the dates and brought me a day late. Not only did I miss out on flinging myself around an inflatable assault course, but I also missed a rare chance to get my paws on a slice of birthday cake. I felt crushed, but I leveraged my disappointment to manipulate Mum into taking me to a local cafe, which served the legendary “death by chocolate” cake. A large slab of multilayered indulgence thudded on to the table. After years of substitute confectionery, I felt its name was a legitimate warning. The warm, buttery fudge at the top was sprinkled with milk chocolate flakes, complemented by layers of sponge as soft as cloud, smooth salted caramel, chocolate ice-cream, and a final layer of sponge stacked on top of a dark chocolate base. Daniel Lavelle

When a traditional sponge cake – known as pound cake in the US and quatre-quarts (describing equal measures of butter, eggs, sugar and flour) in France – is done right, there’s no bettering it. I wouldn’t usually ice it: that dense crumb (from using plain flour, rather than self-raising) defies decoration. Turn it into a Victoria sandwich, though (as I have for my kid from the age of four), and all that air you spend seven minutes beating into the butter and sugar sets the mind afloat with possibility. I’ll bake multiple layers, then sandwich them with raspberry jam into a tall stack, which I lightly buttercream all over (I like a vanilla or white chocolate Swiss meringue buttercream) and cover with rolled-out fondant. Sometimes, I add sculptural elements – Matisse-like chocolate trees with moulded marble leaves, candy-stained-glass shards, misshapen meringue mushrooms, sidings of chocolate bark. I can say these are the best cakes I’ve had, not because I get to taste them but precisely because I usually don’t – no matter how thinly I slice the portions, the cake is simply inhaled before I get the chance. Dale Berning Sawa

Sometimes, the most delicious treats are the ones you’re not supposed to eat. At 15, my friend and I baked and donated cakes as part of the volunteering section for our Duke of Edinburgh awards. On this occasion, what came out of the oven dazzled and, for once, wasn’t burnt. It was the most delicious, golden, glistening lemon drizzle tray bake. As I sliced our masterpiece into bite-size pieces, I snuck a few into my mouth. It was the perfect balance of sweetness and tangy lemon, with a hint of earl grey tea. It was a guilty pleasure, but so worth it. Charlotte Smith

‘A losing battle’: will UK public service broadcasters survive amid US onslaught?

The Guardian Sat, 19 Sep 2026 09:00:43 GMT

Jobs and programme budgets in firing line at BBC, Channel 4 and ITV as they are outgunned by YouTube and Netflix

“I wouldn’t be surprised if the BBC or Channel 4 disappeared,” says one of the thousands of TV staff at risk of redundancy, as British broadcasters face what has rapidly become a fight for survival against US digital rivals.

“My generation grew up with Netflix and YouTube … Honestly, I feel like it is a losing battle.”

Over the course of the summer the crisis facing the UK’s biggest public service broadcasters (PSBs) – the BBC, Channel 4 and ITV – has reached fever pitch amid announcements of deep job cuts and talk of business models unfit to face up to the deep-pocketed streamers.

Earlier this month, Priya Dogra, Channel 4’s new chief executive, announced that 28% of its staff are to be cut, the biggest round of redundancies in the broadcaster’s 43-year history, amid a slump in advertising and increasingly stretched finances.

Meanwhile the BBC’s new director general, Matt Brittin, a former top Google executive, is pushing through up to 2,000 job cuts as he attempts to negotiate a dramatic overhaul of its licence fee funding model with the government to secure its long-term future.

And four years after ITV announced an £800m-plus plan to create a streaming “national champion” to take on Netflix, Disney+ and Amazon, chief executive Carolyn McCall has raised the white flag, arguing that a cut-price £1.6bn sale of its broadcasting arm to Sky is the only way to survive.

“What is happening is not unique to the UK, it is all across Europe and beyond, it relates to ‘local’ broadcasting operations,” says Sir Peter Bazalgette, the former ITV chair who has also sat on the board of the culture department. “I cannot see a future Europe where there are four or five domestic broadcasters in each country with viable financial models.”

US tech companies such as YouTube owner Google, Facebook and Instagram parent Meta, and streamers such as Netflix, have deployed their billions in funding to develop their businesses into viewing, subscription and advertising juggernauts.

The Silicon Valley behemoths are forecast to take almost $50bn (£38bn) in UK ad revenues by 2028 – two-thirds of the $74bn total – at which point 90% of all ad spend will be digital, according to eMarketer.

That expansion leaves a shrinking pool of funding for commercial PSBs, which have struggled to untether from their reliance on traditional TV advertising – a market that is forecast by WPP Media to shrink by 2031 to just £2.4bn, 60% down on 2015 levels.

Meanwhile, the predominantly publicly funded BBC’s licence fee income has fallen by 38% in real terms since 2010, owing to a combination of freezes or below-inflation increases to the licence fee and increasing non-payment.

The BBC has lost 2.7 million payers of the £180 annual charge since the beginning of the decade. Last year it lost a further 539,000, taking the total who still contribute to 23.3 mllion, the lowest level since 1999.

Brittin, now spearheading negotiations with the government over the terms of the renewal of the BBC’s royal charter next year, has called the model a “busted flush” and “insufficient to sustain a universal public service”.

The increasingly financially stretched PSBs face competitors with huge financial resources for programme-making. Netflix alone has a content budget of $20bn this year, and enjoys a larger share of UK TV and streaming viewing than ITV, Sky, Channel 4 or Channel 5, while YouTube is close to overtaking the BBC to become the most popular platform in Britain on the same metric.

“If you think about the shrinking money and budgets I feel we are heading toward a two-tier system,” says a senior executive at a leading TV production company. “It is great that the big US corporates like Netflix, Amazon and Disney have these mega-budgets and do produce great ‘British’ shows like Adolescence, Black Doves and Slow Horses but they are becoming in a class of their own.

“My fear is we end up with a system where the UK public service broadcasters will diminish to such an extent, while facing such big budgets wielded by rivals, they will become a bit like a cottage industry.”

The crisis in which Channel 4 finds itself has renewed talk of whether those who advocated privatisation to ensure its long-term survival may well have been right, or whether a tie-up with the BBC might build the scale needed to survive.

“Channel 4 has always punched above its weight and being a challenger is nothing new,” said a source at the broadcaster. “But it was never meant to operate in isolation – it was designed to be part of the creative ecosystem. So partnerships will be a defining feature of the new era. They’re a way for the channel to compete on reach and scale while maintaining its independence.”

The UK’s PSBs have a patchy record on collaboration, although notable successes include the development of Freeview, and have not been able to come together to map out a streaming future as viewing moves beyond linear TV.

Earlier this year, Carolyn McCall, the ITV chief executive, expressed her frustration that talks to create a British streaming champion comprising the original three PSBs had failed because “we all have such different business models”.

However, as the reality of the scale of the crisis facing the industry becomes ever more apparent, a new wave of collaboration is taking place – some say helped by a change of top executives.

Brittin has said the BBC is in talks to enable Channel 4 content to run with ads on the iPlayer, having told MPs that the commercially funded PSB looked “very subscale” given ITV and Sky are merging.

This week, Channel 4, which relies on advertising for 90% of its income, made a significant move to try to address this scale issue by poaching the £300m-plus contract to sell the TV and digital ads for Paramount UK properties including Channel 5, Nickelodeon and Comedy Central from Sky.

And although ITV, Channel 4 and Channel 5 now make a little over £1bn annually in revenues combined from their respective streaming services, which continue to grow at pace, it is not fast enough to bridge the gap from lost legacy TV revenues in the short term.

“Despite the attention that video sharing platforms receive, public service streaming is the untold success story of the year so far, outpacing viewing growth to YouTube and subscription video-on-demand services,” says the Channel 5 president, Reemah Sakaan. “Audiences and advertisers alike still want trusted, relevant and distinctly British content, and they are choosing our platforms as go-to destinations.”

The UK’s PSBs had realised as far back as 2009 that coming together was necessary to ultimately compete, but the British streaming platform, called Project Kangaroo, was blocked by the competition regulator. Three years later Netflix led the US expansion of the international streaming era to the UK.

The BBC’s Brittin has warned that the issue of scale is now more acute than ever saying UK broadcasters risk being “underweight” as global players dominate content creation and distribution to audiences.

“What is at stake? It is about the criticality of local content, and independent impartial news about our country,” Bazalgette says. “Content made for us, by us about us. There are some marvellous programmes [made by the global streamers] but that is not the same as an absolute commitment to sustained investment in local content.”

The quest for scale extends to working more with rivals, exemplified by the BBC’s recent deal to create bespoke content for YouTube to expand its reach with younger audiences. However, none of the UK’s PSBs have yet pushed collaboration as far as France’s TF1, which has made all its channels available on Netflix.

As the fight for the commercial survival of Britain’s biggest broadcasters continues, many of those affected by a brutal summer of restructuring remain unconvinced there is a bright future for the TV industry.

“I would say it is a watershed moment,” says one TV executive. “Our sector of the media industry has peaked, we are definitely in decline.

“If you are young enough your next job will most likely not be with another broadcaster. It is all about downsizing; it is where your skills and experience might fit into another industry. It is bleak, very bleak.”

Ed Sheeran thought fans didn’t want artists to be politically engaged. He’s finding out how wrong he was

The Guardian Sat, 19 Sep 2026 09:00:42 GMT

Twenty years ago, even Madonna faced radio blacklisting for being overtly political. But in our age of streaming, there’s less excuse for not speaking out

It must have come as a surprise to Ed Sheeran when all of his support acts withdrew from the remainder of the US leg of his tour. The American rapper Macklemore had triggered the walkout when he gave an impassioned speech calling for a “free Palestine” on stage and was dropped for doing so. The decision by the remaining acts to drop out in solidarity exposed a deep divide in the modern music industry. Some artists still insist on keeping politics out of music, while others expect music to speak to our perilous times.

After he was dropped, Macklemore wrote that Sheeran’s “typical apolitical stance was being challenged in a way it never had been before”, to which Sheeran responded: “I am not complicit” and “those who come to my shows do not expect a political forum”.

I think that the concept of expectation is worth probing. The idea that artists should make their political sentiments known is often dismissed as a parasocial delusion, one particularly rampant among young people on social media who “call out” musicians for their silence (indeed, young people are far more likely to be in favour of musicians using their concerts to make political statements). Artists aren’t politicians, the criticism goes, and to consider them as such distracts from, even compromises, the purpose of art as a forum for personal expression and of escapism. In other words, why not just enjoy the music instead of expecting activism from musicians, too?

The problem with that idea is that it treats a separation of art and politics as natural rather than something determined by historical convention. It wasn’t so long ago that expectations were quite different. There used to be a neater division between countercultural musicians who were relegated to the periphery and mainstream artists who would be disciplined if they spoke up.

The MTV era of music in the 2000s prioritised blockbuster, spectacle and glamour, while avoiding political, social and economic controversies. Artists were generally expected to keep politics out of their music. When Madonna challenged that idea in 2003 with her single American Life, which opposed US foreign policy and jingoism at the onset of the Iraq war, the backlash was heavy: she was forced to dump its “un-American” music video, and faced heavy radio blacklisting. It took years for the Chicks, then known as The Dixie Chicks, to recover commercially from the backlash they faced to their criticism of the Iraq War and George W Bush around the same period.

Today, the expectations that audiences have of artists are different from two decades ago. Partly, this is because the economics and the technology behind the music industry has changed. In the age of streaming, it is harder to silence artists who have made politically problematic statements – radio station blacklisting is far less fatal than it was before people discovered music through their phones and algorithms.

Interestingly, this greater political autonomy also means that the biggest artists take less of a commercial hit in their worst moments. After Kanye West’s antisemitic rants (which the rapper apologised for), his album Vultures still reached No 1 on the Billboard charts in 2024. On his most recent tour, he performed at AT&T stadium in Arlington, Texas, one of the venues that banned Macklemore from performing.

In any case, this greater autonomy pushes young fans to ask: why not take the risk? Why not speak? Particularly in the case of Palestine, it has often been smaller and less influential artists who have done so. Think of how the scale of Sheeran’s commercial reach, by contrast, dwarfs that of the artists around him who have risked more by speaking out.

Artists, both alternative and mainstream, have also set this expectation for each other. The stances a musician has taken on pressing issues are no longer just cudgels used against them. Rather, silence on these matters has become a source of shame.

Billie Eilish rebuked her fellow celebrities for not taking a stance against Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) in the US and its killing of civilians. The Irish singer-songwriter CMAT, who I saw at Glastonbury last year leading a “free Palestine” chant on the Pyramid Stage, had this to say while receiving the award for best album at the Ivor Novello Awards this year: “I have a very specific idea of what songwriting is supposed to be for, and I think it is to reflect the times through your own personal view so that everybody can have something to connect to and something to learn from years later. And now I would compel my fellow artists in the room, it is not the time to sit on the fence.”

The political shift in music also reflects a tonal shift. Artists have become more emotionally intimate with their audiences. I was struck by an analysis published earlier this year by the music data company Musixmatch for the Economist, which assessed lyrics from the Billboard charts to conclude that pop music has become “gloomier”. The most popular songs increasingly invoke sadness, angst and heartbreak.

Sign up to Matters of Opinion

Guardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and more

after newsletter promotion

A study in the Times also found that the musical mood has become more downbeat. This is in itself not surprising – listeners increasingly want authenticity from musicians and depend on it for a sense of connection. Think of the music of Eilish and CMAT, both of whom are popular with young audiences and praised for filterless emotion. They invoke that gloom, vulnerability and emotion – in other words, they communicate pain as a central tenor of their sound.

As CMAT said of her music, which muses on isolation, capitalism and disillusionment: “Everyone has the same wants and desires, and if you’re really honest as an artist with your pain, it will always connect.” For many young people, part of the pain they have felt in the past few years has been in witnessing the events in Gaza, as well as the rising global tide of far-right populism, the climate crisis and instability. So for a generation that is increasingly accustomed to having their despair made audible through gloomier music, why would they not increasingly expect artists to draw connections between their personal pain and what is causing it?

Artists, then, cannot assume that the old bargain still holds. Sheeran’s insistence on an apolitical arena of music is increasingly anachronistic – a position that has exposed the faultlines of modern music. Many listeners increasingly seek emotional clarity as well as moral clarity. Whether popular music has risen to that moment will be judged by history. But for now, as the expectation changes, it is down to artists to decide if they change with it.

Jason Okundaye is an assistant Opinion editor at the Guardian

After 20 years of my school dinners campaign, I’m a happy man. At last, we’re going to feed kids properly

The Guardian Sat, 19 Sep 2026 07:00:40 GMT

This week’s government announcement on school food standards is huge. It’s based on common sense and science. Beautiful!

More than 20 years ago, when I started the campaign and TV series School Dinners, I couldn’t believe that we had standards for dog food but no standards for the food we fed our children at school. I have never, and will never, stop banging that drum – even after this week’s momentous announcement on school food standards in England. Because it is so important we remember where we started from.

Children in the state sector are at school for 190 days a year. And if they’re eating breakfast and lunch there, the majority of what they consume each day is in the hands of their school. When we know that children are consuming less than half the recommended fruit and vegetables, but twice the recommended sugar, school food is a massive opportunity to directly improve diets at scale.

But eating good food around a shared table isn’t just important for children’s health. It’s a core part of a child’s social connection and sense of belonging. Well-fed kids are happier, have more energy and fewer days off school due to sickness, and their learning and behaviour improve, too.

It’s no surprise that 80% of teachers agree that unhealthy food at lunch and breaktime can lead to disruptive behaviour, and 85% say diet affects pupils’ ability to concentrate.

But we didn’t need scientific evidence to tell us that – who doesn’t feel and perform better when their bellies are full of the good stuff? Get school food right and the prize is massive. Not just for children today, but for the adults they will become. Feed children well and we give them a better chance of healthier lives, greater productivity and less long-term pressure on the NHS and social care from diet-related disease. That’s no small change when current estimates are that obesity, and its knock-on consequences, costs the UK economy about £126bn each year.

That is why it’s so great to see the government announce new standards, based on the latest science. It’s the first time in a decade. And it means, for this generation of kids, they will be nourished with more fruit and vegetables, fibre-rich proteins and whole grains. Beautiful stuff.

It’s a big and much-needed update, but we know that amazing schools, caterers and chefs can rise to the challenge. Through my Good School Food awards, we have shown amazing school food is possible and affordable, and it’s happening right now in schools across the UK.

Take Chef Russ in Bournemouth. Working out of a cupboard-sized kitchen, he has transformed the food at his school. Not only has the school increased the uptake of meals from 28% to 98%, there’s a waiting list of parents keen to nab their kids a place there.

We see this pattern in schools up and down the country, and we have to keep telling these stories again and again because it goes against what many people think they know – that kids simply won’t eat the “good stuff”. We have heard that for decades. And we get it, because the food environment we all struggle with makes it hard to eat well, and so this seems to chime with our experience. But school is different. It’s a rare, protected space where that noise can be stripped away.

And when it is, remarkable things happen. Children eat – and enjoy – delicious, nutritious food. The evidence is clear: when the food is good and the environment is supportive, over time school meal uptake increases.

What makes me excited is these standards won’t just sit on a piece of paper. There will be proper monitoring to make sure they are actually followed. Not to nit-pick. Not to catch schools out. But so we know what’s working, where schools are doing brilliantly, and where we need to deploy care, love and support to help them get it right. That’s where the School Food Project comes in. We know not all lunch trays are created equal, which is why we are partnering with Bite Back, Chefs in Schools, School Food Matters and the Food Foundation to help to make sure these new standards can really be for everyone.

These new school food standards will finally fix what is on children’s school plates, but it’s only half the job we have to do. A delicious lunch nourishes a child for the afternoon, but teaching them how to cook nourishes them for the rest of their life. You can serve the best meals in the world, but if a child leaves school without knowing how to feed themselves, that’s where it stops.

Sign up to Matters of Opinion

after newsletter promotion

That is why food education must be absolutely central to transforming school food. And it’s why I’m passionate about giving kids (and adults) the skills, knowledge and confidence to cook from scratch. My dream has always been simple: I want every single child to leave school knowing 10 core skills that will save their life.

My free 10 skills food education programme teaches kids basic, bulletproof culinary foundations – how to chop safely, balance flavours, cook a nutritious staple meal from scratch, and stretch simple, fresh ingredients into something delicious. If kids leave school knowing how to cook a fast vegetable stir-fry, a simple soup, or how to make a loaf of bread, not only will they be healthier now, but they have options in the future.

With this cooking superpower they can feed themselves, and their future families, on a budget. That isn’t just a life skill: it’s health insurance for life.

Jamie Oliver is a chef, restaurateur and campaigner

Meditating by the Dnipro: I’m an artist in Ukraine, searching for peace and a life between the missiles

The Guardian Sat, 19 Sep 2026 06:00:39 GMT

Sometimes, you can remember what ordinary life was like before Russia’s invasion. Then reality comes screaming back

Sometimes, where I live in Kyiv, I hear people say: “This feels pre-war.” It refers to situations that remind us of what life was like before. You could call it a “sense of normalcy”.

For example, it refers to being able to walk around at night, travel abroad or plan your life at least six months in advance. Simple, everyday things have become a lost luxury.

Sometimes people say this phrase simply because they feel that the war isn’t completely occupying their entire mental space: while attending a play at the theatre, for example, or reading arguments about Eurovision. But this ability to mentally transport yourself back in time doesn’t remove the reality that will never let you forget where you are. We are in a place where a theatre performance is overshadowed by the threat of ballistic strikes. Where musicians who could have gone to Eurovision are serving in the army. Where a drone yesterday crashed into the coffee shop that people are used to getting their morning coffee from. But today the coffee shop is reopening, and people head over to their new location for a cappuccino, scanning the QR codes posted everywhere, codes that can be used to donate to the military units the coffee shop supports. It’s a place where the missiles and drones strike suddenly. Just this week, another salvo in Kyiv and other cities. More than two dozen injured only hours after US Congress passed a sanctions bill allowing the country to target Moscow.

Recently, I had the opportunity to visit Poland for a few days. The seaside in Sopot, located very close to Gdańsk, is now a very peaceful place. In 1939, Hitler was here with his army. A hotel on the shore served as his headquarters during the invasion of Poland. It is well known that he adored this region. Was this his “happy place”? In 2009, Putin stayed at the same hotel to mark the 70th anniversary of the start of the second world war. All of this, against the backdrop of carefree tourists, made me reflect on the fact that every place has different stories associated with it over time.

I began to think about it when I returned to Kyiv. Sitting on the banks of the Dnipro River one day, I recalled my feelings in Sopot. I thought that a place has as many versions as it has witnesses, and these versions can exist in the same place at the same time.

Nine women in South Africa have been murdered since July. We are being told to be vigilant – but where are the warnings to men?

The Guardian Sat, 19 Sep 2026 06:00:39 GMT

The country has one of the highest femicide rates in the world, and women are yet again being asked to remove themselves from public life to counter it

When I heard the authorities advising women in and around Kempton Park, the site of a recent spate of femicides, not to walk or run alone, to avoid isolated places and to “remain vigilant”, my immediate response was anger. Remain vigilant. How groundbreaking.

Women are already vigilant. We photograph number plates before entering vehicles. We share Uber details with friends. We phone one another while walking. We watch the driver’s route and notice every unexpected turn. We avoid certain roads, certain times and certain conversations. We scan parking areas before getting out of our cars. We check the back seat. We listen for footsteps. We carry pepper spray where we can. We hold our keys in a way that makes us feel slightly less defenceless.

Women have informal safety systems built into our friendships. “Please let me know when you get home” is not simply a polite farewell. It is a survival protocol.

Yet women are still being killed.

Police are investigating the deaths of nine women whose bodies have been found across the Ekurhuleni district, east of Johannesburg, since July. Some were found naked or partially clothed, and several had visible injuries.

One of the women was Elizabeth “Tsontso” Moselakgomo, a 38-year-old who disappeared after leaving her home in Kempton Park for an afternoon run on 9 September. Her body was found three days later.

Now running must be approached like a security operation. Choose a group. Share your route. Check the time. Avoid quiet roads. Stay where people can see you. Keep one earphone out. Carry your phone. Remain visible. Remain alert. Remain vigilant.

But women cannot “vigilance” themselves out of gender-based violence and femicide.

Where are the instructions to men? Where is the urgent public warning telling them not to harm women? Where is the nationwide mobilisation asking men to confront their friends, brothers and colleagues? Where are the campaigns teaching men that affection does not create ownership and that rejection is not humiliation?

Where is the same relentless attention on perpetrators, effective policing, prosecution and prevention?

The truth is, women are not safe anywhere.

In 2019, 19-year-old University of Cape Town student Uyinene Mrwetyana went to collect a parcel from a post office in Cape Town. She was raped and murdered inside that post office by an employee. Her murder shattered the idea that danger is limited to badly lit streets and isolated fields.

If we must avoid every place where another woman has been attacked or killed, where are we allowed to exist?

We are told to stay indoors, although many women are abused in their homes. We are told not to trust strangers, although women are killed by husbands, boyfriends, relatives and former partners. We are told to choose better, as though abusive men introduce themselves honestly and arrive carrying warning labels.

South African women were killed at a rate of 12.2 per 100,000 in 2022, nearly six times the global rate, according to the UN Office on Drugs and Crime. That figure should stop the country in its tracks. Instead, it becomes another statistic repeated during interviews, marches and annual campaigns.

After protests ahead of the G20 summit in Johannesburg in November 2025, President Cyril Ramaphosa declared gender-based violence and femicide a national crisis. Women had already spent years explaining that it was one.

The issue is not whether government has heard us. It has. The issue is hat actually changes after gender-based violence is declared a national crisis?

Which institutions become accountable? What additional resources are committed? Are police stations properly equipped to act when a woman is reported missing? Are officers trained to respond to survivors with care rather than suspicion? Are investigations adequately resourced? Are protection orders enforced? Are shelters funded? Are survivors protected while cases move through courts?

Sign up to Global Dispatch

Get a different world view with a roundup of the best news, features, opinion and photography, curated by our global development team

after newsletter promotion

Who answers when commitments are not fulfilled?

The Commission for Gender Equality has called for an urgent safety audit of the affected areas. It wants attention given to lighting, surveillance, public transport routes, neglected spaces, police visibility and access to emergency assistance. That is necessary.

But the response cannot end at Ekurhuleni’s borders. Women are being killed nationally, therefore prevention strategies must implemented at a national level.

We also need to stop treating every killing as an isolated tragedy with no relationship to the culture around it. Femicide does not begin when a body is discovered. It develops along a continuum.

Through my work with young people, I see why intervention must begin long before violence reaches the criminal justice system. We need sustained education about consent, bodily autonomy, healthy relationships, emotional regulation and positive masculinity.

That is not an excuse for violence. It is part of preventing it.

Men must confront misogyny in their own circles. They must challenge the jokes, controlling behaviour, coercion and entitlement before somebody is dead. Silence is not neutrality. It protects the conditions in which violence thrives.

This responsibility does not belong only to activists, police or women’s organisations. It belongs in homes, schools, churches, workplaces, sports clubs, taxis, universities and friendship groups. It belongs wherever boys learn what manhood means.

I am not arguing that women should ignore immediate safety warnings. I am arguing that those warnings cannot be presented as the solution. There is a difference between sharing information about a specific risk and building an entire response around women limiting their lives.

The state’s responsibility is not to teach women how to stay alive around violent men. Its responsibility is to prevent violence, investigate cases properly, pursue perpetrators and build a country in which women can collect a parcel, go for a run, leave a relationship, take a ride home and simply live.

We have restricted ourselves. We have changed our behaviour. We have remained vigilant. We are still being killed. It is time the authorities, and men, tried something different. Accountability would be a good place to start.

Nolethu Ndude is a South African social entrepreneur, speaker and founder of We Mattah, a youth-centred organisation working across sexual and reproductive health and rights, gender-based violence prevention, mental wellbeing and youth empowerment.
