Deep cuts: how one Londoner’s fake vinyl empire sheds light on ‘industrial scale’ fraud

The Guardian Sat, 19 Sep 2026 06:00:38 GMT

Thousands of knock-off records worth a fortune are being seized in the UK by anti-counterfeit police stings

From 2017 onwards, Rehan Ahmed styled himself as a savvy business owner. But behind the facade of a successful entrepreneur lurked one stark fact: his empire was built on fakery.

On Friday, the man behind the biggest-ever UK case of producing fraudulent vinyl, who sold counterfeit copies of records by some of the world’s biggest artists including Taylor Swift, Coldplay and Kendrick Lamar, was jailed.

Ahmed, a 40-year-old father of three from Southall, west London, pleaded guilty to two charges of breach of artists’ copyright, and acquiring and using criminal property. On the first count, Judge Darren Reed sentenced him to two years and eight months in prison, while the more serious second charge led to a custodial penalty of three and a half years. The sentences will be served concurrently, meaning that the second will dictate the time Ahmed spends in prison.

In a sentencing hearing at Inner London crown court on Friday, the judge highlighted the “sophisticated and planned nature of the enterprise”, and the fact that Ahmed had caused “wider harm to the music industry”.

Operating under the company names Phoenix of Vinyl and Paragon Music, Ahmed produced counterfeit vinyl albums that he supplied to record shops or sold directly to consumers through online platforms such as Discogs and eBay. In 2025, eBay removed about 7.9m potentially counterfeit or prohibited items from the platform.

A spokesperson said: “Counterfeits are strictly prohibited on eBay. Where listings violate eBay policies, we act swiftly to remove them and may take action against the seller’s account.” Discogs did not respond to a request for comment.

Phoenix of Vinyl was no minor operation. When police raided Ahmed’s factory, they found 15,000 records. His previous business endeavours, around which there is no suggestion of criminality, had focused on takeaway food and bodybuilding supplements. But the booming vinyl industry appears to have lured him into the illicit market.

In 2025, UK vinyl sales increased by 13.3% to 7.6m units, maintaining 18 years of constant growth. Led by Swift’s 2025 release of The Life of a Showgirl, the total retail value of vinyl in the US that year reached over $1bn for the first time in four decades.

Rising prices of records inevitably followed this increased demand: some high-profile albums, particularly in “limited edition” versions, are now regularly priced at about £40.

While “bootlegs” of rare and unreleased material have long been part of the music landscape – originally on vinyl and now largely eclipsed by the internet – Ahmed was part of a growing underground industry making counterfeit copies of officially released albums. Over the last two years, the music business umbrella organisation the British Phonographic Industry (BPI) says it has been involved in the execution of 43 search warrants centred on illegal counterfeit vinyl and CDs, and seized about 600,000 items estimated to have a street value of up to £8m.

The fakes can be easily spotted when it comes to particular artists. The American star Frank Ocean, for example, digitally released his Grammy-winning debut Channel Orange in 2012, but only put out a vinyl edition in 2025, leaving a huge gap for the counterfeiters to fill. In my experience reporting on counterfeit vinyl, Ocean’s work is ubiquitous in impounded batches and the stash found at Ahmed’s HQ was no exception.

Ahmed employed “three or four” people at his factory, which operated exclusively at night. When officers from the Police Intellectual Property Crime Unit (Pipcu), a national taskforce based within the City of London force, raided the premises, they found a squalid mess, with chemicals stored in fridges next to cans of lager. Machinery, some of which was believed to be at least 70 years old, and stock were haphazardly arranged over three floors, suggesting little quality control. Receipts and order documents were found randomly scattered around.

In footage of the raid viewed by the Guardian, a framed silver disc apparently presented to Ahmed by “the God of Vinyl” is visible. A representative from the BPI can be heard expressing surprise at the absence of a cutting lathe, the very expensive piece of machinery that commences record manufacturing by producing the “master” disc, from which everything else is copied, which indicated Ahmed’s “masters” were existing records.

Amid the chaos, officers, assisted by vinyl experts from the BPI, found albums with a street value of about £1m alongside production equipment that is considered a relative rarity among illegal British record specialists, who tend to outsource manufacturing. The only things Ahmed did not produce himself were labels and sleeves, which he had printed by a factory in Gravesend, Kent.

I was led to Ahmed while reporting on what appeared to be a sprawling counterfeit vinyl trade across the UK. In summer 2024, I was writing a feature about the case of Richard Hutter, a Hampshire-based rogue trader who avoided a spell in prison, despite having been found to have made £1.2m from selling illicit records by artists including Amy Winehouse and the US metal band Tool under the company name Vinyl Groove UK.

While researching his case, I was told about a Midlands-based inquiry called Operation Typhoon, which had come to life with the seizure of 529 counterfeit vinyl records from a shop in Stoke-on-Trent.

Then there was an enticing new development. The Stoke discovery was followed by a new police inquiry called Operation Imatra, which had started with forced entry into “a three-storey industrial unit in west London”.

Sign up to Headlines UK

Get the day’s headlines and highlights emailed direct to you every morning

after newsletter promotion

Ten days before Ahmed was sentenced, I met DC Daryl Fryatt, who led the investigation. A relative newcomer to the byzantine world of vinyl, he was clearly fascinated by his new line of work. Midway through the investigation, he bought his first turntable, which he used to indulge his love of modern country music.

Phoenix of Vinyl, he explained, had already been issued with a legal cease and desist order in 2017, but blithely carried on its activities for another seven years – something Fryatt put down to the fact that systems designed to detect counterfeits were new, allowing Ahmed’s records to slip through the net. By the time raids took place on Ahmed’s business and family home – a pebble-dashed semi in nearby Southall – at 6am on 20 February 2024, Fryatt and his team still hadn’t grasped the scale of his operation. “Then we searched the premises and we seized a huge amount of records. We found all the production equipment there. And clearly, the factory did the whole lot: made the vinyl, distributed it. Everything,” Fryatt said.

Police and BPI experts faced an arduous task before they were able to bring charges. They needed to contact 108 record labels or artists’ legal representatives to formally confirm that copyright had been breached.

It took until 5 February this year for Ahmed, along with his brother and sister, to be charged with copyright infringement and acquiring, using or possessing criminal property. At a hearing a month later at Westminster magistrates’ court, Ahmed’s siblings pleaded not guilty and the charges against them were later dropped.

When Ahmed was first interviewed under caution by the police in May 2024, he painted an illusory picture of his operation, identifying a number of supposed business partners and presenting the police with packs of their supposed ID documents.

“One of them didn’t exist,” said Fryatt. “One was a heroin addict who struggled with life and the other one was a guy in America that may or may not have been involved, but there were no records on any phone to show he was. So we discredited his account, basically.”

In a second police interview, Fryatt recalled that Ahmed “decided to give us another version: ‘Forget all that: it’s my business, I’m the mastermind behind it all and I’ll take the punishment.’”

Between the first and second interview, Fryatt said, “his demeanour was completely different: he started out confident and cocky, but in interview two he was kind of crushed.” He said he would now plead guilty.

Fryatt believes Ahmed’s motivation for his crime was simple: “Money, getting rich quick … There was no kind of siphoning it off and investing it. It was all just spent.”

Peter Ratcliffe, the BPI’s new director of content protection, appointed nine months after Ahmed’s operation was raided, said there were “absolute shockers” among the seized stock. “They were warped: there were bumps in them. The sound was dreadful. The printing quality was awful.”

The ex-Pipcu officer, himself a vinyl enthusiast – the last album he bought was The Cure’s Songs of a Lost World – is ambivalent about the soaring cost of records, viewing his role as more about protecting quality and ensuring money made from counterfeit records isn’t used to fund other serious crime.

On 22 April, thanks to information provided by BPI vinyl specialists who were present at the subsequent raid, officers from Pipcu forced their way into a warehouse in Luton, where they found counterfeit albums estimated to be worth £260,000, by artists including The Beatles, Queen and David Bowie.

Ratcliffe said that at least 10 other counterfeit vinyl investigations are also taking place. “We’re going to find more,” he said, “and I think we’re going to have bigger finds as well. Just the industrial scale now and the increased popularity of vinyl … It’s all going to lead to very big seizures.”

From Shaun the Sheep to The Split Up: your complete entertainment guide to the week ahead

The Guardian Sat, 19 Sep 2026 05:00:38 GMT

Guardian journalism is independent. We earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link. Learn more.

Aardman’s woolly hero reckons with a mysterious beast and Abi Morgan’s lawyers-in-love TV drama gets a Manchester-set reboot

Shaun the Sheep: The Beast of Mossy BottomOut now The beloved Wallace and Gromit spin-off character returns to topline another film, with a Halloween-themed adventure involving the destruction of a pumpkin patch and a mysterious beast on the loose. Naturally, our hero turns to weird science to address matters.

Bad ApplesOut now A splendidly deranged combination of weird-wave European arthouse sensibility and the aesthetic of a classic British debut sees Saoirse Ronan as a teacher who improbably but deliciously takes justice into her own hands when one of the kids pushes her too far. There are also stunning child-actor performances from Eddie Waller and Nia Brown.

Queen at SeaOut now An acting tour de force, Lance Hammer’s hit from this year’s Berlinale stars the heavyweight trio of Juliette Binoche, Tom Courtenay and Anna Calder-Marshall (the latter two reunited almost 60 years after they played Hamlet and Ophelia together on stage) in a nuanced exploration of dementia and sexual consent.

Resident EvilOut now Director Zach Cregger has been on a run of form with Barbarian (2022) followed by his Oscar-winning horror Weapons (2025). It may be unfair to expect him to bring quite the same level of flair to the eighth live-action Resident Evil film, but at least it’s a standalone: no need to wade through endless lore before you go in. Catherine Bray

How the Light Gets InKenwood House, London, 19 & 20 SeptemberThe London leg of the world’s largest (only?) philosophy and music festival returns with an intriguing lineup of brainy talkers and brainy singers. The latter group includes indie pop duo Prima Queen and the recently rejuvenated Patrick Wolf, who released his seventh album, Crying the Neck, last year. Michael Cragg

Niall Horan22 September to 16 November; tour starts BirminghamNiall Horan and his trusty soft-rock bops arrive in the UK and Ireland for a tour in support of June’s fourth album, Dinner Party. Expect a handful of new tunes to sit nicely alongside hits such as Slow Hands and the gently epic Heaven. MC

Linda May Han Oh & Melissa AldanaWigmore Hall, London, 21 SeptemberBassist-composer Linda May Han Oh, a subtle collaborator with jazz giants including Pat Metheny, shares an exquisitely lyrical and intuitive duo stage partnership here with Chilean saxophone star Melissa Aldana – on both an original and classic repertoire including timeless themes by Charlie Parker, Wayne Shorter, Billie Holiday and many more. John Fordham

Bluebeard’s Castle + Oedipus RexWales Millennium Centre, Cardiff, 20 & 25 September, 2 October; touring to 28 NovemberRebranded and determined to thrive, Welsh National Opera launches its new season with a double bill that pulls no punches, pairing powerful one-acters by Bartók and Stravinsky. The casts feature soprano Christine Rice, tenor Peter Hoare and bass-baritone Nathan Berg. Joe Hill-Gibbins directs, with conductor Lidiya Yankovskaya in the pit. Flora Willson

Amar KanwarSerpentine North, London, 23 September to 3 JanuaryLyrical Indian artist Amar Kanwar is best known as a film-maker. This show functions as a site-specific installation of video work touching on themes of displacement, nationalism, violence and memory.

Raqib ShawCompton Verney, Warwickshire, 19 September to 21 FebruaryShaw’s dense, super-intricate, mythologically influenced fusion of Indian motifs and classical western art references is instantly recognisable, but he hasn’t had a major show of new work in the UK since 2017. Until now, that is, with this exhibition of atmospheric nocturnal paintings and tapestry.

Jenkin Van ZylSomerset House Studios, London, 24 September to 29 NovemberOne of the UK’s most interesting young artists returns with another disturbingly surreal immersive film installation, this time filled with holograms and inflatable cocoons, all about celebrities and obsolete technologies.

Rae Yen SongFact, Liverpool, to 14 FebruaryThe glowing pond at the centre of Rae Yen Song’s exhibition is filled with microscopic life and organic matter. It’s a living ecosystem that allows the artist to explore woozy ideas of mythology, ancestry and spirituality. Eddy Frankel

Celya AB Glasgow, 23 September; Newcastle upon Tyne, 24 September; Sheffield, 25 September; touring to 1 November The cast may have received the bigger profile boost, but it was actually members of the SNL UK writing team who dominated this year’s Edinburgh fringe (including main award winner Chris Cantrill). French comedian Celya AB is among their number: a master joke-constructor whose latest show grapples with standup’s darker side. Rachel Aroesti

Birmingham Royal Ballet: Swan LakeBirmingham Hippodrome, 23 September to 31 October Sometimes you just want to see a classic. No need for boundary-breaking, head-scratching new inventions, just a tried-and-tested hit. That’s where Swan Lake comes in. Here’s how Germany can defend its democracy. Banning the AfD isn’t the answer

The Guardian Sat, 19 Sep 2026 05:00:38 GMT

Instead, constrain it legally and fight it politically. The world is watching

Far-right nationalist populist parties are making the running everywhere from Washington to Warsaw. So why be so alarmed about a little regional electoral victory for one such party, the Alternative für Deutschland (AfD), in one federal state, Saxony-Anhalt? “Because it’s Germany!” is the almost instinctive answer in many heads around the world.

But that “because it’s Germany” needs to be taken apart, like the segments of an orange. Yes, because of Adolf Hitler, two dictatorships (Nazi Germany until 1945, communist-ruled East Germany until 1989) and two world wars. And yes, some of the language used by the AfD will give anyone familiar with Nazi rhetoric a cold shudder down the spine.

Then there’s the fact that Germany is Europe’s central power. The AfD’s national co-leader Alice Weidel says that when her party gets into government after the federal election scheduled for 2029, Germany will abandon the euro and leave the Schengen border-free travel area. What would be left of the EU then?

The great German liberal social and political thinker Ralf Dahrendorf, who died in 2009, told me more than once that he would only feel really confident of the resilience of German democracy when it had withstood the test of a big economic crisis. Well, the country is close to that now.

The final segment of “because it’s Germany!” is perhaps the most interesting. The federal republic’s entire constitutional, political and educational system is designed to prevent anything like the collapse of the Weimar republic into Hitler’s dictatorship in 1933. The federal republic should be a wehrhafte Demokratie – a democracy capable of defending itself.

So how Germany will defend its democracy is a question not just of European but of global significance. Looking at all the answers being frenetically canvassed in Berlin, I think the most convincing formula is: neither ban the AfD nor embrace it, but instead constrain it legally and fight it politically.

The German constitution provides for political parties that are “hostile” to its basic liberal democratic principles to be banned. Senior German politicians have called for an application to be made to the constitutional court to ban the AfD, or at least its most extreme parts, on those grounds. But it’s too late for that. The AfD has been a major force in the Bundestag since its success (off the back of the migration crisis) in the 2017 general election and, like Reform UK in Britain, has led nationwide in opinion polls. To suddenly tell so many citizens “you’re not allowed to vote for the party you support!” would itself be an assault on democracy.

But this is not democracy as the tyranny of the majority: the people have spoken, off with your head! It’s liberal democracy, meaning the outcome of any popular vote is constrained by the rule of law, human and minority rights, and pluralist, anti-majoritarian institutions. The real threats to German democracy today are less like Weimar in 1933 than Budapest in 2010 (when Viktor Orbán took over) and Washington DC in 2025. The mini-Donald Trumps of the AfD have reportedly been quietly exploring Trump-like executive and administrative devices they might use to consolidate their control. The Federal Republic of Germany has the right, the power and the duty to stop them.

Article 37 of the constitution, which allows federal authorities to overrule anti-constitutional behaviour by the states, has never been used in the 77-year history of the republic. Assuming, as now seems likely, the AfD forms the state government in Saxony-Anhalt, all federal powers, up to and including article 37, should be used wherever necessary. For example, they should prevent sensitive intelligence about Russia’s increasing aggression being shared with a Saxony-Anhalt branch of the domestic security service controlled by the pro-Russian AfD; secure the independence of courts and prosecutors, as well as the neutrality of police and civil service; and, I would add, stop any extreme politicisation of education and public service broadcasting. Of course, AfD politicians will cry “foul!”; tough. If, as they say, they want “another republic”, they can go and live in Russia.

Yet even more important than these legal and administrative constraints is the political response. At the opposite end from those calling for the party to be banned are Christian Democrats calling for the “firewall” to be abandoned and AfD politicians to be embraced as part of the normal political process. Letting them take responsibility in a state government will, it’s argued, expose their incoherence, incompetence and lack of real policy answers.

Talking and working with them will end up moderating them, as apparently happened with Giorgia Meloni’s Brothers of Italy. I’ve been tempted by these arguments myself. But evidence collected by political scientists suggests that a strategy of inclusion is just as likely to put more wind in the nationalists’ sails. And AfD activists are themselves warning against the danger of Melonisierung (Melonisation).

So Christian Democrats should not be tempted to get half into bed with the AfD, like a middle-aged man nervously edging into an extramarital affair. Instead, starting already this weekend with elections in Mecklenburg-Vorpommern and Berlin, they should more effectively combat it politically. Rather than defining Christian Democracy by what it’s against (the AfD and the far-left Linke), they should say what it’s for. To renew Germany’s social market economy, they should implement all the labour market, pension, tax and other reforms agreed this summer with their Social Democrat coalition partners – and more. Faced with huge external challenges, from Russian aggression to US and Chinese AI, the Christian Democrats – historically the party of Europe – should boldly advocate the European-scale answers which alone will give any European country the strength to stand up to giants.

Sign up to Matters of Opinion

Guardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and more

after newsletter promotion

But besides AI, Germany’s mainstream parties badly need EI (emotional intelligence). The key to the success of the AfD’s Ulrich Siegmund in Saxony-Anhalt, as with Trump and Britain’s Nigel Farage, is a kind of emotional communication. I’m here with you; I hear you and see you; I share your anger. With me, you can say what you really think and be yourself, because – whether or not I’m a millionaire – deep down I’m a normal bloke like you. So let’s all have a beer and march forward to an imagined past.

It’s fascinating to re-read the exiled German political scientist Karl Loewenstein’s influential 1937 article on “militant democracy” and find him insisting that democracy cannot “devise emotional formulas capable of competing with the fascist Pied Pipers”. Hence the emphasis on constitutional constraints. But in our transformed information environment, with its premium on attention, drama and passion, democracy can’t be defended simply by legal constraints and rational policies. Democrats everywhere need to compete with today’s Pied Pipers on the emotional plane, too. Constant presence on social media and physical presence on the ground are both essential.

Hungary’s new prime minister, Péter Magyar, and to some extent the UK’s, Andy Burnham, have shown how it can be done. So much will now depend on German democrats, and especially Christian Democrats, proving they can do the same.

Timothy Garton Ash is a historian, political writer and Guardian columnist. His new book, Europe in 7 1/2 Chapters, is published in October

‘A maelstrom of his own making’: how Ed Sheeran’s tour turned into a full-blown culture war

The Guardian Sat, 19 Sep 2026 05:00:37 GMT

Moment of reckoning for ‘Mr Nice Guy’ of music, who embraced Macklemore’s political cred only for pro-Palestine rapper to be dropped under pressure from billionaire

Ed Sheeran has long been known as the “Mr Nice Guy” of music. His is an unthreatening kind of pop stardom; he looks and talks like the bloke who might be standing behind you in a pub, rather than someone selling out stadiums. He champions other artists, he celebrates different cultures. His songs are about love, heartbreak and friendship. People get engaged at his concerts.

But this week, one of the most successful musicians in the world faced the biggest controversy of his career, and found himself dragged into exactly the kind of political row he has spent his career avoiding.

It began when Macklemore, the Grammy-winning rapper supporting Sheeran on the US leg of his Loop tour, used his set at MetLife Stadium in New Jersey to call for a “free Palestine”. He performed Hind’s Hall, his 2024 protest song for a five-year-old girl killed by Israeli forces, while footage of pro-Palestine student demonstrations and destruction in Gaza played behind him.

The backlash was immediate. The StopAntisemitism group accused Macklemore of “ambushing” fans with “anti-Israel propaganda”, a post amplified by the singer Pink. The Israeli-American Council called for him to be pulled from the tour, asking where the line should be drawn “when an opening act uses a global concert platform to advance a one-sided political agenda”. There was extra heat given Macklemore’s history: in 2014 he performed in a fake beard, wig and prosthetic nose widely read as a Jewish caricature. He was soon dropped from the remaining tour dates.

But then Macklemore turned the story on Sheeran, accusing his friend of a “determination not to take sides publicly”, and claiming Robert Kraft – owner of the New England Patriots – had pressured Sheeran by threatening to pull his stadium from the tour dates and urging other venues to do the same. Sheeran’s team confirmed multiple venues had objected to Macklemore staying on the bill. Kraft, a prominent supporter of Israel and founder of the Foundation to Combat Antisemitism, has a personal relationship with Sheeran, who sang at his 2022 wedding. In a phone call with Sheeran, the billionaire reportedly acknowledged the sensitivity of Gaza but argued Macklemore’s remarks crossed into hate speech.

“Taking a side can cost you,” Macklemore said. “Money, brand deals, sponsorships, festivals, private shows, relationships and access. I’ve lost all of those things. But there is no neutral position between the oppressor and the oppressed.”

Sheeran’s own statement, published a day later, did little to calm things. He said dropping Macklemore was not his decision and he was “deeply disappointed” by it, but made clear he was not using the moment to declare a position on Israel and Palestine.

He was “appalled by the conflict”, he wrote, adding that the “suffering and pain caused on both sides” was “a human tragedy”. “I am not complicit. Just because I choose not to speak publicly, it doesn’t mean I don’t have [personal views], and it doesn’t mean that I don’t care.” He wanted his concerts to stay places of “safety and sanctuary”, where people could gather regardless of politics.

The Palestinian Campaign for the Academic and Cultural Boycott of Israel (PACBI) was unconvinced: Sheeran’s statement, it said, “attempts to ‘both-sides’ Israel’s ongoing genocide against Palestinians in Gaza” and its appeal to “peace” left out “its crucial condition – justice”.

“The stakes for him would have been very, very high,” said Dorian Lynskey, the author of 33 Revolutions Per Minute: A History of Protest Songs. “Taking a stand meant potentially cancelling the rest of your tour, with all the refunds, people who work on the tour losing their work. It’s an enormous thing.”

Lynskey, who has interviewed Sheeran several times, has “a lot of sympathy” for him, but he thinks the attempt to frame the decision as something that simply happened around him, rather than a choice he made, has backfired. “He may end up being put in another position which is further away from where his sympathies lie. He’s now being seen as a supporter of genocide, when he obviously isn’t.”

Within days, every other support act on the US tour pulled out, including Finneas, Lukas Graham, the Irish band Beoga and Aaron Rowe. Sheeran’s Instagram following dropped by almost 150,000 in 24 hours; Macklemore gained more than 750,000. The actor Hannah Einbinder, Irish musician CMAT and Zara Larsson spoke up for Macklemore. Then Tommy Robinson tweeted his support for Sheeran, yanking the singer into a political camp about as far as possible from where he would want to be.

Suddenly, one rapper’s decision to speak from a concert stage had ballooned into a full-blown culture war. Many were asking: how does a man who has built a fortune on being liked by everyone end up here?

The answer partly lies in the distinction Sheeran has always drawn between having political views and making them part of his public identity. He has never been entirely apolitical. In 2017, he said he was supporting Jeremy Corbyn at the general election, while also saying he did not want to tell other people how to vote. He has campaigned on music education and copyright and supported charities including Crisis. In 2022, he performed at the Concert for Ukraine alongside other artists, raising more than £13.4m for humanitarian relief after Russia’s invasion.

Paloma Faith, who also played at the Concert for Ukraine, highlighted what she perceived as a hypocrisy. “He wasn’t apolitical by doing that and I don’t really understand why one felt more political than the other,” she told Channel 4 News.

The difference, said Lynskey, is that Ukraine reads in the west as a “consensus position” – “like Chris Martin wearing the pride flag, subtly progressive without risk of a massive backlash. That’s the realm Sheeran exists in: generally on the right side of things without talking about them too much. This time he’ll have had people around him going ‘this is how much money you lose’ or ‘this is how you could be tarred as antisemitic’.”

Musicians speaking out is nothing new, from Dylan and civil rights to punk and anti-apartheid – and neither is the price of doing so. In 2003, the Dixie Chicks faced boycotts, radio bans and death threats after Natalie Maines criticised George W Bush over Iraq. What sets Sheeran apart is that he did not say the controversial thing himself – someone he chose to put on his stage did. Choosing Macklemore was not the same as endorsing everything he says. But Macklemore’s politics are not incidental to who he is.

“He can’t say: ‘I didn’t know Macklemore was going to do that’,” said Billy Bragg, who has spent decades making explicitly political music. “Macklemore has been speaking out about Palestine and the war in Gaza for quite some time now. His song Hind’s Hall and its accompanying video are a central aspect of his set. Ed’s people must have seen that on every other night of the tour.”

Stephen Millar, the author of Sounding Dissent, calls it “a maelstrom partly of Sheeran’s own making”. Sheeran had chosen an artist whose politics were well established, he said. “By doing that you could say that was his effort to the cause. But to pull that back is almost like wanting your cake and eating it.”

David Hesmondhalgh, a professor of media, music and culture at the University of Leeds, said while artists should not be compelled to take a position on everything, “Sheeran arguably gains credibility from associating himself with an act like Macklemore whose star persona is based on strong political commitments … So his declarations of neutrality look a bit spineless”.

The episode also points to a broader shift in what people expect of celebrities. Social media and the sheer weight of feeling over Gaza have made the old split between public image and private politics much harder to hold. “If you’re not using your platform, you’re seen as doing something wrong,” Millar said.

At the same time, artists have become proxies for arguments much bigger than themselves. Lynskey pointed to figures such as Gal Gadot and Mark Ruffalo, who have become stand-ins for opposing sides of the Israel-Palestine debate. “There is this sort of proxy war fought out with celebrities. People have been protesting for almost three years and it doesn’t seem to have made any difference, so I think they’re getting more and more angry and frustrated.”

The journalist Lulu Garcia-Navarro made a similar point to CNN: “There’s an increasing antipathy towards Israel, regardless of left or right, and popular culture gives people a way in – they’re not talking about what’s happening in Congress, but this they can understand.” She pointed to a second layer, too: “Both the left and right feel like they don’t have control over their free speech … today there’s a perception that pro-Palestinian voices get censored. So it’s become a real S-storm.”

Lisa Nandy, the UK culture secretary, said she had “enormous sympathy” for Sheeran, calling his position “really difficult and impossible” – he wanted to platform his support acts, she said, while promoters were warning himthey would cancel shows over politics on stage.

Bragg also acknowledged the practical realities. “Undoubtedly Ed has contractual obligations, and he’d get sued and it would cost him money,” he said. “I can understand it.” But he believes Sheeran could have drawn a cleaner line between defending Macklemore’s right to speak and endorsing every word of it.

“He doesn’t have to come out and say ‘free Palestine’. Put purely on the grounds of free speech, he can say an artist must be able to express their view. He needs to let people know how he feels about billionaires deciding what can and can’t be said from a stage,” he said.

“Of course, someone like Kanye West should be banned because of the antisemitic things he’s said. But drawing attention to the suffering of civilians in Gaza is not a reason to lose your gig. Culture has to entertain, but it can also challenge.”

The point found an echo on the American left. “When you see what Robert Kraft did, to line up all of the stadiums to censor speech in that one specific way, it’s become clear this isn’t about one or two music artists – it’s about how a handful of stadium owners and the elite can bury an entire massive issue. In this case, the genocide in Gaza,” Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez told TMZ. “We need to be very clear about how dangerous a precedent this is.”

Lynskey worries about the wider lesson. “Are you just going to vet your support act for politics? Is the lesson that big artists learn that you don’t book anybody who might be a bit spicy? That would be terrible.”

Sheeran is due back onstage at Philadelphia’s Lincoln Financial Field on Saturday – with no support acts and no band. “I can’t think of a clear precedent where a star of that size has been put in that kind of situation because of support acts,” Lynskey said. It’s a sharp contrast to his last tour, one of the best-attended of all time; this time thousands of tickets sit unsold, some going for $65 online. Classic Hits Radio in Ireland has dropped him from its playlist “for the foreseeable future”, citing listener reaction.

“In Ireland, rebel songs were used to resist against British occupation for centuries, so the fact that Sheeran makes so much of his Irishness makes his stance all the more jarring,” Millar said.

Sheeran has tried to answer the controversy on his own terms: through money instead of words. Macklemore has pledged $1m of his Loop tour earnings to humanitarian organisations in Gaza; Sheeran and Kraft have each promised $2m for “aid in the region”. It is a way of showing he cares about the human cost without making any overt political statements – but whether it satisfies the people who wanted him to speak is another matter.

Paul Rieckhoff, the founder of Independent Veterans of America, who was inside MetLife Stadium with his two young children on the night of Macklemore’s statement, told CNN Sheeran might be better placed than most to do some good here: “Maybe Ed Sheeran is the person who can actually bring people together around this. But it’s not going to be by throwing Macklemore under the bus or by appeasing Bob Kraft.”

Bragg said: “By trying to be Mr Nice Guy and not take sides, he’s in danger of becoming a pariah himself. And that would be a shame, because it’s not his fault. He does need to make a choice here, and it’s one I think that will define him in the eyes of the public for a long time.”

I live in the ‘coolest neighbourhood’ in the world. It’s not as great as you’d think

The Guardian Sat, 19 Sep 2026 03:16:30 GMT

A wave of tourists and visitors has changed the character of the Seoul neighbourhood I live in and helped create a place that no longer feels like home

In 2021, I was asked by Time Out to nominate a Seoul neighbourhood for its annual list of the world’s coolest. I didn’t think much of it and put forward the one I live in, Jongno 3-ga, in the old centre of the city. Somehow, it got ranked third.

This week, the same area was named the coolest neighbourhood in the world. I should be pleased, but instead, I’m devastated.

All these lists seem to celebrate the same idea of “cool”: expensive conceptual art galleries, high-end restaurants, and the sort of places that cater to a narrow demographic of people who read lifestyle magazines. Most cities have these places.

But when I moved to Jongno 3-ga, I chose somewhere that was the opposite: humble, raw and completely unpretentious.

I was first drawn to the neighbourhood 20 years ago, fresh out of school. I recollect with sweet nostalgia being one of the few tourists at a time when South Korea was not “cool”, and people often advised me against travelling there, confusing South Korea with North Korea.

There were no English menus, but restaurants were welcoming. Shopfronts were rusty but full of artisanry, while alleys that went nowhere and were slightly dilapidated felt cosy. There were men getting drunk over bottles of soju who occasionally got into a brawl, but nothing that ever felt particularly threatening. I felt at home and eventually made it my home.

It was a refuge for society’s rejects: people with nowhere to go, some of the poorest in Seoul, residents of the city’s tiny-room settlements and people with disabilities. In Tapgol Park, elderly women sold sexual services to older men in plain sight. Outside the park, pensioners played janggi, Korean chess, on the pavement. Around them lived musicians and artists. In Jongno 3-ga, everyone was welcome.

For years, the pojangmacha, the street-food tents that serve everything from fried squid to kimchi pancake, catered to older people drinking through to the early evening. Then at some point – around 9pm – there was an unofficial handover to the gay scene.

South Korea is socially conservative and the LGBTQ+ community is still very much frowned upon. But come the weekend, hundreds of excited men of all ages came to let off steam out in the open, as well as in one of the area’s more than 100 gay bars and karaoke rooms. Jongno 3-ga was a place where people could be themselves, without fear of being outed, harassed or judged.

None of that was cool. But that was the entire point: people could mind their own business in a safe haven amid a culture addicted to consumerism and keeping up appearances.

That all changed after Covid. The street barbecues and pojangmacha are still there, but now they have queues, some up to an hour long. People line up for a seat, take their Instagram shots, and the neighbourhood that used to hide people has become a place to be seen.

With the crowds came the displacement. Gay patrons no longer take over the streets at night. The older drinkers have largely gone. The sex workers have been pushed out. The chess boards outside Tapgol Park were cleared away. Rents have risen sharply.

The area is now littered with kitschy tourist shops, claw-machine arcades and unmanned photo-booths, and, in the streets nearby, bakery after bakery, coffee shop after coffee shop. One by one, the small merchants have left, to be replaced with another dessert shop. It’s now hard to find the humble rice-and-soup places that fed this neighbourhood for decades. The once shabby and unremarkable place is now heavily curated, and doesn’t feel very “Korean” any more.

Locals complain about lost identity and gentrification but put on a brave face for the hordes of tourists, both local and international, who come to gorge on this area.

None of this is the fault of the visitors either. They were told the place was worth seeing, and they are buying exactly what they were sold. K-culture has never been more popular. From the likes of BTS to Squid Game, the whole world is looking to South Korea and keeps coming – and things are changing to accommodate for these tourist dollars.

But in a way, I feel part of the problem. I highlighted a place I loved for being overlooked, and feel I helped create a monster. Now, as the neighbourhood becomes almost unrecognisable, I wonder what effect these rankings have on the people who live in the listed destinations.

Jongno 3-ga becoming the “world’s coolest neighbourhood” is nothing to celebrate. I feel guilty for calling it cool. I’d take the word back if I could.

Five Great Reads: End times fascists, battling patriarchy in the climate crisis, and why Kylie still lives in our heads

The Guardian Fri, 18 Sep 2026 22:30:30 GMT

The Guardian’s weekend wrap of essential reads from the past seven days, selected by Jacqui Housden and Miles Herbert

Get this in your inbox every weekend. Sign up for Five Great Reads here

Hello and welcome to the weekend.

At the moment, it’s easy to feel as if things have taken a turn towards the apocalyptic.

Headlines this week predicted that AI could kill all humans, the climate crisis would exacerbate environmental disasters, and “end time fascists” were plotting their escape from the end of the world.

But there is hope among the pessimism. In this selection of reads from across the Guardian, communities are fighting back, finding joy in music, and staying loyal to the planet as well as each other.

Enjoy.

If the world didn’t feel bleak enough, some startling claims this week made the end truly seem nigh. Warnings from people working in the AI industry that there was a 10% chance humanity could be wiped out by the technology in the next decade was just one of them. But how serious are these claims? Here, six experts give their views.

‘Bizarre nonsense’: Hearteningly, scepticism around the latest claims abounds. Some experts believe the idea that AI bots could take over with their own free will is nonsense, and it’s (you guessed it) the humans who let things go berserk. “The AIs would not decide to do it on their own,” says Prof Alan Woodward from the University of Surrey’s centre for cybersecurity. “It’s the humans that are responsible and the AI is a tool. That is what we need to control, not the AI.”

Should we slow it all down? It appears the industry is divided on what to do, despite loud cries and alarm around the world at how quickly AI is evolving. “The path to better understanding and control of AI is more research, not less,” says Pedro Domingos, an emeritus professor of computer science at the University of Washington. “What would be truly irresponsible is putting up barriers to it.”

How long will it take to read: According to my AI chatbot (kidding!) just under four minutes.

Further reading: How AI ghosts and deathslop are changing the way we mourn, and this very excellent explainer on why tech companies might be only too happy for us to believe AI will “kill us all”.

As fires burn in Indonesian Borneo, and a looming “super” El Niño threatens to exacerbate already fragile conditions, a local group of women have come together to defend their community and battle the patriarchy. Indonesia’s first-ever all female firefighting team, which goes by the name Power of Mama, is made up of more than 140 women, with some as young as 10 years old. They receive rigorous training – from firefighting to operating surveillance drones – in order to help protect the nearby rainforests and peatlands that make up one of the most biodiverse regions on the planet.

Notable quote: “Because we are housewives, we are the ones that feel its effects most.”

Breaking down the village patriarchy: At first, the all women firefighting team faced criticism from the men in their villages. They would tease the women and ask them if they have “other duties to perform” instead of battling fires on the frontlines. But protecting residential properties and local farmland is gruelling work in unforgiving conditions, and Power of Mama members say they now work hand in hand with local communities.

How long will it take to read: About two minutes. Further reading: As the fires destroy precious Indonesian forests, critically endangered Bornean orangutans have no choice but to flee.

The hysteria surrounding tech bros and the super rich at the moment isn’t just because of the rise of AI. As the sharp and thought-provoking author Naomi Klein, and co-author Astra Taylor, write in their new book: “The most powerful people in the world are preparing for the end of the world, an end they themselves are frenetically accelerating.” So what can we do about it? Here they give their vision.

Plotting their escape: “On one side are those of us who have no escape plan, no bunker in the sky or underground,” they write. “On the other are those with rapturous plans to shield themselves and their families from the political and ecological fires burning our planet. Instead of improving conditions for actual people on Earth … end times fascists are plotting their escape, indifferent and oblivious to all that’s worth saving.”

Are we at their mercy? The authors argue that our own human networks could give “basis for a different kind of survivalism”. As they write: “Part of that involves telling new stories, stories that are truthful and inspiring enough to help our depleted fellow humans fall back in love with our one and only home and defiantly recommit to defending it with all they’ve got.”

How long will it take to read: Just over nine minutes

Further reading: This soothing antidote to the ills of the world.

Peer-on-peer violence is on the rise in Australia, with school-age girls making up the majority of sexual assault victims. As cases continue to grow, many victims have no choice but to go back to school and share classrooms with their perpetrators. Experts agree the current frameworks leave educational institutions unable to properly respond to this mounting crisis. Left to manage the aftermath of their assault alone, many female students stop going to campus all together.

Facing abusers at school: One student who experienced sexual assault when she was 14 says: “You go back to school the next day, and you just deal with it.” One social workers says she hears stories of schools not intervening, mishandling a report, or of female students having to keep attending the same school – facing their abuser regularly on the school grounds “many, many times”.

“Hypocrisy”: Prof Michael Salter, a leading researcher into child sexual abuse and exploitation, says if schools are teaching students about respectful relationships and consent, but are not empowered to protect and respond to students who experience sexual assault, “there would seem to be an obvious contradiction, or even hypocrisy”.

How long will it take to read: Just over three minutes.

Further reading: What the research says about choking as a sexual practice, and how to talk to your children about misogyny.

Born on an autumn weekend in a garage studio using a Mac computer-generated drum loop, the minimalist dance-pop opus Can’t Get You Out of My Head would go on to define Kylie Minogue’s career. Twenty-five years later, music writer Michael Cragg looks back on the dance tracks legacy and longevity.

Futuristic escapism: Released in the wake of the 9/11 terror attacks, Can’t Get You Out of My Head seemed to become a “hypnotic balm” for a world trying to make sense of things as the global “war on terror” dominated headlines.

Notable quote: “I really do believe that [Osama] Bin Laden and Kylie represent the polar opposites of human nature; the first all about cruelty without beauty, the second all about beauty without cruelty.”

Posh v Kylie: Back in the early 2000s, music fans were “obsessed with chart battles”, often pitting female songwriters against each other. On the same day Can’t Get You Out of My Head hit the airwaves, Victoria “Posh Spice” Beckham was ready to release her own lead single from her debut solo album. Kylie would emerge victorious, beating out Posh whose Not Such an Innocent Girl came in at No 6 on the charts.

How long will it take to read: About five minutes. Enough time to spin Can’t Get You Out of My Head (three minutes and 50 seconds) at least once.

Further reading: Kylie’s 30 greatest singles, and a refreshingly raw and real encounter with the songwriter.

This Israeli election could be the country’s last – this week I saw that for myself

The Guardian Fri, 18 Sep 2026 17:20:45 GMT

Spend time on the ground and you see how high the stakes are for next month’s contest – for Israelis and Palestinians alike

Candidates always say it, but this time it’s true. When Israel goes to the polls on 27 October, it really will be the most important election in the country’s history – and not just for Israelis. I saw that for myself this last week, in a visit that served as a sharp reminder of both what is at stake – and the role of those watching from afar.

More than one voter I spoke to voiced the fear that, if the coalition headed by Benjamin Netanyahu is returned to power next month, 27 October will not merely be Israel’s most important election: it will be its last. They were not referring to the absence of democracy in the occupied territory of the West Bank – which we’ll come to – but rather to Israel’s internationally recognised, pre-1967 borders: what you might call Israel-proper. There, the last four years have seen a sustained assault on the machinery of liberal democracy by the most rightwing government since Israel’s establishment in 1948 – a committed, focused attempt to remove the checks and restraints on its own power, installing instead a kind of elective dictatorship.

Democratic norms are breaking down all the time. While I was there, Netanyahu joined calls to strip two Israeli film-makers of their citizenship, as a livid mob surrounded the home of the parents of one of the two directors. The film in question is NAZA, produced by the Guardian, which features interviews with two dozen Israeli military insiders, their identities disguised, and which is named for the acronym euphemistically used by the Israeli military when calculating the number of civilians it expects to die in an airstrike. Unlike everyone protesting against it, I have actually seen the film: I have some misgivings about specific choices it makes, but that is irrelevant. A country true to its self-designation as the only democracy in the Middle East would not threaten with expulsion or violence those who say what its rulers do not want to hear.

But such egregious behaviour is becoming commonplace. Last month, Netanyahu’s wife, Sara, implied, without evidence, that Yair Golan, leader of the left-leaning Democrats party, had inside knowledge of the 7 October 2023 attacks that saw the massacre of 1,200 Israelis and the abduction of 251 hostages – the trauma of which still touches every aspect of Israeli life and looms over this election campaign. It’s part of a baseless conspiracy theory pushed by Netanyahu and his “poison machine” of acolytes and media allies to shift the blame for the PM’s own 7 October failures, but it’s especially despicable when directed against Golan. A former general, he leapt into his car on 7 October, drove south and personally rescued six of those who had come under fire. He is a hero of that dark day – and has threatened to sue Sara Netanyahu. As it happens, soon after her intervention, it was reported that someone high up in Israel had indeed been explicitly warned before 7 October that a devastating Hamas attack was on the way. That someone was Benjamin Netanyahu and the warning came from the president of the United Arab Emirates. Netanyahu vehemently denied the allegation.

It is a dirty campaign, filled with disinformation and lies, utterly in keeping with the degraded state of Israeli politics in the age of late-stage Netanyahu. Thanks to Israel’s unwritten constitution, there now remains only one serious obstacle in his way: the courts. He has had the judiciary in his sights since he returned to office nearly four years ago, not least because he wants to halt the ongoing corruption trial that could send him to jail. He tried to gut the supreme court once already, in early 2023, and, if he wins next month, most observers are clear: the court will be gone.

That matters for Israelis, who will find themselves in a Turkey- or Russia-style autocracy poorly disguised as a democracy. But it also matters for Palestinians. Yehuda Shaul, an Israeli anti-occupation activist fully aware of the court’s inadequate record as a defender of Palestinian rights, told me that Israel has been on the wrong road for a long time: “But so long as the courts and basic democratic institutions are standing, we can still turn back. If they’re gone, we’re heading off a cliff.”

I was with Shaul driving around the West Bank, seeing the changing reality there up close. I stood in the burnt-out and broken mosque of what had been the small Bedouin village of Mu’arrajat, its population chased out by settler terrorists – to use the formulation favoured, remarkably, by the US ambassador to Israel, Mike Huckabee. Through harassment and violence, they made the lives of the inhabitants there so unbearable that the villagers could hold on no longer. It was the same story in Ras ‘Ein al ‘Auja, where I stood among similar ruins, including a small, abandoned school, and where a herd of settler-owned goats now grazes. Shaul points out the vast swathe of land, more than 100 sq miles, in the east of the West Bank, close enough to see Jordan, where now next to no Palestinians live. Small wonder that former Israeli prime minister Ehud Olmert speaks of ethnic cleansing, or that UK foreign secretary Ed Miliband does the same.

I saw, too, in what the settlers call northern Samaria, the four settlements that Ariel Sharon dismantled in 2005, now returned and rebuilt along with 14 others either built or approved for construction. Their arrival sees roadside buildings demolished and olive trees uprooted, in the name of safety for settlers as they travel. And dotted, seemingly on every ridge and hilltop, the distinct, bright white caravans that mark a new officially “unauthorised” outpost, popping up with such frequency that Shaul can barely name them all – he estimates 250 new settlements and outposts have gone up since 2023 – and which are steadily encircling the major Palestinian cities, reducing them to isolated enclaves, thereby preventing the territorial contiguity that would be essential for a viable Palestinian state.

Netanyahu’s coalition, with radical settler Bezalel Smotrich in de facto charge of the West Bank, has directed this settlement expansion and turned a blind eye to the pogroms staged by the movement’s most aggressive wing. The best chance to stop it going farther and further comes on 27 October.

Those outside the country appalled by what they see in Gaza or the West Bank sometimes struggle to know what they can do to help. The temptation is to rally around, say, the rapper Macklemore, calling out “Free Palestine” from Ed Sheeran’s stage – but that temptation fades a little when you see that the same Macklemore once performed dressed up as what looked unmistakably like an antisemitic caricature of a Jew, complete with a false, giant nose. He later apologised, saying a “Jewish stereotype” had never crossed his mind.

after newsletter promotion

Or you might want to get fully behind Miliband’s sanctions package, which at long last signals that the settlement enterprise will not be allowed to continue with impunity – until you hear from those involved who say that the immediate impact will fall not on settlers but on Palestinians. That’s because the Netanyahu government’s predictable and predicted response – which included the closure of the UK consulate in East Jerusalem – has robbed Britain of its main mechanism to aid Palestinians through delivering development programmes and the like.

The truth is that, for those desperate to see change, the best hope is the ejection from office of what has been a vile, cruel, bigoted and lethally dangerous government. Be under no illusion: even if Netanyahu is toppled, he will not be replaced by a peacenik who will instantly lead the country in the opposite direction. It doesn’t work like that. But there is a bloc, unofficially led by former general Gadi Eisenkot, which is defined by its opposition to the man who has ruled Israel on and off for much of the last 30 years and there are campaigners and activists, such as Shaul, who are fighting every hour of every day to avert further disaster. They are branded as traitors at home and shunned simply for being Israeli by too many supposed progressives abroad. They need allies and friends, because right now they are all that stands between this moment and the abyss.

Jonathan Freedland is a Guardian columnist

It’s not just ‘spermageddon’ that’s stopping us having children

The Guardian Fri, 18 Sep 2026 16:54:36 GMT

Aubrey Foard and Nina Plummer respond to Zoe Williams’s interview with Camilla Cavendish about the reasons behind plummeting birthrates worldwide

I appreciate Zoe Williams’s excellent interview with Camilla Cavendish (Spermageddon, ‘greedy jobs’ and abject fear: why birthrates are plummeting – and why it matters, 17 September), but I have to take issue with one of her statements: “Of course, the climate crisis is playing a big part in that, but it still doesn’t wholly stack up – in the 80s, there was the wraparound threat of nuclear annihilation and it didn’t seem to dent anyone’s joie de vivre.”

Yes, the buildup of nuclear arms and the terror surrounding it reached its peak in the 20th century, but it was kept in check by policies of Mutually Assured Destruction: a singular launch of a nuclear arsenal would have instantly ended humanity.

As an older, childless millennial, climate change figures profoundly in my desire to not have children: the cause of climate change has been known for 50 years, it’s happening before our eyes, and there is not enough being done about it.

While it’s true that we may overcome rising emission rates with renewable energy, the current and near-future effects of the climate crisis mean we are in for a very difficult road ahead as a society – and that’s if we succeed. If I’m going to go through the financial, physical, emotional and psychological burden of raising a child, I don’t want to also have to explain to them that there’s a very good chance that they’re doomed, because billionaire, capitalist greed couldn’t figure out how to stop itself from ruining the world for human civilisation. Aubrey FoardBaltimore, Maryland, US

Camilla Cavendish notes that the falling birthrate is fundamentally “a story about pessimism”. I would like to offer an additional perspective we can begin to hold alongside (not in lieu of) this bleak view.

The link between women’s education and empowerment and the falling birthrate is well established. It is only two generations since contraception became widely available in western countries. It is therefore only a split second since human beings have collectively been given the opportunity to consider what other forms of joy, meaning and fulfilment are available to us as a species. While children are an enormous source of joy and meaning for many, we are now also discovering other ways to build beautiful, meaningful, fulfilling lives that include loving communities of non-biological kin, as well as deep affinity for our home and the other beings that inhabit it.

Beyond pessimism, choosing not to have children or to have fewer children might be the exact investment of hope in the future that Cavendish is struggling to see. It is not just an act of “giving up”, but an investment in the belief that the decisions we make today can create a better future. By acting now to reduce the strain on the planet while simultaneously reducing competition for future generations; by becoming more mindful of our individual limitations as potential parents as well as the systemic limitations of our circumstances; by considering deeply and ethically whether here and now is the best time to bring more people into the world; by learning to savour deep connections alongside our biological relatives; and by finding a story of hope, meaning and fulfilment beyond the cycle of biological reproduction alone, people, and women in particular, might be making hope out of the freedom that has been offered through being able to control our own fertility.

For some, choosing not to have children, or choosing to have fewer children, in order to dedicate ourselves more fully to helping, as well as savouring, the world already here, might be as much an act of hope as deciding to have (more) children is for others. Nina PlummerEdinburgh

On assisted dying, MPs grappled with a difficult bill

The Guardian Fri, 18 Sep 2026 16:53:26 GMT

Readers respond to the bill’s narrow defeat in the Commons earlier this month

For many, the failure of the assisted dying bill (MPs vote against legalising assisted dying in England and Wales, 11 September) has brought relief that a manifestly unsafe law will not be entering the statute book. But it should also prompt reflection about how it got this far.

Two hundred and seventy MPs voted for the bill despite multiple warnings from the medical royal colleges and other professional groups responsible for implementing it that it was unsafe and unworkable. Supportive MPs appeared to be voting on an abstract principle rather than engaging with the concerns raised.

But an MP’s role is not that of a campaigner. If MPs believe there is a case for assisting some people to end their lives, their role is to consider whether and how that could be achieved safely. Instead, parliament was presented with the latest iteration of a proposal first drafted in the 1930s by medical eugenicist Killick Millard, who held disturbing views about “a last service to society by relieving it of a useless burden”. His proposal has returned to parliament repeatedly over the past century, vigorously promoted by the organisation he founded, now calling itself Dignity in Dying. Only its justification, not its content, has been updated as social values have changed.

If parliament returns to this issue, it should approach it afresh and honestly grapple with the complex ethical and practical trade-offs. I, and many others with relevant expertise, would welcome the opportunity to help. Lucy ThomasPalliative care and public health doctor

Andy Burnham talked at length about the importance of leadership in his recent campaigns. His decision to abstain in the assisted dying bill gave a clear compass bearing to those Labour MPs keen to follow their leader. It led to the defeat of the bill and will literally cause untold suffering to innocent citizens. This is not leadership, and to hide behind the barricade of “we must improve social care and palliative care first” is disingenuous in the extreme. Gary NethercottWoodbridge, Suffolk

Sweden’s soul and worrying political shift

The Guardian Fri, 18 Sep 2026 16:52:44 GMT

Alvin Engström and Jean Fridh respond to an article by Martin Gelin in which he argues that the country has entered a new era of cruelty

I am writing in response to Martin Gelin’s article (How Sweden lost its soul – and stopped being Sweden, 11 September). Gelin is right to lament how far Swedish politics has moved from the liberal internationalism of the Fredrik Reinfeldt era. Having grown up in Malmö, I have seen how border controls with Denmark affect an Öresund region whose everyday life has long depended on easy movement across the strait. Gelin is right to see this retreat from openness as consequential.

But to say that Sweden has therefore “lost its soul” goes too far. Its political shift is neither uniquely Swedish nor evidence that the country has somehow ceased to be itself. Reinfeldt’s “open your hearts” Sweden faded in much the same European political moment as Angela Merkel’s “Wir schaffen das” Germany. Across the European mainland, mainstream parties have adopted more restrictive positions on migration.

The cases involving British citizens that Gelin describes are troubling, but Britain’s departure from the EU is also part of the explanation for why Britons in Sweden now face immigration rules from which freedom of movement once spared them. Sweden has changed. So has Britain. Neither exists in a vacuum.

There is nothing wrong with romanticising an open, internationalist Sweden. As a young Swede studying at Cambridge, I am susceptible to that image myself. But defining one particular political settlement as Sweden’s “soul” risks turning nostalgia into national essentialism.

Perhaps Jantelagen – the Scandinavian suspicion of thinking oneself exceptional – offers a more Swedish conclusion. We should not imagine that our political upheavals make us uniquely fallen. Sweden has changed, considerably and sometimes regrettably. It has not stopped being Sweden. Alvin EngströmCambridge

Martin Gelin’s analysis of how Sweden is losing its soul rings true – unfortunately. After living in Sweden for 33 years, I have never felt more like a foreigner than I do now. I am British (of Scottish origin) and moved to Sweden in 1993, at the age of 37, to live with my Swedish husband and our two children. I remember being so impressed by the social benefits, the access to good and affordable childcare and the job opportunities for women – precisely the ideals Martin describes. Over the past 10. years, opposition to immigration has grown in the wake of the so-called refugee “flood” of 2015, when the door was wide open. Sadly, that door is now permanently closed, and locked.

In recent years, I have repeatedly been asked whether I consider myself Swedish (I have dual nationality). At first, I didn’t think much of it, but over time, I began to find the question very irritating. On one occasion, an older Swedish woman said it didn’t matter if I didn’t feel Swedish, because “we see you as one of us anyway”. I am ashamed to admit that I snapped at her over the word “us”; I know she meant well, but it made me realise just how divisive the question was. The mere fact that it was being asked by nice, ordinary, polite people was playing right into the hands of the far right.

I love my life in Sweden and have no plans to move, but the divisiveness has got under my skin and is hard to ignore. Jean FridhKatrineholm, Sweden

Spot the conversation hogger – and do something about it

The Guardian Fri, 18 Sep 2026 16:50:11 GMT

Penelope Mavor suggests that listening is not a passive act, so you could interrupt the flow

These conversational hoggers … don’t they know we were born with two ears and one mouth for a reason? Thank you, Anita Chaudhuri, for a fun, well observed and useful article (‘But enough about you …’ How to survive in a world of monologuists, interrupters and trauma dumpers, 13 September).

It is an interesting reflection to see which of the five hoggers more frequently turn up in our own lives. As a people pleaser and introvert, I have a track record of meeting many monologuists. I pretend to listen, but secretly resent them and their audacity. I just want them to ask about me.

I have learned that although interruption can feel violent, sometimes it is a courageous act. When the speaker has just lost connection with the audience and themselves, we have to bring them back. That is what I loved most about the article – it reminded us that we do have options. We can start noticing how we turn up. How am I listening and speaking? What is my responsibility here?

A great listener can help to transform the conversation – listening is not a passive act. And in talking, am I actually being interesting? Am I talking as if being listened to?

Life is always inviting us into a conversation … with ourselves and each other. Penelope MavorDirector, Earth Converse

The Guardian view on NAZA’s persecuted directors: journalism is not treason

The Guardian Fri, 18 Sep 2026 16:46:30 GMT

Politicians who threaten filmmakers rather than investigate alleged military crimes expose not strength but a leadership frightened of the evidence

Across Israel, politicians, military leaders and much of the media are trying to discredit a documentary that almost none of them have seen. Produced by the Guardian, NAZA examines the AI-powered targeting systems used by the Israel Defense Forces to bombard Gaza after Hamas’s brutal 7 October 2023 attacks. Named after the Israeli military acronym euphemistically used for “collateral damage”, NAZA features interviews with 24 anonymous insiders who reflect on their role in the death-dealing. Israeli leaders have branded the film a “blood libel” and “fiction”. Its Oscar-winning directors, Rachel Szor and Yuval Abraham, face being stripped of their citizenship for treason.

This is absurd. NAZA shows how bureaucratic distance and routine can turn extreme violence into ordinary work. More than 73,000 Palestinians, including more than 20,000 children, have been killed in the campaign by Israel’s military. A democracy that values life would at least investigate the film’s claims. Instead Israel’s government, which says it is committed to democratic accountability, is attacking journalists.

The allegations in NAZA come from military insiders. For many, it does not appear to be remorse that drives them to speak out. Some are proud of what they have done. One recalls the “insane fun” of planning airstrikes in Gaza. Crucially, Israeli soldiers describe the military accepting large numbers of Palestinian casualties as the price for killing a single Hamas operative. When civilian fatalities rise to as many as hundreds for one enemy combatant, proportionality looks less like a military assessment and more like a licence for mass death.

NAZA’s story is not only about death and destruction but also some of the people behind it: polite, educated members of Israel’s liberal middle class, much like the directors themselves. They built and operated a system that told them women and children would die in large numbers. Yet they told themselves that responsibility for the deaths of innocent Palestinians lay elsewhere. The acronym, NAZA, turns possible fatalities into a number per target. By the time an operator approves a strike, morality has disappeared up the chain of command.

An election campaign has seen Israeli politicians shamefully weaponise controversy to outflank each other on the right. If such leaders are saying that the conduct of the Israeli military is beyond independent review, that can hardly be consistent with the commitment to the rule of law. Israel’s government might invoke national security to defend its actions. But the film builds on revelations first published by the Israeli-Palestinian publication +972 Magazine, the Hebrew-language outlet Local Call and the Guardian between 2023 and 2025. Ominously, Israel’s domestic intelligence service may be involved in a leak investigation. By turning the army on the documentary’s directors, Israel is making an example of them. Far-right activists target their families by making threats. If the filmmakers were to return to Israel now, their lives might well be in danger.

The Committee to Protect Journalists and 10 other press-freedom groups have warned that Israel must protect its journalists and filmmakers – not brand them traitors and paint targets on their backs. Yet the country’s prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, has seized on the controversy to threaten anyone who “defames” Israeli soldiers with loss of citizenship. Rather than investigate alleged crimes, he would punish those who expose them. Israel’s leaders ought to be protecting those who scrutinise power, not pointing a mob towards them.

The Guardian view on youth unemployment: too few jobs in too many places

The Guardian Fri, 18 Sep 2026 16:45:29 GMT

Young people in Britain’s poorer towns have far fewer opportunities. Changing this will require targeted support – and industrial strategy

The ideas that Neets (young people not in education, employment or training) simply aren’t trying hard enough to find a job, or don’t want one, are “myths,” Alan Milburn wrote in his interim report on the subject earlier this year – “sometimes cruel ones”. Although 84% of Neets say they want to work, their prospects are unfairly limited by where they live. Rotherham has one suitable vacancy for every 22 young adults. The Cotswolds has one for every four. For too many young people, particularly those in deprived parts of Britain, there simply aren’t enough jobs.

This is the finding from an index published last week by the Institute for Public Policy Research (IPPR), which ranked British towns according to the availability of jobs for young people. Like so many features of Britain’s Neet crisis, from poor mental health to school drop-out rates, the index is a map of disadvantage. At the top are affluent towns in southern England that account for nine in 10 of the areas with the highest numbers of vacancies. At the bottom are places such as Inverclyde and East Renfrewshire, where young people might once have followed their parents into manufacturing and industry. Deindustrialisation destroyed those jobs, and such places never recovered.

Given that half of the rise in Neets aged 18 to 24 since 2019 is due to changes in the labour market, jobs are a good place for the government to focus. In 2024, the Starmer government launched a “youth guarantee,” including a pilot jobs programme that provides six months’ paid work to 18 to 24-year-olds who have been receiving universal credit for 18 months. This was a positive step, but 18 months is far too long for young people to wait for support, and almost half of Neets don’t claim benefits, so aren’t eligible for this scheme.

The IPPR has called for the creation of a new “youth contract”, comprising short-term placements for all people at risk of becoming Neet in areas where jobs are scarce, more apprenticeships at the smaller firms that dominate Britain’s labour market, and more dedicated work coaches. These would all be improvements to the status quo. But if today’s young people are to find employment that will sustain them into adulthood, the government will need an industrial strategy capable of creating long-term opportunities in places where few exist.

The devolution of vocational training to local authorities, which are better placed to understand the demands of regional labour markets than Whitehall civil servants, is welcome. But ministers will need a dose of realism about where “good” jobs will come from. Andy Burnham’s talk of “reindustrialising” regions resembles a Westminster pipe dream. As manufacturing has developed, it has lost the ability to reliably create widespread employment. Even in the US and China, where governments have generously subsidised industry, manufacturing jobs continue to fall as a share of total employment.

As the economist Dani Rodrik recently observed in an essay collection about reindustrialisation, much of Britain’s future employment won’t be in manufacturing or high-productivity service sectors, but in industries such as retail, hospitality and care. If Mr Burnham wants to create “good growth in every postcode”, his government must transform the conditions of work in these industries so they provide gainful employment – and opportunities for today’s young people to build future careers.

Premier League action, Celtic v Rangers, T20 cricket and NFL – follow with us

Michael Butler rises early to barge open the door to Saturday’s football activity. After a summer spend in excess of £300m, things were supposed to be different this season ⁠after successive 17th-placed finishes.
