Defeat ended Newcastle’s unbeaten start this season and an injury-hit squad now face high-flying Hull at St James’ Park. Sergej Jakirovic’s side are fourth in the table with two wins and two draws, holding Chelsea 2-2 in their last outing.

Renée Slegers’ Gunners stride out at the Emirates Stadium unbeaten, although they were frustrated in a scoreless draw with promoted Crystal Palace last weekend. Eva Olid’s Manchester United tenure has begun with defeats in both their opening games, and they have conceded seven goals, more than any other WSL team so far. Olid is expecting a response from their 5-0 trashing by Chelsea last weekend. “My main message is about being themselves,” she said. “I am not sure they are showing in the first two matches who they are and what they can do. For me it is so important that they show that to perform. We had a day to reflect and analyse the game, to see what we can do better and we know what we have to do.” Will Magee has minute-by-minute coverage, and Tom Garry reports.

Sunday brings four Premier League matches plus an Old Firm derby and a spicy clash at Molineux as Wolves host old foes West Brom. Emillia Hawkins is on hand bright and early with all the breaking news at the helm of our essential football live blog. Join the conversation by emailing your thoughts and queries to matchday. live@theguardian. com

Celtic have a 100% league record but are in something of a tailspin, having been thumped 3-0 in the League Cup by their Glasgow rivals at Ibrox on Sunday and then beaten 3-1 by Ferencvaros at Parkhead in the Europa League on Thursday. So it is less than an optimal moment to be going up against Rangers, who will be striving to make it six wins in succession across all competitions when they visit Celtic Park. Martin O’Neill certainly understands his side are a world away from last season’s uplift, calling their latest loss “a huge frustration” and “psychologically damning”. He admitted: “It’s not the start we wanted. Really need to concentrate now on Sunday [against Rangers] … Sunday’s a big game.” John Brewin helms the blog with Jonathan Liew reporting.

Liverpool remain unbeaten under their new head coach, Andoni Iraola, in all competitions but managing three draws from four Premier League games has stifled any early-season momentum. Iraola will be back in familiar surroundings as his side travel to Bournemouth, the south coast club the Spaniard consistently had punching above their weight. Bournemouth are yet ‌to win in the league under Iraola’s replacement, Marco Rose, but three draws and a rather unlucky loss at Manchester City are scant return for some eye-catching football under the German. Daniel Harris has the live blog, with Ben Fisher reporting.

One month into the Premier League season, excuses about bedding-in processes and newly assembled squads needing time to gel are wearing thin and for Manchester United there is ⁠an acute sense of urgency as the international break looms. After so much pre-season optimism, the spotlight has turned on the ⁠manager, Michael Carrick. Only one ​win in four league games – at home to promoted Ipswich – has been compounded by Wednesday’s League Cup exit at home to Brighton, having led 2-0. Another setback at Craven Cottage against a ⁠Fulham side without a league win would increase the pressure on Carrick and deepen the sense that United’s season is in danger of drifting before it has properly begun. United will be buoyed by the fact they ‌have not lost at Fulham since 2009, but while the London club have made a slow start under Álvaro Arbeloa, a draw at Liverpool last week and a League Cup win at West Ham in midweek offered glimpses of better things to come. Taha Hashim brings the noise in the live blog, with David Hytner and Jacob Steinberg our reporting team at Craven Cottage.

Graham Searles is back for the best of week two’s action. He will be concentrating on Vikings v Bears and Steelers v Patriots from the eight 6pm fixtures. Minnesota opened their season with a comeback win over Green Bay, rallying from a 12-point deficit late in the third quarter to overwhelm the Packers. The Vikings’ defense will bid to shut down Caleb Williams in a battle of unbeaten teams after the Chicago quarterback inspired a record-breaking start to the season. Williams threw two touchdowns and ran for two more as the Bears pounded the Carolina Panthers 59-37 last weekend in the highest-scoring opener in NFL history. Pittsburgh, meanwhile, are coming off the successful debut of their new coach, Mike McCarthy, after the departure of Mike Tomlin, and a vintage effort from their 42-year-old quarterback Aaron Rodgers in their opening win over Atlanta. The Patriots will be entering their second home opener under Mike Vrabel, the architect of New England’s renaissance in the post-Tom Brady era, and with a third-year quarterback in Drake Maye whose post-Super Bowl run honeymoon appears to be over after one of the worst performances of his young career in last week’s 13-10 loss to Seattle.

The New York Times has been publishing for 175 years. Some of that history may be sitting in a shoe box under your bed.

By The New York Times

This story is part of a series marking 175 years of eyewitness journalism from The New York Times. Read more here.

The New York Times turns 175 this September. As part of the celebration, we’re going to be reaching back into our archives. We’d like you to reach into yours.

What stories from The Times have you collected over the years? Are there informal archives you’ve created by saving articles on a specific topic — or around events you felt were momentous?

As we look through our history, we hope you’ll look through your own — at least the one you’ve curated via The Times — and consider sharing it with us.

This might include archives that have been passed down through generations: yellowed clippings sent by a parent, say, or recipes tucked in a treasured cookbook.

And this fall, your archive might wind up alongside ours.

We read every submission. A reporter may follow up to learn more. Nothing gets published without us following up with you, and hearing back.

In Significant Escalation, Houthis Attack Saudi Capital

The New York Times September 19, 2026

Advertisement

Supported by

The Houthis, an Iranian-backed militia, said they had fired a wave of missiles and drones at Riyadh, and on Saudi oil facilities.

By Vivian NereimIsmaeel Naar and Pranav Baskar

Vivian Nereim reported from Riyadh, Saudi Arabia, and Ismaeel Naar from Dubai, United Arab Emirates.

The Houthi militia in Yemen said on Saturday that it had attacked Saudi Arabia’s capital and oil facilities with a barrage of missiles and drones, a significant escalation in the renewed war between the kingdom and the Iranian-backed group.

The Saudis intercepted a Houthi missile launched toward Riyadh, the capital, according to Maj. Gen. Turki Al-Maliki, the spokesman for the Saudi-led military coalition in Yemen.

He added in a statement that air defenses had fended off assaults on “civilians and civilian infrastructure” in several other cities in the kingdom, including coastal Yanbu, where the Houthis said they attacked oil facilities.

The Houthi strikes, the first on Riyadh in months, left the city on edge. Emergency alerts sounded in Riyadh earlier on Saturday, with residents reporting loud explosions, and flights were severely disrupted at the city’s airport. There were no immediate reports of casualties.

The Houthis and Saudi Arabia have accused each other of mounting intensifying attacks in recent weeks. Strikes on Saudi Arabia have disrupted critical oil infrastructure, fueling alarm over threats to global energy supplies.

Yahya Saree, a spokesman for the Houthi military, said the group had fired a “large number of ballistic and cruise missiles and drones” targeting “sensitive sites” in Riyadh and facilities for Saudi Arabia’s national oil company in Yanbu, a crucial Red Sea terminal.

Mr. Saree said the attacks were retaliation for more than 700 Saudi airstrikes in Yemen, where the kingdom has been backing government forces trying to wrest back territory from a lightning Houthi offensive.

Saudi Arabia has not acknowledged launching any airstrikes in recent days, and Saudi officials generally say that such strikes are being carried out by the Saudi-backed Yemeni government. The Saudi authorities did not respond to a request for comment on Saturday, but General Al-Maliki said in his statement on Saturday that the Houthi attacks demonstrated the militia’s “intransigence.”

Starting in 2015, Saudi Arabia led a disastrous bombing campaign to rout the Houthis but failed to push the group out of power, leaving Yemen in the fragmented control of government forces and the militants. A truce reached in 2022 has unraveled amid worsening fighting in recent months, as the Houthis have sought to seize strategic territory in Yemen and enforce a naval blockade on Saudi Arabia in the Red Sea.

But the attacks on Riyadh were a “huge” escalation, said Farea Al-Muslimi, a Yemen specialist at Chatham House, a London-based research group. He said they reflected that the “Houthis are not going to stop anywhere,” particularly at a time when they feel emboldened by recent battlefield victories.

In his statement, Mr. Saree, the Houthi military spokesman, said that the group was pursuing a policy of “escalation for escalation” until Saudi Arabia stops its “aggression” in Yemen and lifts restrictions on Yemeni airspace, which the militia refers to as a blockade.

FlightRadar24, a flight tracking website, showed major delays on Saturday afternoon at the King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh. Photographs and video by the Reuters news agency showed a plume of smoke rising in the vicinity of the airport.

Overnight, Riyadh residents received two emergency alerts warning of a “hostile aerial threat.” On Saturday, two booms rattled western Riyadh, home to a diplomatic quarter hosting foreign embassies. Saudi Civil Defense officials said early-warning systems were also activated in nine other cities.

It was the first time alerts were sounded in Riyadh since tensions with the Houthis flared in July. Recent strikes had largely targeted southern Saudi cities, sparing the capital, where Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman of Saudi Arabia is scheduled to host the Future Investment Initiative, a major gathering of billionaires and international financiers, next month.

The reported explosions in Riyadh followed Houthi accusations on Friday that Saudi Arabia had attempted a “criminal” attack on Sanaa, the Yemeni capital, which the Houthis seized in 2014. Mr. Saree said the group had foiled the attacks, without detailing their nature.

On Tuesday, Saudi Arabia’s air defenses intercepted a Houthi drone approaching Mecca, the Saudi authorities said — a direct accusation that the militia had targeted Islam’s holiest site. Abdulmalik al-Houthi, the movement’s leader, dismissed the assertion as “slander and fabrication.”

The Houthis also claimed on Wednesday that last week they had shot down a Saudi F-15 fighter jet over Marib Province, Yemen, using a locally made missile.

The hostilities are the most dangerous since the 2022 truce frayed this summer. Fighting reignited in July after the Houthis accused Saudi Arabia of bombing Sanaa’s airport to prevent an Iranian aircraft from landing. In response, the Houthis launched drone and ballistic missile barrages at Saudi military bases, ports and airports, while targeting oil tankers in the Red Sea in what they called a naval blockade

The Houthis have reported several Saudi air raids on their positions in several provinces. Domestic fighting in Yemen has also intensified following the Houthi capture of the country’s entire western Red Sea coastline, heightening risks for the Bab el-Mandab Strait, a vital global trade choke point.

Shuaib Almosawa contributed reporting from Sanaa, Yemen, and Saeed Al-Batati from al-Mukalla, Yemen.

Vivian Nereim is the lead reporter for The Times covering the countries of the Arabian Peninsula. She is based in Riyadh, Saudi Arabia.

Ismaeel Naar is an international reporter for The Times, covering the Gulf states. He is based in Dubai, United Arab Emirates.

Pranav Baskar is an international reporter at The Times, based in New York.

‘Nervous and Skeptical,’ Greenlanders Question the New Deal With Trump

The New York Times September 19, 2026

Trump Administration

Advertisement

Supported by

The U. S. president’s threats to seize Greenland left its people on edge, and with details scarce, the news of an agreement didn’t seem to be putting minds at ease.

By Jeffrey Gettleman and Maya Tekeli

Jeffrey Gettleman and Maya Tekeli have been covering Greenland closely since President Trump threatened to annex it last year. Ms. Tekeli reported from Copenhagen.

First, President Trump wanted to buy their homeland.

Then he threatened to seize it by force.

On Friday, he announced that he had worked out an “Infinite Life” deal between the United States, Denmark and Greenland, the gigantic Arctic island and semiautonomous Danish territory that has been an obsession of Mr. Trump’s for years.

As news of the deal spread across Greenland on Saturday, some Greenlanders expressed relief. But there also seemed to be confusion, anxiety and a nagging question: What, exactly, had been agreed to?

“My immediate reaction is that it makes me nervous and skeptical,” Ellen Frederiksen, a retired teacher in Narsaq, a town in southern Greenland, said by telephone.

“The way Trump presents it, it sounds as if he is being given a monopoly over Greenland,” she said. “I sincerely hope that isn’t the case.”

For months, Mr. Trump’s aides had been tasked with finding a way to defuse a crisis the president himself provoked last year among America’s NATO allies, especially Denmark, when he threatened to take over the island. On Friday, American officials said the new deal would expand the U. S. security presence on the island. But the details of the agreement are not expected to be revealed until next week.

Mr. Trump asserted that the United States had secured “permanent control over security, and all other needs” in Greenland. But Greenlandic and Danish officials were much more measured about what the deal portends, and they have said little about it.

On Saturday, Lars Lokke Rasmussen, Denmark’s foreign minister, said the agreement could end “a long period of uncertainty” and that “next week could be a good week.”

Some analysts suggested that Mr. Trump could be exaggerating the deal’s importance. Under a defense treaty that dates to the 1950s, the U. S. military already enjoys sweeping access to Greenland. Greenlanders and Danes have never questioned that. And Greenlanders had already said they were interested in doing more business with Americans.

“In terms of rights, they were already allowed quite a lot under the original agreement,” said Mikkel Runge Olesen, a researcher at the Danish Institute for International Studies in Copenhagen.

Mr. Trump said on Friday that the new deal would prevent Russia and China from ever establishing military bases in Greenland. But Mr. Olesen made the point that since Greenland is a NATO territory, there had never been a realistic possibility that China or Russia would put troops there.

“Is there anything here that one could not have achieved without this crisis?” Mr. Olesen asked.

It’s been an exhausting year and a half for Greenlanders. Ever since Mr. Trump threatened to seize the island in early 2025, his administration’s threats and warnings have seeped into everyday life.

Many people became newshounds, constantly scanning the headlines for any word out of Washington. Some said they struggled to sleep, worried about what might happen next.

Aka Hansen, a filmmaker and member of an opposition political party in Nuuk, the capital, said that earlier this year she had been told to prepare for the worst. She even stored five days’ worth of water, in case the Americans invaded.

“Now, suddenly, everything is fine,” she said. “What happened in between?”

The answers matter deeply in Greenland, where questions about sovereignty and outside influence have never been abstract. The island is bigger than Mexico but home to fewer than 60,000 people.

For more than 300 years, it has been part of the Danish kingdom, and today, many Greenlanders follow a blended lifestyle — part Scandinavian, part Indigenous Inuit culture. Many people still hunt seals, for instance.

Large parts of the island, with their glistening snowfields, dramatic fjords and icebergs and ice mountains, are stunningly beautiful. Protecting the environment has always been a priority, which is why some Greenlanders said they didn’t feel comfortable with Mr. Trump’s talk of expanding America’s military presence.

Already, the Pentagon has taken the first steps toward a bigger buildup. Just this week, American soldiers were spotted surveying an airstrip in Narsarsuaq, a town in southern Greenland.

“If it becomes a daily routine for them to fly around here near us, then it will be a complete change,” said Aana Uulat Bach, a retired teacher living in Nuuk. “We are not soldiers. We are people of nature, and we want to preserve that.”

Still, some people were hopeful.

“If the agreement is finalized, it will create all the conditions needed to restore more normal relations,” said Naaja Nathanielsen, one of two Greenlanders in Denmark’s Parliament. “I don’t think there can be much disagreement that this would be a good thing.”

Jeffrey Gettleman is an international correspondent based in London covering global events. He has worked for The Times for more than 20 years.

Sherrod Brown Tries a New Retort to Criticism on Transgender Issues

The New York Times September 19, 2026

Advertisement

Supported by

the ad campaign

A spot from the Senate candidate in Ohio seeks to dismiss the Republican Party’s focus on transgender rights as a distraction from economic issues.

By Emily Davies

Sherrod Brown, the Democratic candidate for Senate in Ohio, has spent more than $200,000 on a 30-second advertisement responding to attacks from his opponent and an Elon Musk-backed PAC regarding transgender issues, according to AdImpact.

Here’s a look at the ad, its accuracy and its major takeaway.

The ad opens with voters identified as Beth and Warren in Johnstown, Ohio, an agricultural hub northeast of Columbus that has historically leaned Republican.

Warren speaks first, looking directly at the camera, and says, “Here they go again, those same attacks against Sherrod Brown.”

The ad then pans to a voter in Granville, a Democratic island in a conservative part of the state, who says, “With everything going on, that’s what they’re talking about?”

As another voter speaks, a text overlay on an image of a dark, empty hospital hallway reads: “IN OHIO IT’S ILLEGAL TO PERFORM TRANSGENDER SURGERIES ON CHILDREN.”

A series of voters in different parts of the state then denounce Senator Jon Husted, Mr. Brown’s Republican opponent, accusing him of voting to increase the cost of groceries, kicking hundreds of thousands of Ohioans off health care, writing a law letting utility companies “jack up our electric bills,” and failing to address the cost of gas.

The ad ends with Beth in Johnstown, who faces the camera and says “Jon Husted, why don’t you start working for us?”

Mr. Brown is in a high-stakes race against Senator Jon Husted, who was appointed to fill the Senate seat of JD Vance when he left to become vice president. Mr. Brown has faced a torrent of negative advertising focusing on transgender issues.

“Here they go again, those same attacks against Sherrod Brown. With everything going on, that’s what they’re talking about. In Ohio, it’s against the law to perform transgender surgeries on kids. That’s right, it’s illegal. Jon Husted, why’d you vote to increase the cost of groceries? To do nothing about the cost of gas. You kicked 490,000 Ohioans off their health care. And Jon Husted wrote the law on letting utility companies jack up our electric bills. Jon Husted, why don’t you start working for us? I’m Sherrod Brown and I approve this message.”

The advertisement is correct that an Ohio law passed in 2024, over the Republican governor’s veto, forbids doctors from prescribing medications that assist minors seeking gender transitions. The law also restricts transgender girls and women from competing in girls and women’s sports.

The law is being challenged before the state Supreme Court, which is made up of six Republican justices and one Democrat.

It is misleading to say that Mr. Husted voted to “increase the cost of groceries,” because there was not a specific vote on that issue in the Senate. But he has supported sweeping tariffs and the war with Iran, among other policies, that have contributed to the rising prices, including of groceries and gas.

Mr. Husted also voted for President Trump’s signature domestic policy bill, which included significant cuts to Medicaid and Medicare. The Joint Economic Committee, a bipartisan group, estimated that more that 489,815 Ohioans would lose health insurance as a result of the cuts.

The claim that Mr. Husted wrote a law that allowed utility companies to raise prices is accurate and complicated. Mr. Husted, then a lieutenant governor, was highly involved in passing a 2019 energy law that later became the center of a massive bribery scheme that landed another lawmaker, the former speaker of the Ohio House of Representatives, in prison.

The law allowed utility companies to add extra fees and surcharges to electricity bills as a bailout for two struggling nuclear power plants. Mr. Husted has denied any knowledge of wrongdoing in the high-profile scandal.

This spot represents a new response to the Republican Party’s effort to use transgender issues to paint Democrats as radical and unelectable, regardless of their specific stances, which tend to be more nuanced than portrayed by their opponents.

Instead of engaging on the topic, Mr. Brown’s campaign is seeking to dismiss it as irrelevant, and a distraction from the economic issues that they hope will drive voters to the polls.

An earlier version of this article misstated the location of Johnstown, Ohio. It is northeast of Columbus, not south of Columbus.

We acknowledge mistakes in our reporting with corrections. If you spot an error, please let us know at corrections@nytimes. com. Learn more.

Emily Davies is a political correspondent for The New York Times.

India Is Again Squeezed Between the Threat of Trump Tariffs and Russian Oil

The New York Times September 19, 2026

U. S. Tariffs and Trade

Advertisement

Supported by

India is trying to secure affordable energy while preserving a crucial relationship with Washington, a balancing act made harder by turmoil in global energy markets.

By Alex Travelli

Reporting from New Delhi

A new sanctions law giving President Trump broad authority to impose steep tariffs on countries that buy Russian oil adds a new layer of uncertainty to India’s already fraught trade relationship with the United States.

The bill, signed by President Trump on Friday, gives him the power to impose tariffs of up to 100 percent on goods from countries that continue to buy Russian energy. The aim of Congress was to choke off the revenue that finances Moscow’s war in Ukraine.

The law, however, gives Mr. Trump considerable discretion over when and how to wield those tariffs, and it’s not clear when — or even whether — he would impose tariffs that would raise the cost of American imports of Indian goods.

To India, the law is seen as a threat, potentially increasing Mr. Trump’s leverage even as he explores business deals with Russia.

The timing puts the Indian prime minister, Narendra Modi, in a tight spot. India imports more than 90 percent of the crude oil it consumes, and its reliance on Russia has climbed again as the war in Iran has disrupted supplies from the Middle East. Russian crude accounted for roughly half of India’s imports this summer, according to Kpler, a global maritime data company.

The new law is the latest in a series of shifting American policies that have repeatedly forced India to adjust its Russian oil purchases.

In February, days before the war against Iran started, Washington and New Delhi struck a trade agreement under which the United States would lower tariffs and India would reduce its intake of Russian oil.

Then, in quick succession, the assumptions underlying that bargain fell apart. The Supreme Court curtailed Mr. Trump’s ability to use the tariff powers that had helped him negotiate with India. The war in Iran made it difficult to get oil from the Persian Gulf. And the Treasury Department allowed India and other countries to compensate by buying more Russian oil.

Now Washington is again threatening to punish India for buying oil that has become harder to replace.

India has responded forcefully.

“India remains firmly committed to ensuring energy security for its 1.4 billion people,” the country’s foreign ministry said on Thursday, adding that it would continue to diversify its suppliers according to market conditions. The ministry warned of “potential implications for not just the bilateral relationship” with the United States but also the international energy market.

India has faced a similar predicament before. Washington has pressed New Delhi to stop buying oil from Venezuela and Iran, only for American policy toward those suppliers to shift as diplomatic relations and energy prices changed.

This has forced India to balance two imperatives. It wants to preserve its relationship with the United States, while securing enough affordable energy for the world’s most populous country.

Complicating that balance, the United States is an increasingly important energy supplier to India even as it threatens penalties over New Delhi’s purchases elsewhere. Since the war began, India’s share of cooking gas imports from the United States rose to more than 50 percent, up from 8 percent in December.

Ajay Srivastava, a former Indian trade official who runs the Global Trade Research Initiative in New Delhi, said India should not be overly fixated on American tariffs. Tariffs can damage some Indian exporters, he argued, but they are collected from American importers and ultimately raise costs in the United States.

In Mr. Srivastava’s view, the new law restores some of the bargaining power Mr. Trump lost when the Supreme Court restricted his earlier tariff authority. The trade agreement negotiated with India has remained in limbo. But the new authority would give Washington something substantial to offer — a lower tariff in exchange for Indian concessions.

“My problem,” Mr. Srivastava said, “is that signing the trade deal does not buy you peace from any of this.”

India has watched the United States strike deals with major trading partners, only for disputes over tariffs and the terms of those agreements to re-emerge.

And India is not the only country trying to determine what the new law means for its relationship with Washington.

China buys more Russian oil than India and also falls within the new law’s reach. Indian officials and analysts are looking to see whether Washington applies the same pressure to Beijing that it does to New Delhi. The question carries weight because India has spent years drawing closer to the United States, partly as a counterweight to China.

Last weekend, Xi Jinping, China’s top leader, and President Vladimir V. Putin of Russia joined Mr. Modi in New Delhi for the BRICS summit, posing together in a conspicuous display of non-Western cooperation. Mr. Xi is expected to meet Mr. Trump in Washington in the coming days.

Among the major BRICS powers, India has had a strong strategic incentive to deepen its partnership with Washington. C. Raja Mohan, a professor at Jindal Global University, described India’s dilemma as a choice between two uncomfortable alternatives.

“Do you want to jump from the American frying pan into the Chinese fire?” Mr. Mohan said.

China’s growing power gives India a powerful reason to preserve its relationship with Washington. But repeated shifts in American demands over energy and trade have also raised questions in New Delhi about how durable any new bargain would be.

“India should not do any deal until U. S. policy stabilizes,” Mr. Srivastava said.

Alex Travelli is a correspondent based in New Delhi, writing about business and economic developments in India and the rest of South Asia.

Newsom Signs Bills Meant to Prevent Trump’s Interference in Midterms

The New York Times September 19, 2026

Advertisement

Supported by

Gov. Gavin Newsom of California signed legislation that would make it illegal to interfere with ballots or election records in response to efforts by the president to restrict voting.

By Laurel Rosenhall

Reporting from Sacramento

Gov. Gavin Newsom signed legislation on Saturday that is meant to prevent interference in California’s midterm elections in response to efforts by President Trump and other Republicans to restrict voting participation.

Mr. Newsom and fellow Democrats in the State Legislature crafted the bills to broadly combat involvement by the Trump administration, without knowing specifically whether or how the federal government might engage in California’s elections. The state relies heavily on mail ballots, and Mr. Trump has taken particular aim at that form of voting.

One bill prohibits the seizure of ballots, election records or voting technology before an election is certified. Another makes it a felony for people in positions of authority to direct their workers to interfere with the delivery of a mail ballot or its return to election officials.

Mr. Newsom signed a package of 13 bills, including a measure that prohibits arrests within 200 feet of a polling place on Election Day, with exceptions for acts related to disrupting the election or crimes against people or property. Democrats have feared that the Trump administration could send federal agents to polling places in immigrant communities.

Mr. Trump, who has voted by mail twice this year, has claimed that absentee voting is rife with fraud. He and his administration said in July, without evidence, that California and three other states had allowed about 278,000 noncitizens to vote in federal elections.

California’s Democratic leaders said they were responding to a spate of unusual challenges from Mr. Trump, and local officials aligned with him. Mr. Newsom signed the bills in Los Angeles at the Japanese American National Museum, where Border Patrol agents showed up outside a rally the governor held last summer.

Mr. Trump signed an executive order in March that sought to restrict the use of mail ballots. And earlier this year, Chad Bianco, the Republican sheriff in Riverside County, seized more than 650,000 ballots that voters had cast last year because he said he was investigating a discrepancy in the count. California challenged both actions in court. The Supreme Court on Monday sided with California and other Democratic-led states by blocking Mr. Trump’s plan to restrict voting by mail.

The new state laws add small but meaningful protections to California’s ability to prevent outside involvement in its ballot process, said Justin Levitt, a law professor at Loyola Marymount University who worked on voting rights for the Biden administration.

“There’s a vigilante mood afoot,” Mr. Levitt said. “This acts as a little bit of a deterrent for people who are cosplaying election officials.”

Shannon Grove, a Republican state senator who voted against the bills, said she believed one of the laws would allow criminal charges against U. S. Postal Service workers who handle ballots as a routine part of their job. Under that bill, it would be a misdemeanor for anyone in charge of a mail ballot to interfere with delivering it to a voter.

“This is about the postal workers, and that’s pretty bold,” she said.

In a brief interview last month, Mr. Newsom said the legislation wasn’t aimed at prosecuting postal workers who are doing their jobs properly.

The bills are targeted at those “carrying out illegal activity or illegal orders and directives,” Mr. Newsom said. “With these enhanced sanctions, if you break the law we’re going to hold you accountable, and it doesn’t matter who you are.”

Among the other bills that Mr. Newsom signed are two that took aim at “deepfake” ads generated by A. I. that mimic a politician’s voice or appearance to deceive voters.

In 2024, voters in New Hampshire received a voice message that was made to sound like President Joseph R. Biden Jr. urging them not to vote. That same year, an online ad imitated the voice of Vice President Kamala Harris saying Mr. Biden was senile.

California passed legislation cracking down on deepfake political ads that year, but it was later blocked by courts for violating free speech. The new legislation takes a narrower approach meant to strengthen it against constitutional challenges.

Mr. Newsom also signed a bill that could accelerate California’s notoriously slow process for counting votes.

It calls for election officials to tell people how to vote early, which reduces the glut of envelopes that arrive on Election Day. It also requires informing voters that they can submit mail ballots at a polling place. Doing so allows election officials to count ballots faster by eliminating the envelopes that are cumbersome to process.

Most election-related bills relied on Democratic support to pass, but the legislation to encourage early voting and in-person submission of ballots had sweeping bipartisan support.

Rick Hasen, an election law professor at the University of California, Los Angeles, said he was skeptical that California would be successful in stopping officials from the U. S. Department of Justice if they tried to collect ballots during an election, a scenario that has not occurred in modern times.

But, he said, the laws could be enforced against state and local officials. The state has already sued Mr. Bianco, and the parties in that case are awaiting a decision from the California Supreme Court.

Laurel Rosenhall is a Sacramento-based reporter covering California politics and government for The Times.

times investigation

Data science helps determine who receives betting incentives, but the company has resisted using similar technology to protect gamblers at risk of addiction.

Credit... Hokyoung Kim

Supported by

By Alex KlavensWalt Bogdanich and Jenny Vrentas

The reporters obtained internal documents and interviewed dozens of former DraftKings employees, many of whom worried that the company’s efforts were harming problem gamblers.

About a year into his job as a data analyst at DraftKings, Jayden Butts received a new assignment.

The online gambling giant was spending hundreds of millions of dollars every year on promotional incentives: “Free” betting money advertised through emails and phone alerts. But the company knew little about their effectiveness.

So in 2023, DraftKings took customer betting records and built a machine learning model, a form of artificial intelligence that seeks patterns in data, to answer the question: Who was more likely to respond to promotions by gambling — and losing — more?

Mr. Butts’s task was to test that model, prioritizing free bets and bonuses for those likely losers. Soon, a question began to gnaw at him: Aren’t many of these same people prone to addiction? “We are looking for traits and features that we can target that indicate a good investment,” he said. By strict financial logic, “the best investment would be a problem gambler.”

Mr. Butts had reason to be concerned. DraftKings makes money when gamblers lose money. And the model sought to identify those it could get to lose the most. It scored each customer based on their habits: The higher the score, the more money a gambler was likely to lose for each promotion offered.

Since Mr. Butts ran those tests, DraftKings has continued to hone its methods, using data science, to target losing gamblers with promotions that encourage more betting, according to six former employees who worked on them. At the same time, four other former employees said, DraftKings has stalled or squashed efforts to use similar technology to predict who might develop a gambling problem based on their betting activity.

Silicon Valley firms spent years analyzing every digital interaction to predict what will keep users clicking on advertisements. Now, as companies like DraftKings have made gambling accessible to millions on smartphones, they too have collected an extraordinary wealth of data.

An investigation by The New York Times shows what DraftKings has chosen to do — and not do — with that power.

The Times interviewed more than 40 former DraftKings employees, and obtained internal research memos, presentations and Slack messages as well as betting records from experiments conducted on customers.

The documents show how the model Mr. Butts worked on analyzed dozens of data points for each gambler, including how frequently they played, their daily account balances and how much they typically lost compared with how much they bet. It also incorporated another model that calculated how likely a user was to stop gambling.

This betting data may also contain signs that a person is headed for trouble. Yet when employees developed a machine learning model that would have assigned users “risk scores,” the company sidelined it, according to two former employees who worked on that project.

In late 2024, DraftKings fired Mr. Butts for performance reasons, he said, amid a short blip in business that led some in the company to believe its promotional experiments weren’t working as intended. The company briefly paused some of its data science work — before revving back up again with a flurry of new machine learning projects.

Mr. Butts and five other former DraftKings employees who worked on promotional targeting told The Times they regretted building technology they now viewed as dangerous.

“It is as predatory as it sounds,” said a former DraftKings analyst who, like many interviewed for this article, requested anonymity because he feared retribution. “If you lose more, we give you more, so you keep playing more.” He quit in 2024.

In a statement, DraftKings said it “rejects any implication that its marketing practices are unfair or improperly targets customers.” The company disputed how some former employees characterized its use of promotions, saying they are “directed toward customers who demonstrate sustained, engaged use of our platform, not toward customers based on their losses.” It also said it disagreed with Mr. Butts’s account of his firing, but did not elaborate.

Lori Kalani, who as DraftKings’s chief responsible gaming officer leads the company’s efforts to prevent problem gambling, said in an interview that its business depended on “customers who are betting within their means, are betting for entertainment and betting for fun.”

Ms. Kalani said DraftKings does monitor customers for “potentially risky behaviors.” But she acknowledged that the company has declined to use risk prediction technology, saying there wasn’t evidence that it was helpful.

In 2018, when the Supreme Court ruled that states could legalize online sports gambling, it ushered in a new era in which betting has moved beyond casinos and racetracks. Professional sports games are now saturated with celebrity advertisements, encouraging people to wager on their phones.

DraftKings and its rival FanDuel dominate this new industry, which has expanded into online casino games and, more recently, prediction markets. DraftKings says it has 11 million customers, compared with five million in 2022.

Health experts have long recognized gambling as addictive, but many critics see this modern version, where people can bet from their couch on the outcome of a single baseball pitch, as especially dangerous. A study published last year in JAMA Internal Medicine cited a rise in Google searches like “Am I a gambling addict?” Calls about sports betting to Ohio’s problem gambling help line have more than quadrupled since the state legalized it in 2023. The state’s outgoing governor, Mike DeWine, told The Times that signing that law was his biggest regret.

Promotions, which take on forms like a free bet, a “profit boost” or a deposit bonus, play a vital role in DraftKings’s business: The company brought in around $8.7 billion in gross revenue from sports and casino gamblers last year, and gave out about $3 billion in promotions, according to research by Citizens Bank.

DraftKings and some competitors, including FanDuel, have boasted publicly about their use of customer data for promotions — without disclosing what those efforts entail. A DraftKings executive recently told investors that data science and analytics helped it improve its margins on promotion-driven sports bets by 13 percent in 2025 and that it used A. I. to personalize hundreds of millions of promotional dollars.

The New York Times would like to hear from readers who want to share messages and materials with our journalists.

One former DraftKings data scientist who worked on promotions, Jacob Shulkin, said that they were effective because they take advantage of gamblers’ psychology. “I feel I’m getting free money,” he said, “but really it’s dragging me back in.”

Several gamblers told The Times that promotions fueled their addictions. Bryan Biehl lost nearly $70,000 gambling online, more than half of it at DraftKings. Mr. Biehl recalled how in late 2024, when he started therapy for his addiction, his email inbox began to feel like a relapse risk.

“I would get flooded with bonuses and deposits,” Mr. Biehl said. “If you are in addiction, you are not going to say no.”

In the first two weeks of December 2024, Mr. Biehl received 40 promotions from DraftKings, emails show. He succumbed to temptation one last time on Christmas Day before putting himself on self-exclusion lists, which blocked him from gambling apps.

DraftKings declined to comment on Mr. Biehl’s account.

Asked whether promotions contribute to problem gambling, Ms. Kalani said they are “a marketing tool that every company out there uses,” comparing DraftKings to businesses like Amazon. Other industries face similar issues, she said. “Shopping can be problematic for people.”

Jayden Butts grew up watching his grandfather’s gambling addiction play out — three trips a week up I-95 to Oxford Casino in Maine.

Fresh out of college and eager for a high-paying tech job, he joined DraftKings’s casino division in May 2022 as a data analyst. He initially didn’t think much about customers like his grandfather. Then he had his own string of losses playing online slots through an offshore website. He later quit gambling with a new appreciation for people who might be struggling.

DraftKings is famous for sports betting, but its online casino games, including slots and blackjack, bring in nearly one-third of the company’s revenue, even though it offers them in only a handful of jurisdictions.

The online casino is where, in mid-2023, DraftKings set out to build a model for predicting how promotions would translate into a user’s eventual wins or losses.

The core question was, “Is this person going to give us more than we’re giving them?” Mr. Butts said. “And if the answer is yes, open the floodgates.”

DraftKings already had a system that weighed factors like a gambler’s skill, how much they bet and tax rates on gambling revenue in the state where they lived.

But it was relatively crude. According to one internal memo, it offered “no information or insight on expected user-level profitability of reinvestment dollars” — in other words, DraftKings did not know how effective its promotions were at inducing gamblers to lose.

Figuring this out required machine learning. Unlike traditional data analytics, where researchers decide which patterns to look for, machine learning models can sift through hundreds of variables on their own to find combinations that help predict particular behaviors.

Data scientists had trained the new casino model on historical data. It was Mr. Butts’s job to test it on real customers. Each week, the model vacuumed up information about a user’s recent activity. The score it calculated was known internally as “elasticity,” a term borrowed from economics.

Users with below-average scores were deemed “inelastic” and marked for fewer incentives. The “elastic” bettors remained.

In September 2023, Mr. Butts tested using the elasticity model to influence promotions for about 5,000 casino players. He later expanded the tests to a larger population.

He initially thought DraftKings aimed to save money by avoiding people who were unlikely to be profitable. But he said his supervisors told him that the company did not want to reduce its promotional spending but rather to “redeploy” it. He understood this to mean the goal was to direct more promotions toward the biggest losers.

Mr. Butts said he also worried that his experiments might lead DraftKings to send more promotions to players who played more addictive games, including his own former vice: online slots, widely regarded by public health experts as among the most addictive forms of gambling.

It’s not clear the extent to which DraftKings has targeted slots players more than others. But in a 2023 internal memo, researchers reported that slots revenue was “more elastic” than earnings from other casino games, meaning that promotions were particularly effective at driving users to those games. A Times analysis of internal DraftKings casino betting data from early 2024 also found that bettors with high elasticity scores gambled more on slots, on average, than those with low scores.

DraftKings said that it could not provide a “definitive response” to Mr. Butts’s tests, the 2023 memo or the Times analysis because it had not “seen or verified” the material. But it said Mr. Butts’s test “appears preliminary and inconclusive,” and that his views do not “reflect DraftKings’ approach to promotional investment.”

Around the same time that Mr. Butts ran his tests, DraftKings began building similar models for sports betting promotions, according to eight former employees. It has continued to develop techniques for targeting sports and casino bettors as recently as this year.

One former employee said he had worked on a system that looked for people at risk of leaving the platform and tried to coax them back. Another said he helped develop a program that ramped up promotions for people gambling more aggressively than usual.

Two other former analysts who worked on targeting projects told The Times that they independently raised concerns with their superiors that these models would identify vulnerable gamblers as promotional targets, and asked to put protections in place.

Both received the same response: no. That would be handled by another part of the company, they said they were told.

Ms. Kalani, DraftKings’s responsible gaming head, said she was not familiar with those requests.

The job of limiting problem gambling at DraftKings largely falls to its responsible gaming division, a group of around 50 employees at the 5,000-person company.

DraftKings offers a variety of tools for gamblers who need them. Its advertisements feature phone numbers for 24/7 gambling help lines. “Cool-off periods” let people turn off access to the app for up to a year, and those with a longer-term problem can put themselves on self-exclusion lists for years — or indefinitely.

Gamblers with a high degree of self-awareness may find these tools helpful. But they put the onus on the gambler. “When someone is struggling with an addiction, a rational suggestion that this is not in your best interest is falling on deaf ears,” said Mark Gottlieb, a lawyer who has sued DraftKings and other internet gambling companies, accusing them of practices that lead to addiction.

Although many at DraftKings feel proud of their work to protect problem gamblers, their efforts have created friction with the wider business, according to six former employees who worked on responsible gaming projects. One described the responsible gaming group as “at odds with the rest of the company,” because it aims to slow gamblers down, which in turn makes them less profitable for DraftKings.

DraftKings said there was “no tension” between its business goals and its responsible gaming efforts.

But Hassel Velasco, a former member of DraftKings’s customer service team, told The Times that on about a dozen occasions he heard complaints from problem gamblers who continued to receive promotions.

“It pushes people to almost chase their losses,” Mr. Velasco said. “They’re going, ‘Oh, I’m getting a bonus so I can make up whatever I lost.’” Troubled by these conversations, Mr. Velasco struggled to sleep. He quit in 2024 after five months on the job.

DraftKings said its representatives were required to report problem gambling concerns to the company. Ms. Kalani said the company did not send promotions to bettors who have been flagged or who have taken themselves off the platform.

The company does monitor for vulnerable customers, even if they don’t reach out for help. DraftKings follows guidelines from New Jersey regulators, who have instructed operators to set automatic triggers for specific indicators of potentially reckless betting, such as a customer depositing more than a certain amount during a set time period or a notable spike in time spent gambling.

DraftKings said that it does this nationwide, watching for more than two dozen such indicators. The company declined to share the thresholds it uses to prompt a response — how much someone would have to deposit, for instance — “because doing so could enable customers to circumvent our systems.”

When a customer trips one of these triggers, DraftKings can take three escalating steps. It first sends a message about responsible gaming, then an educational video and finally a questionnaire about gambling habits. Sometimes, DraftKings will close a gambler’s account.

But there are limitations. Intervention is based on customers demonstrating a specific behavior, and even if that happens, they can deny that they have a problem.

DraftKings described the system as “advanced technology” and said that it allowed the company to reach out to gamblers who have not yet asked for help. The company declined to share how many accounts it had suspended using this system.

Inside DraftKings, some employees believed the company could go much further.

One was a data scientist named Nestor Hernandez, who in mid-2024 began building a system that would help the responsible gaming division identify gamblers in trouble.

Mr. Hernandez, a computer science Ph. D., had spent years using algorithms to detect unusual patterns in large amounts of data.

He reviewed academic research into problem gambling, then developed a machine learning model to analyze the betting records — the same used for promotional targeting — of customers the company had already flagged for risky behavior.

His model scanned, among other things, deposits and withdrawals, attempts to chase losses and even age and gender, for patterns that might anticipate a gambler’s impending crisis. The risk score it assigned each user could theoretically help the company step in early with warnings or an outright ban.

“The idea of this model is to be more proactive instead of being reactive,” Mr. Hernandez said. “You will basically predict that a user will be in trouble, let’s say, a few days or a few weeks in advance. And you can act accordingly.”

Mr. Hernandez left the company that November for personal reasons, his model still unfinished. A new team of data scientists continued the work. Just a few months later, he received news from two former colleagues: The project had been shut down.

One member of that team was Jake Shannin. “Our conclusion was that it is possible even with simple rules to get a better-than-guessing sense” of whether a customer would end up needing an intervention, Mr. Shannin said.

In early 2025, Mr. Shannin said, the team prepared to share the new model with company officials, including Ms. Kalani. But the day of the presentation, the meeting was canceled. Two other attempts by DraftKings employees to build similar algorithms have also been shelved, according to two former employees.

Ms. Kalani said that company leaders made a “collective decision” not to use predictive technology for problem gambling. “We evaluated that it wasn’t evidence-based,” she said. The company decided that its existing system was a “better methodology.”

Several third-party firms offer their own versions of risk scoring. Other gambling companies say they have signed up for this, including two of DraftKings’s largest rivals, FanDuel and Fanatics.

Phil Sherwood, senior director of responsible gaming at PrizePicks, another competitor, said his company had a “moral obligation” to use these tools. “Frankly, without technology like this, I can’t look you in the eye and say, ‘We’re doing our best,’” he said.

DraftKings does not use any of these tools. “We’re always considering our options,” Ms. Kalani said. The company said its “primary commitment is to approaches that demonstrably help customers, not simply to adopting technology for its own sake.”

DraftKings shared one example of its using A. I. for responsible gaming: It deploys large-language models, the technology behind chatbots like ChatGPT, to monitor communications from gamblers to company representatives for signs of distress.

But the technology cannot flag customers who say nothing.

Georgia Gee and Susan C. Beachy contributed research.

Over the past few years, I've covered the rapid growth of the online gambling industry and how Americans have been affected. Our investigation examines the internal business practices of one of the leading online gambling platforms in the U. S., DraftKings, including how it deploys promotional offers to keep customers betting.

My interest in addiction issues goes back to the 1990s, when I reported on how cigarette companies used nicotine to addict smokers. In subsequent years, I've reported how gambling companies paid universities to encourage their students to bet on sports and how illegal offshore bookmakers operate. Now, our team of reporters examined the rise of online gambling and why it is so popular.

Alex Klavens is a data journalist at The Times, building computational tools that power data-driven reporting.

Walt Bogdanich joined The Times in 2001 as investigative editor for the Business desk. Since 2003, he has worked as an investigative reporter. He has won three Pulitzer Prizes.

Jenny Vrentas is a Times reporter covering money, power and influence in sports.

The Rise of A. I. Is Raising Threats From Drones, Police Group Warns

The New York Times September 19, 2026

Advertisement

Supported by

The leaps being made in artificial intelligence and the plunging costs of drones pose dangers to cities across the United States, according to the Police Executive Research Forum.

By Hurubie Meko and Maria Cramer

The confluence of rapidly advancing artificial intelligence technology and cheaper and deadlier drones pose an increasing threat to cities and towns across the United States, according to a report from the Police Executive Research Forum, a Washington-based think tank.

The report, titled “A Clear and Present Danger,” is not the first time the group has warned about the growing threat from drones. While there have been no publicly reported major attacks by drones within the United States, the easier access to cheaper drones has dramatically increased the technology’s “potential to inflict chaos and carnage,” the report states, particularly if they were to be used with A. I.

Most drones used in the United States are for commercial and civilian use, and fall under federal jurisdiction. Law enforcement should treat the dangers of the technology with the same urgency that federal investigators should have treated terrorism threats that led to the Sept. 11 attacks, the report states.

According to data collected by the group, unauthorized drones are flying into football stadiums on game days, highlighting how serious of a public safety issue this has become. In New York City, about 23,000 illegal drone flights are reported monthly, the report said. And during the World Cup this summer, hundreds of drones were seized this summer near World Cup games across the United States.

“Twenty-five years ago, our nation paid a terrible price for a failure of imagination,” Chuck Wexler, the executive director of the group, wrote in the report. “We cannot afford to make the same mistake again.”

Anxiety about artificial intelligence and its potential risks — to the environment and to safety — have reached a flashpoint in the nation. The growing use of drones in wars across the world and rising use of A. I. technology, has brought the issue of autonomous weapons back to the forefront.

Earlier this year, Ukrainian officials said a Russian drone was guided by A. I. when it killed three people after crashing into a wall and exploding. Ukrainian officials have said that Russia was testing self-targeting A. I. systems. In the war in Iran, the U. S. military modeled and deployed low-cost drones to respond to Iran’s own arsenal of drones, called the Shahed drones.

In June, federal officials said they foiled a plot to attack the Ultimate Fighting Championship matches that took place on the White House lawn. According to charging documents, the plot involved explosive-laden drones and rifles.

Jessica Tisch, the commissioner of the New York Police Department, has spoken about the proliferation of drones, which were once limited to the military but are now in the hands of more individuals.

“If there is one threat that keeps me up at night, it is from drones,” Ms. Tisch said during a news conference in May as the city was preparing for the World Cup. “Commercial drones can be easily adapted into weapons of war. That reality matters in New York City.”

Last month, during the U. S. Open, Ms. Tisch announced that the New York Police Department now had federal approval to bring down unauthorized drones during major events in the city.

That authority was granted under the Safer Skies Act, which Congress passed in December, giving local governments permission to disable and take down drones that are a threat to public safety.

Before the policy change, local law enforcement agencies didn’t have the proper training or equipment and had to rely on federal officials, Mr. Wexler said. The policy change is a turning point for local law enforcement, Mr. Wexler said. The Federal Bureau of Investigation has opened the National Counter-UAS Training Center in Huntsville, Al., to train officers from around the country, according to the report.

Since the Police Executive Research Forum’s first drone report in 2019, the group has held meetings with private security executives, local law enforcement leaders and federal officials, including the deputy chief of the Kyiv region in Ukraine.

Christopher O’Leary, a former senior F. B. I. counterterrorism official who retired in 2023, said drone technology has “alarming potential” for terrorists to use it in the United States and “our ability to counter it is limited.”

“The evolution of drone technology and the ubiquitous nature of it and the ease of acquisition makes it something anyone can get their hands on, and also alter and tinker with to meet their needs,” he said.

Most drones used for public safety in the United States are made in China, making the technology a national security threat, the report said. The Federal Communications Commission banned some new foreign-made drones from being sold in the country last year, but the technology continues to enter the United States through “rebranded products sold under shell company names,” according to the report.

Sean Patterson, chief of the University of Tennessee Police Department, said a trip he took to Ukraine with Mr. Wexler last year changed how he thought about drones. Chief Patterson, who served for 22 years in the N. Y. P. D. and was a rookie on Sept. 11, 2001, said he has “seen firsthand the lethality of terrorist organizations.” His visit to Ukraine showed him how easy it can be to use that technology for harm, he said.

“If police leaders that are in places that have large venues are not thinking about it, they need to think about it now,” he said, adding that in his case, more than 103,000 come to University of Tennessee’s campus for football games.

William K. Rashbaum contributed reporting.

Hurubie Meko is a Times reporter covering criminal justice in New York, with a focus on the Manhattan district attorney's office and state courts.

Maria Cramer is a Times reporter covering the New York Police Department and crime in the city and surrounding areas.
