Trump Has Finally Lost the Plot

The New York Times September 19, 2026

Advertisement

Supported by

Guest Essay

By Jonathan Rauch and Peter Wehner

Mr. Rauch is a senior fellow at the Brookings Institution. Mr. Wehner, a senior fellow at the Trinity Forum, is a contributing Opinion writer.

The frantic pace of the Trump presidency makes days seem like weeks and weeks like months — if not years. Finding rhyme or reason amid President Trump’s erratic conduct is impossible. Even so, while 2026 has not brought calm, it has brought more clarity.

Twenty months into his second term, Mr. Trump has remade the presidency and changed what Americans will tolerate from their government and from one another. Yet that transformation, sweeping as it is, may prove less important than what Mr. Trump and his allies could not do. They failed at the most ambitious project that they brought to his second term: using the state to remake American society. That failure is a central fact of the past 20 months, and it is why the country is in a less dangerous place than it was a year ago.

When Mr. Trump took office for the second time, he arrived with several overlapping but distinct agendas. The one he cared most about would convert the executive branch to a form of government that scholars call patrimonialism, in which the state is run as the leader’s personal property and family concern. In a patrimonialist system, expert bureaucracies and neutral rules are replaced by — or subordinated to — the head of state’s will. Where they can, patrimonialists personalize and weaponize law enforcement, pardons, programs and grants, appointments, promotions and all the other aspects of state power.

Patrimonialism is manifest in Mr. Trump’s enrichment of himself and his family, reportedly by several billion dollars — and in his effort to extract almost $1.8 billion from taxpayers by means of a sham legal settlement. It is manifest, too, in his systematic repurposing of the executive branch to serve his personal and political interests.

He uses his Justice Department to wage personal vendettas and his pardons to indemnify his cronies. He has staffed the department’s senior ranks with his own criminal defense attorneys, and the F. B. I. with a fierce political loyalist whose chief qualification was a career spent attacking the investigators who had scrutinized Mr. Trump. And he has purged the government’s internal checks on corruption, including by firing inspectors general, career prosecutors and F. B. I. agents whose offense was to follow the rules.

Mr. Trump uses faits accomplis, such as the demolition of the United States Agency for International Development, to elbow aside Congress and impose his will without regard for constitutional boundaries. With some help from the Supreme Court, he has concentrated federal power in the office of the presidency; and with his patrimonialist agenda, he has remade that office to serve not the Constitution but himself and his desires.

The re-norming of political standards is another area in which Mr. Trump has made a lasting imprint. By “re-norming,” we mean the deliberate degradation of what is considered acceptable in American public life.

Examples are far too many to enumerate, but recall just a few: Mr. Trump described his political opponents as “vermin” and said immigrants were “poisoning the blood of our country.” When Robert Mueller died in March, Mr. Trump posted that he was “glad he’s dead.” When Rob Reiner and his wife were murdered in their home, he blamed the killings on Mr. Reiner’s criticism of him. He courted and excused political violence — winking at threats against officials who crossed him, joking about the near-fatal attack on Nancy Pelosi’s husband, and praising and then pardoning Jan. 6 rioters. He revels in bullying, cruelty and hate as no president ever has. Beneath it all is the normalization of lying on an industrial scale: tens of thousands of documented false claims as president, including false accusations against Americans and false representations to courts.

Many Americans are sick of wading through the sludge and understandably want to look away. That is what Mr. Trump is counting on. He wins not by persuading us that the conduct is acceptable, but by wearing us out until we no longer object. Each violation makes the next easier; each unpunished transgression resets the baseline. What is being broken is not this standard or that one; it’s the idea that standards apply. Thanks largely to Mr. Trump and his allies, the country today accepts political speech and behavior that only a few years ago would have been disqualifying, if not unthinkable. It is no longer clear what a president could say — about a dead man, about a murdered family, about women he has abused, about incitements to violence — that would cost him anything.

So why, despite all that, does the second year of Mr. Trump’s second term seem less menacing than the first year? Because the patrimonialism and the re-norming, damaging as they are, were only part of what he and his followers set out to do. The largest of their ambitions was something else: the remaking of American society itself.

The Trump administration’s cultural reset was ambitious. While it had the president’s support, it was devised and pursued mostly by people around him. They included top officials such as Stephen Miller, Russell Vought, and JD Vance on the inside of the administration, plus Elon Musk for the four months he worked in it; outside activists such as Christopher Rufo of the Manhattan Institute, Kevin Roberts of the Heritage Foundation, and Steve Bannon of the “ War Room” podcast; intellectuals such as Patrick Deneen, Michael Anton and Charles Kesler; and institutions such as the Heritage Foundation, the Claremont Institute, and the America First Policy Institute.

This group saw Mr. Trump’s second term as their best chance to block and reverse the left’s takeover and makeover of the country’s culture and institutions. By deploying government power against the commanding heights of the culture, they sought to supplant liberal hegemony not just in Washington but throughout society.

In his 2023 book “Regime Change: Toward a Postliberal Future,” Dr. Deneen, a political scientist at Notre Dame, made clear that the regime that had to be changed included not just government offices, but elite positions throughout society. The goal was to achieve “the peaceful but vigorous overthrow of a corrupt and corrupting liberal ruling class,” he wrote. “Where necessary, those who currently occupy positions of economic, cultural and political power must be constrained and disciplined by the assertion of popular power. However, merely limiting the power elite is insufficient. Instead, the creation of a new elite is essential.”

In keeping with their revolutionary ambitions, Mr. Trump’s cultural warriors spoke in revolutionary terms. Mr. Bannon, in 2017, announced the “deconstruction of the administrative state.” Mr. Vought, an architect of Project 2025, said the goal was for career civil servants to be viewed as “villains.” Mr. Rufo, widely credited with designing the administration’s campaign against universities, described the MAGA movement as a “revolution against revolution” that “has to use what many see as radical techniques” to put universities “in an existential terror” and “set them back a generation or two.”

Their project, in other words, was to use government power and the unmatched influence of the presidency to dominate and rewire civil society. They sought to strike at “wokeness” wherever they saw it, an all-of-society project. The campaign proceeded domain by domain.

Universities: Mr. Vance, in 2021, endorsed President Richard Nixon’s claim that “professors are the enemy,” and Mr. Trump, in 2023, promised to “choke off the money to schools that aid the Marxist assault on our American heritage.” True to their word, they froze billions in federal research funds at Harvard, Columbia, Penn and others as leverage over admissions, hiring, and governance — brazenly violating the universities’ due-process rights in order to exert unprecedented sway over core academic matters. Had courts not intervened, Mr. Trump might have effectively commandeered America’s private universities.

Law firms: Mr. Trump signed executive orders aimed at punishing or crippling major law firms by stripping their security clearances and federal access. That was partly because some firms had challenged Mr. Trump or represented his adversaries. But more broadly, the administration sought to intimidate the legal profession and drive it away from liberal causes and clients. (Several of the firms settled on the Trump administration’s terms; those that fought the orders in court won.)

Media: Among the president’s early second-term actions was an attempt to force The Associated Press and other news organizations to rename the Gulf of Mexico. While bizarre, that effort heralded persistent efforts to bully and reshape the media. The president sought to marginalize legacy news outlets by displacing them from the White House and Pentagon. His personal lawsuits against ABC, CBS and other news organizations extracted multimillion-dollar settlements, while his Federal Communications Commission chairman publicly threatened broadcasters’ licenses — pressure under which Jimmy Kimmel was pulled off the air (temporarily, it turned out).

Culture: Also among his first actions, Mr. Trump installed himself as chairman of the Kennedy Center — the country’s congressionally chartered cultural showcase — and renamed it to include himself. He defunded public broadcasting, canceled funding for humanities councils in 56 states and jurisdictions, and effectively shut down the Corporation for Public Broadcasting. He ordered a review of Smithsonian exhibits and programming for ideological content. He pressured national parks to remove references to slavery. He and his defense secretary remade the military as a culture-war showcase — restyling the Defense Department as the “Department of War,” restoring Confederate base names, scrubbing web pages honoring the Tuskegee Airmen and Navajo Code Talkers (later restored), and pulling nearly 400 books from the Naval Academy library.

Sports: Executive orders created White House task forces for the 2026 World Cup and the 2028 Los Angeles Olympics, with Mr. Trump installing himself as chairman of both. He demanded that Washington’s N. F. L. team, the Commanders, and baseball’s Cleveland Guardians revert to their former names. He attacked athletes with the goal of intensifying cultural divisions. He personally called the international soccer federation’s president and got an American striker’s red-card suspension lifted in the middle of the World Cup. He spent $60 million or more to stage a U. F. C. cage match on the White House lawn for his 80th birthday.

The Streets: Probably most important, the administration used displays of force in an attempt to teach Americans docility. It deployed National Guard troops in the nation’s capital and in other cities, ostensibly to reduce crime but actually to own the streets. It deployed masked, unidentified, paramilitary-style agents against American cities and instructed them to use ostentatiously forceful tactics. In “Operation Metro Surge,” thousands of agents poured into Minneapolis–St. Paul, with parallel deployments and shows of force in Chicago, Portland, Los Angeles, and beyond. Journalists were arrested covering the operations.

Those operations were not law enforcement as it is ordinarily understood; they were the state’s effort to instill fear in its citizens. In the CECOT affair, hundreds of migrants were flown to El Salvador’s mega-prison without hearings — and the secretary of homeland security made a well-publicized visit there to gloat about their harsh treatment. As federal agencies posted triumphant videos of raids and arrests, and Mr. Trump suggested that American citizens should be next, the message was: Be afraid.

Every administration tries to shape the culture. What sets this one apart is not the ambition, but the means and the scale — not persuasion but coercion, and not on one front but everywhere all at once, in ways that were unprecedented and found by courts to be unlawful. Mr. Trump and his administration sought to bully and commandeer private institutions, to redirect the culture, and to remake society from above by force and fear.

In a few ways, the Trumpian social revolution succeeded: by slowing, and even reversing, the momentum of so-called D. E. I. (diversity, equity and inclusion) in elite institutions and of what conservatives called “gender ideology” — though both of those changes were already underway before Mr. Trump took office. On the whole, though, the administration’s effort to remake the culture in its image has failed.

History may one day judge that the tide turned in Minneapolis. In January of this year, Operation Metro Surge made mass arrests, invaded homes, fired pepper balls and shot dead two American citizens, Renee Good and Alex Pretti, without plausible cause — and then, after their deaths, defamed them.

The architect of the operation, Stephen Miller, one of the most powerful presidential aides in modern history, was explicit about the method. He ran Operation Metro Surge through daily calls with the leadership of the Department of Homeland Security, wielding the authority of the president — reportedly directing agents to “force confrontations” with protesters to win the “P. R. battle” and saying that if Minnesotans came to believe “their protesting is successful,” the administration’s interior operations would fail nationwide. Protesters, he reportedly said, “need to be vanquished by any force necessary.”

The people of Minneapolis answered with disciplined, peaceful resistance: tens of thousands marching in Arctic cold, luminaria spelling “ICE Out 4 Good,” a statewide “economic blackout,” a state lawsuit in federal court, citizen networks that tracked ICE and documented its activities, and a population that refused every provocation.

The administration backed down; within days, its border czar announced a “drawdown plan.” Key figures in the effort to break the city’s will were subsequently removed: Greg Bovino, the operation’s enforcement commander, was pulled out of the city and sent back to California. Kristi Noem was fired. Noticeably less was heard from Mr. Miller.

By demonstrating that they could face the spectacle of force and win, Minnesotans shook off their despair and found that they were not powerless. The moment became a catalyst far beyond the Twin Cities. The mass public saw what was being done in their name and many were repulsed by it. What they glimpsed was that a country can, in fact, be lost, and that theirs had come nearer the edge than they had believed.

The president and his forces lost other key cultural battles, too. From outside his home country, but speaking pointedly to it, the first American pope not only defied Mr. Trump but transcended him, demonstrating a moral authority against which the president had no power. Within the United States, No Kings marches staged some of the largest single-day protests in American history, deploying anger and humor without fear. Lawsuits on behalf of Harvard, U. C. L. A. and law firms fought and won key rulings. Federal judges, including some of Mr. Trump’s appointees, blocked action after action. Mr. Musk’s demolition crew disbanded in failure and disrepute.

At the same time, and equally important, the president’s approval rating collapsed. Voters wanted an orderly border and criminal immigrants removed, not a culture war waged brutally in the streets. Mr. Trump’s unpopularity — abetted by his twin fresh failures on Iran and high prices — reached near-record lows for a second-term president.

Had Mr. Trump’s ratings been in the 50s instead of the 30s, he might well have had the confidence to foment a true constitutional crisis by defying the Supreme Court or invoking the Insurrection Act — and he probably would have gotten away with it. Instead, when the Supreme Court invalidated his signature tariffs in February, he felt compelled to comply. (He rebuilt some of them under a different statute.) His efforts to bully the culture have not stopped; he is still menacing universities and attacking free speech. No one should be relaxed about that. But his preoccupations have shifted away from intimidating and dominating civil society and toward building monuments to himself.

Revolutions can fail but still scar the landscape. And Mr. Trump, with just under two-and-a-half years left in his second term, might emotionally and psychologically blow apart. But things are different than they were. The 80-year-old president is losing his grip on power and even his own base. The MAGA movement is fracturing. And the president no longer inspires the fear he once did. We know something today that wasn’t altogether clear a year ago: America’s civil society is harder to intimidate and rewire than MAGA’s cultural revolutionaries hoped.

Conservatives have every right to influence and change the culture, as progressives assuredly have done. But they should do it Ronald Reagan’s way: by moral inspiration and persuasion, not force majeure. Progressives have something to learn, too. Mr. Trump and his culture warriors lost by moving too far out of the moral mainstream; Democrats should claim and occupy that mainstream, not lurch well out to the left, as they seem tempted to do.

Those who played a role in Mr. Trump’s rise to power have acted not just unwisely, but culpably. Even so, it is now apparent that many Americans — probably enough Americans — are determined to live within the truth rather than the lie, to fight for their civic and political self-respect, to return a sense of humanity to a nation that has grown too cold, too callous and too cruel.

Jonathan Rauch and I have co-authored several essays for the Times during the Trump era. We see the world differently in some respects, but not on the threat Donald Trump and his administration pose, and not on our judgment that the second term has been worse than the first. Mr. Trump has transformed the presidency in fundamental ways. But in this essay we argue that his administration's most ambitious project — using state power to remake American society — has largely failed. The turning point came in Minneapolis, where peaceful mass resistance to Operation Metro Surge forced the administration to retreat. That failure, together with collapsing approval ratings, the debacle in Iran, defeats in court and a fracturing MAGA coalition, has left Mr. Trump weaker and the country less endangered than a year ago. Enormous damage has been done, and real dangers remain. But MAGA's cultural revolutionaries have been slowed, and Americans, having discovered they are not powerless, are rising up.

Jonathan Rauch is a senior fellow at the Brookings Institution and the author of “The Constitution of Knowledge: A Defense of Truth.” Peter Wehner, a senior fellow at the Trinity Forum who served in Ronald Reagan’s, George H. W. Bush’s and George W. Bush’s administrations, is a contributing Opinion writer and the author of “The Death of Politics: How to Heal Our Frayed Republic After Trump.”

Mexico Dispatch

In the eastern city of Xalapa, what started as a joke among friends over two decades ago has become a vibrant annual tradition that highlights creativity and absurdity with melons.

Credit...

Supported by

By James Wagner

Visuals by Luis Antonio Rojas

Reporting from Xalapa, Mexico.

The line stretched the entire length of the steep cobblestone bridge in the historic part of town. Many had waited a year to participate in the event and were anxious to register before the spots filled up.

All of them held the same thing in their hands on Tuesday afternoon: a melon.

Mexico is full of unique and vibrant traditions, both ancient and new. There is a century-old radish-carving competition, and a race of people with potbellies in Oaxaca State. There is a mascot obstacle dash in Mexico City.

The annual melon race in Xalapa is not only one of Mexico’s most colorful traditions but also one of its most random. What began as a mockumentary among friends two decades ago — filming melons racing down the city’s sloping cobblestone bridge while streets were closed on Mexican Independence Day — morphed into a yearly tradition, drawing hundreds of participants and thousands of spectators.

“I really love seeing people come together for something that isn’t just mindlessly spending money,” said Sabrina Salem, 28, an actress from Xalapa who lives in Spain but planned a visit back to see her family during the melon race.

“Plus it’s seeing your city united by something that’s absurd,” she added. “To me, that feels like the most Mexican thing ever.”

TEXAS

mexico

VERACRUZ

Xalapa

Mexico City

300 miles

The New York Times

Xalapa, the capital of Veracruz State in eastern Mexico, is often known as a surrealist city. Its nearly half a million people are surrounded by volcanoes and cloud forests, which creates a daily fog that adds a magical element. It is dotted with steep, winding cobblestone streets. House numbers sometimes lack logical order and skip around in odd ways. A local tradition has diners eating pizza with yogurt.

“I wouldn’t say that just Xalapa is surreal, but various places in Mexico,” said Kevin Sameer, 25, wearing a Spiderman lucha libre mask and holding a melon decorated in the same style. “You could keep walking on the bridge here and say, ‘Hey, why is there a gorilla planted on top of that building?’”

(There is indeed a large gorilla statue on top of a nearby building.)

“But there are artistic and novel things that you’d hardly see anywhere else in the world, only here,” he added.

Manuel López Rocha, 39, one of the original organizers of the race, said that he and his friends never ended up finishing the mockumentary because people started cheering and betting on the fastest melons. The following year, he said, his friends decided to hold the race again — and it caught on.

“Because, ultimately, it’s people going out into the street to play,” he said. “That’s really powerful. And it has been especially powerful during times when the city was going through really difficult moments.”

A group of 10 residents, including Mr. López Rocha, a university professor, volunteer to organize the annual event. They find local businesses to sponsor it. The prizes are coupons to those places, such as free cinnamon rolls from a bakery, a haircut from a barbershop and a consultation with a psychotherapist.

A few years into annual race, Mr. López Rocha said they added another competition: the most handsome melon.

Anyone can participate in either contest. They are free and held rain or shine. Participants must use a melon of any size of the Cucumis melo species — honeydew or cantaloupe — for the race. (Sorry, watermelons.) Prizes are awarded for most handsome for the children’s and general categories, and to the top three finishers in the race.

The most handsome melons are determined by applause. People filled a square underneath the bridge to judge, many peering over the sides to hoot and holler for their favorite fruit.

There were melons decorated with serious themes, such as a woman in a wheelchair, submitted by a local group of survivors of sexual violence. A group of researchers entered a melon decorated as a vulture, hoping to raise awareness about the bird’s importance to the ecosystem.

And there were melons decorated with more comical themes or pop culture, from Minions to Charlie Brown to Pokémon.

Ms. Salem and her girlfriend, Anna Marchessi, 34, a Spanish actress and screenwriter also visiting from Madrid, had two entries: a depiction of the famous Olmec colossal head statue at Xalapa’s anthropology museum and another of President Trump, who recently said Mexico offered the United States few things it needed beyond tamales.

Their Trump melon showed him selling tamales with the words, Make Melones Great Again.

“We get pleasure from seeing Trump’s head roll around here,” Ms. Salem said.

The three entries that won in the general category all depicted themes from Mexican culture. First place used six small melons to recreate the ancient Indigenous ceremony of the Veracruz fliers, who spin atop a tall pole. The runners-up portrayed the famous Mexican singer Juan Gabriel, during his well-known Palace of Fine Arts performance, and a traditional Veracruz musician of Son Jarocho, an energetic, communal folk genre, with the melon’s arm moving to play a small guitar-like instrument.

Diego Mortera, 40, and Ángel Mena, 32, said they decorated their Veracruz musician melon in five hours. The friends met in Xalapa last year and decided to compete after hearing so many residents talk about the event.

Others have been competing for many years.

Mara Yerena, 36, an architect from Xalapa, has participated 15 times. She said the entries have gotten more elaborate over the years and she loved how the event fostered a sense of community, with so many young people participating.

She and her friend, Marbet Salazar, 39, also an architect who was visiting from Mexico City just for the race, won second place in the race last year. This year, they finished third.

For the race, there were nine rounds of 25 melons each, with the top five advancing to the two semifinals and then the top 10 from each to the final. The melons were lined up at the top of the cobblestone bridge and then all released at the same time.

Some zipped downhill, while others bounced slowly over the bumpy street. The sidewalks of the bridge were stuffed with spectators, cheering on slow melons and laughing as participants chased after their rolling fruit.

“I didn’t think it would get so crowded,” said Marcel Trinidad, 21.

She and Iván González, 22, medical students at a local university, finished first in the race and walked away with their arms full of gifts, coupons, a plaque, a trophy and their nine-pound melon with a snail painted on it. They bought it for $9 at a market earlier in the day.

The secret to picking a winning melon? “It has to be very round, smooth and have lots of luck,” Ms. Yerena said.

I’ve had my eye on the Melon Race in Xalapa for a while. After coming across videos last year of both the race and the decorating competition, I was drawn to its sheer creativity and randomness. While it isn’t an ancient Mexican cultural tradition, it shows how new customs are born — and how quickly they gain meaning, especially with young people.

James Wagner covers news and culture in Latin America for The Times. He is based in Mexico City.

Aaron Sorkin Goes Off Script

The New York Times September 19, 2026

Trump Administration

The Interview

The Interview

Credit... Devin Oktar Yalkin for The New York Times

Supported by

By Lulu Garcia-Navarro

The walk-and-talks. The soaring monologues. Aaron Sorkin has, for the last quarter-century, dramatized the institutions at the center of American society. From his first play, “A Few Good Men,” in 1989, which he then adapted into the blockbuster movie (and is now bringing back to Broadway), to “The West Wing,” “The American President,” “The Newsroom” and beyond, Sorkin has created work that in many ways has shaped our understanding of how politics, the media and the military work. Or should work.

Sorkin’s script for the 2010 film “The Social Network” not only won Sorkin an Oscar for best adapted screenplay but became the defining story of how Mark Zuckerberg created Facebook, even if it wasn’t all exactly true. Now Sorkin has returned to Facebook with “The Social Reckoning,” which opens on Oct. 9 and focuses on the real-life Facebook product manager and whistle-blower Frances Haugen, who leaked thousands of internal documents to the Wall Street Journal reporter Jeff Horwitz, showing that the company knew its platforms were having a number of negative effects and resisted doing anything to address them.

Sorkin’s movies and television shows are often more idealistic than realistic, and “The Social Reckoning” is no exception. This impulse to romanticize is something Sorkin is often dinged for, and on the two occasions we spoke — once before Meta settled a landmark lawsuit about harms its social media platforms cause teenagers, and once after — he defended and explained his trademark uplift to me in ways that surprised us both.

Subscribe: Apple Podcasts | Spotify | YouTube | Amazon | iHeart

Andrew Breitbart, the founder of the right-wing website Breitbart News, would often say that politics is downstream from culture — essentially that Hollywood has more sway over our politics than Washington does. How do you view your role in that equation? It’s not a political agenda. Before a movie can be anything else — before it can be thought-provoking or relevant — it has to be good. It has to work as something that you watch while you’re eating popcorn. That’s what I’m thinking about while I’m writing. Beyond that, I write idealistically and romantically. I find that these areas — government, the news, journalists — are where the stories are that really suit the way I like to write.

I want to talk about how that view fits into your new movie, “The Social Reckoning.” In 2022, you told The Guardian: “I very much doubt that I or anyone else is going to write a sequel to ‘The Social Network.’” What changed your mind? First, I’m not really sure you can call this a sequel. This is another movie about Facebook, written by the same writer who wrote “The Social Network.” And one of the characters from “The Social Network” is in this as well, but played by a different actor. It’s as if the character of Henry Hill [from “Goodfellas”] showed up in “Casino.” To answer your question, there were two reasons in 2022 I said that. There had been a few people in my world asking me for a while to write something else about Facebook after Cambridge Analytica. I just didn’t want to be the writer of “Jaws 2.” I was afraid of that. But mostly I just couldn’t find the story. I couldn’t find the movie part of what they were talking about, until I started learning about Frances Haugen and Jeff Horwitz and what they uncovered.

I went back and watched “The Social Network” again. I was really shocked by how skeptical you were of social media back then. This came out in 2010, the height of tech optimism, when we were still happily connecting with our high school friends and former sweethearts. What did you see that the rest of us didn’t? What I remember is that I thought, Here’s an interesting story: This very successful social network is being built by an extraordinarily antisocial guy. That this person who was uncomfortable in the social structure of college, the way many of us are, invented his own social structure that he couldn’t be shut out of. And he’d be the mayor of that social structure.

You’ve been asked before about your responsibility to be fair to people when you’re writing stories that involve real-life characters, and you’ve said you’re making a painting and not a photograph. But looking back, some of the details you changed are pretty big. That idea of this antisocial person creating this social network — Zuckerberg was dating his now-wife, Priscilla Chan, at the time. So it wasn’t exactly true, but it’s become the origin story that everyone understands about Facebook now. Whether Mark was dating Priscilla Chan at the time or not, I honestly don’t know. In all of the research, her name never came up, but I think broadly speaking, your question is: What am I willing to fictionalize when I’m telling the story of a real person who’s still living?

Right, because it is the way so many people understand things. I would never defame someone. By the way, I could never defame someone. It’s a really interesting area for me because I have especially lately done a lot of nonfiction, and in some cases about people who are still alive: “The Trial of the Chicago 7,” “Molly’s Game,” “Steve Jobs.” One critic once said — and they didn’t mean it as an insult, and I didn’t take it that way — that when I write nonfiction, I am really just using the characters for parts. And they had a point. There’s an idea that I’ll get about a character’s motivation, like Mark’s. I’ll do my research. I’ll learn everything I can about the reality. But in the process of thinking about it, and then the process of writing it, it becomes the same as a fictional character for me. It becomes my character that I’m creating. The studio’s legal department will make sure that I’m staying inside the lines. But it’s this imaginary thing, and it has my voice, and eventually it’s going to be played by an actor and it’s going to have that face. But I will tell you that in terms of Mark, in both cases, “The Social Network” and “The Social Reckoning,” or any antihero — which is what Mark is, not a villain — I, as the writer, can’t judge that character. I write that character as if they’re making their case to God why they should get into heaven.

You don’t think Mark Zuckerberg is a villain? Are we talking about real Mark or my Mark?

Well, tell me what the distinction is. I don’t want to pass judgment on real Mark. I’m not here for that. The Mark in “The Social Reckoning” is an antihero, not a villain. And I just want to add that the character and the person not only have me trying to defend them, but Jeremy Strong, who blows the doors off the place playing this part, was constantly defending Mark to me. Not just on the set. He’d write to me late at night. And as soon as his last shot was over, on his last day of shooting, as soon as I called, “Cut!” Jeremy Strong marched up to me — and this was the first time I heard him use his own voice on the set, not Mark’s voice — and in his own voice said, “If I’d been playing Jeff, I’d have been defending Jeff.”

What is Mark Zuckerberg’s case to God now? That’s he’s bringing people closer together. That’s been his mission from the beginning, and I imagine that the advances that he’s making with A. I. and with the dumb glasses, he imagines those are steps forward for all of us.

Just to stay with Jeremy Strong’s portrayal, Jesse Eisenberg turned down the role. Part of the reason he said he didn’t want to do it is because he felt like he had been so identified with that role and he was tired of people coming up to him and saying —— It’s the only reason he said he didn’t want to do it. He does not want to be conflated with this character anymore. He really doesn’t like Mark Zuckerberg. He would talk about being in airports at the baggage claim and young kids coming up to him, wanting him to sign a business card that said “I’m C. E. O., bitch,” and things like that. He doesn’t like that he kind of looks like the guy. Just wouldn’t do it. And he meant it, too, because he was offered every incentive that usually works with actors. Jeremy was the next call, and as it turned out, it was like replacing Joe DiMaggio with Mickey Mantle.

In a recent interview, Strong said he reached out via email to Zuckerberg, and Zuckerberg wrote back. Yeah, I read that.

Did you know? No, I had no idea.

That’s interesting. Why do you think he didn’t tell you? I don’t know. I’m not shocked that he didn’t. Jeremy does a lot of his own work. He does a tremendous amount of work before he shows up on your set. He did not speak in his own voice on the set or walk the way Jeremy walks. I told all the other actors in his scenes: “Guys, he’s not going to be hanging out with you at craft service. He’s not going to be yucking it up with you between takes. He’s probably not going to speak to you at all. He is going to treat you the way he imagines Mark treats the people around him.” And that’s what happened. You cannot argue with the results.

Was it hard to get the movie made? Because we’ve seen other films about technology companies having trouble in Hollywood these days. I’m thinking of “Artificial,” the film about Sam Altman, which got dropped by Amazon MGM Studios, and Laurene Powell Jobs, the widow of Steve Jobs, tried to kill your biopic of Steve. Has Meta ever warned or threatened you over “The Social Reckoning?” It’s my understanding that Sony did get letters from Meta, and I do not think those letters said: “We’re wishing you all the luck in the world. Send us some tickets for opening night.” Under ordinary circumstances, with a piece of nonfiction, the studio’s legal department would do a thorough vet. With this movie, they hired an outside law firm just to handle the legal vet to make sure that every single thing that is presented as a fact is a fact.

Was that nerve-racking? Oh, it’s agonizing, and the things that I wasn’t able to say or do are agonizing. The irony wasn’t lost on anybody that we were doing a thorough fact check of a movie about a company unwilling to do the same thing.

In 2019, you had this very public back-and-forth with Zuckerberg. You wrote an open letter to him in The New York Times Opinion pages where you said that Facebook was “assaulting truth” by allowing lies to be pumped into the ecosystem. And then in what seemed like a response, Zuckerberg posted a quote from your “America isn’t easy” speech from “The American President,” which talks about the value of free speech. Is this new film a continuation of that argument that you two seem to be engaged in over time? As a matter of fact, it is. I wrote that in 2019 as a response to Facebook announcing that they were no longer fact-checking political ads, which is an argument that happens in this film. I saw the response that you’re talking about where he quotes [President] Shepherd’s speech from “The American President” about free speech and about how American citizenship is hard. I found it a little aggravating because there’s no chance that Mark, who’s a very smart guy, and the people around him, who are very smart people, don’t know the difference between an unpopular opinion and a lie. The First Amendment doesn’t protect lies. If it did, nobody would ever win a libel suit.

So in some ways this is your response? I found a story to tell. [Smiles] I found a good story to tell where you can eat popcorn and Milk Duds.

This is a classic underdog story, and there is something really hopeful about a regular person taking on a behemoth like Facebook. But I was just reading an interview that Frances Haugen gave [this past spring] and she said that we “may be worse off today than when I leaked the documents.” And Jeff Horwitz, the watchdog reporter who is also lionized in the film, was effectively downsized out of his job at The Wall Street Journal. He’s now working at Reuters. And Congress doesn’t seem to be anywhere close to regulating online safety. You’re saying it hasn’t been fixed? [Laughs] I thought it was fixed!

Aren’t things bleaker than perhaps you’re portraying in the film? Yes. But let me just expand a little bit on what you just said. Frances Haugen is someone who is an incredibly employable person, a young woman who could have gotten a job anywhere, wanted to come work at Facebook because Facebook had at the time something called a Civic Integrity Team, the one team at Facebook that does not care about growth — their only thing is safety. It was the Civic Integrity Team that came to Mark and said, We have found ways to reduce misinformation. The Civic Integrity Team was dissolved, and that’s part of what sent Frances on her way to being a whistle-blower. As she says in the movie, she did this because she wanted to help Facebook and not hurt it. She really believed in its mission, believed in what it could be, and believed that people like her could help it get there. This movie — and I want to say this without giving away the end or really anything in the third act — but it ends on an optimistic note. Because of who wrote it. [Laughs]

I’m glad to hear you acknowledge that. It ends on an optimistic note, but not a rose-colored one. It’s up front about what’s still wrong. It’s just that David threw a rock at Goliath and connected.

Why do you keep on being attracted to those particular types of characters? You are asking me a very interesting question, and I don’t know the answer. I think it has something to do with my father. I always felt like he had one foot in another century, you know? He was just a very sweet, very bright man for whom decency was the measure of a man.

I actually wanted to talk about the way you grew up. Part of your family fled the Russian ghettos to come to the U. S., right? Yeah, my father’s parents were chased out of Russia by the czar’s police because they were Jewish, and they came here with $3 in their pocket, as teenagers. Then they had my father, who on his 18th birthday signed up for the Army in the middle of World War II. When the war was over, he went to college on the G. I. Bill and then law school. In the course of one generation, the Sorkins went from lower middle class to upper middle class.

What did your parents understand about patriotism and duty? What they understood about patriotism wasn’t the kind of bumper-sticker patriotism that we get sold so often. I was very little at the time of the Watergate hearings, but I do remember watching them that summer, and I didn’t feel like my parents thought this was a national shame. I thought my parents felt like, Look at these guys railing against the most powerful person in the world. And on that day in August, when Nixon resigned, it was nothing but pride that the most powerful person in the world is giving up power and there isn’t a tank in the street. And so, Jan. 6 becomes a lot more heartbreaking.

Without giving too much away, Jan. 6 plays a role in your new film. It comes up. But I believe in all of us, even now. I believe in this country, I really do. A couple of years ago, I was reading an interview with Adam McKay, who is one of my very favorites, and the interviewer asked him: Who is you in Hollywood but a Republican? Who’s the Republican Adam McKay? And Adam said, Aaron Sorkin. I thought: What?! Are you out of your mind? And it was because of this romantic idea I have about our institutions, which I do have.

I’m going to come back to this, but I want to talk a little bit about your writing. You have this very recognizable style of dialogue: supersmart people exchanging supersmart quips, super fast. Have you been tempted to go on a chatbot and ask it to do an Aaron Sorkin scene? Because I can imagine that is a prompt that it would know exactly how to emulate. Thanks!

Emulate, not improve on! “I imagine a robot would be able to do what you do.” [Laughs]

Because you have a very distinctive style! It would understand what the prompt meant. I appreciate that. No, I haven’t done it. But would you like to hear my theory of why I’m optimistic about A. I.? It’s because I don’t think it’s going to work. I remember being at a dinner party a while back and there was an abstract painting on the wall. I kind of liked it. Whatever you’re supposed to get from art, it was happening. And the host of the party came up to me and he said, “A machine painted that.” And I was impressed with the technology, but whatever I was feeling about that painting was gone. If you’re someone who plays video games, those people you’re shooting in Call of Duty, you don’t have an emotional connection to them. And that would be your experience watching A. I. “Schindler’s List.”

But people are using this technology in ways that shortcut the difficult process that you do to try to come up with an idea. And the fact of the matter is, especially given how difficult it is for me to get started, if I went to one of these sites and said, “Hey, do me a favor, write an opening scene for a story about … ” and it was able to do it, or even come close in a way where all I had to do is a little dialogue polish, I think that would be all I’d ever do. I don’t think I’d ever try to have an idea again.

So why are you optimistic? First of all, it’s how I earn a living. [Laughs] At first I thought, Well, maybe the future is going to be that you’ll just find non-A. I. films in art houses. Every once in a while, you’ll hear about a town that’s got a great non-A. I. theater, but I don’t believe it. I want a Scorsese movie, I want a Spielberg movie, I want an Adam McKay movie, I want a Greta Gerwig movie. And I’m going to feel about an A. I. movie the same way I felt about that A. I. painting.

I want to talk about how your writing has evolved. In your 20s and 30s, you would take drugs and stay up all night writing. You’re sober now. It did make me wonder what the difference is between writing high and writing sober. Did you find that there’s a certain level of creativity that is more accessible to you sober, contrary to the myth that a lot of addicts have that the only way they can get the creative juices flowing is through chemical intervention? Well, that’s what I thought. It was the creative juices and also the energy. I mean, there was a time when I would not begin writing until after the sun went down and my dealer came over. And I was using coke. I was a late bloomer when it came to drugs. I went through high school, college, even my early 20s without ever having even tried marijuana, and it all changed in one night.

What was the night? I was 25 and I was sharing an apartment in Hell’s Kitchen in New York. One of my roommates got a job on a national tour or something and sublet their third of the apartment out to someone else. I was trying to write “A Few Good Men,” and I was probably complaining about having some trouble. And she said, “Here, smoke this, relax.” I had been offered weed a million times before in my life and had said no every time. For some reason, this particular time, I said yes. About a half-hour later, she laid out some lines on the table, and I said yes. And in my mind, I did the coke and wrote “A Few Good Men” the next day. That’s how my mind thought of it. And I thought: “I know this is bad for me. But if it’s the difference between being able to do this and not being able to do this, I’m sorry.” And I lost a decade of my life to drugs.

It must have been very frightening to get sober with that connection, that your livelihood and your addiction were so closely aligned. It was. I got a phone call out of the blue from someone I’d never met or spoken to, Carrie Fisher. I’d become friends with Warren Beatty. He has a gravitational pull, and people come into his orbit. And I began to be one of the people in his orbit. I got a phone call from Carrie Fisher because Warren told her to call me. And she said, “I know you think you can’t write without it, and I’m telling you, you’re going to write better than you’ve ever written before.” So I went to rehab. And when I got out, my big fear was relapsing — you’re always terrified of relapsing — and going through the “trying to have an idea” phase again, and that I was going to get frustrated and think, “I know the secret, I know how to get past this, I know the phone number to use.” So at the beginning, I just took uncredited dialogue polish, like two weeks on a Jerry Bruckheimer movie, to get back in the groove of it.

What was the first time that you thought: “OK, this is good. I’m writing it and I’m OK writing it sober?” The “West Wing” pilot. Not even the whole pilot, just a couple of scenes in there, in particular the last five or 10 minutes. I was like, I can do this sober.

We’re going to talk again, but before we end —— Oh, no. I was hoping we were going to talk more about my drug use. [Laughs]

The reason I ask about the drug use is that it informs the way you think about things. It does, and I thought this was where you were going, actually, which is that, yes, I am a suburban kid who’s been very lucky in my life, but there was a lot of terrible darkness. My drug use wasn’t partying. I never did it with anyone else. It was something I did alone, isolated. I went from snorting coke to smoking coke, freebasing. That’s a rough place to go. I thought you were going to say: “I don’t understand how that squares with the optimism and romanticism in your writing. Why aren’t you writing more about the darkness?”

It’s a great question from Aaron Sorkin about himself. Let me ask you the question. Why? Why did I bring this up? [Laughs] There have been plenty of times where I’ve thought, Why aren’t I writing about that? Here’s what I think it is. Honestly, I’ve always been aware of it, but right now is the most thought I’ve ever given it. So here goes. I think the problem is that if I write more autobiographically, you’re not going to like that character. And I want you to like me from my writing. [Pause] How’s that for a confession?

It’s a good one. Damn it. There’s someone off-camera letting me know just how wrong that was [to say]. But I think that’s what it is. For instance, my second movie [“Malice,” 1993] is one I’m not proud of at all. Everything went wrong. This movie starred Alec Baldwin and Nicole Kidman. It was an R-rated thriller. We were in rehearsal, we’re about a week away from shooting, and the director, Harold Becker, said, “We need a sex scene with Alec and Nicole. It’s ridiculous that there’s no sex scene with Alec and Nicole. So I want you to go to your hotel room and write one.” So I went back to my hotel room and I wrote four pages of sexy banter, ending with “they fall onto the bed as we cut to the quad the next morning.” Harold read this and said, “No, no — I mean a sex scene.” I was young, early in my career, and he saw the panic in my face, and he said, “It’s no big deal. Just go to your hotel room and write down what you’d like to see Nicole do.” And I thought, You want me to write down what I’d like to see Nicole Kidman do and then distribute it to the cast and crew, including Nicole Kidman and her husband, Tom Cruise, who I just did a movie with? I was simply unable to do it. As a result, Alec and Nicole and the director went into the director’s trailer and they mapped out what they were going to do. It’s not sexy. It’s not erotic. It’s just crude. It’s bad writing! And I hate that people seeing that movie — fortunately not many of them did — think that that’s what I think is charming or sexy or a come-on. That’s not me.

I talked to Sorkin again a few weeks later, just after Meta agreed to pay up to $17.1 billion in a landmark settlement.

Meta agreed to a major settlement where it has promised to make changes to its apps and how they are used by teenagers. This comes out of one of the things that Frances Haugen brought to light, which is how Meta’s apps negatively impact young people. What did you think when you saw that? It’s great news. It’s terrific. A couple of things: Yes, Frances provided some of the information that served as the foundation for those lawsuits. This settlement was about the addictive nature of Facebook and that Mark and senior people there knew it was addictive, just like the tobacco companies and nicotine. What “The Social Reckoning” is about is Facebook’s role in the rise of divisiveness, extremism and hyper-partisanship. It’s about something a little different. But the settlement is great; it’s a step in the right direction. I was listening to someone who’s an expert the other day say this is a terrible problem that just got 5 percent better. It does nothing for what the movie is about.

I’m assuming then that the news hasn’t changed the way that you ended the film? No.

I do wonder about how you tell the story of real events. Too soon, and you don’t have the full context; too late, and things have moved on and the story can feel dated. I don’t want the movie, or any movie I do, to be timely. I want it to be timeless. I don’t want it to feel like it was ripped from yesterday’s headlines. I want this movie to be just as good 10, 20 years from now as it is when you see it in October and November. I make decisions based on that. In fact, you asked me if we changed the end of the movie because of the settlement. A couple of people at the studio had suggested, Well, there’s a postscript on the end of the film and you should put there that Meta settled for $17 billion, and I didn’t do that, because I didn’t want to feel like we just made the movie yesterday.

Last question: You’ve said that you’re romantic about the institutions of American democracy. I want to confess that watching “The Social Reckoning” was a little bit disorienting because of its reverence for working within the system — Congress, the courts, journalism — to achieve this goal. We’re at this moment where people are angry at our institutions. They feel the system is rigged. Do you not despair sometimes that your reverence is misguided? It may well be, but what’s the alternative? I mean, what would I do if it was misguided? If I said, “Hey, these institutions, they’re terrible, they’re rigged,” what do we do? All we have are elections. Other than taking to the streets, that’s the only time we get to raise our hand.

This interview has been edited and condensed from two conversations. Listen to and follow “The Interview” on Apple Podcasts, Spotify, YouTube, iHeartRadio or Amazon Music. Follow us on Instagram and TikTok.

Director of photography (video): Aaron Katter

Lulu Garcia-Navarro is a writer and co-host of The Interview, a series focused on interviewing the world’s most fascinating people.

What Does Trump Want With Greenland?

The New York Times September 19, 2026

Trump Administration

Advertisement

Supported by

President Trump insisted for months that the Danish territory should be part of the United States. Now, a security deal — not a takeover — seems to be on the table.

By Maya TekeliLynsey Chutel and Amelia Nierenberg

Maya Tekeli reported from Copenhagen.

After months of threats, retorts and closed-door negotiations, the United States has reached a deal to expand its security presence in Greenland, the semiautonomous Danish territory, according to President Trump.

The specifics of the agreement, announced on Friday, were not immediately made public. But it clearly falls short of the outright American takeover that Mr. Trump had demanded, a threat that roiled the NATO alliance, of which Denmark is a member.

In a social media post, Mr. Trump said the deal gave the United States “permanent control over security, and all other needs” in Greenland. But the Danish prime minister, Mette Frederiksen, stressed that the agreement “recognizes the sovereignty and territorial integrity” of Denmark.

Mr. Trump had said since his first term that the United States wanted to acquire Greenland, and he became more insistent about it after returning to office last year. One of his aides said Mr. Trump wanted to buy the island, and another suggested that the United States could simply take it by force.

The leaders of Greenland and Denmark rejected such ideas, and European leaders grappled with how to respond to the threat to seize territory from a NATO ally. In the end, negotiators from the United States, Greenland and Denmark met in Washington for high-stakes talks.

Mr. Trump said the agreement would enable the United States to expand its current military presence in Greenland. Under its terms, he said on social media, “no U. S. adversary can EVER have a base in Greenland, have a military presence in Greenland, or make sensitive investments in Greenland, without our express written approval.”

American negotiators had insisted on veto power over any major investment deals in Greenland to box out competitors like Russia and China. Greenlanders and Danes strongly objected to that, and it was not clear how the agreement would address the issue.

Mr. Trump also said the deal ensured that the United States would “FOREVER have the complete ability to do what is necessary in Greenland in order to secure and defend the security of Greenland,” calling it “an ‘Infinite Life’ Agreement,” even though the current pact authorizing the U. S. military presence on the island has no time limit.

Ms. Frederiksen said the new deal would strengthen “our common security in the Arctic and the North Atlantic area and is therefore also good for NATO and Europe.”

Mr. Trump initially said that American ownership of the island was vital to U. S. national security. He later pitched it as a matter of global importance.

“Greenland is a big problem for us,” he said during a NATO summit in July. “We need it for protection of the world, not just the United States, and it’s very important. It doesn’t help Denmark.”

Most of Greenland is inside the Arctic Circle, where superpowers are vying for military and commercial dominance. Controlling the island would give Washington an outpost in an important naval corridor connecting the Atlantic Ocean and the Arctic, where climate change is melting the ice and making once unnavigable territory a theater of competition.

“If we don’t do it, Russia or China will take over Greenland,” Mr. Trump told reporters on Jan. 9.

The Chinese and Russian Navies are active in the Arctic, and critical undersea communications cables have made the region a site of renewed superpower conflict.

Greenland also has huge stores of the rare-earth minerals used for making batteries, electric vehicles and other high-tech items. Currently, China dominates the global market for such minerals.

Mr. Trump said in a January interview with The New York Times that nothing short of U. S. ownership of Greenland was acceptable.

“Because that’s what I feel is psychologically needed for success,” he said. “I think that ownership gives you a thing that you can’t do, whether you’re talking about a lease or a treaty.”

Asked whether it was psychologically important to him personally or to the United States, he responded, “psychologically important for me.”

Greenland is a semiautonomous territory of Denmark, which colonized it more than 300 years ago. Greenland achieved home rule in 1979, taking control over most of its internal affairs.

Since 2009, Greenlanders have had the right to hold a referendum on independence. But Denmark manages Greenland’s foreign policy, defense and other matters. And the island is largely economically dependent on Denmark: Greenland receives an annual subsidy that pays for its schools, cheap gas and strong social services.

While Greenlanders are happy to do business with the United States, polls have indicated that a vast majority of the population does not want to become American.

The United States has had troops in Greenland since World War II and operates a small missile defense base there.

Under a 1951 treaty, the United States already has the right to “construct, install, maintain and operate” military bases across Greenland, “house personnel” and “control landings, takeoffs, anchorages, moorings, movements and operation of ships, aircraft and waterborne craft.”

Reporting was contributed by Jeffrey Gettleman, Zolan Kanno-Youngs, Anton Troianovski and Jeanna Smialek.

Lynsey Chutel is a Times reporter based in London who covers breaking news in Africa, the Middle East and Europe.

Amelia Nierenberg is a Times reporter covering international news from London.

Connections Coach

OpinionGuest Essay

Credit... Damon Winter/The New York Times

Supported by

By Damon Winter

Mr. Winter is a staff photographer for Opinion.

Over nearly two decades as a photographer for The Times, I’ve spent innumerable hours in the subway system. It’s not always the most pleasant place to work. Sometimes, as a diversion from the relentless onslaught of train clatter and the endless flood of humanity — hustling, jostling, trying to make it through the commute inside traveling bubbles of indifference — I stop to look for art. I don’t mean the excellent sculptures and mosaics commissioned by the Metropolitan Transportation Authority to brighten up the commute. I mean the accidental kind.

I look for the colorful scenes of decay on the tunnel walls, the rusted iron beams, patterns formed in crumbling tiles and peeling paint. I’m drawn to the strange forms found in discarded bubble gum and to the delicate sketches etched in HVAC soot. They appear to me as secret works of art just waiting to be noticed and appreciated. I like to imagine them under glass, on pristine white mats inside deep black wood frames on the walls of the Museum of Modern Art. I’ve come to think of it as the “M. T. A. Modern,” a public museum open to all New Yorkers for a mere $3 — if only they knew where to look.

Water is the key medium for much of the naturally occurring art within the subway. It acts as both builder and destroyer. As water permeates the surrounding bedrock, it picks up mineral passengers and slowly deposits them where it seeps through, streaks and evaporates. Shallow beds of milky white and amber crystals emerge, glistening, from the primordial solution. As water oxidizes steel, the chemical transformation creates streams of leathery ocher hues.

The M. T. A. estimates that its workers — and 753 pumps — drain the equivalent of 15 Olympic-size swimming pools of groundwater every day. When there’s a storm or a water main break, the volume becomes almost unfathomable. It courses through an aging system, much of which still relies on its original infrastructure, sometimes more than 120 years old. It forces that water to surface in strange and surprisingly beautiful ways.

It pushes its way under thick layers of “M. T. A. Green” paint slathered on structural supports and emerges in bright orange streaks that seem perfectly picked from the opposite side of a color wheel. Several I-beams in Times Square Station display this kaleidoscope of texture and color. On a tunnel wall at 47th-50th Streets-Rockefeller Center, storm clouds stream down showers of acid rain against a foreboding night sky, while farther down the platform a form reminiscent of a Georgia O’Keeffe painting blossoms from an ivory canvas.

But water isn’t the only creative force at work. Over 4 million people ride the subway on an average day. Thousands of hands run down railings, thousands of feet shuffle over platforms, leaving their mark. Countless footsteps over a pandemic-era social distancing mat at Marcy Avenue unearthed years of layered texture and color. On a platform bench at 110th Street-Malcolm X Plaza, the repetition of daily seatings and the resulting abrasion of cloth on wood revealed a sinister portrait.

Sometimes, the slow, grinding creative rhythm is broken: A sharp, even violent action by a single person can spark a riveting new piece. A blow to an M. T. A. digital display at Times Square creates a spider web of faceted cracks, reflecting and refracting pinks, greens and blues from the LEDs beneath. At the Bowery station, an extravagant splash of matte gray paint — hurled onto glazed ceramic tiles — creates a striking monochromatic abstract. And at Brooklyn Bridge-City Hall, a long-since-removed object has left mounting anchors, broken tiles and rust stains, bringing to mind a primitive ceremonial mask.

The forces of nature and humanity collaborate. It’s reminiscent of the slow procession of time and water that hews away at, say, Bryce Canyon, leaving divine peaks in its wake. Or how the steady dripping of calcium carbonate-rich water formed the stalactites of Carlsbad Caverns. They remind me of places where water has carved deep, winding gashes through miles of stone over the millenniums or constructed intricate crystalline structures with mathematical precision.

The M. T. A. Modern’s accidental art reminds me of the fine pigments suspended in liquid polymers that are splattered, carved and swirled, over days and weeks and months, layer by layer, onto canvases hung in museums and galleries around the world. Here, underground, are the swirls of van Gogh’s “Starry Night,” Mark Rothko’s minimalist blocks, Richard Serra’s seemingly weightless steel sculptures.

During a visit to the Guggenheim decades ago, I stood beneath a towering canvas that was entirely black. It was a monumental, leaden void on a powdery white sweep of museum wall. Time and close inspection revealed the slow, painstaking process the artist must have undertaken to create it, stroke after stroke. It would have been easy to ignore, but its barren austerity taunted me, and the sheer audacity of its size and prominence dared me to pass it by. I didn’t. It was perplexing, even infuriating, but I was fascinated. It changed the way I thought about art.

I felt that same way again years later, marveling at some of the subway’s creations. The system is almost a living, breathing — and quite prolific — abstract artist. The tunnels, beams and platforms are the studio, where works of startling, unintended beauty are created — sometimes by human interaction, more often by the forces of nature and time.

You only have to pause your subterranean scurrying and look.

There is a pleasure to be had in finding beauty in unexpected places and taking time to contemplate it. Next time you see a rusted pipe or a slow trickle of water down an I-beam, stop. Let this train go. Take a minute to explore what water, time and your fellow riders have created. You’ll have the museum to yourself until the next train arrives.

The idea of finding beauty in unexpected places is certainly nothing new. I've been observing these subterranean gems for well over a decade and have attempted to capture them in the past but it was really the refinement of the modern smartphone camera that made this work possible. All of these photos were shot on an iPhone. It allowed me to operate with a very small profile in crowded stations and to maneuver the lens into some pretty tight and awkward situations. What unexpected places inspire you?

Damon Winter is a staff photographer for Opinion.

Gold Statues and Staff Cuts: How Trump Has Disrupted America’s Parks

The New York Times September 19, 2026

Trump Administration

Maintenance projects have been put off around the country and resources diverted to the president’s favored projects in Washington.

Maintenance projects have been put off around the country and resources diverted to the president’s favored projects in Washington.

An unstaffed entrance station at Zion National Park in Utah. Credit... Erin Schaff/The New York Times

Supported by

By Maxine Joselow

Reporting from Washington

Ever since Theodore Roosevelt ventured into the wilderness of California’s Yosemite Valley in 1903 and emerged with a sweeping conservation policy, presidents in both parties have valued the country’s national parks.

The public has, too. Polling shows that Americans of all stripes and political persuasions overwhelmingly love their parks.

But President Trump’s administration has thrown the 433 sites managed by the National Park Service into turmoil, shifting funding and workers to pet projects in Washington, slashing staff across the country and scrubbing exhibits that it says “inappropriately disparage Americans.”

Moves like putting Mr. Trump’s face on some park passes have been largely symbolic. Others have upended the lives of Park Service workers and marred the experiences of some of the hundreds of millions of people who visit national parks each year.

The changes have come one after the other, affecting everything from the rugged shorelines of Acadia National Park in Maine to the high desert of Joshua Tree National Park in California.

Early last year, the Trump administration began making steep cuts to the Park Service work force, leaving at least 20 percent of parks significantly understaffed. This spring, the administration used at least $67 million generated by entrance fees from parks to help fund projects in Washington favored by Mr. Trump, like the botched Reflecting Pool repairs. As a result, hundreds of repairs and upgrades around the country may go unfunded this year, according to government documents reviewed by The New York Times.

Then there is the contentious proposal to trade away a small parcel of land in Yosemite National Park, a crown jewel of the park system, to a private developer. A bipartisan group of 153 lawmakers pledged this week to block the land exchange, declaring that “public lands belong in public hands.”

“Any one of these changes could be catastrophic in its own right, especially as it relates to staffing and funding,” said Dan Wenk, who retired as superintendent of Yellowstone National Park after nearly 43 years with the Park Service. “When the next administration comes, Republican or Democrat, funding may be restored, but it’s going to be incredibly difficult to rebuild.”

Fran P. Mainella, who led the Park Service under President George W. Bush, said that Mr. Trump may not realize the value of parks to the public and the economy.

“We have to find a better way to tell that story to him, so he understands that these parks are here for current and future generations, and part of his responsibility is to make sure they stay that way,” said Ms. Mainella, a Republican.

It is unclear if Mr. Trump has ever visited a national park, either while in office or as a private citizen; his forays outdoors typically involve a golf course. Taylor Rogers, a spokeswoman for the White House, would not say if Mr. Trump had been to a park but said he “loves our national parks and is personally invested in making them great.”

Charlotte Taylor, a spokeswoman for the Interior Department, which oversees the Park Service, said in an email that the agency “remains focused on its longstanding mission: protecting America’s natural and cultural resources, telling the nation’s history accurately and welcoming visitors to these extraordinary places.”

Senator Steve Daines, a Montana Republican who leads a subcommittee on national parks, said in an interview that Mr. Trump “has been an incredible supporter of the parks.” He dismissed reports of funding and staffing issues at parks as “fear-mongering” by the president’s critics before the midterm elections.

“You know, there’s always room for improvement, but I think some of this is just, it’s the political season,” Mr. Daines said.

As he tried to do on the facade of the Kennedy Center, Mr. Trump has left his stamp on the parks and monuments in the capital.

In one flashy example, the administration awarded a no-bid contract to cover four statues near the National Mall in 23.75-karat gold leaf before the country’s 250th birthday. It also repaired nine ornamental fountains in Washington that had been dry for years.

These cosmetic fixes siphoned money from urgent upgrades elsewhere.

While the administration added Washington sites to a list of White House priorities, it relegated about 1,500 other projects at more than 200 sites nationwide to a separate list labeled “low priority,” according to government documents reviewed by The Times.

Work was approved for many of those projects this year. But now most may not be funded before the end of the fiscal year on Sept. 30, according to two former Park Service employees, who spoke on the condition of anonymity because they feared retaliation.

At Big Bend National Park in Texas, where the administration wants to build a border wall over the objections of local leaders, a project to pay “water haulers” to provide drinking water for visitors has been shelved, the documents show.

Another stalled project would replace enormous batteries that store power from solar panels that help supply electricity for visitors and staff members at Natural Bridges National Monument in Utah.

“These batteries serve as critical park utility infrastructure and failure to complete would impact health and life-safety as well as the ability to keep the park open and operational for visitors,” the documents say.

Emily Thompson, the executive director of the Coalition to Protect America’s National Parks, an advocacy group of current and former park employees, said the administration should be tackling the $24 billion backlog of deferred maintenance projects across the country.

“While the fountains look lovely and regilding statues has value, is that really more important than some of these other very strong needs at parks throughout the system?” Ms. Thompson said.

But Steve Coleman, the executive director of Washington Parks & People, a nonprofit group focused on urban parks, welcomed the influx of federal funding in the capital. He said the District’s many federally owned sites often get short shrift because the city lacks voting representation in Congress.

“It’s funny, because we have a lot to criticize about the ways that this Trump regime is attacking our parks, but even a broken clock is right twice a day,” Mr. Coleman said. “And it’s a long-overdue thing to have the country supporting the capital. If you look at other countries, they really invest in their capitals.”

In addition to funding, the Park Service deployed more than 1,000 employees from sites nationwide to Washington this year, according to government documents reviewed by The Times. The employees typically stayed for two to three weeks to assist with events related to the 250th anniversary, and about 40 remain this month, the documents show.

Controversy is not entirely new for the Park Service. During the George W. Bush administration, the agency was accused of promoting religious or conservative content at parks, including on plaques bearing biblical verses at the Grand Canyon.

But Ms. Mainella, the Park Service director at the time, said the Trump administration had gone much further, pointing to Mr. Trump’s directive to remove or revise exhibits that “inappropriately disparage Americans.” To comply, Park Service workers dismantled an exhibit on slavery at Independence National Historical Park in Philadelphia, a sign about climate change at Fort Sumter in South Carolina and a sign about Indigenous people at Acadia National Park in Maine.

“Our parks tell the history of this country,” Ms. Mainella said. “You may not like the history, but it is the history, and so you should tell the story that did take place, not come in and edit.”

Ms. Rogers, the White House spokeswoman, said that Mr. Trump “has put an end to the radical left and the media’s divisive and inaccurate characterization of our nation’s history, which infiltrated our national parks and museums.”

In another contentious move, the Park Service canceled at least $25 million worth of proposed agreements with outside organizations, including nearly $13 million with the Great Basin Institute, a nonprofit conservation group, according to documents reviewed by The Times and first reported by The Washington Post.

Some of the scuttled agreements would have supported efforts to reduce wildfire risk and remove hantavirus-carrying rodents in Joshua Tree National Park in California. Others would have helped the Park Service research and address record-low water levels at Lake Powell, one of the nation’s largest reservoirs, within Glen Canyon National Recreation Area along the Utah-Arizona border.

Peter Woodruff, the chief executive of the Great Basin Institute, said he only learned of the cancellations through a two-sentence message relayed by staff members at partnering parks.

The funding requests were denied, the message said, because of a change in administration priorities.

Maxine Joselow covers climate change and the environment for The Times. Contact her securely on Signal: @MaxineJ.55
